title: Single press-and-hold button
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (0-30 min mechanical dial with bell); Hold-to-heat button (Magnetron runs only while finger is on one big button); Set cooking duration (User decides how long to heat)
rationale: No settings at all: press means heat, release means stop, which nobody needs to learn.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is very simple and intuitive, though the clockwork timer adds a redundant element and holding a button for minutes is tiring.

title: Foot pedal timer
new_elements: Foot pedal (Sewing-machine style pedal replaces timer knob; harder press = more power); Set cooking duration (Hands-free intuitive control)
rationale: Borrows a universally understood pedal metaphor and frees hands holding the plate.
judge_comment: A pedal is a familiar metaphor and keeps hands free, but it needs floor space, and variable power by pressure is unclear and hardly simpler.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Sand hourglass switch (Flip the glass; a light sensor stops the magnetron when sand runs out); Optical sand-level sensing (Cheap phototransistor at base of glass)
rationale: Everyone already knows how an hourglass works; time is literally visible.
judge_comment: A visible hourglass is a whimsical, intuitive timer, but fixed durations limit it and the optical sensing adds complexity.

title: Door-close-starts-cooking
new_elements: Door latch start switch (Closing the door starts heating; opening stops it; fixed 60 s burst); Door push-release button (Existing mechanical door opener)
rationale: Removes the start step entirely; the only action is putting food in.
judge_comment: Removing the start step is the most direct route to no learning curve, though a fixed 60 s is inflexible and the reversal of normal safety logic needs care.

title: Weight-based auto timer
new_elements: Spring scale turntable (Turntable sits on spring; heavier load = longer fixed cam time); Infer cooking duration from mass (No user input needed)
rationale: Replaces the timer knob with a mechanical scale so the user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Mass-based auto time requires no input, but weight is a poor proxy for the heating needed and the mechanical cam would be hard to make accurate.

title: Steam-stop sensor replaces timer
new_elements: Humidity cutoff sensor (Stops heating when cavity humidity spikes, i.e. food is hot); Capacitive humidity sensing (Low-cost sensor in exhaust duct)
rationale: The microwave knows when food is done, so there is no duration to learn or guess.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-cutoff removes the need to choose a time and is technically proven in sensor-cook models, though it is not very radical.

title: IR food-temperature cutoff
new_elements: Infrared thermopile (Reads surface temp; stops at 70 °C eating temperature); Heat to eating temperature (Outcome-based instead of time-based)
rationale: The user asks for 'hot', not minutes and watts.
judge_comment: An outcome-based 'heat to eating temperature' control is intuitive, but IR only reads the surface and the metal-free cavity adds complexity.

title: Two-button Hot/Warm
new_elements: Hot / Warm buttons (Two big tactile buttons replace both knobs with fixed presets); Power knob (Existing 5-step duty-cycle cam)
rationale: Reduces every decision to one binary choice in plain words.
judge_comment: Very simple and easy to build, but fixed presets are common and not radical; it also keeps the power knob, which undercuts the simplicity.

title: Coin-slot style token timer
new_elements: Minute-token slot (Drop plastic tokens, each = 1 minute, mechanical counter advances)
rationale: Counting physical tokens is more intuitive than reading a dial scale.
judge_comment: Quirky and tangible, but tokens can get lost and add a step, so it is not simpler than a dial.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Pull-cord retract timer (Pull cord out like a talking doll; retraction speed sets time); Escapement spring retractor (Same clockwork, different interface)
rationale: Length pulled is a visible, bodily measure of time with no numbers.
judge_comment: A pull-cord is a playful, numberless interface, but it is imprecise and not obviously easier than a dial.

title: Mug-size shaped cavity
new_elements: Cup-shaped mini cavity (Cavity fits a mug only; fixed power and time for one beverage); Reheat a drink (Single-purpose appliance)
rationale: Form dictates use so there is nothing to configure.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug cavity removes all configuration and is easy to build, but its narrow use limits how widely it serves the need, and it is a modest substitution.

title: Dial with pictograms only
new_elements: Pictogram dial (Replaces minute scale with icons: cup, plate, pizza, popcorn mapping to cam positions)
rationale: Users match a picture to their food instead of estimating minutes.
judge_comment: A pictogram cam dial is cheap and intuitive, but icon-based presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline voice module ('Heat my soup' parsed by keyword chip; no buttons or knobs); Edge speech recognition (Low-cost keyword-spotting MCU)
rationale: Speaking a wish is the lowest possible learning curve.
judge_comment: Offline keyword voice control is plausible and needs no learning, but it is vague about how it knows food quantity, and speech recognition adds cost and can fail.

title: Barcode cooks the packet
new_elements: Barcode reader window (Wave package at door; lookup table sets time/power); 1D barcode scanning (Commodity scanner module)
rationale: Packaging already knows the instructions, so the user never reads them.
judge_comment: Scanning the package barcode removes the need to read instructions, but it needs a database of cooking times and does not work for food without a barcode, such as leftovers.

title: Bimetal auto-stop
new_elements: Bimetal cavity thermostat (Cuts magnetron when exhaust air hits set temperature; no timer at all); Bimetallic strip switching (Cents-level cost)
rationale: Cheaper than a clockwork timer and needs no user setting.
judge_comment: A bimetal thermostat that replaces the timer is a radical and cheap substitution, but exhaust air temperature is an unreliable proxy for doneness and the approach risks overheating or underheating the food.

title: Transparent casing, no lamp
new_elements: Metal-mesh glass cavity (Full transparent cavity walls with fine Faraday mesh; ambient light only); Interior incandescent lamp (Existing 20-25 W bulb)
rationale: Seeing food from any angle removes the mental model of a hidden box.
judge_comment: A transparent mesh cavity adds visibility but does not simplify operation, and it contradicts its own title by keeping the lamp; it is also hard to build robustly.

title: Open-top toaster microwave
new_elements: Choke-sealed top slot (Drop plate through top like a toaster; lever starts and pops up when done); Quarter-wave choke seal (Leak suppression without hinged door)
rationale: Reuses the universally known toaster lever gesture.
judge_comment: The toaster lever is a familiar gesture, but a top-loading cavity with a choke seal is hard to make safe and it limits which dishes fit.

title: Drawer instead of door
new_elements: Slide-out drawer cavity (Pull drawer, place food, push closed to start)
rationale: Push-to-start on close removes the door button and start step.
judge_comment: A drawer that starts when pushed closed is plausible and removes steps, but the cook time is still unspecified and drawer microwaves already exist.

title: Kitchen-timer twist egg
new_elements: Detachable egg timer (Standard twist egg timer docks on top and is the only control)
rationale: Uses an object people already own and understand.
judge_comment: A twist egg timer as the sole control closely mirrors old mechanical microwave dials, so it is very simple and cheap, though not very radical.

title: Colour-coded cups
new_elements: RFID cookware tags (Branded bowls carry tag; microwave reads it and cooks preset); NFC reading (Antenna under turntable)
rationale: The dish carries the settings so the user carries none.
judge_comment: Dish-embedded RFID presets make cooking zero-input, but they lock users into branded cookware and cover limited cases.

title: Loudness bell to talking bell
new_elements: Mechanical bell (Existing end-of-cycle bell); Chime-and-voice chip (Says 'Done, careful it's hot')
rationale: Explains the state rather than making users decode a sound.
judge_comment: Voice bell is easy and clearer than a beep, but it only helps at the end of the cycle and is an incremental swap.

title: Light = heat indicator
new_elements: Thermochromic door panel (Door glass tints red while cavity is hot, no lamp); Thermochromic film (Passive, zero electronics)
rationale: State is communicated by colour without any display to read.
judge_comment: A passive thermochromic door panel is a clever, cheap state indicator, but it shows heat rather than operation, and the door glass must also keep the microwave shielding.

title: Turntable removed by mode stirrer
new_elements: Glass turntable (Existing rotating plate); Fan mode stirrer (Flat fixed floor; stirrer blade spreads field)
rationale: No plate to align or wedge means no setup errors.
judge_comment: A mode stirrer is a real, existing substitute for a turntable and removes a setup error, but it barely affects how the user operates the microwave and may heat less evenly.

title: Gesture-free proximity start
new_elements: Load presence switch (Micro-switch under floor starts a 90 s cycle when weight detected and door shuts)
rationale: Cooking begins automatically with zero controls.
judge_comment: Auto-start on load and door close removes all controls, but a fixed 90 s cycle and the risk of accidental or unsafe starts (empty cavity, wrong food) limit it.

title: Smartphone as the only panel
new_elements: Bluetooth control-less chassis (No knobs; phone app shows photos of food to tap); BLE link (Removes all mechanical UI parts)
rationale: Uses a UI people already know and updates it over time.
judge_comment: A phone-only interface is technically easy, but it adds pairing and app steps, which works against the no-learning-curve need.

title: Dumb inverter power knob to slider
new_elements: Fader slider (Linear slide 'gentle ↔ strong' replaces 5-step cam)
rationale: Linear more/less is grasped instantly compared to numbered steps.
judge_comment: A slider is easier to grasp than numbered steps, but it is an incremental change and still leaves a separate time control.

title: Single knob merging time and power
new_elements: Compound cam knob (One knob: turning further = longer and stronger)
rationale: Halves the controls to one monotonic dial.
judge_comment: One dial for time and power cuts the controls in half, though coupling the two limits flexibility and some foods will heat badly.

title: Camera doneness vision
new_elements: Cavity webcam (Also replaces lamp via IR LED; tiny classifier detects boiling/bubbling and stops); Embedded image classification (MCU-level model)
rationale: Visual judgement is outsourced to the device.
judge_comment: Removing timing decisions entirely would give zero learning curve, but a camera classifier in a hot, steamy cavity is hard to make reliable and adds cost.

title: Microphone pop detector
new_elements: Acoustic popcorn sensor (Stops when pops slow; also detects boiling splatter)
rationale: Listening replaces user timing for noisy foods.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection is plausible and proven, but it covers only a narrow set of foods, so it helps ease of use only a little.

title: Candle-style burn timer
new_elements: Fusible minute strip (Disposable fuse strip lengths = minutes; burns through to stop)
rationale: Wildly simple consumable: tear a length, insert, done.
judge_comment: A burnable fuse strip is wild and memorable, but a combustible inside a microwave is dangerous, and it adds consumables and hassle.

title: Water-clock timer
new_elements: Drip cup timer (Fill a cup; drip-through float switch ends heating)
rationale: Fill level is an intuitive analogue for duration.
judge_comment: Whimsical and novel, but a water-based timer in a microwave is messy, imprecise and arguably harder to use than a dial.

title: Door window as whole front
new_elements: Full-front mesh door (Entire front is transparent mesh glass, no control panel at all)
rationale: Removes the panel that intimidates; controls go to one top button.
judge_comment: Removing the panel simplifies the look, but a single button leaves duration and power unresolved and a transparent front is vague.

title: Magnetic lid instead of latched door
new_elements: Magnet-held choke lid (Lift-off lid with magnetic seal and interlock; no hinge, no button)
rationale: Lid-like access is as familiar as a saucepan.
judge_comment: A saucepan-like lid is a familiar metaphor, but RF sealing and safety interlocks without a latch are hard, and it does not simplify the controls.

title: Tactile Braille-free big knob
new_elements: Oversized click knob (One palm-sized knob with 4 loud detents labelled by raised icons)
rationale: Few, physical, loud positions are learnable by feel in seconds.
judge_comment: A single large detented knob with raised icons is directly learnable by feel and easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Continuous low power only
new_elements: Fixed 350 W magnetron (Removes power knob; everything heats gently with one timer)
rationale: Eliminating power choice removes the hardest concept to learn.
judge_comment: Fixing a single gentle power level removes the hardest concept and is feasible, but slower heating is a trade-off.

title: Plate-shaped slot
new_elements: Horizontal plate slot (Insert dinner plate like a CD; spring-loaded eject when done)
rationale: Single affordance; nothing to open, nothing to set.
judge_comment: Radical single-affordance concept that removes learning, but it only fits flat plates, the eject mechanism is unclear, and it is hard to substitute for a cavity and door safely.

title: Printed instruction window
new_elements: Glass-etched cheat chart (Door glass printed with food → knob-position chart)
rationale: Cheap substitute for a manual, always in view.
judge_comment: Cheap and practical, but it still needs a chart to be read and a knob to be set, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Door light from outside
new_elements: External LED edge-lit door (LEDs in door frame shine through glass; no cavity lamp or socket)
rationale: Simpler service, brighter view, fewer parts.
judge_comment: Concrete as a part swap, but it does nothing for ease of operation, and lighting through the door glass is questionable.

title: Smart plug energy timer
new_elements: Timed mains plug (Microwave is always 'on'; a plug-in timer on the cord is the only control)
rationale: Replaces internal timer with a familiar external one.
judge_comment: A familiar external timer is simple to use, but a microwave that is always on is a safety problem, and it needs a door interlock and power-level control.

title: Doneness ribbon
new_elements: Mechanical progress ribbon (Coloured ribbon winds out of slot showing time left, replaces dial scale)
rationale: Remaining time becomes a visible length.
judge_comment: The visible time-left ribbon is intuitive and tangible, but it adds mechanical complexity and does little to simplify setting the time.

title: Rotary phone dial
new_elements: Return-spring finger dial (Dial a digit of minutes; spring return starts it)
rationale: Dialling a single number is self-explanatory and self-starting.
judge_comment: A rotary dial is intuitive and self-starting, feasible with a mechanical spring and escapement, though dialing a single digit of minutes limits flexibility.

title: Self-labelling knob by lid
new_elements: Snap-on preset caps (Knob caps with words 'Coffee','Dinner' that mechanically limit range)
rationale: User chooses a word, the cap does the setting.
judge_comment: Word-labelled caps that mechanically limit the knob range are simple and understandable, but the caps are somewhat incremental and preset-dependent.

title: Weight+IR fully blind oven
new_elements: Zero-control sealed box (No door window, no lamp, no knobs: scale + IR sensor decide everything)
rationale: The most radical reduction: nothing to see or set.
judge_comment: A zero-control blind oven removes learning entirely, but reliably deciding cook time from weight and IR is hard, and removing the window and lamp undermines user trust and visibility.

title: Steam-whistle done signal
new_elements: Exhaust whistle (Kettle-style whistle in vent sounds when steam flows, replacing bell)
rationale: Kettle whistle is a globally understood 'it's ready' cue.
judge_comment: A kettle whistle is a familiar cue, but microwaves produce little steam flow through the vent and it only replaces the done signal, not the operation.

title: One-minute cam only
new_elements: Fixed 60 s push timer (Button pushes a cam for exactly 1 min; press again for more)
rationale: Counting presses beats reading a scale.
judge_comment: A fixed 60-second push cam is very simple and feasible, but it is a modest and not very radical change, and it is inflexible for different foods.

title: Door as the knob
new_elements: Door-angle timer (How far you swing the door before closing winds the timer)
rationale: Merges loading and setting into one motion.
judge_comment: Merging loading and timer setting is intuitive, but door angle as a timer input is awkward and hard to make precise, and the door interlock safety design adds complexity.

title: Tilt the oven
new_elements: Rocking base timer (Tilt the whole unit back to wind a pendulum timer)
rationale: Playful whole-body gesture, no panel.
judge_comment: Tilting a heavy appliance is impractical and unsafe, and a pendulum timer is a weak fit; the gesture is not intuitive for setting time.

title: Heat-sensitive sticker on plate
new_elements: Reusable temp sticker (Sticker on turntable edge changes colour; user stops when colour matches)
rationale: Visible done-ness replaces numeric planning.
judge_comment: A visual done-ness cue is simple, but a sticker on a turntable edge reads the plate rather than the food, and the user must still decide when to stop.

title: Shared preset dial from kettle
new_elements: Kettle-style rocker switch (One rocker, clicks off automatically like a kettle)
rationale: Copies the simplest kitchen control that exists.
judge_comment: A kettle-style single rocker is very easy to use and cheap, but it is not a radical idea and needs some auto-termination logic, such as a sensor or a fixed time.

title: Window-less camera mirror
new_elements: Periscope mirror window (Angled mirrors show cavity from top; cheaper than perforated glass and lamp)
rationale: Viewing from above is a natural pot-watching posture.
judge_comment: A periscope mirror is a cheap substitution for the window, but it does little for operation simplicity and the mirrors could get dirty or heat-damaged.

title: Self-opening door at end
new_elements: Spring auto-open latch (Timer release pops the door open when done; replaces bell and button)
rationale: An open door is the clearest possible 'done' signal.
judge_comment: A spring-loaded auto-open door is already standard on most microwaves (the open button), so it's easy to build and gives a clear 'done' signal. It does little to simplify the input side of operation, and it isn't radical, because it replaces the bell with something similar rather than rethinking the controls.

title: One Hot Button
new_elements: Single HOT button (Replaces timer and power knobs; IR sensor stops heating at eating temperature); Zero-decision heating (User presses once, machine decides time and power)
rationale: Removes every setting the user had to learn.
judge_comment: A single button with IR sensing removes all settings, though judging the right time and power for varied foods is hard and the idea is somewhat expected.

title: Weigh-and-go turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Mass of food sets heating time automatically); Auto time from weight (Replaces clockwork timer)
rationale: No minutes to guess; placing food is the input.
judge_comment: A load-cell turntable is concrete and feasible, but weight alone is a crude proxy for heating needs and some food-type input may still be needed.

title: Glass-box cavity
new_elements: Fully transparent metallised-glass casing (Replaces lamp and perforated door window); See food from anywhere (Visual feedback needs no light switch)
rationale: Checking progress is obvious and effortless.
judge_comment: A transparent casing is only loosely tied to ease of operation, and RF shielding with fully transparent glass is difficult.

title: Hold-to-heat deadman button
new_elements: Hold-to-heat paddle (Magnetron runs only while the paddle is held; release stops); Direct manual control (Replaces timer with the user's own hand)
rationale: Behaves like a tap: hold for hot, let go to stop.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat has no learning curve and is simple to build, but it is tiring for long heating and has safety and ergonomic drawbacks.

title: Flip-hourglass timer
new_elements: Sand hourglass switch (Flip the hourglass to start; optical sensor stops heating when sand runs out); Intuitive visible countdown (Replaces clockwork dial and bell)
rationale: Everyone already understands an hourglass.
judge_comment: An hourglass is a familiar metaphor and easy to implement, but users still have to choose a duration, and the fixed sand time limits flexibility.

title: Close-door-to-start
new_elements: Door-latch start switch (Closing door starts a default 60 s cycle; opening stops); No start button needed (Replaces timer knob for quick reheats)
rationale: The only action is putting food in and shutting the door.
judge_comment: Zero-step operation that matches the need, but a fixed 60 s default risks accidental starts (e.g., running empty) and is inflexible beyond reheats.

title: Tap-to-add-30s panel
new_elements: Whole-front tap sensor (Each tap anywhere on the front adds 30 s); Knob-free time entry (Replaces timer knob)
rationale: One gesture, impossible to get wrong.
judge_comment: Simple single gesture, though it needs a capacitive or vibration sensor on the front and tapping is slightly less discoverable than a door-close start.

title: Pictogram dial
new_elements: Food-icon dial (Dial positions are coffee, soup, plate, pizza, frozen; replaces minutes and power); Select by food not numbers (Preset time/duty cycle per icon)
rationale: Users think in dishes, not watts and minutes.
judge_comment: Intuitive and easy to build, but food-icon presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.

title: Steam-stop sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor in vent (Heating stops when food starts steaming); Self-ending cycle (Replaces timer)
rationale: Food tells the oven when it is done.
judge_comment: Self-ending cycles remove time entry, but humidity-based stopping is inconsistent across foods and still needs a start action.

title: Package barcode reader
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode/NFC reader (Scans ready-meal packaging and runs printed instructions); Instruction-free cooking (Replaces both knobs)
rationale: Nobody reads the box or sets anything.
judge_comment: Removes settings for packaged meals, but it depends on packaging standards and does not cover non-packaged food, and scanning adds a step.

title: Voice-only microwave
new_elements: Offline voice chip ('Two minutes' or 'reheat' replaces knobs); Spoken control (Natural language instead of controls)
rationale: Talking requires no learning.
judge_comment: Offline voice commands remove the controls entirely and need no learning, but noise, accents and the limited command set are real weaknesses, and voice-controlled microwaves already exist.

title: Auto-pop door
new_elements: Spring door release at end (Door pops open when done, replacing bell); Unmissable done signal (Physical state change instead of sound)
rationale: Open door means ready; no interpretation needed.
judge_comment: A spring-loaded door pop gives a clear physical done signal, but it only helps at the end of the cycle and does nothing for setting up the cook.

title: Talking bell
new_elements: Speech chip (Says 'your food is ready' instead of ringing); Explicit status (Replaces mechanical bell)
rationale: No ambiguous sounds to decode.
judge_comment: A speech chip is cheap and easy to build, but it only clarifies the done signal and is an incremental change.

title: Hob-style intensity dial
new_elements: Off-low-high dial (Runs continuously like a stove knob until turned off or door opened); Familiar stove mental model (Replaces timer+power pair)
rationale: Borrows a control everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A stove-style dial uses a familiar mental model, but running with no timer risks overcooking and has safety and food-quality problems.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord (Length pulled sets time; cord retracts as it counts down); Tangible time setting (Replaces clockwork knob)
rationale: Longer pull = longer heat, visibly.
judge_comment: A retracting pull-cord makes time visible and intuitive and is quite radical, though the mechanism is awkward and imprecise and its reliability is questionable.

title: Door-handle-is-the-timer
new_elements: Twist-handle timer (Door handle rotates to set time and pushes to close/start); One control for open, set, start (Merges handle, button and timer)
rationale: Only one thing on the product to touch.
judge_comment: A single twist-and-push handle that opens, sets time and starts is simple and plausible, though a time dial still requires some thought.

title: Top-loading pot microwave
new_elements: Lift-lid cavity (Drop food in from the top like a pot; lid closes and starts); Pot-like use (Replaces front door and release button)
rationale: Mimics the most basic cooking vessel.
judge_comment: A top-loading pot-style microwave is radical and intuitive, but it brings ergonomic, spillage and leakage-shielding challenges, and it doesn't say how time gets set.

title: Stirrer instead of turntable
new_elements: Mode stirrer fan (Flat cavity floor; no plate to seat or clean); Nothing to position (Replaces glass turntable)
rationale: Removes a part users misplace or misalign.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist, and removing the turntable helps cleaning more than operation, so its effect on the learning curve is marginal.

title: Three-button bar
new_elements: Reheat / Defrost / Boil buttons (Only three sensor-ended presets); Choose a verb (Replaces two knobs)
rationale: Three words cover 95% of uses.
judge_comment: Three verb buttons make operation very simple, but presets are common and not very radical.

title: Plate thermometer stop
new_elements: IR thermopile on ceiling (Stops when food surface reaches 70 °C); Target temperature not time (Replaces timer)
rationale: Users want 'hot', not '2:30'.
judge_comment: Targeting a temperature rather than a time matches user intent, but IR sensing only reads the surface and is affected by steam and containers.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Cavity camera + tiny classifier (Identifies food class and runs matching program); Automatic program choice (Replaces all settings)
rationale: The oven sees what you put in.
judge_comment: Auto food recognition removes nearly all settings and learning, but it is unreliable on varied foods and the substitution framing is a stretch (adds components rather than simplifying).

title: Glowing cavity walls
new_elements: Electroluminescent enamel (Cavity liner glows; no bulb, socket or shade); Even interior light (Replaces incandescent lamp)
rationale: Clear view of food with zero bulb maintenance.
judge_comment: Interesting substitution of the bulb, but it barely affects operation simplicity and electroluminescent enamel in a microwave cavity is implausible.

title: Countdown light bar
new_elements: Shrinking LED bar (Full-width bar empties as cooking proceeds); Room-visible progress (Replaces numeric dial reading)
rationale: Progress is understood at a glance from across the kitchen.
judge_comment: A shrinking LED bar is easy to build and intuitive for progress, though it covers only the display and not setting the time.

title: Sliding door
new_elements: Side-sliding door (No release button, no swing space); Push-aside access (Replaces button + hinge)
rationale: Opening is a single obvious motion.
judge_comment: A sliding door makes opening obvious, but microwave seals and choke requirements make it harder, and it does not address operation of the controls.

title: Magnetic pull door
new_elements: Magnet-held door (Pull anywhere on the door to open); Buttonless opening (Replaces push-release button)
rationale: No hunting for the right button.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch with a pull-anywhere door is simple and feasible, but it is a modest change that is similar to existing pull-handle designs.

title: Wave-to-start gesture
new_elements: Proximity gesture sensor (Wave hand once per minute wanted); Touchless setting (Replaces timer knob)
rationale: Works with messy hands and no instructions.
judge_comment: Wave-per-minute counting is easy to build, but it assumes users know the gesture and it is hard to use for long cook times, so it is not truly zero-learning.

title: Colour-coded dishes
new_elements: RFID-tagged bowls set (Each bowl encodes its own program; oven reads it); Dish selects program (Replaces power/time knobs)
rationale: Choosing a bowl is the entire interface.
judge_comment: Choosing a bowl as the whole interface is intuitive, but it ties the user to proprietary dishes and limits flexibility, and it adds cost rather than cutting it.

title: 2-D touchpad
new_elements: Single touchpad (x=time, y=power) (One tap sets both parameters); One-touch dual setting (Replaces two knobs)
rationale: Two settings collapse into one gesture.
judge_comment: A single touchpad is simple and cheap, but the x/y mapping to time and power must be learned and is imprecise.

title: Sound-of-doneness mic
new_elements: Cavity microphone (Stops on popcorn silence or boiling sound); Acoustic auto-stop (Replaces timer for popcorn/liquids)
rationale: Listens so the user doesn't have to.
judge_comment: Acoustic auto-stop removes the need to set a timer for popcorn and liquids, but it is unreliable for other foods and noisy in a real kitchen.

title: Inverter gentle/strong switch
new_elements: Inverter PSU with 2-way toggle (Continuous power replaces 5-step duty cam); Gentle or strong only (Replaces power knob)
rationale: A toggle is simpler than five numbered levels.
judge_comment: A two-way toggle is easy to understand and cheap to build, but the idea is incremental and limits control.

title: Labelled slider warm→boiling
new_elements: Linear outcome slider (Marks: warm, hot, piping, boiling); Set outcome not duration (Replaces timer)
rationale: Users describe the result, not the process.
judge_comment: Outcome-based slider is very intuitive, but without sensing it is hard to map reliably to food types and quantities, and it is not very radical.

title: Countertop heating pad
new_elements: Near-field phased antenna pad (Flat pad heats a plate placed on it, shielded by a drop-over cover); Pad + cloche (Replaces cavity, door, turntable)
rationale: Set plate down, cover it, lift when hot.
judge_comment: Radical and simple to use, but near-field phased pad heating with safe shielding is technically doubtful and the cloche leakage risk is high.

title: Projected READY on counter
new_elements: Under-oven LED projector (Projects 'READY' on the worktop); Silent obvious completion (Replaces bell)
rationale: Status readable without any learned cue.
judge_comment: Easy and feasible, but it only improves completion feedback rather than operation, so the effect on the learning curve is modest.

title: Fan-driven turntable
new_elements: Airflow-spun turntable (Cooling-fan exhaust spins plate; no separate motor); Fewer parts to fail (Replaces turntable motor)
rationale: Simpler product means fewer things for the user to troubleshoot.
judge_comment: Reduces parts but does almost nothing for user operation, and airflow-driven rotation is hard to make reliable under load.

title: Press-harder-for-longer
new_elements: Force-sensitive start pad (Light press 30 s, firm press 2 min, hard press 5 min); Force encodes time (Replaces timer knob)
rationale: One button, intuitive mapping of effort to duration.
judge_comment: Single-button force mapping is clever and buildable, but pressure levels are not self-evident and need learning and consistent force control.

title: Roll-top transparent door
new_elements: Tambour polycarbonate shutter (Rolls up with one push; mesh laminated inside); Push-up access and view (Replaces hinged door, button, window)
rationale: Open like a bread bin, no latch logic.
judge_comment: A roll-top shutter is a fresh swap for the hinged door, but sealing microwave leakage around a tambour is very hard and it does little for the learning curve.

title: Disposable paper mat floor
new_elements: Peel-off paper liner (Fixed ceramic floor with tear-off liners); No turntable cleaning (Replaces removable glass plate)
rationale: Cleaning becomes peel-and-bin, nothing to reassemble.
judge_comment: Liners are feasible and simplify cleaning, but they have little to do with operation, and paper in a microwave raises safety concerns.

title: Mug slot preset
new_elements: Mug-shaped side cradle (Dropping a mug into the cradle triggers a drink program); Shape-triggered program (Replaces settings for drinks)
rationale: The physical fit tells the user and the oven what to do.
judge_comment: A physical mug cradle that triggers a program removes settings for a common task, though it only covers one use case.

title: Thermal-image doneness map
new_elements: Low-res thermal array (Stops when whole item is uniformly hot; shows cold spots on door); No-cold-spot auto stop (Replaces timer and guessing)
rationale: Ends the cycle of reheat-check-reheat.
judge_comment: Thermal sensing with automatic stop removes timer guessing, which fits zero learning curve well, though low-res IR through a microwave cavity is challenging.

title: Door window as webcam
new_elements: Cavity webcam + door display (Replaces lamp and mesh window with a screen); Bright magnified view (Clear feedback without peering)
rationale: Mistakes are visible instantly.
judge_comment: A webcam and screen replace the window but add complexity and cost, and cameras in a hot, humid cavity are a problem, with little help for ease of use.

title: Frozen-detect auto defrost
new_elements: Floor contact thermistor (Detects frozen load and runs defrost without asking); Automatic defrost mode (Replaces defrost power setting)
rationale: User never has to know defrost exists.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes the need to know about defrost, though a floor thermistor may struggle to sense the load's temperature reliably.

title: Pass-through conveyor
new_elements: Belt tunnel microwave (Place plate at entry; exits hot at the other side); Put in, take out (Replaces door, button, timer)
rationale: The interaction is literally one motion.
judge_comment: A conveyor tunnel makes operation a single motion, but it faces serious challenges with RF leakage, size, cost and variable food loads.

title: LED lamp swap
new_elements: Sealed LED strip (Replaces 20-25 W incandescent bulb); Maintenance-free light (No bulb change ever)
rationale: Eliminates a confusing maintenance task.
judge_comment: An LED lamp swap is easy to build but barely touches the need for simple operation, and it is not radical.

title: Haptic-detent dial of tasks
new_elements: Clicky task dial (Each click is a named task (coffee, leftovers, soup), not a minute); Count clicks not minutes (Replaces numeric timer)
rationale: Tactile presets need no reading.
judge_comment: A task dial with detents is intuitive and easy to build, but presets already exist and the dial still needs labels to be read.

title: Foot-pedal start
new_elements: Floor pedal (Hands-free start/stop like a bin pedal); Hands-busy operation (Replaces front start control)
rationale: Step on it: universally understood.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is easy to grasp and feasible, but it only replaces the start button, leaving time and power unresolved, and it is awkward to use.

title: Lid-weight clockwork
new_elements: Gravity-driven timer weight (Lift a weight to set time; it descends and cuts power at bottom); Visible mechanical countdown (Replaces hidden clockwork)
rationale: Cuckoo-clock clarity: higher means longer.
judge_comment: A mechanical gravity timer with a visible countdown is intuitive and a cheap substitution for electronics, though the 'lid-weight' placement is a bit odd and time precision is limited.

title: Plate-size infers portion
new_elements: Floor capacitive footprint sensor (Reads dish diameter to set time); Portion from footprint (Replaces timer)
rationale: Bigger plate, longer heat, no input.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is appealing, but plate diameter is a poor proxy for food quantity or type, and a capacitive floor sensor under a turntable is questionable.

title: Open-to-stop only
new_elements: Door-open sole stop control (No stop/cancel button; opening the door is the only stop); Single stop affordance (Replaces cancel logic)
rationale: One way to stop means nothing to remember.
judge_comment: Simple and already common behavior, so it reduces the learning curve a little but is not radical or a true substitution.

title: Fixed-power, single knob
new_elements: Fixed 100% magnetron drive (Deletes power knob; adaptive pulsing handled by load sensor); Time-only control (Replaces 5-step cam)
rationale: Half the controls removed outright.
judge_comment: Removing the power control simplifies operation sensibly, but the idea is incremental and relies on a load sensor to do the adaptive work.

title: Smart-lid vessel
new_elements: Bundled lid with temp sensor (Lid transmits food temp; oven stops at eating temp); Vessel controls oven (Replaces timer)
rationale: Cover food, close door, eat when it opens.
judge_comment: A lid that senses temperature removes time-setting entirely and is intuitive, though a microwave-safe wireless temperature sensor is challenging and the lid is an extra part to supply.

title: Colour-change cavity glow
new_elements: RGB cavity light (Blue=cold, orange=warming, red=hot; replaces bell and lamp); Colour tells doneness (Ambient status cue)
rationale: Status understood from across the room with no sound or numbers.
judge_comment: An RGB cavity light is cheap and technically easy, and it gives an intuitive ambient status cue. It only addresses feedback, though, not how to operate the microwave, and the cold/warm/hot colour mapping is not very radical or clearly tied to actual doneness.

title: One-button 'Heat It' with IR doneness sensor
new_elements: Single HEAT button (One pushbutton replaces timer and power knobs; cooking stops automatically.); IR thermopile surface-temperature sensing (Non-contact sensor reads food surface temperature through a waveguide-safe window.)
rationale: Zero settings to understand: press once, food stops when hot.
judge_comment: A single button with automatic stop fully removes the learning curve, but IR surface sensing is unreliable for uneven or covered food.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Momentary hold-to-heat paddle (Magnetron runs only while the user holds the paddle; release stops it instantly.)
rationale: Nothing to set or read; the user's own hand is the timer.
judge_comment: Very simple and safe to build, but holding the paddle for minutes is tiring, and it is arguably a step backward.

title: Toaster-style lever microwave
new_elements: Spring-loaded pop-up lever (Push lever down to start; it pops up with a click when done, like a toaster.)
rationale: Borrows a control everyone already knows from toasters.
judge_comment: The toaster metaphor is familiar, but it still needs a time setting, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Pictogram food dial replaces power and time
new_elements: Food-icon selector dial (Dial positions are pictures (mug, plate, pizza slice, frozen block) mapped to fixed power/time pairs.)
rationale: Users pick what they have, not watts and minutes.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and cheap to build, but similar preset dials already exist, so it is not radical.

title: Turntable is a weighing scale that sets the time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Three load cells under the turntable ring weigh the food and compute heating duration.); Strain-gauge load cells (Low-cost strain gauges with simple amplifier.)
rationale: Put food in, close door, it already knows how long.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic timing is plausible and removes the settings, but weight is a weak proxy for food type and starting temperature.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop replaces the clockwork timer
new_elements: Cavity humidity sensor (Detects steam burst from food and ends the cycle.)
rationale: No timer to misjudge; food tells the oven when it is done.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop already exists on sensor-cook microwaves, so it is a proven but not very radical way to remove timer guesswork.

title: Barcode scanner reads the packet's instructions
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Reads packaged-food barcode and applies the printed heating program automatically.); Machine vision (Optical code reading.)
rationale: Students never read the back of the box; the oven does it for them.
judge_comment: Barcodes usually don't encode heating programs, so it needs a database or new packaging standard, but it removes all input for packaged food.

title: RFID smart containers set the program
new_elements: RFID reader in cavity floor (Tagged mugs/bowls carry their own heating profile; the oven applies it on door close.)
rationale: The container is the interface, so no control panel is needed.
judge_comment: Containers carrying their own profile make for a novel zero-interface concept, but it requires an ecosystem of tagged containers and RFID inside a microwave cavity is difficult.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline speech-command module (Recognises 'heat', 'defrost', 'stop' without cloud.); Speech recognition (Keyword spotting on microcontroller.)
rationale: Talking is the only interface with truly no learning curve.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is feasible, but voice still needs time or quantity input and noisy kitchens and discoverability limit the no-learning-curve claim.

title: Single 'more/less' knob merges time and power
new_elements: Unified heating-amount knob (One knob scales total energy delivered; firmware picks power/time combination.)
rationale: Two confusing knobs become one intuitive 'how much' control.
judge_comment: A single 'how much' knob is simple, cheap and intuitive, though it is a modest simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Colour-band timer scale instead of minutes
new_elements: Green/amber/red timer dial (Dial printed with coloured zones labelled 'warm', 'hot', 'cook' instead of numbers.)
rationale: Replaces numeric estimation with a glanceable traffic-light scale.
judge_comment: A glanceable colour scale removes number estimation and is trivially cheap, but it is a modest rather than radical change.

title: Mug-count scale on the timer
new_elements: Timer dial marked in mugs/plates (Scale reads '1 mug, 2 mugs, 1 plate' instead of minutes.)
rationale: Units match the student's mental model of what they are heating.
judge_comment: Units that match what the user is heating remove translation effort, though the mapping from mugs to time is imprecise.

title: Two-position power switch (defrost / full)
new_elements: Rocker switch: Defrost / Heat (Replaces 5-step cam with a simple two-way rocker.)
rationale: Removes four meaningless power steps nobody understands.
judge_comment: A two-way rocker is easy and clearer, but simplified power switches are already common.

title: Fixed-power oven with no power knob at all
new_elements: Hard-wired 100% duty magnetron drive (Delete cam and knob; only a timer remains.)
rationale: Cheaper and simpler: one knob, one decision.
judge_comment: Removing the power control cuts decisions to one, but it loses defrost and gentle heating, so it is not very radical.

title: Inverter power supply replaces transformer, diode and doubler
new_elements: Switch-mode HV inverter (High-frequency SMPS drives the magnetron with continuous, variable power and no large HV capacitor.)
rationale: True continuous power lets a single slider mean exactly what it says, with no stored lethal charge.
judge_comment: Inverter technology is real and specific, but it is more complex and costly, and it is not a simplification of operation.

title: Solid-state GaN RF source replaces the magnetron
new_elements: GaN solid-state microwave generation (Low-voltage transistor amplifiers with reflected-power feedback for closed-loop heating.); RF power electronics (Solid-state amplifier design.)
rationale: Reflected-power feedback makes auto-stop reliable, so the user never sets anything.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power feedback enables true auto-cook and no settings, though cost and power levels are still hurdles; it is not cheaper, so it fits SUBSTITUTE only loosely.

title: Thermal fuse replaces bimetal thermostat
new_elements: One-shot thermal fuse on magnetron (Cheaper, non-resettable thermal cut-off.)
rationale: Lower cost and fewer parts keeps the product simple and affordable for students.
judge_comment: A cost-saving swap that does nothing for operation simplicity, and a non-resettable fuse can worsen the user experience.

title: Capacitor-free design eliminates bleed-down
new_elements: Resonant inverter without storage capacitor (No energy stored after switch-off; bleeder resistor and warnings removed.)
rationale: Removes a hidden hazard and its warning labels, making the product worry-free.
judge_comment: Removing the stored-energy hazard is appealing but only tangentially related to ease of use, and a high-voltage magnetron supply without any storage capacitor is questionable.

title: Mode-stirrer fan replaces turntable and motor
new_elements: Waveguide mode stirrer (Rotating metal paddle in the waveguide spreads the field; flat cavity floor, no turntable.)
rationale: No plate to misalign, break or clean; square dishes just fit.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are well-established and remove the turntable hassle, giving modest simplicity gains.

title: Rotating antenna under the floor
new_elements: Sub-floor rotating radiating antenna (Antenna spins beneath a flat ceramic floor to even out heating.)
rationale: Flat floor removes the ‘did I seat the turntable?’ failure mode.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas are already in commercial products; they remove the turntable seating error and ease cleaning.

title: Airflow-driven turntable (no motor)
new_elements: Cooling-fan-driven turntable turbine (Magnetron cooling air spins a small turbine under the plate; no separate motor.)
rationale: Fewer parts and cheaper, keeping the basic model basic.
judge_comment: Clever part substitution, but it does nothing for ease of operation, and fan airflow is unlikely to turn a loaded plate reliably.

title: Silicone mat replaces glass turntable
new_elements: Microwave-safe silicone turntable mat (Unbreakable, dishwasher-safe, rolls up.)
rationale: Nothing to shatter or drop; one less thing to think about.
judge_comment: Safer and easier to handle, but a floppy mat may not rotate well on the roller ring and the benefit to operation is marginal.

title: Ceramic glass plate replaces mica waveguide cover
new_elements: Glass-ceramic waveguide window (Wipe-clean non-porous cover; no mica that chars or absorbs grease.)
rationale: Users never need to learn about replacing a mica sheet.
judge_comment: Plausible and practical for maintenance, but it is unrelated to operating the microwave without learning.

title: Magnetic door with Hall-effect interlocks
new_elements: Magnetic door catch + Hall sensor interlock (Door held by magnets; redundant Hall sensors replace mechanical microswitches and latch hooks.)
rationale: Pull the door like a fridge; no button to find.
judge_comment: A magnetic pull-open door with Hall-sensor interlocks removes the button-finding step and is technically plausible, though safety certification of the interlocks needs care.

title: Pull-handle door replaces push-release button
new_elements: Fridge-style pull handle (Handle directly lifts the latch hooks; button and lever deleted.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to open a door with a handle.
judge_comment: Highly intuitive and easy to build (some models already use it), but it is not radical.

title: Drawer-style cavity replaces hinged door
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (Food sits in a drawer that slides into the shielded box; choke is on the drawer rim.)
rationale: Open, place, push shut — the same gesture as every kitchen drawer.
judge_comment: Drawer gesture is intuitive and fairly radical, though RF choke on a sliding drawer and spill handling are tough; it also substitutes the door rather than just a part.

title: Wave-to-open proximity door release
new_elements: Capacitive proximity door release (Solenoid latch opens when a hand approaches, like a sensor bin.)
rationale: Hands full with a hot plate? No button to press.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening is easy to implement with proven sensors, but accidental triggering is a risk and the benefit to learning curve is modest.

title: Mechanical RF shutter replaces electrical interlock logic
new_elements: Door-driven waveguide shutter (Opening the door mechanically slides a metal shutter across the waveguide, blocking RF regardless of electronics.)
rationale: Intrinsic safety needs no explanation and no user caution.
judge_comment: A mechanical shutter is a safety feature that is invisible to the user, so it does little for ease of operation and adds complexity.

title: Hinge contacts as the interlock
new_elements: Conductive hinge-pin interlock (Door hinge completes the magnetron circuit only when fully closed.)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail or confuse, keeping the appliance trouble-free.
judge_comment: A single hinge-contact interlock is unreliable and unsafe by regulation, and has little connection to the user's learning curve.

title: Optical door-closed sensor replaces monitor switch
new_elements: Reflective optical door sensor (IR LED/phototransistor pair confirms door seating as the monitor channel.)
rationale: Removes the 'door not quite shut' confusion by sensing seating directly.
judge_comment: An optical seating sensor is plausible but only marginally reduces confusion; it is not a safe standalone monitor channel.

title: Conductive mesh gasket replaces quarter-wave choke
new_elements: Knitted-wire RF gasket (Compressible metal mesh seals RF at the door rim with simpler stamping.)
rationale: Cheaper manufacture funds a simpler, better-labelled front panel.
judge_comment: The mesh gasket is a manufacturing substitution, and its link to simpler operation is indirect, resting on a hoped-for better-labelled panel.

title: Transparent conductive glass door (no mesh, no lamp)
new_elements: ITO-coated full-glass door (Transparent conductive oxide film shields RF while giving an unobstructed view by room light.)
rationale: Seeing clearly means fewer mistakes without reading any display.
judge_comment: ITO glass is a named, concrete substitution, but ITO shielding at 2.45 GHz while staying transparent and surviving heat is doubtful, and visibility only modestly helps usability.

title: Transparent mesh cavity 'pod'
new_elements: Fine-mesh see-through cavity (Entire cavity is fine Faraday mesh in a plastic shell; food is visible from all sides.)
rationale: Total visibility replaces the need for feedback displays.
judge_comment: A fully see-through mesh cavity is radical, but it has serious problems with RF leakage, hygiene, and cleaning, and it only addresses feedback, not operation.

title: LED strip in door frame replaces incandescent lamp
new_elements: Door-frame LED strip (Cool, long-life LEDs outside the RF cavity light the food through the window.)
rationale: A bulb the user never has to replace means no maintenance to learn.
judge_comment: LED lighting is already common and barely touches the learning-curve need.

title: Window glows green when done, replacing the bell
new_elements: Colour-shifting edge-lit window (Window lights amber while heating, green when finished.)
rationale: Status is understood at a glance across the room without sound or text.
judge_comment: Colour status on the window is intuitive, feasible, and replaces the beep with a glanceable signal that needs no learning.

title: Spoken 'Done' replaces the bell
new_elements: Voice-prompt speaker (Plays short spoken cues: 'heating', 'done', 'let it stand'.)
rationale: Plain words beat symbolic beeps for first-time users.
judge_comment: Talking microwaves already exist; it helps clarity but does not simplify operation or substitute much.

title: Talking knob: audio hints when touched
new_elements: Touch-triggered audio guidance (Touching any control speaks what it does and a suggested setting.)
rationale: Replaces the printed manual with just-in-time spoken help.
judge_comment: Touch-triggered spoken help removes the need for a manual, but the idea is fairly incremental and the speaker adds cost rather than substituting a part.

title: Pull-string timer (pull length = heating time)
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pull the cord out to a marked length; it retracts slowly and stops the oven at zero, like a toy.)
rationale: A playful, bodily gesture replaces reading a dial.
judge_comment: The pull-cord timer is a tactile, intuitive input that replaces the dial, though precision and retraction mechanics are a concern.

title: Hourglass sand timer as the visible clock
new_elements: Flip-hourglass with optical end sensor (Flip the glass to start; a sensor stops the magnetron when sand runs out.)
rationale: The remaining time is literally visible, no numbers required.
judge_comment: The visible sand timer is charming and number-free, but fixed durations limit flexibility and the sensor adds complexity.

title: Hand-crank energy timer
new_elements: Wind-up crank timer (Number of crank turns sets both the clockwork timer and the power cam together.)
rationale: More cranking = more heating, an intuitive physical metaphor.
judge_comment: The crank-wound clockwork and power cam is a playful metaphor and mechanically plausible, but the turns-to-power mapping is not obvious and the crank is effortful.

title: Detented 'coffee / soup / dinner' presets on the timer knob
new_elements: Timer knob with labelled hard detents (Mechanical clicks at 45 s, 2 min, 4 min with icon labels.)
rationale: Cheap fix: the right short setting snaps into place without guessing.
judge_comment: Very practical and simple to use, but a labelled detented knob is hardly radical and only covers a few presets.

title: Foot-pedal start for hands-full users
new_elements: Kick-plate start/stop pedal (Toe-operated plate at the base starts and stops heating.)
rationale: One obvious control that works even with hands occupied.
judge_comment: Foot-pedal start is unusual and feasible, but it doesn't reduce the learning curve and adds hygiene and safety issues like accidental starts.

title: Camera in the door replaces lamp and window grid
new_elements: Internal camera with small door display (Shows food live and flags boiling-over automatically.)
rationale: Automatic mistake detection means the user needs no technique.
judge_comment: The camera with automatic boil-over detection is novel and reduces the need for technique, but cost, steam fogging and the added interface work against simplicity.

title: Built-in stir stick prevents superheating
new_elements: Ceramic nucleation stick in cavity (A rough ceramic rod the user drops in any mug; no need to know about superheating.)
rationale: Substitutes user knowledge with a physical object.
judge_comment: A nucleation stick is a cheap physical substitute for knowledge, but it only addresses superheating and the user must remember to use it.

title: Non-metallic cavity liner immune to arcing
new_elements: Arc-detecting auto-cutoff (Microphone/current sensor detects arcing and shuts off before damage.)
rationale: Users need not learn the 'no metal' rule; the oven forgives them.
judge_comment: An arc-detecting cutoff forgives the 'no metal' mistake and removes a rule to learn, but the liner and sensor details are vague and arcing detection is hard to make reliable.

title: Retractable cord replaces loose cord and plug
new_elements: Spring-retract cord reel (Vacuum-cleaner-style cord reel in the base.)
rationale: Set-up is plug in and go; no cable to manage in a dorm.
judge_comment: A retractable cord eases setup but does nothing for operating the microwave, and it's an incremental, familiar mechanism.

title: Wall-plug microwave (plug built into the casing)
new_elements: Integral wall-mount plug chassis (A small 300 W unit that hangs directly on the socket like a night-light.)
rationale: No installation decisions at all: hang it on the wall socket.
judge_comment: A wall-hanging 300 W unit is odd and simplifies installation, but the weight, heat and socket load make it hard, and it barely addresses operation.

title: USB-C PD 'slow microwave' for mugs
new_elements: 100 W USB-C powered mini cavity (Solid-state RF mug warmer powered by a laptop charger.); Portable heating anywhere (Dorm, office, car.)
rationale: One button, one cable students already own.
judge_comment: A USB-C solid-state mug heater is novel and has one-button simplicity, but 100 W RF over USB-C is weak and barely plausible for heating food.

title: Door-close equals start
new_elements: Auto-start on door close (Closing the door begins a sensor-controlled cycle; opening it stops.)
rationale: The only action is opening and closing the door.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start removes nearly all controls and learning, though it needs sensing of the load and raises safety and accidental-start concerns.

title: Big single knob: turn to start, press to stop
new_elements: Oversized rotary-push controller (A single large knob with pictograms; turning starts, pushing stops, nothing else.)
rationale: Two knobs and a button collapse into one obvious control.
judge_comment: A single big knob is clear, easy to build and intuitive, though a simple control consolidation is not radical.

title: One Big Button (30 s per press)
new_elements: Single oversized add-30s button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; nothing else to set.); Single-chip pulse-count timer (Cheap 8-pin MCU counts presses, drives relay and buzzer.)
rationale: Two knobs collapse into one obvious action anyone can perform without reading.
judge_comment: Very simple and practical, though similar to existing quick-start buttons, so not very radical.

title: Hold-to-Heat Dead-Man Button
new_elements: Hold-to-heat momentary switch (Magnetron runs only while the button is held; release stops it.)
rationale: No duration to think about: user watches the food and simply lets go when done.
judge_comment: Zero-setting operation is intuitive, but holding a button for minutes is tiring and not suited to elderly users.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand hourglass timer module (User flips a sand glass; an optical gate under the lower bulb cuts power when sand finishes.); Granular-flow optical gating (Photo-interrupter sees sand column empty and opens magnetron relay.)
rationale: A universally understood object replaces a numbered dial; the remaining sand shows progress at a glance.
judge_comment: Charming and intuitive, but flipping a glass and sand-sensing is unreliable, and fixed durations are imprecise.

title: Water-Clock Drip Timer
new_elements: Drip-fed float timer (User pours a cup of water into a funnel; drip rate drains it, float drops and opens contacts.)
rationale: Mains-frequency independent and visually self-explaining: more water equals more time.
judge_comment: Pouring water into an appliance next to a magnetron is messy and unsafe, and it adds steps instead of simplifying.

title: Pull-String Toy Timer
new_elements: Pull-string spring-return timer (Pull a cord out; it retracts over minutes via an escapement and breaks the circuit at home.)
rationale: A single gross-motor pull with visible string length as the time display suits elderly hands.
judge_comment: Pull-cord mechanical timer is intuitive with visible time and plausible, similar to old mechanical timers, though it needs a robust escapement.

title: Linear 'Longer' Slider
new_elements: Long linear slider timer (A 25 cm slide potentiometer labelled only 'shorter ↔ longer' sets duration; slider creeps back to zero.)
rationale: Linear travel maps directly to time, is readable from across the room, and has fine short-duration resolution.
judge_comment: Intuitive and easy to build, but it is still a manual timer with a different form factor, and it is not very radical.

title: Food-Icon Wheel Instead of Minutes
new_elements: Pictogram selector wheel (Dial shows only pictures (cup, plate, bowl, frozen block); each hard-wires a time/power pair.)
rationale: Users pick what they have, not numbers, eliminating any mental conversion.
judge_comment: Pictograms remove the number conversion and are easy to implement, but similar preset buttons are already common.

title: Weighing Turntable Sets Time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable auto-timer (Turntable weighs the dish; time is derived from mass, start on door close.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost load cell under turntable motor.)
rationale: Zero settings: put food in, close door, it heats proportionally to how much is there.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is ideal, but weight is a poor proxy for the heating needed (food type, starting temperature), and the load cell must work in a microwave environment.

title: Steam-Stop Auto Timer
new_elements: Humidity-burst cutoff sensor (Cavity vent humidity sensor stops heating when steam release peaks.)
rationale: Replaces the timer with a sensor so the user never sets a duration at all.
judge_comment: Humidity sensors for auto-cooking already exist and need no input, but they work poorly for foods that don't steam.

title: IR Thermometer 'Warm / Hot' Knob
new_elements: Target-temperature knob with IR pyrometer (Two-position knob 'warm' / 'hot'; non-contact IR sensor stops heating at target.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not 'how many minutes at what %'; the oven does the translation.
judge_comment: A warm/hot knob matches how people think, but an IR sensor only reads surface temperature and the cavity has to be designed around it, which limits reliability.

title: Thermal-Camera Closed Loop, No Controls
new_elements: Low-res thermal array controller (8x8 thermopile watches dish, pulses magnetron until uniform target temp.); Thermopile array imaging (Sub-$5 MEMS thermopile sensor.)
rationale: The entire control panel disappears; close door and it finishes when food is evenly hot.
judge_comment: Removes all controls and fits the zero-learning-curve need, though an 8x8 thermopile sees only surface temperature through steam and a metal-mesh door, which makes accurate closed-loop control hard.

title: Door-Close Starts, Door-Open Stops
new_elements: Door-as-switch fixed-dose controller (Closing the door fires a fixed 60 s burst; opening cancels; close again for another.)
rationale: The only interaction the user already must perform—closing the door—becomes the only control.
judge_comment: Very simple and easy to build, but a fixed 60 s dose is inflexible and needs repeated door cycling.

title: Gentle/Fast Rocker Replaces 5-Step Power Knob
new_elements: Two-position gentle/fast rocker (Rocker selects 30% or 100% duty via a single bimetal flasher.)
rationale: Five ambiguous power steps become one binary choice with plain words.
judge_comment: A cheap, plausible simplification, but it still leaves a control and a time setting to learn, so the gain is incremental.

title: Continuous Inverter Dial 'Low ↔ High'
new_elements: Inverter continuous magnetron drive (Switch-mode supply varies anode current for true continuous power.); Unmarked low-high analogue dial (Potentiometer with no numbers, like a stove knob.)
rationale: Behaves exactly like a hob knob everyone already knows.
judge_comment: The stove-knob metaphor is familiar, but inverter drives cost more than they save, which runs against SUBSTITUTE, and the dial still needs a time control.

title: Height-Shelf Power Control
new_elements: Three-level insert shelf (Food placed higher or lower in the cavity receives more or less field; no electrical power setting.)
rationale: Power becomes a physical placement decision ('top shelf = fast') with no knob to learn.
judge_comment: Using shelf height for power is wild and removes the knob, but standing-wave hot spots make the effect unpredictable and the placement rule is less intuitive than it sounds.

title: Delete the Power Knob Entirely
new_elements: Fixed 500 W always-on setting (Magnetron sized to a medium power that reheats without needing defrost modes.)
rationale: One fewer control is the simplest control.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob does simplify operation and is easy to build, but a fixed 500 W setting limits versatility and is hardly radical.

title: Recipe Punch-Card Slot
new_elements: Notched card reader slot (Insert a stiff card (sold with food or printed) whose edge notches set time and power mechanically.)
rationale: Settings come pre-made; the user only pushes a card in.
judge_comment: A mechanical notched-card reader is a cheap substitute for the electronic panel and needs no learning, though it depends on cards being available.

title: Barcode-on-Packaging Scanner
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Hold the ready-meal under the scanner; GS1 code maps to stored time/power.)
rationale: No reading of pack instructions or dial numbers; scan and go.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning is feasible and removes manual entry, but it needs a database and only works for packaged food.

title: NFC Tag Reader in Turntable
new_elements: Turntable NFC reader (Tagged packaging or dishes placed on the turntable transmit cook settings.); Passive NFC tagging (13.56 MHz coil under glass plate; tags cost cents.)
rationale: Placing the food is the whole interaction.
judge_comment: Placing the food is the whole interaction, which fits the need very well, but it requires tagged packaging and NFC reading inside a microwave cavity is hard.

title: Voice-Only Control
new_elements: Offline keyword speech module (Recognises 'two minutes', 'stop', 'defrost' locally; no panel.)
rationale: Speaking a duration is the most natural interface for users who struggle with knobs.
judge_comment: Offline voice control is natural and workable, but it is common in existing products and raises noise and accent issues.

title: Wave-to-Add-Time Gesture Sensor
new_elements: IR gesture bar (Each hand wave past the front adds 30 s; wave backwards cancels.)
rationale: Touch-free, no fine motor skills, one gesture to learn.
judge_comment: Touch-free wave-to-add-time is easy to grasp, but accidental triggers, no feedback on the total, and no power control limit its usefulness.

title: Joystick Combined Time/Power
new_elements: Single 2-axis joystick (Push forward for longer, sideways for stronger; spring-centre starts.)
rationale: Two parameters, one hand, one object.
judge_comment: A single joystick is plausible and compact, but mapping axes to time and power is not intuitive and needs some learning.

title: Quantity Dial Instead of Time
new_elements: 'How much food' dial (Dial graduated in cups/plates; fixed power; time computed internally.)
rationale: Users estimate quantity far more easily than cooking seconds.
judge_comment: Setting by quantity removes the abstract time and power decisions, and it is feasible with a lookup table, though food type still matters.

title: Turntable-Revolution Counter Timer
new_elements: Revolution-count stop dial (Dial sets 'number of turns' (1-10); a reed switch on the turntable counts down.)
rationale: Progress is literally visible as the plate turns; no abstract minutes.
judge_comment: Counting turntable revolutions is a wild and visible progress cue, but 'turns' is no more intuitive than time and the rotation speed is variable.

title: Quartz Electronic Timer Replaces Synchronous Motor
new_elements: Crystal-oscillator timing IC (32 kHz crystal timer independent of mains frequency; same knob, better accuracy.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar knob but makes short times reliable so first-try results are right.
judge_comment: A quartz timer is a sensible, feasible substitution, but it is nearly invisible to users and does little for the learning curve.

title: Bimetal Thermal Timer
new_elements: Heated bimetal delay switch (Knob sets contact gap; a heater coil warps bimetal until contacts open—no motor.)
rationale: Simpler, cheaper mechanism with the same one-knob operation.
judge_comment: Plausible cheap thermal timer that keeps the one-knob control, but it is not much simpler for the user and likely less accurate than the mechanical timers already in use.

title: Hydraulic Dashpot Timer
new_elements: Oil-damped piston timer (Knob compresses a spring against a viscous dashpot; slow return opens contacts.)
rationale: Silent, motorless and voltage-independent while keeping the familiar twist.
judge_comment: Oil dashpot timers do exist and keep the familiar twist, but the user gets little new and accuracy and temperature drift are concerns.

title: Egg-Timer Dock
new_elements: Removable kitchen egg-timer cradle (Any wind-up egg timer drops into a cradle whose ring-detect mic/latch stops the oven.)
rationale: Users bring the timer they already know how to use.
judge_comment: Reusing a familiar egg timer is a clever way to avoid learning anything, but detecting the ring reliably and cutting power is clunky and unreliable.

title: Coin-Slot Duration Tokens
new_elements: Token slot timer (Drop colour-coded plastic tokens (1 min, 5 min) in a slot; each token trips a fixed delay.)
rationale: Tangible countable units replace reading a scale.
judge_comment: Tokens give a tangible and wild way to set time that is easy to grasp, but they can be lost and make flexible timing harder.

title: Spoken 'Done' Instead of Bell
new_elements: Voice chip end-of-cycle announcer (Replaces mechanical bell with a sound chip saying 'Your food is ready'.)
rationale: Unambiguous feedback removes guessing about what the ding meant.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build and it makes the end of the cycle clearer, but it only affects feedback and not operation, and it is hardly radical.

title: Lift-Off Magnetic Door Panel
new_elements: Hinge-less magnetically seated door plate (Door is a flat shielded plate held by magnets and choke flange; lift it off with one hand.)
rationale: No button, no swing arc, no latch to learn—just pick up the lid.
judge_comment: A lift-off magnetic door is novel and has no latch to learn, but it still leaves operation of the controls unaddressed, and the safety interlock and RF sealing are challenging.

title: Pull Handle with Magnetic Catch
new_elements: Grab-handle magnetic catch (Door held shut by magnets and interlock reed switch; pulling the handle opens it.)
rationale: Works like a fridge door, the most familiar door in any kitchen.
judge_comment: Very feasible and familiar, but it is close to existing doors and only addresses opening, so it is not radical.

title: Drawer Cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Whole cavity floor slides out like a drawer; shielding by choke rails.)
rationale: Food is loaded from above with no reaching into a box; drawers need no instruction.
judge_comment: A drawer is intuitive and has some precedent in drawer microwaves, but the choke-rail shielding and the controls remain open issues.

title: Top-Loading Well with Lid
new_elements: Top-loading shielded well (Cylindrical cavity opened from the top with a hinged lid like a rice cooker.)
rationale: Drop-in loading is intuitive and gravity keeps the lid sealed.
judge_comment: Rice-cooker-style top loading is familiar, but cylindrical cavity heating and loading ergonomics are questionable and the idea says little about how to start or set it.

title: Toaster-Style Pop-Up Cavity
new_elements: Pop-up lift cage (Push the cage down to start; a spring-latch timer pops the food up when done.)
rationale: Everyone can use a toaster; start and finish are one physical motion.
judge_comment: Merging start, timing and finish into one toaster-like motion directly removes the learning curve, though a mechanical timer and pop-up for varied foods are tricky.

title: Rotating Carousel Cavity
new_elements: Rotate-out turret cavity (Cavity is a drum that turns 180° to present its open side; closed position seals against choke.)
rationale: Turn to load, turn to cook—a single rotary motion with no door at all.
judge_comment: Very radical doorless turret is intriguing, but RF sealing on a rotating drum and food spillage when rotating make it hard, and the single-motion benefit is only moderate.

title: Chain-Mail Curtain Door
new_elements: Conductive mesh roller curtain (Fine stainless chain-mail curtain rolls up like a blind; edges run in grounded tracks.)
rationale: No swing clearance and no latch; push it up like a blind.
judge_comment: Chain-mail curtain is novel and intuitive like a blind, but mesh gaps, leakage at edges, and cleaning are significant concerns.

title: Garage-Style Roll-Up Shutter
new_elements: Segmented steel roll-up shutter (Interlocking stamped slats roll into the top; closing completes the interlock.)
rationale: One up/down motion with nothing protruding into the user's space.
judge_comment: Roll-up shutter is concrete and plausible with interlocking slats forming a choke, though it is bulky and less simple than a normal door.

title: Drop-Down Oven Door
new_elements: Bottom-hinged fold-down door (Door folds down to form a shelf for dishes, like a conventional oven.)
rationale: Mirrors the oven people already own and gives a landing spot for hot plates.
judge_comment: Familiar oven-style door is highly intuitive with no learning curve and easily built, but it is hardly radical and the weight of a loaded door is a minor issue.

title: Foot-Pedal Door Opener
new_elements: Foot pedal latch release (Pedal at base pulls a Bowden cable to the latch lever.)
rationale: Hands-full users open the door without finding a small button.
judge_comment: Foot pedal with Bowden cable is simple and practical for full hands, but it adds a hidden control to discover rather than removing learning.

title: Elbow Paddle Release
new_elements: Full-height side paddle (A long bar down the door edge releases the latch when nudged anywhere.)
rationale: Impossible to miss, operable with elbow, wrist or hand.
judge_comment: Easy door-opening bar helps a bit, but only addresses door release, not operation overall, and is similar to existing push-bar designs.

title: Proximity Auto-Open Door
new_elements: Capacitive approach auto-latch (After cycle ends, a hand near the door pops the latch via solenoid.)
rationale: The door opens itself; nothing to find or press.
judge_comment: Auto-opening door removes a step with a plausible capacitive sensor and solenoid, though it only covers the end-of-cycle opening.

title: Auto-Open at Bell
new_elements: Timer-cam driven door pop (The same cam that rings the bell also kicks the latch lever so the door swings ajar.)
rationale: 'Done' is signalled by the door itself opening—no button and no bell to interpret.
judge_comment: Clever mechanical substitution where one cam both rings the bell and pops the door, giving an intuitive done signal, but it is limited to old timer-style units.

title: Gravity Latch
new_elements: Gravity-drop hook latch (A weighted hook falls into the keeper on close; lifting the door handle slightly frees it.)
rationale: No spring, no button: lift and pull is self-evident.
judge_comment: A simple gravity hook replaces the spring and button latch, but a lift-to-open action is not obviously more intuitive and the safety interlock needs care.

title: Transparent Conductive Film Window
new_elements: ITO / silver-nanowire shielding glass (Fully clear glass pane with transparent conductive coating replaces perforated mesh.)
rationale: A clear view of the food lets users judge doneness without understanding settings.
judge_comment: A clear window helps judge doneness, but it does little for operation simplicity, and transparent conductive coatings at microwave shielding levels are technically challenging.

title: Mesh-Embedded Polymer Door
new_elements: Insert-moulded mesh polycarbonate (Mesh overmoulded in a single clear polymer shot forms the whole door, no glass, no steel frame.)
rationale: Lighter door is easier to swing for elderly users and cheaper to build.
judge_comment: A cheaper, lighter door is plausible, but it barely addresses zero-learning-curve operation, and a clear polymer with mesh must still shield microwaves while staying see-through.

title: Living-Hinge Flexible Door
new_elements: Conductive-silicone living hinge (Door attached by a flexible conductive elastomer strip; no pins or stamped hinges.)
rationale: Door flops open any way it is pushed; nothing to align or jam.
judge_comment: A floppy door is a wild idea, but a conductive silicone hinge would struggle to seal against microwave leakage and to hold the interlock reliably, and it does little for operation simplicity.

title: Faraday Cloche Over a Hot-Plate Base
new_elements: Shielded dome cloche (Magnetron in a base plate; a metal-mesh dome cloche placed over the dish completes the cage and interlock.)
rationale: Cover the plate, it heats; lift the cover, it stops—no box, no door, no buttons.
judge_comment: A cover-to-heat cloche is a radical, intuitive interaction with essentially no learning curve, though shielding at the seam and controlling power need engineering.

title: Tip-Out Serving Tray at End
new_elements: Timer-released tilting tray (Cam end-stop releases a tilt tray that slides the dish forward through a flap for pickup.)
rationale: The oven hands the food back; the user never operates the door.
judge_comment: Automatic hand-back removes the door-opening step and is concrete, but it ignores the start and setup controls and adds mechanical complexity and a leakage path through the flap.

title: Remote Key-Fob Start
new_elements: Two-button RF fob (Go / Stop) (Car-key style fob replaces panel; Go = 1 min full power each press.)
rationale: Two large labelled buttons, usable from an armchair, no panel to decipher.
judge_comment: A two-button fob is very simple and easy to build, but remote controls are a familiar idea, and a remote start raises safety concerns when nobody is watching the oven.

title: Thermochromic Cavity Floor as Timer Display
new_elements: Colour-change glass turntable (Thermochromic ring on the turntable turns red when the plate reaches serving temperature; a photodiode stops the oven.)
rationale: 'Red means ready' is understood instantly and needs no timer setting.
