judge_comment: Removing timer-setting with a 'red means ready' cue strongly serves zero-learning-curve operation, but a thermochromic ring on the turntable reflects plate/surface temperature rather than food temperature, and the photodiode sensing and heat-resistant microwave-safe pigment add reliability doubts.

title: Cook-until-hot button
new_elements: Single large HEAT button (One button; cooking stops when an IR food-surface sensor reaches eating temperature.); Thermopile IR food-temperature sensing (Non-contact IR element views the turntable through a waveguide-safe window.)
rationale: Removes both knobs so the only decision is 'press'; serves directly.
judge_comment: One-button heat-until-hot is ideal for zero learning, though IR surface sensing is unreliable for uneven food and a single button gives no control over different foods.

title: Weigh-and-go timer
new_elements: Load-cell turntable auto-timer (Food mass sets duration automatically via a mechanical spring scale coupled to the timer cam.)
rationale: User never chooses a time; weight decides it, so zero learning.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing removes user choice, but weight is a poor proxy for needed time, and the description is internally inconsistent (load cell vs. mechanical spring scale).

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand hourglass with optical end sensor (Flipping the glass starts heating; empty upper bulb trips a photo-interrupter.)
rationale: Everyone already understands an hourglass; the control is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A familiar hourglass metaphor is quirky and clear, but the user still has to pick a duration and the glass fixes it to one time.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Pull-cord spring timer (Pull the cord out; its retraction length equals cooking time, like a toy.)
rationale: A single intuitive gesture replaces reading a dial.
judge_comment: Pull-cord spring timer is simple, mechanical and cheap, though judging how far to pull still requires estimating a time.

title: Toaster lever start
new_elements: Push-down lever that pops up when done (Lever depth sets time; it pops up with a click and opens the door.)
rationale: Borrows the universally known toaster interaction.
judge_comment: The toaster lever is a universally understood interaction and mechanically plausible, though lever depth as time setting is imprecise.

title: Hold-to-heat paddle
new_elements: Dead-man's paddle switch (Magnetron runs only while the big paddle is held; release stops it.)
rationale: No numbers at all; user watches food and lets go.
judge_comment: A hold-to-run paddle removes all numbers and learning, and a dead-man switch is simple and safe, though holding it for minutes is tiring.

title: Pictogram dial
new_elements: Food-icon selector dial (Cup, plate, popcorn, frozen icons map to fixed time/power cams.)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating instead of how.
judge_comment: Icon-based dial with fixed cams is cheap and intuitive, but presets are less flexible and similar presets already exist.

title: One-minute tally button
new_elements: Add-a-minute ratchet button (Each press advances the timer cam one minute; a row of lamps shows the count.)
rationale: Counting presses needs no reading of a scale.
judge_comment: A press-per-minute button with lamps is very easy to understand and mechanically simple, but it's close to existing quick-start buttons.

title: Package tag auto-set
new_elements: NFC/barcode reader in cavity floor (Reads heating instructions printed on the food packaging.); Low-cost NFC reader IC (Near-field tag reading through plastic packaging.)
rationale: Food tells the oven what to do; user just loads it.
judge_comment: Needs no user input if it works, but it depends on packaging tags that don't exist and NFC reading inside a metal cavity is hard.

title: Turn-count dial
new_elements: Turntable-revolution counter dial (User selects 'how many turns'; a cam on the turntable motor counts them.)
rationale: Visible rotations are easier to grasp than abstract minutes.
judge_comment: Counting turntable revolutions is highly original, but it is less intuitive than time and offers little real benefit.

title: Shelf-height power
new_elements: Adjustable-height turntable shelf (Raising/lowering food in the standing-wave field changes absorbed power continuously.)
rationale: Physical 'closer = hotter' is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: Height-based power is novel but standing-wave hot spots make it unpredictable, and a raised shelf isn't self-explanatory to users.

title: Waveguide shutter
new_elements: Sliding metal iris on waveguide port (A lever slides a plate partially over the feed aperture, attenuating power continuously.)
rationale: A tap-like slider is more intuitive than numbered duty steps.
judge_comment: A mechanical iris on the waveguide is a concrete way to get continuous power, though it risks magnetron mismatch and reflected power, and a slider still needs some user understanding.

title: Water-load dimmer
new_elements: Lossy water-load slider (Moving a sealed water tube into the cavity absorbs a share of power, giving smooth control.)
rationale: Behaves like a stove flame: slide for gentler heat.
judge_comment: The stove-flame analogy is intuitive, but a movable water load wastes energy and adds mess and complexity.

title: Gentle/Fast toggle
new_elements: Two-position rocker (Gentle / Fast) (Replaces five numbered steps with two plain-language settings.)
rationale: Fewer, worded choices eliminate the power-level guessing game.
judge_comment: Two plain-language settings directly remove the learning curve and are easy to build, but the idea is not radical.

title: No power knob at all
new_elements: Fixed-power with mode stirrer (Delete the knob; a stirrer fan evens heating so one power suits most foods.)
rationale: One fewer control is the simplest learning curve.
judge_comment: Removing the power control is the simplest possible operation, though one power level may not suit all foods and mode stirrers are already known.

title: Target-temperature dial
new_elements: Warm/Hot/Boiling thermostat dial with IR sensor (User sets desired food temperature; oven cycles until reached.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Intuitive 'how hot' interface replaces time/power, though IR sensing of food temp through a cavity is imperfect and the approach is not entirely new.

title: Steam-stop sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor auto-stop (Cooking ends shortly after the vent humidity spikes.)
rationale: Removes the need to estimate time.
judge_comment: Humidity sensor cooking exists in sensor-cook models, so it is feasible and helpful but not radical.

title: Popcorn microphone
new_elements: Acoustic pop-rate sensor (Microphone stops heating when popping slows below one per two seconds.)
rationale: Listening does the timing for the user.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection exists in some products, but it is a clever, specific use that serves only one food.

title: Door-close autostart
new_elements: Close-to-start / open-to-stop interlock (Closing the door starts a sensor-ended cycle; no start button exists.)
rationale: The only gestures are load and close.
judge_comment: Removing the start button makes operation truly two-gesture, though accidental starts with empty or unsuitable loads need safeguards.

title: Push-to-open door
new_elements: Push-latch door (cabinet style) (Pressing the door face itself releases a push-push latch; no separate button.)
rationale: No button to find; the door is the button.
judge_comment: A push-latch door is simple and cheap and removes a button, but it only addresses opening and is a minor gain.

title: Magnetic pull handle
new_elements: Magnetic catch with large grab handle (Fridge-style magnetic seal; pulling the handle opens the door and the interlock.)
rationale: Fridge gesture everyone knows, fewer parts.
judge_comment: Familiar fridge-style pull is intuitive and simple, but it only addresses opening, not the controls, and magnetic seals offer weak microwave leakage protection.

title: Foot-pedal door
new_elements: Foot pedal door release (Bin-style pedal opens the door while both hands hold the dish.)
rationale: Hands-free opening is simpler for loaded hands.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening is handy, but a pedal adds a new thing to learn and does little for the core operation.

title: Auto-eject door
new_elements: Timer-triggered spring door opener (Bell cam also releases the latch so the door swings ajar when done.)
rationale: An open door is the most obvious 'ready' signal.
judge_comment: A door that springs ajar when done is an obvious completion cue and is feasible with a cam release, though it only helps the end of the cycle.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Whole cavity floor slides out on rails; choke flange seals when closed.)
rationale: Drawers need no latch, no button and no reach-in.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar, intuitive motion and removes the latch, but sealing a sliding cavity and its rails is difficult.

title: Top-loading lid
new_elements: Lift-up canopy lid (Food placed from above like a slow cooker; gravity closes the lid onto a choke seal.)
rationale: Setting a bowl down from above is the most natural loading motion.
judge_comment: Top-loading is highly intuitive and radical, but gravity-closed lids raise safety-interlock and leakage concerns, and steam and spills make it hard to use.

title: Roll-shutter door
new_elements: Tambour roll-up conductive shutter (Metal-slat shutter rolls into the roof; slats overlap below aperture limit.)
rationale: No swing arc, no button; just push up.
judge_comment: Roll-up shutter removes the swing and latch button, but RF sealing along slat gaps and tracks is hard, and it does little for control simplicity.

title: Sideways pocket door
new_elements: Sliding pocket door (Door slides into the side wall on a rail; no hinge or latch lever.)
rationale: One linear motion replaces button-plus-swing.
judge_comment: A sliding door is plausible and simple to use, but the RF choke along the rail is a challenge and it does not address the controls.

title: Revolving-drum loader
new_elements: Rotating cylinder cavity (Turn the drum to expose the shelf, turn back to seal; the drum wall is the door.)
rationale: A single twist loads and seals; nothing to latch.
judge_comment: The rotating drum loads and seals in one twist, which is intuitive, but the rotating RF seal and the food spill risk make it hard.

title: Iris aperture door
new_elements: Camera-iris metal door (Interleaved steel leaves close like a lens; one ring twist opens it.)
rationale: Wildly simple twist-to-open gesture.
judge_comment: An iris door is eye-catching, but it is mechanically complex, an RF seal across the leaves is nearly impossible, and the opening is awkward for loading dishes.

title: Conductive clear door
new_elements: ITO-coated glass RF shield (Transparent conductive film blocks 2.45 GHz without a perforated mesh.)
rationale: Clear view of food means less need to interpret controls.
judge_comment: ITO-coated glass is a real, concrete substitute for the mesh, but it barely affects operation simplicity.

title: Single combined knob
new_elements: Twist-for-time, push-for-power knob (One oversized knob; pushing it in toggles gentle/full.)
rationale: Halves the controls on the panel.
judge_comment: Practical and simple, but a twist-and-push knob is close to existing microwaves and only modestly radical.

title: Big-button minute bank
new_elements: Row of five labelled minute buttons (1,2,3,5,10) (Each button is a dedicated cam preset; no dial reading.)
rationale: Discrete large buttons suit elderly and first-time users.
judge_comment: Dedicated minute buttons need no learning and suit first-time users, but the idea is incremental, and the fixed presets limit flexibility.

title: Tactile braille dial
new_elements: Oversized detented dial with raised tactile marks (Strong clicks per minute and embossed numerals readable by touch.)
rationale: Settable without glasses or light.
judge_comment: Detents and embossed numerals are cheap and accessible, though a dial that is easy to set is not a new idea.

title: Light-arc timer ring
new_elements: Capacitive ring with LED countdown arc (Swipe around the ring; glowing arc shrinks as time passes.)
rationale: Visual remaining-time arc is understood at a glance.
judge_comment: The glowing arc is intuitive for showing time remaining, but swiping a capacitive ring adds a small learning step and costs more than a dial.

title: Water-clock timer
new_elements: Visible drip water-clock (Tilt reservoir to fill; a float switch ends heating when it drains.)
rationale: Timing is physically visible and mains-frequency independent.
judge_comment: A visible water-clock is wild and easy to understand, but water near the electronics is a hazard, and filling and tilting it is awkward and imprecise.

title: Door-swing winds timer
new_elements: Hinge-wound spring timer (Opening the door winds a spring; cooking length is set by how long the door stays open.)
rationale: Eliminates the separate timing act entirely.
judge_comment: Clever mechanical substitution that removes the timing step, but holding the door open for the cooking duration is unintuitive and arguably adds a learning curve.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline keyword microphone ('heat', 'stop') (Two-word offline recogniser on a low-cost MCU replaces both knobs.)
rationale: Speaking is the lowest learning curve for.
judge_comment: Offline two-word recognition is plausible and easy to learn, but it cannot specify duration, and noisy kitchens and accents cause errors.

title: Cup-shaped cradle
new_elements: Mug-detecting cradle preset (A mug placed in a moulded cradle closes a switch that runs a fixed 'drink' cycle.)
rationale: The most common task becomes zero-input.
judge_comment: A mug cradle that triggers a fixed cycle gives true zero-input operation for a common task, though it covers a narrow use case.

title: Frozen/Fresh switch
new_elements: Frozen / Fresh slide switch (Selects defrost cam or full power using plain food states.)
rationale: Describes the food, not the machine.
judge_comment: A simple two-state switch is very easy to use and cheap, but it is incremental rather than radical, and the two settings limit flexibility.

title: Thermochromic done-glass
new_elements: Thermochromic turntable glass (Glass changes colour when food above it is hot; user stops when they see the colour.)
rationale: A colour cue replaces mental timing.
judge_comment: A visual doneness cue is a creative idea, but thermochromic glass would heat unreliably and slowly, reflecting plate rather than food temperature, and would degrade in a microwave.

title: Inverter with soft/hot slider
new_elements: Inverter magnetron supply (Continuous true power control replaces on/off cycling.); Unmarked soft-to-hot slider (A fader with a gradient instead of numbers.)
rationale: A gradient slider is understood without instructions.
judge_comment: A gradient slider is intuitive, and inverter power control is real technology, but it replaces rather than substitutes cheaply and still needs a time setting.

title: Living-hinge door
new_elements: Polymer living-hinge door with metal mesh insert (Moulded flexure replaces stamped steel hinges and pins.)
rationale: Light, soft door is easier for frail hands.
judge_comment: A polymer living-hinge door is a plausible cost substitution, but it does little for no-learning-curve operation and raises RF-shielding and heat concerns.

title: Gas-strut self-closing door
new_elements: Soft-close damped hinge (Door closes itself from any angle and seats the interlock; no slam, no latch button.)
rationale: Users never worry whether the door is properly shut.
judge_comment: A self-closing damped door removes the latch worry and is feasible, though the benefit to learning is modest and the idea is fairly incremental.

title: Slosh-sensing stop
new_elements: Turntable motor-current boil detector (Boiling liquid shifts load torque; the oven stops at first boil.)
rationale: Liquids heat to 'just right' with no setting.
judge_comment: Detecting boil from turntable motor current would remove settings for liquids, but the signal is likely too weak and unreliable, and it only works for liquids.

title: Timer by dish diameter
new_elements: Spring-loaded dish-size feelers (Guides on the turntable measure plate diameter and set a proportional time.)
rationale: Bigger plate, longer cook, nothing to set.
judge_comment: Mechanical plate-size feelers that set the time are novel and need no input, but plate diameter is a poor proxy for food load and the mechanism is awkward.

title: Light-fade finish
new_elements: Dimming cavity lamp as countdown (Lamp brightness decays with remaining time; dark means done.)
rationale: Progress is readable from across the room without a display.
judge_comment: An intuitive countdown through lamp dimming needs no learning, and it is cheap and plausible, though it does not address how to set the time.

title: Snap-ring stirrer power
new_elements: Even/Fast stirrer selector (Replaces power steps with a choice between stirred even heating and direct fast heating.)
rationale: Outcome words instead of wattage numbers.
judge_comment: Outcome-based wording simplifies power choice, but it is a modest change and the stirrer mechanism is only loosely described.

title: Choke-tunnel open front
new_elements: Quarter-wave choke tunnel (industrial conveyor style) (A deep lossy-walled tunnel attenuates leakage so no door is needed.); Doorless shelf with RF choke tunnel (Slide the plate in; interlock is a light curtain.)
rationale: No door means nothing to open, close or latch.
judge_comment: A doorless microwave is radical and removes the door interaction, but leakage and safety make it very implausible for a home appliance, and it needs a new way to keep food from spilling.

title: Dial-by-sound ticks
new_elements: Audible-click timer that announces minutes (Each detent plays a spoken number from a cheap sound chip.)
rationale: Removes the need to read small dial markings.
judge_comment: Spoken detent numbers are simple and cheap, but talking appliances already exist, so the idea is not very novel.

title: Pressure-plate time
new_elements: Press-harder-for-longer pad (A force-sensing pad: light tap = quick warm, firm press = full cook.)
rationale: One gesture, intensity intuitively maps to heat.
judge_comment: Pressing harder to cook longer or hotter is a single gesture, but its mapping is ambiguous and hard to repeat precisely.

title: Hand-wave stop
new_elements: IR hand-wave sensor on door (Waving stops cooking and pops the door; no button or knob to touch.)
rationale: Touch-free stop/open is obvious and hygienic.
judge_comment: A hand-wave stop and open is intuitive and technically easy with an IR sensor and a door-release solenoid, but it covers only stop/open and not the harder setup of time and power, and it replaces a button rather than simplifying operation, so it is not radical.

title: Single 'Heat' button replaces timer and power knobs
new_elements: One-touch heat button with auto-stop (A single large button; pressing starts full power, a humidity sensor stops it when food is hot.); Humidity-based doneness sensing (Cheap capacitive humidity sensor in vent detects steam burst signalling food is hot.)
rationale: Removes both knobs so the user has literally one control and zero settings to learn.
judge_comment: One button with humidity auto-stop nearly eliminates the learning curve, though sensing reliability varies across foods like dry or covered items.

title: Door-close starts cooking
new_elements: Door-as-start-switch (Closing the door starts a fixed 60 s cycle; opening stops it. No separate start control.)
rationale: The only gesture the user already knows (shutting the door) becomes the entire interface.
judge_comment: Door-close starting a fixed 60 s cycle is very simple, but it risks accidental starts and inflexible durations, and an empty-run hazard.

title: Weight-scale turntable sets time automatically
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (Strain gauge under turntable weighs food; time scales linearly with mass.); Low-cost strain-gauge load cell (Kitchen-scale grade load cell integrated into motor coupling.)
rationale: User never guesses minutes; the oven infers them from weight.
judge_comment: Weight-based time is intuitive and feasible, but weight is a poor proxy for heating needs, and the load cell adds cost.

title: Replace clockwork timer with hourglass-style sand timer
new_elements: Optical sand-glass timer (User flips a sealed sand glass; an IR gate detects when sand runs out and cuts power.)
rationale: Everyone intuitively understands an hourglass; no dial markings to read.
judge_comment: Sand timer is a charming, radical substitution that is familiar, but it is less precise and flipping a glass is arguably no simpler than a dial.

title: Power knob replaced by 'Gentle / Normal' rocker
new_elements: Two-position rocker switch (Binary choice: 30% duty for defrost/melt, 100% for everything else.)
rationale: Five power steps nobody understands collapse to one obvious binary decision.
judge_comment: A binary Gentle/Normal rocker is highly feasible and easy to grasp, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Infrared surface thermometer stops at eating temperature
new_elements: Cavity IR thermopile sensor (Non-contact sensor halts magnetron when food surface reaches 70 °C.); Thermopile IR sensing (Mass-produced ear-thermometer sensor behind mica window.)
rationale: Temperature, not time, is what users actually want, so no time estimation is needed.
judge_comment: Auto-stop at target temperature removes time estimation, though surface-only IR readings and steam or covered containers limit accuracy; it also fits the SUBSTITUTE operator reasonably well.

title: Fixed-duty magnetron eliminates power selection entirely
new_elements: Single-power inverter supply (Low-cost inverter fixed at 500 W continuous, gentle enough for most tasks.); Switch-mode inverter HV supply (Replaces transformer+doubler; continuous rather than duty-cycled output.)
rationale: With no power choice at all, there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Removing power selection simplifies the interface and is technically easy, but it lowers capability (poor defrosting) and still leaves the user to set a time.

title: Door window as the whole timer: wipe-to-set
new_elements: Capacitive slider printed on door glass (Swipe along the window edge; length of swipe equals minutes, shown by LED strip.)
rationale: A phone-like swipe gesture replaces reading a dial scale.
judge_comment: A swipe gesture is intuitive, but a capacitive slider on door glass is awkward near the microwave and swiping to set time is not clearly simpler than a dial.

title: Preset buttons with pictures instead of numbers
new_elements: Four icon buttons (mug, plate, popcorn, snowflake) (Each button hard-wired to a fixed time/power cam; no numerals anywhere on the panel.)
rationale: Pictograms are language-free and need no instruction.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are easy to use and cheap to build, but they are common and inflexible for varied food quantities.

title: Voice-free sound cue: cavity sings when done
new_elements: Resonant steam whistle in vent (Steam escaping the vent passes a whistle; pitch rises as food gets hot, telling the user to stop.)
rationale: Like a kettle, the appliance tells you when it is done without a timer to set.
judge_comment: A whistle that signals doneness is a charming idea, but steam output is unreliable across foods and the user still has to stop the oven manually.

title: Foot pedal replaces door button
new_elements: Foot-pedal door opener (Bin-style pedal opens door hands-free; interlocks unchanged.)
rationale: Hands full of plates? The familiar pedal-bin gesture needs no thought.
judge_comment: Familiar pedal gesture helps hands-free opening, but it only touches door opening, not the overall learning curve, and a pedal on a countertop appliance is awkward.

title: Magnetic-latch door with no button
new_elements: Pull-to-open magnetic latch (Fridge-style magnetic gasket holds door; Hall sensors replace mechanical interlock actuation.); Hall-effect door sensing (Redundant Hall sensors keep three-channel logic.)
rationale: Opens exactly like a fridge, the one kitchen door everybody already knows.
judge_comment: Fridge-style opening is intuitive, but magnetic latches must meet strict safety interlock regulations, and Hall sensors alone are a hard sell for those.

title: Turntable motor replaced by mode stirrer
new_elements: Fan-driven mode stirrer in waveguide (Rotating metal paddle scatters field so flat cavity floor needs no turntable.)
rationale: No glass plate to align, remove or break; any dish just goes in.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, so this is a proven swap that removes the plate-seating step, though it is not radical.

title: Air-bearing turntable: no motor, no coupling
new_elements: Cooling-fan-driven passive turntable (Exhaust air from the magnetron fan spins a vaned plate via air jets.)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail and no plate-seating puzzle for the user.
judge_comment: An air-driven turntable is creative, but it only removes a part and does little for operation, and the airflow is probably too weak and unreliable.

title: Solid-state RF replaces magnetron and HV chain
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF module (Low-voltage transistor amplifier; no HV capacitor or diode.); Solid-state RF power amplification (GaN HEMT at 2.45 GHz with adaptive frequency for even heating.)
rationale: Even heating means no stirring or rotating instructions; power is set internally.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with adaptive frequency gives even heating and automatic power control, which is plausible and radical, though still costly.

title: Bleeder resistor replaced by self-discharging capacitor film
new_elements: Leaky-dielectric HV capacitor (Capacitor with engineered dielectric leakage self-discharges in seconds.)
rationale: Removes a part and a safety warning the user would otherwise need to read.
judge_comment: Internal component swap that the user never sees, so it does almost nothing for operational simplicity, and leaky HV capacitors are questionable.

title: Thermal fuse instead of snap-disc thermostat
new_elements: PTC self-limiting heater element in magnetron mount (PTC ceramic raises resistance when hot, throttling current without a switch.)
rationale: Overheat protection becomes invisible and automatic; no reset button for the user.
judge_comment: Invisible overheat protection removes a reset step, but it is tangential to learning-curve simplicity and a PTC can't realistically replace a safety thermostat on a magnetron.

title: Cavity floor as weight-sensing 'start' pad
new_elements: Pressure-mat cavity floor (Place a dish and close door: presence of weight plus closed door starts a default cycle.)
rationale: Putting food in is the instruction; no buttons at all.
judge_comment: Placing food and closing the door starts the oven with no buttons, which is a strong zero-learning concept, though a default cycle risks overheating or misfires and a weight mat must survive heat and spills.

title: Printed-label timer: stick-on NFC cards for favourite meals
new_elements: NFC reader in door frame (Tap a pre-printed card (soup, rice, tea) to load time and power.); Passive NFC tags (Sub-cent tags on cardboard cards shipped with the oven.)
rationale: Choosing a card is simpler than setting two knobs and never wrong.
judge_comment: Tapping a card is very simple and uses cheap, proven NFC, though cards can be lost and it is not radical.

title: Packaging barcode scanner sets cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Reads ready-meal barcode and applies manufacturer-specified time/power.)
rationale: Students heating ready meals never read instructions; the oven reads them instead.
judge_comment: The oven reads the package instructions, which removes user input for ready meals, but it depends on barcode-to-cooking-data coverage and works only for packaged food.

title: Thermochromic turntable shows heat distribution
new_elements: Thermochromic-coated glass turntable (Glass changes colour where hot, visible through the door.); Leuco-dye thermochromic glazing (Reversible colour-change coating stable to 150 °C.)
rationale: Users see when food is hot instead of interpreting timer numbers.
judge_comment: Visual heat feedback is intuitive, but food heats unevenly and the turntable is hidden under the food, so it doesn't replace the timer or the substitute logic much.

title: Mica cover replaced by self-cleaning PTFE panel
new_elements: PTFE waveguide cover (Non-stick, dishwasher-safe clip-in panel; no cleaning instructions needed.)
rationale: Eliminates the maintenance step and arcing confusion from soiled mica.
judge_comment: PTFE is a plausible low-loss cover, but it reduces maintenance rather than operation learning, so relevance to the need is weak.

title: Choke seal replaced by conductive elastomer gasket
new_elements: Conductive silicone RF gasket (Compressible metal-loaded silicone seals the door edge with no precision rim.)
rationale: Door tolerates careless slamming or crumbs, so no 'close firmly' lesson is needed.
judge_comment: Conductive gaskets are real RF-sealing tech and forgiving, but door closing is already trivial, so the benefit to the learning curve is marginal.

title: Arc detector auto-stops instead of warning labels
new_elements: Acoustic arc-detection cutoff (Microphone hears arc crackle and cuts magnetron, then beeps 'remove metal'.)
rationale: Users need not learn the metal rule; the oven forgives the mistake.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on arcing removes a real rule to learn, though acoustic detection in a noisy oven is tricky and it replaces a label with more electronics.

title: Built-in stirring stick for liquids
new_elements: Turntable-driven cup stirrer (Ceramic paddle dips into mug via lid and is spun by turntable gear, preventing superheating.)
rationale: Removes the superheating warning the user would otherwise have to remember.
judge_comment: It removes the superheating hazard by design, but a stirrer paddle in a mug is awkward, adds mechanical complexity, and fits only some containers.

title: Rough-surface turntable nucleates boiling
new_elements: Micro-etched boiling-chip turntable (Glass surface micro-pits act as nucleation sites for cups placed on it.)
rationale: Safety by material, not by user knowledge.
judge_comment: Clever safety idea against superheating, but it addresses a hazard rather than operational simplicity, and its effect on microwave heating is questionable.

title: Plug-timer: cord has the timer
new_elements: Inline mechanical cord timer (Timer dial lives on the plug; oven itself has no controls.)
rationale: A one-dial oven body with the control in a familiar plug-timer form.
judge_comment: Moving the timer onto the plug is a familiar, simple control, but it is awkward to reach and the oven would have no door-interlock or stop control.

title: Retractable cord reel replaces loose cord
new_elements: Spring cord reel (Vacuum-cleaner style reel inside base.)
rationale: Setup is plug-and-go with no cable management.
judge_comment: A cord reel is feasible but barely relates to operating the oven without learning.

title: Timer scale in food icons instead of minutes
new_elements: Icon-graduated clockwork dial (Dial marked with coffee cup, soup bowl, dinner plate at corresponding durations.)
rationale: Zero-cost substitution of numbers for meaning.
judge_comment: Food-icon dial removes the need to know times and is easy to build, though the substitution is not very radical.

title: Detent-free 'twist and release' spring timer
new_elements: Torsion-spring momentary timer (Twist knob against spring; duration equals twist angle, runs back in seconds-accurate escapement.)
rationale: Short durations become accurate without introducing digital controls.
judge_comment: A twist-to-set spring timer is intuitive and mechanically plausible, with a clear mechanism and accurate short durations.

title: Hold-to-heat deadman button
new_elements: Momentary heat button (Oven runs only while finger is pressed; release stops it.)
rationale: Perfect for 10-second reheats; the user is the timer.
judge_comment: A momentary-contact heat button is trivially understood and easy to build, though it is tiring for long cycles and hold-to-run controls already exist in other appliances.

title: Transparent cavity replaces lamp
new_elements: Fine-mesh glass cavity walls (Laminated mesh glass panels let ambient light in; no bulb.)
rationale: Always visible contents reduce the need to open and check.
judge_comment: Transparent walls would leak microwaves unless the mesh is a proper shield, and the idea only loosely relates to simple operation.

title: Door-mounted light pipe from room light
new_elements: Acrylic light pipe into cavity (Collects ambient light at top of door and spreads it inside; no bulb, no wiring.)
rationale: One less part to burn out and replace.
judge_comment: A passive light pipe is plausible and cheap, but it depends on room light and barely affects ease of operation.

title: Progress shown as a heating-up colour bar on the door
new_elements: Electroluminescent progress strip (Door strip fills from blue to red as cycle proceeds.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood at a glance, no numbers.
judge_comment: A numberless color progress bar is intuitive, though it adds an electroluminescent part instead of substituting a cheaper one.

title: Fixed 30-second cycles counted by presses
new_elements: Press-counting ratchet timer (Each press adds a fixed 30 s; ratchet advances a mechanical escapement.)
rationale: Counting presses is simpler than reading a dial.
judge_comment: A press-counting mechanical timer with fixed 30 s steps is simple, cheap and concrete, and it needs no learning.

title: Dish-type recognition camera sets power
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-device classifier (Recognises mug / plate / frozen block and picks a program.); Edge image classification (Tiny CNN on microcontroller.)
rationale: The oven decides so the user never has to.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting the food removes all user decisions, directly meeting zero-learning-curve, though accuracy and steam or lighting issues in the cavity are challenges.

title: Door window becomes a webcam view on phone
new_elements: Wi-Fi cavity webcam (Replaces lamp+mesh; cavity imaged by camera behind mica, streamed to phone.)
rationale: Checking from the sofa is simpler than peering through a mesh.
judge_comment: A phone webcam view adds complexity and an app, and doesn't simplify operation; heat and the mesh also pose camera challenges.

title: Turntable replaced by rotating antenna under ceramic floor
new_elements: Rotating feed antenna beneath flat floor (Flat-bed design: the antenna rotates, the food stays still.)
rationale: Square dishes fit; nothing rotates or jams for the user to fix.
judge_comment: Flat-bed designs with rotating stirrers already exist; this removes the turntable and helps usability modestly, but doesn't change the controls.

title: Combined timer-power single knob (push = power, turn = time)
new_elements: Push-turn single knob (Pushing cycles two power states shown by colour ring; turning sets time.)
rationale: Halves the controls while preserving mechanical familiarity.
judge_comment: A single knob does reduce controls and remains familiar, but it is incremental and the push-to-cycle power states add a small learning step.

title: Interlock switches replaced by a single sealed reed-switch module
new_elements: Triple-reed sealed interlock cartridge (Three reed switches in one potted block; no lever adjustment at assembly.)
rationale: Door never needs 'slam harder' to register; consistent, foolproof operation.
judge_comment: A more reliable door interlock fixes a real annoyance, but it is mostly an internal change with little effect on the learning curve.

title: Reusable snap-on 'cook card' overlay for the dial
new_elements: Interchangeable printed dial bezels (Bezels printed with meal names at correct positions; student swaps bezel for their diet.)
rationale: Personalised guidance with zero electronics.
judge_comment: Easy to produce, but it adds a swap step and only loosely substitutes a part; meal-specific dial positions are plausible but not very radical.

title: Door glass replaced by polymer with embedded mesh and printed tips
new_elements: Polycarbonate door with printed quick-guide (Cheaper than glass; instructions silk-screened directly on the window margin.)
rationale: Help is where the eyes already are; no manual.
judge_comment: Printed tips near the window are helpful, but polycarbonate is poor for heat and the door needs a metal mesh, and the idea is mostly cosmetic.

title: Grill-browning substitute: susceptor plate built into turntable
new_elements: Ferrite susceptor crisp plate (Turntable top layer absorbs microwaves and gets hot enough to brown.)
rationale: Crisping happens automatically with no extra mode to select.
judge_comment: Susceptor plates already exist and do remove the need for a separate browning mode, though the link to learning curve is modest.

title: Audio bell replaced by smell: vanilla scent puff at end
new_elements: Scent capsule triggered by timer release (Mechanical timer end also opens a scent vent.)
rationale: A playful, unmistakable done-signal needing no interpretation.
judge_comment: A scent cue is playful and replaces the bell, but it is less reliable than sound, and the scent may taint the food or fade.

title: Tilting cavity: door opens by tipping, not latching
new_elements: Drawer-style gravity-sealed cavity (Food sits in a pull-out drawer; the drawer face is the door, sealed by choke in drawer rim.)
rationale: Pull the drawer, drop in the mug: a motion everyone already uses in the kitchen.
judge_comment: The drawer's familiar motion is very intuitive, but the microwave choke seal and drawer design are hard, though microwave drawers do exist.

title: Shelf of fixed mug-shaped 'cups' instead of free cavity
new_elements: Dedicated mug well with embedded temp probe (A side-mounted well heats only beverages to exactly 65 °C.)
rationale: The most common student task becomes a single-purpose, zero-setting slot.
judge_comment: A single-purpose beverage well removes settings for a common task, but it adds a separate heating zone and the probe is hard to engineer in a microwave.

title: Capacitor and diode replaced by voltage-multiplier module with fault LED
new_elements: Potted HV doubler module with self-test LED (Single plug-in block; green LED when safely discharged.)
rationale: Removes servicing fear and simplifies assembly.
judge_comment: A plug-in HV module is plausible, but it serves servicing and assembly rather than user operation, so it barely addresses the need.

title: Bell replaced by door auto-pop
new_elements: Timer-released door spring (At zero, the clockwork trips the latch and the door cracks open a centimetre.)
rationale: Like a toaster popping up: the signal and the next action are the same thing.
judge_comment: A door that pops open when the timer ends is intuitive and replaces the bell, but it does nothing for the start or setup steps.

title: Toaster-lever start control
new_elements: Push-down lever with bimetal release (Push lever down to start; bimetal strip principle) releases it when exhaust air is hot.)
rationale: Borrows the one appliance interface nobody ever needed a manual for.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever is a familiar interface that simplifies starting, though the bimetal release on exhaust heat is unreliable for timing.

title: Chalkboard panel replaces printed control legend
new_elements: Writable matte front panel (User writes their own notes ('noodles = 3') next to the dial.)
rationale: Users teach the oven their own habits at zero cost.
judge_comment: A writable panel is cheap and personalizable, but it relies on the user to create the instructions and does not simplify the operation itself.

title: Mains cord with integral RCD and 'one green light' status
new_elements: RCD plug with single status LED (Protective plug replaces internal fuse holder; one light means 'ready'.)
rationale: All safety state reduced to one unambiguous indicator.
judge_comment: An RCD plug with a status LED is technically plausible and reasonably concrete, but it mostly addresses electrical safety rather than operating simplicity, so it barely reduces the learning curve, and it is not very radical.

title: Single 'Heat' lever
new_elements: Spring-loaded heat lever (One lever: push down to heat, lifts itself when done; replaces timer knob and power knob); One-gesture start (User performs a single intuitive action)
rationale: Replaces two knobs with one toaster-style lever anyone already knows how to use.
judge_comment: Toaster-style lever is highly intuitive and easy to build, but it isn't very radical and the cook duration and power setting remain unclear.

title: Door-as-timer
new_elements: Hinge-coupled clockwork (Closing door winds the timer; opening angle sets duration); Set time by closing door (Timer knob eliminated)
rationale: The only control is the door, which the user must touch anyway.
judge_comment: Setting the time by door angle is clever, but it's unintuitive because the closing angle doesn't map to a duration, and it conflicts with how doors actually close.

title: Weight-scale turntable timer
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable (Food weight compresses spring and mechanically sets cook duration); Auto time by mass (No time entry required)
rationale: Substitutes timer knob with a passive scale so the user just puts food in and presses go.
judge_comment: Auto time from weight is appealing, but weight is a poor proxy for cook time, and a mechanical spring-scale link through a rotating tray is hard to build.

title: Steam-cutoff switch
new_elements: Humidity bimetal switch (Vent-mounted bimetal strip opens the magnetron circuit when steam appears); Stop when hot (Replaces timer with physical doneness signal)
rationale: User never thinks about minutes; the oven stops itself when food steams.
judge_comment: Steam-triggered shutoff removes timing decisions and is plausible, similar to sensor cooking, though bimetal humidity sensing is unreliable and unsuited to foods that don't steam.

title: Thermochromic turntable
new_elements: Thermochromic glass tray (Tray changes colour at 70 C visible through door); Show doneness without display (Replaces lamp and bell cue)
rationale: Colour is universally readable with no instruction.
judge_comment: Color doneness cue is easy to read, but it only informs and doesn't control the oven, and a thermochromic tray in a microwave is questionable since the tray itself barely heats.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip sand timer with float switch (Flip hourglass to start; sand exhausting releases a switch); Visibly elapsing time (Time remaining is physically obvious)
rationale: Replaces graduated knob with a device humans have understood for centuries.
judge_comment: An intuitive hourglass with a float switch is easy to grasp, though it's coarse and fixed-duration, and the sand-based switch release is a bit fiddly.

title: Coin-slot cook tokens
new_elements: Token slot (Drop a 1-minute token; mechanical counter runs one minute per token); Count minutes by tokens (Discrete, tangible time units)
rationale: Vending-machine mental model requires zero learning.
judge_comment: Tokens are a tangible time metaphor, but losing or managing them adds friction and the mental model is not obviously better than a dial.

title: Pull-cord lawnmower start
new_elements: Pull-cord clockwork (Pulling cord length winds spring; longer pull = longer cook); Analog effort-to-time mapping (Bodily proportional control)
rationale: Replaces numbered knob with an intuitive 'pull more for more' gesture.
judge_comment: Pull-more-for-more is intuitive and a clockwork spring timer is plausible, though precision and the effort required of some users are concerns.

title: Fixed-dose button bank
new_elements: Three cam-timer buttons (Mug / Plate / Bowl buttons, each a fixed mechanical timer); Pick by vessel (No time or power reasoning)
rationale: Substitutes continuous knobs with three self-explanatory pictograms.
judge_comment: Vessel-based pictogram buttons remove time reasoning entirely and are easy to build, though they are less flexible and fairly conventional.

title: Rotate-the-whole-cabinet timer
new_elements: Rotating oven body on base (Twist oven on its base to wind timer; body turns back as it cooks); Oven is the knob (No small controls)
rationale: A giant single control with huge visual feedback is impossible to misuse.
judge_comment: A twisting oven body is wildly novel with huge feedback, but it is mechanically awkward with power cords, weight, and safety.

title: Hold-to-heat deadman button
new_elements: Momentary foot/hand switch (Microwave runs only while button is held); Cook while pressing (Timer eliminated entirely)
rationale: Direct cause-effect control like a tap; no settings exist.
judge_comment: A deadman switch removes all settings and is instantly understandable, but it is tedious for long heats and is more a removal than a substitution.

title: Food-contact thermal probe in tray
new_elements: Bimetal probe under tray centre (Tray transfers food temperature; bimetal trips at eating temp); Stop at eating temperature (No timing decision)
rationale: Replaces timer knob with passive physics so the user only loads and closes.
judge_comment: A passive bimetal probe is a clever substitute for the timer, but it is a poor fit for microwave fields, where metal arcs, and food-contact temperature is unreliable.

title: Wax-pellet cutoff
new_elements: Reusable wax thermostat cartridge (Wax expands at target temp and pushes the door interlock open); Thermal auto-stop (No electronics)
rationale: Cheaper than a clockwork and removes the need to understand minutes.
judge_comment: A wax thermostat is an inventive passive cutoff, but it is unclear how it senses food temperature, and a reusable cartridge adds complexity for the user.

title: Power knob replaced by shelf height
new_elements: Two-position wire rack (Lower rack = full power zone, upper = gentler field; power knob removed); Power by placement (Spatial instead of numeric)
rationale: Removes an abstract 5-step cam in favour of 'high or low shelf'.
judge_comment: Spatial power selection is intuitive in concept, but shelf height does not reliably change microwave power, and metal racks are hazardous.

title: Single-power magnetron, no power knob
new_elements: Fixed 500 W gentle magnetron (Lower constant output tuned to be forgiving for all foods); One power level fits all (Power selection eliminated)
rationale: Deleting the power cam removes the least-understood control.
judge_comment: A fixed power level is simple and highly feasible, but it is an obvious deletion and heats some foods poorly.

title: Tally-mark knob
new_elements: Knob with food icons instead of minutes (Dial positions labelled cup, soup, plate, pizza); Choose food not time (Icon-based duration)
rationale: Same clockwork, cheaper to understand by swapping numbers for pictures.
judge_comment: Icon-based dial directly removes the need to know cooking times and is easy to build, but similar presets already exist and the name 'tally-mark' does not match the idea.

title: Fully transparent cavity, no lamp
new_elements: Metal-mesh-laminated clear polycarbonate shell (Whole oven see-through, ambient light replaces 25 W bulb); Always see food (No light to switch or replace)
rationale: Removes bulb and perforated window; visual check requires no action.
judge_comment: A transparent mesh-laminated shell is bold, but it only loosely relates to simple operation, and microwave shielding, heat and cleaning make it hard to build.

title: Phosphorescent cavity paint
new_elements: Glow-in-dark cavity coating (Charged by room light, glows enough to see food; bulb removed); Passive interior illumination (Zero-power lighting)
rationale: Removes a component that can fail and never needs user attention.
judge_comment: Glow paint is a quirky substitution for the lamp, but the glow would be too dim to see food, and the paint must survive heat and food splatter.

title: Light pipe from room
new_elements: Acrylic light-pipe into cavity (Channels kitchen light into oven; replaces lamp); Borrowed illumination (No bulb, no switch)
rationale: One less thing to break or understand.
judge_comment: A light pipe from the room is a plausible idea, but it would give weak, inconsistent light and it barely changes how easy the oven is to operate.

title: Door-handle wind-up
new_elements: Ratchet handle timer (Pump the door handle like a bicycle pump; each pump adds 30 s); Pump to add time (Push-button and timer knob merged)
rationale: A single handle both opens the door and sets time by repetition.
judge_comment: Pumping the handle to add time is an intuitive, radical merge of the door and timer that needs no instructions, though precision, durability and the risk of accidental time input are concerns.

title: Egg-timer twist cap on door
new_elements: Large door-mounted twist bezel (The window frame itself rotates as the timer); Big obvious single dial (Control cannot be missed)
rationale: Replaces small side panel with one oversized control in the user's eyeline.
judge_comment: A big rotating door bezel as the timer is intuitive and visible, though a rotating window frame adds sealing and mechanical complexity.

title: Bell replaced by steam whistle
new_elements: Kettle-style vent whistle (Escaping steam sounds whistle when food is hot); Natural doneness alert (Alert tied to actual heat, not timer)
rationale: Everyone knows what a kettle whistle means.
judge_comment: A whistle is a familiar cue, but microwaves have no pressurized steam and it does nothing to simplify operation of the controls.

title: Self-opening door at end
new_elements: Spring-eject door latch on timer cam (Timer end pops door open; bell removed); Door opens means done (No sound to interpret, no button to press)
rationale: Removes push-release button and bell; outcome is self-evident.
judge_comment: A spring-eject door on timer end is a cheap, mechanical, self-evident done signal, though it still needs a way to set the time.

title: Tray pops out like a toaster
new_elements: Spring-lift turntable (Tray rises and food is presented at end of cycle); Food presents itself (Completion is physical)
rationale: Uses the universally understood toaster mental model.
judge_comment: The toaster pop-up metaphor is clear, but a lifting tray in a microwave is awkward and risks spills and hot dishes.

title: Door is a drawer
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Drawer replaces hinged door and push button; closing drawer starts default cycle); Push in to cook (One motion operation)
rationale: Removes door button and start step; drawer is intuitive.
judge_comment: A drawer with push-to-start is radical and very simple to use, but microwave leakage sealing and a default cycle make it challenging.

title: Fixed-time cartridge slot
new_elements: Keyed cardboard time cards (Food packaging includes a notched card; notch depth sets timer mechanically); Package sets the cook (User reads nothing)
rationale: Substitutes user's timing judgement with a mechanical punch-card.
judge_comment: Package-encoded cook time removes all decisions and is mechanically plausible, though it requires packaging ecosystem adoption and still needs a way to handle non-packaged food.

title: Gravity timer by tray tilt
new_elements: Tilting tray with ball-race timer (Tilt tray back to load; ball rolls slowly to trip stop); Load-and-forget (Loading gesture is the timing gesture)
rationale: No separate controls to learn.
judge_comment: Loading gesture doubling as timer is clever and intuitive, but the fixed ball-race time and tray tilt mechanism are hard to make accurate and flexible.

title: Rotary turntable crank as timer
new_elements: Hand-crank turntable spring (User cranks turntable a few turns; spring runs motor and timer together); Crank to cook (Turntable motor and timer merged)
rationale: One physical input replaces motor, timer and start.
judge_comment: A wind-up crank merging timer, motor and start mimics old mechanical timers, is cheap and intuitive, though cranking spring power for the magnetron is limited to timing.

title: Mug-only microwave
new_elements: Cup-shaped cavity with lid (Cavity fits one mug; lid closing starts fixed 90 s cycle); Single-purpose heating (No choices at all)
rationale: Radical scope reduction leaves nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug microwave with lid-start is simple and very buildable, but limits utility and is not especially radical.

title: Voice-free sound trigger
new_elements: Clap-start acoustic relay (Cheap sound relay starts fixed cycle on a clap); Touchless start (No panel)
rationale: Replaces timer and button with the simplest gesture known.
judge_comment: Clap start is easy to do but prone to false triggers, safety concerns, and is a common gimmick that still gives no control over time.

title: Proximity-start, walk-away-stop
new_elements: PIR presence relay (Runs only while someone stands in front; replaces timer and button); Presence-gated cooking (Attention equals operation)
rationale: Nothing to set; standing there is the instruction.
judge_comment: Presence-gated cooking removes all settings and is intuitive, though it is inconvenient to stand there and PIR sensors detect motion rather than presence.

title: Infrared doneness LED
new_elements: Cheap thermopile with single LED (Green LED when surface exceeds 65 C; replaces timer judgement); One-light status (Binary feedback)
rationale: Replaces reading a dial with a traffic-light colour.
judge_comment: A simple traffic-light cue is easy to understand, but surface infrared readings of food are unreliable and the user still has to start and stop the oven.

title: Bell replaced by scent release
new_elements: Wax scent pellet on timer cam (Timer end punctures a food-safe aroma pellet); Smell means ready (Non-verbal, non-visual cue)
rationale: Intuitive multisensory cue needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Scent is a novel cue, but it is a consumable that doesn't reduce operation steps and may taint food.

title: Timer knob replaced by countdown balloon
new_elements: Inflatable bladder timer (Squeeze bulb inflates bladder; slow leak deflates and releases switch); Squeeze to set time (Visibly shrinking time)
rationale: Remaining time is a physical size anyone can read.
judge_comment: A squeeze-bulb bladder timer is wild and visually intuitive, but it would be inaccurate and hard to make reliable and safe near microwaves.

title: Default cycle on door close
new_elements: Door-switch-triggered fixed 60 s cam (Closing door starts one minute; close again for another); Close equals start (Start button and timer removed)
rationale: Reduces operation to the one action already required.
judge_comment: A door-close fixed 60-second cycle is very simple and cheap to build, though it is inflexible for different foods.

title: Big single knob with haptic stops
new_elements: Oversized detented timer knob (Hard detents at 1, 2, 5 min only; power knob removed); Few obvious choices (Reduced decision space)
rationale: Same clockwork, far simpler by constraining positions.
judge_comment: A big detented knob with only a few fixed times removes decisions and is easy to build, though it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Dual-cavity instead of power knob
new_elements: Two cavities: Hot / Gentle (Each with fixed power; user picks the box); Choose a box, not a setting (Spatial substitution for cam)
rationale: Physical doors are more intuitive than numbered power steps.
judge_comment: Two cavities with fixed power levels is a bold spatial substitution, but it adds cost, size and complexity, which defeats the 'cheaper or simpler' goal.

title: Timer replaced by music box
new_elements: Wind-up music box drive (Tune plays while cooking; silence means done); Audible progress (Continuous intuitive status)
rationale: Replaces bell and numbered dial with a cue even children understand.
judge_comment: A wind-up music box timer gives an intuitive audible progress cue and is quirky and memorable, though it is hard to make accurate and silence as the done signal could be missed.

title: Shadow sundial timer
new_elements: Rotating pointer casting shadow on door (Timer drives a large pointer; visible progress replaces small dial); Glanceable remaining time (Readable across the room)
rationale: Same cheap clockwork, much easier to read.
judge_comment: A large pointer whose shadow shows remaining time is readable from across the room, but it helps with reading time more than with operating the oven, and shadow visibility is questionable.

title: Interlock replaced by magnetic door
new_elements: Magnetic catch with reed switch (No push button; pull to open, push to shut); Fridge-like door (Familiar mental model)
rationale: Removes a button that confuses first-time users.
judge_comment: A magnetic fridge-style door catch uses a familiar mental model and removes a button, but safety interlock requirements add complexity and the idea is not very radical.

title: Food-shaped buttons
new_elements: Moulded 3D icon buttons (A mug-shaped and plate-shaped button each triggers a fixed cam); Tactile iconography (Usable by eye or touch)
rationale: No numbers, no reading, no language.
judge_comment: Tactile, language-free icon buttons simplify operation, but the mechanical cam mapping to fixed programs is vague and the idea is only moderately radical.

title: Turntable replaced by rocking tray
new_elements: Spring-rocked tray driven by fan airflow (No motor; even heating still achieved; fewer parts to misplace); Motorless even heating (Simpler to clean and reassemble)
rationale: Removes ring-and-coupler assembly users often reinstall wrong.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable helps cleaning and reassembly, but a fan-driven rocking tray is dubious for even heating and touches the operation need only indirectly.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Fan-driven waveguide stirrer (Flat fixed floor; no turntable parts); Flat floor cavity (Nothing to remove or align)
rationale: Eliminates a component that creates confusion and breakage.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves and are very feasible, but this is not radical and has little effect on operating simplicity.

title: Timer replaced by candle-style burn strip
new_elements: Replaceable fusible time strip (Heat from magnetron slowly melts a strip holding the relay closed); Disposable self-timing (No mechanism to wind)
rationale: Tear off a strip and go; cheap and wordless.
judge_comment: A wordless, tear-off timing strip is wild, but melting a strip with magnetron heat is imprecise and unsafe, and consumables are a hassle.

title: Thermal-image window
new_elements: Low-res thermal sensor to LED matrix on door (Shows hot/cold spots as colours; replaces lamp); See heat, not light (Doneness obvious at a glance)
rationale: User judges readiness directly, no timing skill required.
judge_comment: Showing doneness as a thermal image removes the need for timing skill and is novel, though a low-res sensor behind a door and reading colours has limits.

title: Lid-on-top kettle microwave
new_elements: Top-loading cavity with lift lid (Replaces door, button and interlock complexity with a pot-lid); Pot-like loading (Cookware-familiar form)
rationale: Borrows the saucepan mental model everybody already has.
judge_comment: A familiar pot-lid mental model helps, but a top-loading microwave still needs a safe interlock and some way to set time, and leakage and spill risks are significant.

title: Pressure-mat start
new_elements: Floor pressure mat switch (Placing food on tray closes a switch and starts fixed cycle); Load to start (No buttons at all)
rationale: Operation is implicit in placing food.
judge_comment: Starting on placement is very simple, but a fixed cycle suits few foods and risks accidental starts, so it needs a weight sensor and a fixed or auto-detected cycle.

title: Power knob replaced by pulse pedal
new_elements: Foot pedal duty-cycle (Tap pedal rhythmically to pulse heating; hands free); Bodily duty cycle (Intuitive intensity control)
rationale: Like a sewing machine: more tapping, more heat, no abstraction.
judge_comment: A pedal is novel and easy to build as a switch, but holding a pedal for long cooking is tedious and it does not match how people use microwaves.

title: Printed instructions replaced by embossed arrow
new_elements: Single embossed arrow on knob and door (Only affordance cue is a direction arrow; all labels removed); Instruction-free affordance (Zero reading)
rationale: Substitutes labelling with shape, cheaper and universal.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build, but removing all labels makes it ambiguous, and a single arrow cannot convey time or power.

title: Timer by stacked rings
new_elements: Stackable minute rings on a post (Each ring is one minute; stack height depresses a cam timer); Physical minute counting (Tangible, countable units)
rationale: Counting rings is simpler than reading a graduated dial.
judge_comment: Physical minute rings are intuitive and countable, with a clear mechanism, though the rings can be lost and long cook times need many of them.

title: Done-cue via door frost
new_elements: Thermochromic door film (Door window turns from clear to tinted as cavity air heats; lamp removed); Window shows progress (Ambient status indicator)
rationale: Replaces lamp and bell with a passive, obvious visual change.
judge_comment: A passive thermochromic door film is an inventive swap for the lamp and bell, but it only signals status and does nothing to simplify operation (setting time/power). It is also questionable technically, since cavity air temperature is a poor proxy for food doneness, the door gets hot, and removing the lamp makes the food hard to see.

title: One-Button Microwave
new_elements: Single large start/stop button (Press once to run at full power until pressed again or auto-stop; no timer, no power level.)
rationale: Reduces the whole interface to one obvious action, eliminating any learning curve.
judge_comment: Very simple, but full power until stopped risks overcooking and food-dependent results, and it's more a removal than a radical substitution.

title: Doneness Dial
new_elements: Single 'cold-to-hot' doneness dial (One knob with snowflake-to-steam icons that internally maps to combined time and duty cycle.)
rationale: Users think in 'how hot', not minutes and watts, so one intuitive dial replaces two abstract ones.
judge_comment: An intuitive single dial is easy to build and understand, though users still guess at the setting for different foods.

title: Weighing Turntable Sets Time
new_elements: Load-cell weight sensing (Strain gauge under the floor measures food mass and computes heating duration.); Weighing cooking floor (Replaces timer input: the heavier the food, the longer it runs.)
rationale: The user never sets a time; placing food is the only input.
judge_comment: Weight-driven time removes the timer input, but weight alone poorly predicts heating needs for different foods and starting temperatures.

title: Infrared Target-Temperature Stop
new_elements: Non-contact IR thermopile sensing (Thermopile reads food surface temperature through a small waveguide-filtered port.); IR food thermometer auto-stop (Runs until food reaches 'eat' temperature, then stops.)
rationale: Replaces guessed minutes with a closed loop so there is nothing to learn or get wrong.
judge_comment: Closed-loop temperature stopping gives the right result with no input, though IR reads only surface temperature and the port must be shielded from microwaves.

title: Steam-Sniffing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent (Detects the steam burst that signals food is hot and ends the cycle.)
rationale: A cheap sensor replaces the timer so users just press go and the oven knows when to stop.
judge_comment: Steam-sensing auto-stop is cheap and already exists in sensor cooking, giving press-and-go use, but it's unreliable for covered or dry foods.

title: Voice-Set Microwave
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognition (Low-cost MCU recognises 'heat', 'defrost', 'two minutes'.); Microphone control input (Replaces knobs and fascia with spoken commands.)
rationale: Speaking plain language needs no instruction and also serves visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Offline voice commands remove the learning curve and help accessibility, though noisy kitchens and accents can cause errors, and the idea is not radical.

title: Mug Slot Microwave
new_elements: Mug-shaped cavity insert with drop-in start (A cup-sized recess; inserting a mug triggers a fixed hot-drink cycle automatically.)
rationale: The physical shape of the appliance communicates how to use it; no controls at all.
judge_comment: A shape-driven, controlless hot-drink cycle is intuitive and bold, but it is limited to one use case and needs reliable mug detection.

title: Three Pictogram Buttons
new_elements: Three preset icon buttons (Drink / Plate / Defrost) (Each button encodes a fixed time-and-power recipe shown as a picture.)
rationale: Pictures of outcomes replace abstract numbers, so anyone can operate it at first glance.
judge_comment: Three icon presets are very easy to use and cheap to build, but they are a common simplification and fix the recipes.

title: Inverter Replaces Power Knob
new_elements: Switch-mode inverter magnetron drive (High-frequency HV supply delivers continuously variable true power without on/off cycling.); Inverter power module (Replaces transformer, capacitor, diode and duty-cycle cam with a single board.)
rationale: Power becomes an invisible automatic ramp so the user never has to understand 'power levels'.
judge_comment: Inverter drives already exist and mainly improve cooking quality, so the link to zero learning curve is indirect, even though the part swap is concrete.

title: Fridge-Style Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic gasket door with pull handle (No push button or latch lever; just pull to open like a refrigerator.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to open a fridge, so the door needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A fridge-style pull door is familiar and easy to build, but it only affects opening and leaves the rest of the operation untouched.

title: Drawer Microwave Auto-Start
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity with close-to-start switch (Food goes in a drawer; pushing it shut starts a default cycle, pulling it open stops.)
rationale: Opening and closing a drawer is the entire interaction model.
judge_comment: Drawer close-to-start is intuitive and zero-learning, though drawer microwaves exist and a default cycle may not fit every food or risk running when closed on empty.

title: Roller-Shutter Door
new_elements: Conductive tambour roller shutter (Interlinked metal slats roll up into the top; no swing clearance, no hinges, no latch.)
rationale: A one-motion roll-up front is simpler to use in tight kitchens and has fewer parts.
judge_comment: A conductive roller shutter is novel and concrete, but RF sealing around slats is very hard and the usability gain is marginal.

title: Door Is the Start Button
new_elements: Door-close triggered run cycle (Closing the door begins heating; opening it ends the cycle; no separate start control.)
rationale: Removes the concept of 'starting' entirely; the door already does it.
judge_comment: Removing the start button is intuitive, but a default run time is undefined and accidental starts are a concern; it is also a close cousin of idea 1.

title: LED Cavity Lighting
new_elements: High-temperature SMD LED module (Low-power solid-state light rated for cavity heat, lifetime exceeds appliance life.)
rationale: No bulb ever needs replacing, so there is nothing to learn about maintenance.
judge_comment: Highly feasible but already common and barely related to operational simplicity.

title: Daylight Light-Pipe
new_elements: Acrylic light pipe from top surface into cavity (Pipes ambient kitchen light through a choke-protected opening; no lamp at all.)
rationale: Zero-electronics lighting that always works and never confuses the user.
judge_comment: Clever zero-electronics idea but a light pipe would give poor illumination and has little bearing on ease of operation.

title: Spoken 'Ready' Announcement
new_elements: Tiny speech chip saying 'Your food is ready' (Replaces the bell with a plain-language spoken cue.)
rationale: Unambiguous feedback that needs no interpretation of beeps or dings.
judge_comment: Spoken cue is clear and cheap, but talking appliances already exist and it only addresses end-of-cycle feedback, not operation.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: Spring-ejected door at end of cycle (The timer cam releases the latch so the door swings ajar, signalling completion visually and venting steam.)
rationale: Like a toaster popping up, the signal is physical and self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A toaster-like pop-open door is intuitive and physical, though a door springing open raises safety and steam-burn concerns and needs a reliable latch release.

title: Phone Push Notification Instead of Bell
new_elements: Low-cost BLE beacon end-of-cycle notifier (Broadcasts a 'done' event to a paired phone; no bell hardware.)
rationale: Notification arrives in the channel people already know how to read.
judge_comment: Requires pairing a phone, which adds learning burden and runs against the no-learning-curve need.

title: Thermochromic 'Hot' Window
new_elements: Thermochromic pigment film (Film on the door window turns red when the cavity is hot and fades when safe to touch.)
rationale: A colour everyone understands replaces a sound, with no need to learn what the signal means.
judge_comment: An intuitive hot/safe color cue, but thermochromic film near a microwave cavity has durability limits and it doesn't simplify operating.

title: Mode Stirrer Replaces Turntable
new_elements: Fan-driven metal mode stirrer in ceiling (Rotating reflector blades scramble the standing-wave pattern; flat fixed floor, nothing to align or wash.)
rationale: No tray to seat on rollers or re-fit after cleaning means one less thing to get wrong.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common in microwaves, and removing the turntable only marginally eases use, but the mechanism is concrete and feasible.

title: Seamless Molded Ceramic Cavity
new_elements: Metallised one-piece ceramic cavity liner (Smooth cornerless cavity with reflective metallised exterior; no seams to trap food.)
rationale: Cleaning becomes a single wipe with no instructions on seams, rollers or covers.
judge_comment: Easier cleaning is only tangentially related to operation with no learning curve, and a metallised ceramic cavity is costly and awkward to make.

title: Handle Is the Only Control
new_elements: Push-to-run door handle (No fascia: pushing the handle inward runs heating while pushed-in; pulling it stops and opens.)
rationale: The only part you touch is the handle, so there is no control panel to learn.
judge_comment: Push-to-run with the handle eliminates the control panel, but it has no way to set time or power and the door-interlock mechanics are awkward.

title: Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: Spring-driven escapement kitchen timer (Mainspring and escapement replace the synchronous motor; works on any mains frequency or none.)
rationale: Same familiar twist-knob feel as an egg timer, cheaper and region-independent.
judge_comment: Wind-up mechanical timers are already common on microwaves and are intuitive, so this is feasible but not very radical.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down lever with pop-up release (Push the lever down to start a fixed cycle; it pops up with a clack when finished.)
rationale: Borrows the universally understood toaster gesture for both start and finish.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever metaphor is instantly understood and easy to build, though a fixed cycle limits flexibility.

title: Tagged Containers Program the Oven
new_elements: Passive NFC tag reading (Reader in the floor reads a tag moulded into the bowl or mug that encodes its heating recipe.); NFC recipe reader (Replaces both knobs: the container sets time and power.)
rationale: The dish itself tells the oven what to do, so the user makes no decisions.
judge_comment: Containers that carry NFC tags and set the program remove all decisions, but tags must survive microwave fields and the user needs tagged dishes.

title: Camera Food Recognition
new_elements: Embedded image classification (Small camera and on-device model identify food type and portion to select time and power.); Cavity camera module (Replaces knobs and lamp; also streams a view to the front display.)
rationale: Put food in, press start; the oven figures out the rest.
judge_comment: Directly removes all user decisions via food recognition, though accuracy, cost and the SUBSTITUTE framing (camera replacing knobs) are moderate concerns.

title: Weight + IR 'Just Start' Sensor Pack
new_elements: Combined mass and temperature sensing controller (Weight estimates energy needed; IR confirms endpoint; single start button.)
rationale: Two cheap sensors remove every user decision except 'go'.
judge_comment: Cheap, plausible sensors enable one-button operation, though they are less able to identify food type and are somewhat incremental.

title: Low-Voltage Solid-State Magnetron Replacement
new_elements: LDMOS/GaN RF power amplifier (Runs from ~50 V DC; no lethal capacitor, no filament wear, instant on.)
rationale: Instant, continuously controlled heat with no warm-up quirks the user must learn around.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a genuine radical substitution, but it is expensive today and only loosely tied to learning-free operation.

title: Switch-Mode HV Supply
new_elements: Compact flyback HV power supply (Universal-input SMPS replaces the heavy transformer, doubler cap and diode; same board for all regions.)
rationale: Lighter, one-model-worldwide oven with smoother power behaviour the user never notices.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies already exist and the user benefit is invisible, so it barely serves the simplicity need.

title: Fanless Heat-Pipe Cooling
new_elements: Heat-pipe to rear finned heatsink (Passive conduction cooling of the magnetron; no fan, no noise, no louvres to block.)
rationale: Silent operation removes the confusing 'why is it still running' fan noise after the cycle.
judge_comment: Passive cooling is hard to make work for a magnetron, and its link to ease of operation is tenuous.

title: PTC Polymer Thermal Protection
new_elements: Self-resetting PTC thermistor limiters (Polymer PTC devices replace bimetal snap discs; reset automatically without user action.)
rationale: Overheat recovery is invisible and automatic, so the user never meets a fault state.
judge_comment: Auto-resetting thermal protection is plausible and removes a rare fault state, but it barely touches everyday operation and isn't radical.

title: Transparent Conductive Film Window
new_elements: ITO / silver-nanowire shielding film on glass (Transparent conductive coating blocks 2.45 GHz without a perforated mesh.)
rationale: A clear window shows exactly what is happening without peering through a grid.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive films are real and give a clearer window, but the microwave-shielding attenuation and durability are challenging, and the learning-curve benefit is marginal.

title: Top-Loading Pot Microwave
new_elements: Lift-off metal lid with choke rim (Cavity is a deep well; a lid like a saucepan lid closes it and carries the λ/4 choke.)
rationale: Using it is as familiar as putting a lid on a pot.
judge_comment: A radical top-loading pot form with familiar lid use is intuitive, but the lid choke, leakage and safety interlock make it hard to realize.

title: Silicone Mat Instead of Glass Tray
new_elements: Removable silicone cooking mat (Unbreakable, dishwasher-safe mat on a fixed floor; nothing to align.)
rationale: Drop-in mat removes the fiddly tray-on-rollers assembly users often get wrong.
judge_comment: Removes tray alignment confusion, but silicone mats limit turntable-free heating evenness and arcing/heating behaviour need checking.

title: Tap-Count Minute Button
new_elements: '+1 minute' tap button with click feedback (Each tap adds a minute and starts immediately; one input, one rule.)
rationale: A single rule ('tap = a minute') is learned instantly and fixes short-duration imprecision.
judge_comment: A one-button, one-rule input is learned instantly and simple to build, though many microwaves already offer a similar +30s/quick start.

title: Lamp and Fan Off as the Only 'Done' Signal
new_elements: Silent completion cue via light and sound ceasing (End of cycle is indicated by the cavity going dark and quiet; bell deleted.)
rationale: The state change itself is the feedback; nothing extra to understand, nothing extra to pay for.
judge_comment: Removing the bell is cheap, but a silent completion cue is less clear than a beep and could make operation less obvious, and it is not radical.

title: Tactile Large-Icon Knob
new_elements: Oversized knob with raised pictograms and detents (Embossed cup/plate/snowflake symbols and firm clicks readable by touch alone.)
rationale: Settings are felt and seen as pictures, so elderly and visually impaired users need no instructions.
judge_comment: Tactile pictogram knobs are very feasible and clearly lower the learning curve, but similar designs already exist.

title: Three Dish-Size Buttons
new_elements: Mug / Bowl / Plate buttons (Each button is shaped like the container it serves and launches a tuned cycle.)
rationale: Matching a button to the dish in your hand requires zero thought.
judge_comment: Container-matched buttons map intuitively to the task and are easy to build, though the tuned cycles for each size are underspecified.

title: Electroluminescent Cavity Wall
new_elements: Electroluminescent phosphor panel behind cavity window (Thin, cool, shock-proof glow panel replaces the hot incandescent bulb.)
rationale: A lifetime glow source means users never encounter a dark, confusing cavity.
judge_comment: An electroluminescent panel swaps the lamp, but it barely affects operation simplicity and would be too dim and hard to mount in a microwave cavity.

title: Gravity-Close Latchless Door
new_elements: Top-hinged drop door with weighted self-close (Door falls shut under its own weight onto the choke seal; no latch, no button.)
rationale: You can never leave it half-latched; let go and it is closed.
judge_comment: A self-closing door removes the half-latched error, but a top-hinged drop door is awkward to use and the safety interlock and seal are problematic.

title: QR-Scan Packaging Programs Cycle
new_elements: Front barcode scanner window (Hold the ready-meal pack to the scanner; printed heating instructions become the program.)
rationale: Nobody has to read or translate the box instructions into knob positions.
