judge_comment: Scanning the pack removes the need to read or translate instructions, and the barcode and scanner technology exists, though it depends on packaging standards and does not cover non-packaged food.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord duration setter (Pull a cord out; its length is the cooking time and it slowly reels back in, stopping the oven at zero.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible as cord length, an analogue cue anyone grasps instantly.
judge_comment: A retracting cord gives an intuitive analogue timer that shows the remaining time, and it is mechanically simple, but it is imprecise and long times need a long cord.

title: Fan-Air-Driven Turntable
new_elements: Air turbine turntable drive from cooling fan exhaust (Cooling airflow spins a small turbine coupled to the tray; no separate motor or wiring.)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail means fewer confusing 'tray not turning' situations for the user.
judge_comment: A clever part substitution that cuts the motor, but the user never sees it, so it barely helps ease of use, and the airflow may not give reliable torque.

title: Drink-Boil Detector
new_elements: Acoustic boil-onset microphone stop (Listens for the pre-boil hiss of a liquid and stops before superheating; preset for hot drinks.)
rationale: Heating milk becomes a single press with no timing judgement and less eruption risk.
judge_comment: A one-press drink mode is easy to use, but detecting pre-boil sounds in a noisy microwave is unreliable and it serves only a narrow use case.

title: Foot-Pedal Start
new_elements: Hands-free foot pedal run switch (Hold the pedal to heat, release to stop; the whole fascia is deleted.)
rationale: A dead-man pedal is the simplest possible control: press to run, let go to stop.
judge_comment: A hold-to-run pedal is radical and has no learning curve, but holding it through a multi-minute cook is tiring, and it gives no power control and raises safety and regulatory problems.

title: Smart-Speaker Completion Alert
new_elements: Wi-Fi 'done' event to household smart speaker (Oven sends a completion message to Alexa/Google which announces it anywhere in the home.)
rationale: The ready signal reaches the user wherever they are, in plain speech.
judge_comment: Technically easy, and a few connected microwaves already do this, but it only adds a completion alert. It needs Wi-Fi setup, which adds learning, and it does not simplify operation or substitute a part with something simpler, so it fits neither the brief nor the radical ask.

title: One-tap +30s button
new_elements: Single large 'Heat' button (each press adds 30 s, auto-start) (Momentary switch and cheap RC/one-chip counter replace the cam timer.)
rationale: One button, one action, nothing to read—anyone can operate it instantly.
judge_comment: Very simple and workable, but +30s buttons already exist on many microwaves, so it's not radical.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand hourglass with tilt switch (Flipping the glass closes a switch; when sand runs out a float drops and opens it.)
rationale: Everyone already understands an hourglass; no numbers or dials to learn.
judge_comment: Charming and intuitive, but a sand-timer-driven float switch is imprecise, fragile, and awkward for varying cook times.

title: Doneness slider
new_elements: Single 'cold→hot' linear slider (One potentiometer maps to a combined time×power profile.)
rationale: Collapses two controls into one intuitive 'how hot do you want it' gesture.
judge_comment: Intuitive single-control gesture and easy to build, but the mapping to food types is vague and the result is unpredictable.

title: Weigh-to-cook turntable
new_elements: Load cell under turntable auto-setting duration (Food mass sets heating time by a fixed J/g rule; no user input.)
rationale: User just puts food in and closes the door—zero settings.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is ideal for the need, but mass alone poorly predicts heating needs and a load cell adds cost and complexity.

title: IR thermometer stop
new_elements: Thermopile IR surface-temperature sensing (Sensor in cavity roof stops magnetron when food reaches a target temperature.); Three-icon 'warm / hot / boiling' selector (Replaces minutes with a target temperature.)
rationale: Users think in 'hot enough', not minutes—removes guesswork.
judge_comment: Targeting temperature matches how people think, but IR only reads surface temperature and the sensor is not cheaper, so it's not really a substitution.

title: Steam-stop sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent, stops on steam burst (Cheap capacitive humidity sensor replaces timing logic.)
rationale: Press start and walk away; the oven decides when it's done.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on steam is plausible (some ovens already have humidity sensors) and removes the need to set a time, but it doesn't suit foods that don't steam, such as drinks, and it is not very radical.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognition (Low-cost MCU recognises 'heat', 'defrost', 'stop'.); Microphone replacing both knobs (No front-panel controls at all.)
rationale: Speaking is the most natural interface, ideal for elderly or visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Voice control is natural for some users, but it's noisy and error-prone, it has no way to specify a duration, and it needs the user to learn the commands, so it isn't a cheap substitute.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Wind-up pull cord (pull length = cooking time) (Toy-style string spring motor drives the cam shaft.)
rationale: Pulling a cord is a universal, self-explanatory gesture.
judge_comment: A wind-up pull cord is a quirky, intuitive mechanical substitute for the timer, but it is awkward and imprecise for longer times and is not obviously cheaper.

title: Food-icon dial
new_elements: Dial with pictograms (cup, plate, pizza, frozen) instead of minutes (Each detent selects a fixed time/power preset.)
rationale: Removes the need to know how many minutes anything takes.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is simple, cheap and easy to build and does cut learning, but it already exists on some products and is not radical.

title: Package barcode reader
new_elements: Barcode/NFC scanner in door frame reads package heating instructions (Cooking program comes from the product label.)
rationale: Scan and go—no reading of instructions or setting of controls.
judge_comment: Scanning package instructions is clever and effortless, but it depends on a database and on label support, and it adds cost and fails on unlabelled food and leftovers.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: On-device image classification (Tiny neural net recognises food type and portion.); Cavity camera replacing the timer (Auto-selects program on door close.)
rationale: The oven does the thinking; the user does nothing but close the door.
judge_comment: Zero-interaction operation fits the need perfectly, but food recognition and heating accuracy are hard, and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: No power knob at all
new_elements: Fixed full-power operation (knob deleted) (Removes cam switch; defrost handled by longer time at intermittent magnetron via timer cam.)
rationale: Fewer controls means literally nothing to learn and lower BOM.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob simplifies things and is feasible, but full power only hurts results for delicate foods and the intermittent defrost is vaguely defined.

title: Inverter gentle/fast rocker
new_elements: Inverter continuous power control (Switch-mode HV supply varies magnetron output continuously.); Two-position 'gentle / fast' rocker switch (Replaces 5-step cam.)
rationale: Binary choice in plain words is instantly understood.
judge_comment: A plain-language two-way switch backed by an inverter is easy to understand and plausible, though the inverter is not cheaper.

title: Defrost/cook slide
new_elements: Two-position slide switch 'defrost / cook' (Single cam position swap, cheaper than 5-step.)
rationale: Reduces a five-way decision to the only two most people ever use.
judge_comment: A simple and cheap switch that is easy to use, but it is an incremental change with little novelty.

title: Gravity pendulum timer
new_elements: Weighted swing arm timer (lift arm, it falls slowly via dashpot) (Oil dashpot sets rate; arm position shows remaining time.)
rationale: Visual, tactile, mains-frequency-independent and obvious to use.
judge_comment: A tactile pendulum timer that shows remaining time is intuitive and wildly different, but dashpot accuracy and temperature sensitivity are practical concerns.

title: Foot pedal door
new_elements: Foot pedal door release (Bowden cable to latch lever like a pedal bin.)
rationale: Hands-full opening with a gesture everyone knows from pedal bins.
judge_comment: Pedal-bin gesture is familiar and the Bowden cable is plausible, but it only addresses door opening, not the real learning curve of operating the controls, and it is awkward on a countertop unit.

title: Magnetic pull door
new_elements: Magnet-held door with handle and reed-switch interlock (No latch, no button; just pull.)
rationale: Works like a fridge door—zero instruction needed.
judge_comment: Pull-to-open is highly intuitive, but magnetic retention must withstand safety and leakage requirements, and it only simplifies the door, not the controls.

title: Roll-top tambour door
new_elements: Metal tambour roll-top door with conductive slats (Slides up into the housing; no swing clearance, no hinges.)
rationale: Push up to open, pull down to close—intuitive and space-saving.
judge_comment: A tambour door is novel and space-saving, but conductive slats create RF leakage, sealing, and cleaning problems that make it very hard to build.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity with choke seal (The whole cavity floor slides out like a kitchen drawer.)
rationale: Drawers are universally understood and let elderly users load from above.
judge_comment: A drawer microwave is a known concept with easy loading, but the choke seal and spill handling are challenging, and it still leaves the controls unaddressed.

title: Auto-open at end
new_elements: Solenoid auto-pop door at end of cycle (Replaces bell: the open door is the signal.)
rationale: Done means open; no bell to interpret, no button to find.
judge_comment: Auto-opening the door at cycle end replaces the bell with an obvious signal and removes a step, which is simple and feasible, though a popping hot door raises some safety and annoyance concerns.

title: Top-loading toaster style
new_elements: Top lid with spring-loaded lift platform (Food sits on a platform that rises when done, like a toaster.)
rationale: Borrows a mental model everyone already has from toasters.
judge_comment: The toaster mental model is intuitive, but a spring-lift platform for liquids and plates is awkward and the mechanism and shielding at the top opening are unresolved.

title: Wave-to-open sensor
new_elements: Capacitive/IR proximity sensor triggering latch solenoid (Wave a hand in front of the door to open.)
rationale: No button to locate or press force needed—good for arthritic hands.
judge_comment: It is feasible and easy to use for opening, but it only removes one step and does not simplify setting power or time.

title: Conveyor tunnel, no door
new_elements: Waveguide-below-cutoff entry tunnels (Long narrow tunnels attenuate leakage without any door.); Pass-through belt tunnel oven (Food goes in one side, comes out heated the other.)
rationale: Place plate on belt and it comes out hot—no door, no knobs.
judge_comment: A door-free belt tunnel is radical and the cutoff-waveguide principle is real, but it is bulky, costly and hard to control for heating consistency in a home oven.

title: One-lever open-and-start
new_elements: Big lever: pull to open door, push to close and start fixed cycle (Lever stroke winds a fixed 1-min spring timer.)
rationale: Whole interaction is one physical motion.
judge_comment: A single lever motion that opens, closes and starts a spring timer is very simple and mechanically plausible, though the fixed time limits flexibility.

title: Transparent conductive glass door
new_elements: ITO / metal-mesh-on-glass transparent shielding (Conductive coating gives Faraday shielding with clear view.)
rationale: Clear view lets users judge doneness by eye without learning timings.
judge_comment: Shielded transparent glass is feasible and mildly helpful for judging doneness, but it is close to existing mesh doors and only tangentially serves operation simplicity.

title: Thermochromic door panel
new_elements: Thermochromic strip on door showing cavity/food heat colour (Blue→red colour change replaces readouts.)
rationale: Colour is a universal, language-free indicator of 'hot'.
judge_comment: Colour shows heat but doesn't help operate the microwave, and a door strip can't truly show food temperature, so it only addresses feedback.

title: Knock-to-set
new_elements: Piezo knock sensor on cabinet (each knock = 30 s) (No knobs; knock the top to add time.)
rationale: Playful, discoverable, and needs no panel at all.
judge_comment: Knocking to add time is playful and radical, but it is not obviously discoverable, and there is no way to cancel or confirm.

title: Dedicated cup slot
new_elements: Cup-shaped docking recess with limit switch auto-starting a mug program (Drop in a mug; it heats to drinking temp.)
rationale: Form dictates function—the slot only fits one thing and does one thing.
judge_comment: A drop-in slot with a limit switch is simple and zero-learning, but it covers only mugs and not general use.

title: Plate-size detection
new_elements: Optical plate-diameter sensor setting time (Bigger plate = longer heat, no input needed.)
rationale: Removes the time decision for the most common use case.
judge_comment: Removing the time decision is a strong fit for the need, but plate diameter says little about food type or quantity, so the heating would be unreliable.

title: Big-number egg timer
new_elements: Oversized wind-up kitchen-timer knob with 3 cm tactile digits (Same cam tech, redesigned for legibility and grip.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar knob but makes it readable and grippable for elderly users.
judge_comment: A familiar mechanical timer knob has no learning curve and is highly feasible, but it is barely novel and is close to existing designs.

title: Colour-band dial
new_elements: Timer dial with green/yellow/red bands instead of numbers (Short/medium/long encoded as colour.)
rationale: Eliminates numeracy and language from the interface.
judge_comment: Removes numbers, but colour bands are vague about actual times and may reduce precision and be a problem for colour-blind users.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Hold-down 'heat while pressed' palm button (Magnetron runs only while the button is held; release to stop.)
rationale: Direct cause-and-effect control with no timing abstraction.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive with direct cause and effect, though holding for minutes is tiring and safety interlock details are missing.

title: Swipe-length touch strip
new_elements: Capacitive strip—swipe length sets minutes, LEDs count down (No moving parts.)
rationale: Longer swipe = longer cook is self-explanatory and precise for short times.
judge_comment: A swipe-length strip with LED countdown is intuitive and plausible, though capacitive strips can be affected by wet or greasy hands.

title: Food-shaped preset buttons
new_elements: Four physical buttons moulded as mug, plate, pizza slice, snowflake (Shape tells function; each triggers a fixed program.)
rationale: Tactile icons are usable without sight or language.
judge_comment: Shaped presets are easy to use and accessible, but fixed programs limit flexibility and food-type results are uncertain.

title: 30-s detent dial
new_elements: Detented timer dial with 30-s clicks up to 5 min, coarse beyond (Non-linear cam profile.)
rationale: Clicks give haptic certainty for the short times people actually use.
judge_comment: A detented dial with 30-second steps gives clear haptic feedback and is very practical, but is an incremental refinement of existing dials.

title: Light signal instead of bell
new_elements: Flashing cavity lamp at end of cycle replacing bell (Reuses existing lamp; no bell striker.)
rationale: Visible-from-across-room 'done' signal, fewer parts.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap, but it only changes the done signal and does little for operation or learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Rotating drum door
new_elements: Rotating cylindrical cavity with open sector that turns to face user (Spin the drum to load; spin back to seal.)
rationale: One rotary motion replaces door, button and latch.
judge_comment: A single rotary motion is intuitive, but sealing microwave leakage in a rotating drum is hard and it does not address start or time setting.

title: Rice-cooker lid
new_elements: Hinged top lid with magnetic catch, cavity loaded from above (Lid is a flat steel pan with choke rim.)
rationale: Lid-pot mental model is universal across cultures.
judge_comment: The familiar lid metaphor and choke rim are concrete, but top loading has ergonomic and spill issues and the controls are still unaddressed.

title: Sensitivity dial for sensor
new_elements: Single 'a bit less / a bit more' trim dial for auto-sensor cooking (Replaces power knob once sensing takes over.)
rationale: User only ever expresses preference, never technical settings.
judge_comment: Reducing input to a more/less preference is very simple to use and feasible with existing sensor cooking, though it is not very radical.

title: Spring-scale timer
new_elements: Turntable on spring that mechanically winds timer by food weight (Purely mechanical weight-to-time linkage.)
rationale: Automatic timing with no electronics and nothing to set.
judge_comment: Weight-to-time automation removes setting entirely, but food weight poorly predicts cook time and the mechanical linkage is imprecise.

title: Temperature probe plug
new_elements: Shielded food probe with single 'eat' button (Stops at 70 °C core temperature.)
rationale: Guarantees food is safely hot without any timing knowledge.
judge_comment: A probe with a single 'eat' button removes the need to know times or power levels, though a metal probe inside a microwave is hard to make safe and food-contact hygiene is a concern.

title: Pull-cord door
new_elements: Dangling pull cord releasing door latch (Cord on front lifts the latch lever.)
rationale: Tug-to-open is obvious and works with elbows or bandaged hands.
judge_comment: A pull cord is easy to understand and cheap, but it only affects door opening, which is a small part of operating a microwave, and it risks becoming a snag hazard.

title: Pass-through two-door oven
new_elements: Doors on both front and back for hatch installation (Second door shares hinge/latch tooling.)
rationale: Load from kitchen, retrieve at table—no juggling the hot plate.
judge_comment: Doors on both sides are a quirky idea with little connection to learning-free operation, and they complicate shielding and installation.

title: Metal-fibre polymer window
new_elements: Injection-moulded polymer with embedded conductive fibre mesh (One-shot window replaces glass + stamped mesh.)
rationale: Lighter, cheaper door that is easier for elderly users to swing.
judge_comment: A molded polymer window with embedded conductive fibre is a genuine substitution that cuts cost and weight, but it does little for ease of operation and the shielding and heat resistance are uncertain.

title: Tactile wedge knobs
new_elements: Wedge-shaped knobs with braille and ratchet clicks (Orientation of wedge = setting, felt not seen.)
rationale: Settings can be confirmed by touch alone.
judge_comment: Wedge knobs with braille and ratchet clicks let users set and confirm by touch, which is intuitive and feasible, though the idea builds on existing tactile knob designs.

title: Push-the-door to open
new_elements: Push-push latch: press door panel to pop it open (Cabinet-style push catch replaces button and lever.)
rationale: The door itself is the button—nothing else to find.
judge_comment: Push-push latch is simple and plausible, but it only simplifies opening, not the main operation of setting time and power.

title: Defrost mat
new_elements: Blue silicone mat with RFID tag; placing it triggers defrost duty (Physical token replaces power selection.)
rationale: Power level becomes a physical object you either use or don't.
judge_comment: An RFID mat as a physical token for defrost is clever and concrete, but it adds an accessory and covers only one function.

title: Talking oven
new_elements: Speech output chip announcing 'ready' and counting down (Replaces bell with spoken status.)
rationale: Plain-language feedback needs no interpretation of chimes.
judge_comment: Speech feedback is easy to build and clear, but it is common and does not simplify input controls.

title: Close-to-start door
new_elements: Door-close switch starts a fixed 1-min full-power cycle automatically (Timer knob removed; reopen door to stop.)
rationale: The only control is the door—impossible to misuse.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start a fixed 1-minute cycle removes nearly all controls, though the fixed duration limits usefulness and there are safety and overcooking concerns.

title: Clear glass cavity
new_elements: Full transparent conductive-coated glass cavity and door (No lamp, no mesh; whole oven is see-through.)
rationale: Users monitor food directly from any angle, learning nothing but 'look'.
judge_comment: A fully transparent conductive glass cavity is radical, but it is barely linked to ease of operation and is very hard to make while containing microwaves.

title: Single Start button with humidity auto-stop
new_elements: Start button + exhaust humidity sensor (One button; magnetron runs until steam burst detected, then stops); Humidity-based doneness sensing (Capacitive humidity sensor in exhaust duct detects food steam release)
rationale: User presses one button and never thinks about minutes.
judge_comment: One-button operation with humidity-based auto-stop removes time-setting entirely and is plausible, though steam sensing is already used in premium microwaves and fails on dry foods.

title: Food-icon dial replaces minutes scale
new_elements: Icon dial (cup, bowl, plate, pizza) (Same cam timer but scale printed as food pictures with pre-tuned durations)
rationale: Turn to the picture of what you are heating; no mental time arithmetic.
judge_comment: Cheap and easy to build and understand, but it is an incremental relabel of the timer dial and the preset durations are only approximate.

title: Weighing turntable sets time automatically
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Mass of food maps to heating duration via fixed J/g rule); Mass-proportional energy dosing (Energy delivered = k × mass, k selected by a reheat/defrost toggle)
rationale: Place food, press start; machine deduces time from weight.
judge_comment: Weight-based dosing is clever and mostly automatic, but a load cell under a rotating turntable adds cost and complexity, and the toggle remains.

title: One knob: Cold–Warm–Hot
new_elements: Single outcome knob (warm/hot/boiling) (Merged cam sets both duration and duty cycle from one temperature-feel scale)
rationale: User chooses the result they want, not the engineering parameters.
judge_comment: An outcome-oriented knob is intuitive, but food type and quantity still change the result, and the mechanism is only loosely defined.

title: Inverter replaces duty-cycle cam
new_elements: Inverter continuous power control (Switch-mode supply varies magnetron anode current for true continuous power); Continuous power slider (Linear potentiometer labelled gentle→blast)
rationale: Behaviour is predictable like a stove dial, no confusing pulsing.
judge_comment: Inverter power control already exists and mainly improves predictability, so it does little to remove the need to choose time and power.

title: Delete the power knob entirely
new_elements: Fixed 500 W gentle-only magnetron drive (Lower fixed output makes over-cooking forgiving; only time remains)
rationale: One control is simpler than two; forgiving power removes need for the second.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob is simple and feasible, but a fixed low power makes cooking slow and only partially helps the no-learning-curve need.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline keyword speech module (Recognises 'heat', 'defrost', 'stop', 'two minutes' without cloud); Embedded keyword spotting (Low-power DSP speech recognition)
rationale: Speaking is the zero-learning-curve interface, especially for.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is plausible and intuitive, though noise and accents, and the tendency to still require a time, limit it.

title: Heat-to-temperature button with IR eye
new_elements: IR thermopile + 'Eat temp' button (Cooks until surface reaches 65 °C then stops); Non-contact infrared food thermometry (Thermopile through choke-protected aperture reads food surface temperature)
rationale: User asks for 'ready to eat', never for watts or minutes.
judge_comment: A single 'eat temperature' button removes the need for time and power settings, though IR only reads surface temperature and must work through the cavity's shielding.

title: Magnetic pull door, no button
new_elements: Magnet-held door with grab handle (Ferrite catch holds door; reed switch is the interlock); Magnetic catch + reed interlock (Replaces lever latch and hook mechanism)
rationale: Pulling a fridge-like door needs no instruction.
judge_comment: A magnetic pull door with a reed switch interlock is intuitive and cheap, but it only simplifies opening and raises safety-interlock redundancy concerns.

title: Drawer cavity replaces hinged door
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Food sits in a drawer; closing it is the only action)
rationale: Drawers are universally understood and need no latch button.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar interaction, but sealing microwaves around a drawer and spill containment are hard, and the idea gives few details.

title: Roll-up metal shutter door
new_elements: Conductive tambour shutter (Interlocking steel slats roll up into the top; contact strips keep RF seal)
rationale: Push up to open, pull down to cook; no swing clearance or button.
judge_comment: Novel mechanism, but RF sealing with sliding slats is hard and it does not actually simplify operation of cooking settings.

title: Top-loading pot-lid microwave
new_elements: Hinged top lid with choke flange (Cavity opens from above like a saucepan lid)
rationale: Lifting a lid is a cooking gesture everyone already knows.
judge_comment: Familiar lid gesture is intuitive, but it only addresses opening and top-loading brings spill and ergonomics issues.

title: Hand-wound spring timer (no mains clock)
new_elements: Escapement clockwork timer (Wind-up spring with balance escapement, independent of mains frequency)
rationale: Same egg-timer twist everywhere in the world, identical feel.
judge_comment: A wind-up egg-timer dial is universally understood and mechanically plausible, directly eliminating the learning curve.

title: Hold-to-heat pad
new_elements: Capacitive dead-man pad (Magnetron runs only while a hand rests on the pad)
rationale: No setting at all: you heat for as long as you touch, like a tap.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is very intuitive with zero settings, though tiring for long cooks and the safety logic needs care.

title: Foot pedal operation
new_elements: Foot pedal (press=heat, double-tap=open) (Hands-free control for users carrying dishes)
rationale: One pedal, two obvious actions; no front panel to read.
judge_comment: A simple pedal is easy to build, but the double-tap to open is less obvious and it lacks time control.

title: Barcode scanner reads cook instructions
new_elements: Front barcode scanner (Reads packaging code and looks up time/power in onboard table)
rationale: Swipe the package; the oven sets itself.
judge_comment: Workable and concrete, but scanning a package is an extra step and barcodes don't encode cook times, so it needs a big database; it's also not very radical.

title: NFC containers carry their own settings
new_elements: NFC reader under turntable (Tagged bowls/mugs announce their recommended program); Passive NFC tagging (Heat-resistant tags embedded in glass containers)
rationale: Put the mug in, press start; the mug knows.
judge_comment: Put the mug in and press start is very low-learning, but it only works with tagged containers, and NFC tags near microwaves are a heat and RF challenge.

title: Camera food recognition sets program
new_elements: Cavity camera + on-device classifier (Recognises soup/plate/frozen block and selects a program); Edge image classification (Tiny CNN on microcontroller)
rationale: Zero inputs from the user beyond closing the door.
judge_comment: Needs no user input, which fits the need strongly, but recognition accuracy and safe doneness across varied foods are risky; the camera also has to survive steam and splatter.

title: Toaster-style lever
new_elements: Push-down lever with pop-up release (Push down to start; depth = duration; pops up with click when done)
rationale: Borrows the most intuitive kitchen gesture there is.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster gesture removes the learning curve, and it is mechanically simple, though duration precision and power-level control are limited.

title: Braille/tactile detent dial
new_elements: Raised-dot detent dial (1 click = 30 s) (Strong clicks and raised numerals for eyes-free setting)
rationale: Counting clicks is simpler than reading a fine scale.
judge_comment: Easy to build and good for accessibility, but it is an incremental tweak to the existing dial and still needs the user to choose a time.

title: 0–5 minute big-scale timer
new_elements: Short-range 0–5 min cam timer (Same clockwork but gearing spreads 5 minutes over full 300° travel)
rationale: Most tasks are under 5 min; a wide scale makes 30 s easy to hit.
judge_comment: A simple, practical wide-scale mechanical timer that eases operation, but it is an incremental tweak rather than a radical idea.

title: Crystal-clocked electronic timer in a knob
new_elements: Quartz-timed knob encoder (Rotary encoder + MCU emulates cam timer, mains-independent)
rationale: Keeps the familiar twist but makes it accurate everywhere.
judge_comment: It keeps the familiar twist interaction and adds accuracy, but the benefit to a no-learning-curve experience is modest and the idea is not radical.

title: Talking done-signal replaces bell
new_elements: Voice chip + big green lamp (Says 'your food is ready' and lights a large indicator)
rationale: Unambiguous feedback removes guessing about what the ding meant.
judge_comment: Voice and lamp feedback clarify completion, but they address only the output side and talking appliances are well known.

title: Transparent conductive film window
new_elements: Conductive oxide (ITO/metal-mesh) laminate glass (Sheet resistance low enough to shield 2.45 GHz while fully clear)
rationale: A clear window shows progress plainly, so no interface needed to 'check'.
judge_comment: Conductive films for microwave shielding are plausible and specific, but a clear window only loosely helps operational simplicity.

title: Doorless cut-off tunnel for mugs
new_elements: Open-front mug chimney cavity (Opening below waveguide cut-off diameter; no door, no latch, no hinge); Below-cutoff waveguide attenuation (Narrow deep opening attenuates 2.45 GHz exponentially)
rationale: Nothing to open or close: slide the mug in, press one button.
judge_comment: A doorless below-cutoff mug tunnel is a radical substitution that removes the door and latch, and it is physically plausible, though limited to mugs and tricky for leakage and safety compliance.

title: Three preset buttons only
new_elements: Buttons: Drink / Meal / Defrost (Three fixed programs, nothing else on the panel)
rationale: Three choices cover 95% of use with zero reading.
judge_comment: Highly relevant and very feasible, but this is a common simplification and not radical, with limited detail on the programs.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Pull-string spring timer (Pull length sets minutes; cord retracts as it counts down, visible progress)
rationale: Progress is physically visible; longer pull = longer heat, intuitive.
judge_comment: A spring-wound pull-cord timer is intuitive, shows progress, and substitutes for a keypad, though precision and cord safety need work.

title: Knee-press door opener
new_elements: Lower-front knee bar release (Wide bar at knee height trips the latch)
rationale: Opens with hands full of plates; no small button to find.
judge_comment: A knee bar makes opening easy with full hands, but it addresses only door opening and may cause accidental opens.

title: Living-hinge polymer door frame
new_elements: Moulded living hinge with metallised door (One-piece polymer door/hinge, vacuum-metallised for shielding)
rationale: Lighter door with no pinch points is easier for frail hands.
judge_comment: A living-hinge door is a creative substitution, but it barely affects the learning curve, and metallised polymer faces durability, heat and RF-leakage problems.

title: Metallised fabric curtain door
new_elements: Conductive textile curtain with magnetic hem (Silver-coated fabric drops over opening; hem magnets seal to frame)
rationale: Brush it aside like a shower curtain; nothing to operate.
judge_comment: A fabric curtain door is wildly novel, but it is unlikely to seal microwave leakage safely or to meet regulations, and it does little for operational simplicity.

title: Door-is-the-switch
new_elements: Close-to-run door with auto-stop sensor (Closing door starts heating; steam sensor or opening stops it)
rationale: Removes the start step entirely.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start removes a step and is intuitive, but a steam sensor can't tell when food is done, and closing the door to run is a safety and accidental-start concern.

title: Caregiver-preset, no front panel
new_elements: Single big button + BLE preset by caregiver (Family member sets the program once via phone; user only presses GO)
rationale: Elderly user faces exactly one button.
judge_comment: A single button with a caregiver-set preset removes nearly all decisions for the user, though it is inflexible and relies on a smartphone setup by someone else.

title: Bimetal thermal timer
new_elements: Heated bimetal strip delay switch (Resistor warms strip; bend time sets duration, no motor)
rationale: Cheaper, frequency-independent, same simple knob feel.
judge_comment: A bimetal thermal timer is a real, cheap substitute for the timer and keeps a simple knob, but it is imprecise and gives only a modest gain in learning-curve terms.

title: Shelf height sets power
new_elements: Multi-level rack cavity (Field intensity varies with height; upper shelf = gentle, lower = strong)
rationale: Power becomes a physical placement decision, like an oven rack.
judge_comment: Setting power by shelf height is a radical and intuitive idea, but microwave field patterns are uneven and hard to control, so it would heat unreliably.

title: Waveguide vane attenuator
new_elements: Mechanical waveguide attenuator slider (Lossy vane inserted into waveguide absorbs power continuously)
rationale: A smooth slider behaves like a volume knob—no steps to learn.
judge_comment: A slider that attenuates the waveguide gives continuous, volume-knob-like power control and is mechanically plausible, but it wastes energy as heat and is not a major simplification overall.

title: Only a +30 s button
new_elements: Single large +30 s button with countdown lamp bar (Each press adds 30 s and starts; bar of LEDs shows remaining)
rationale: Press once or several times—nothing else to understand.
judge_comment: Very simple to use and easy to build, but one-button microwaves already exist, so it is not radical.

title: Traffic-light doneness indicator
new_elements: Red/amber/green doneness lamp (IR sensor drives lamp; user stops when green, timer optional)
rationale: Universal colour code replaces numeric settings.
judge_comment: A color-coded doneness lamp is intuitive and fairly novel, but IR sensing of food doneness is unreliable and the user still has to stop the oven.

title: Vessel-detent dial
new_elements: Timer with click stops labelled Mug / Bowl / Plate (Cam timer detents at pre-tuned durations)
rationale: Turn until it clicks for your dish; done.
judge_comment: A detented dial labeled by vessel is easy to use and cheap, but the preset times may not match the food, and it is a modest variation on the mechanical timer.

title: Gravity drop-down door, no latch
new_elements: Bottom-hinged weighted door (Door falls shut under its own weight; reed switch interlock)
rationale: Lift to open, let go to close—no button, no slamming.
judge_comment: Removes the latch and button, but a door that closes under its own weight does not address operating the controls, and it is not very radical.

title: Push-push cabinet latch
new_elements: Push-to-open cabinet catch (Press door face to pop it open; press again to latch)
rationale: Whole door is the button; nothing to locate.
judge_comment: A push-to-open door is intuitive and easy to build, but it is a common mechanism and only affects opening the door.

title: Turntable-rotation timer
new_elements: Rotation-counting turntable timer (Knob sets number of turns; turntable motor shaft drives cam, no separate timer motor)
rationale: Fewer parts, and 'three turns' is a tangible unit for users.
judge_comment: Turns as a time unit is not intuitive for cooking and the cam link is plausible, but it does little for ease of use.

title: Push-depth drawer sets time
new_elements: Drawer with graduated push-in travel (How far the drawer is pushed in winds the timer; it slides back out as it counts)
rationale: Loading and setting time become one motion.
judge_comment: Merging loading and time-setting is a clever single motion, but a push depth is imprecise and the mechanics are awkward and unsafe with food.

title: Program cartridge slot
new_elements: Coded plastic card slot (Insert 'Soup' or 'Rice' card; notches set cam positions mechanically)
rationale: Picking a card is choosing a dish, not a setting.
judge_comment: Choosing a dish card needs no learning, and notched mechanical cams are simple and workable, though cards limit flexibility.

title: Visible ball-run timer
new_elements: Marble-run gravity timer (Drop N marbles; each takes 30 s to roll through and trip a switch)
rationale: Time is counted in physical objects you can see and understand.
judge_comment: A marble-run timer is whimsical and visible, but it is bulky, impractical, and awkward to count in 30 s units.

title: Spiral combined time-power dial
new_elements: Spiral-scale single dial (First turn = defrost power, second turn = full power; angle = minutes)
rationale: One knob instead of two halves the interface.
judge_comment: One dial is simpler, but the spiral scale with two turns meaning different power levels adds some confusion.

title: Thermostat dial with closed loop
new_elements: Target-temperature dial + IR feedback (Set 40–90 °C; oven cycles magnetron to hold that temperature then stops)
rationale: Works like a room thermostat, a control everyone already understands.
judge_comment: A thermostat-style dial is instantly understood and swaps time and power settings for one familiar control, though IR sensing of food temperature through a cavity is hard to do reliably.

title: Hold-door-closed to heat
new_elements: Spring-open door with hold-to-run interlock (Door springs open when released; heating only while user holds it shut)
rationale: Impossible to misuse: let go and it stops and opens.
judge_comment: Hold-to-run needs no learning and is safe, but standing and holding the door through a whole cook is impractical and frustrating, and it still needs a way to set the time.

title: Minute tokens
new_elements: Token slot timer (Drop wooden 1-minute tokens into a slot; each token advances the cam)
rationale: Counting tokens is concrete and playful, no scale reading.
judge_comment: Tokens make time concrete and are mechanically simple, but they can be lost and are tedious for longer cooks.

title: Gesture wave control
new_elements: ToF gesture sensor (Wave up = +30 s, wave down = stop, hold palm = open door)
rationale: Touch-free, wipeable, three gestures only.
judge_comment: Three gestures are few, but invisible gestures have to be learned and can misfire, which works against the no-learning-curve need.

title: Juke-box tilt lever for power
new_elements: Big tilt lever Low/High (Two-position lever drives duty-cycle cam; no five-step confusion)
rationale: Binary choice is the simplest possible power control.
judge_comment: A two-position lever is trivially simple and cheap, but it only covers power and is not very radical.

title: Open-plan sliding glass door
new_elements: Side-sliding ITO glass panel (Door slides sideways in rails; conductive gasket closes the seam)
rationale: Slide like a patio door; no swing, no button, full visibility.
judge_comment: A sliding ITO glass door is a concrete substitution for the swing door, but it barely reduces operational complexity (opening a door is already trivial), and sealing microwave leakage along a sliding seam with a conductive gasket is a serious safety and engineering challenge.

title: One-Button Oven
new_elements: Single large GO button (fixed 30 s per press, auto-accumulating) (Replaces both knobs; each press adds 30 s at full power, long-press clears.)
rationale: A single control with one obvious action removes every decision point, giving zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Very simple and feasible, but not very radical, since it is similar to existing +30 s buttons; it does fit the simplicity need well.

title: Toaster-Lever Timer
new_elements: Spring-loaded depth lever with escapement (Push depth sets minutes; lever rises as it counts down and pops up at the end.); Toaster-style start lever (Push down to start, lever position shows remaining time, pop-up ends cycle.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to use a toaster, so the interaction transfers with no instruction.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster metaphor with a mechanical escapement is clever and concrete, though the lever-height display and microwave-door interlock integration add some complexity.

title: Food-Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Pictogram program dial (mug, plate, frozen, butter) (Single cam dial where each icon encodes a fixed time+power pair; numbers removed.)
rationale: Users choose what they are heating, not watts and minutes, so no mental conversion is needed.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are easy to understand and highly feasible, but food-type presets already exist and fixed times may not suit all portions.

title: Weight-Set Timer
new_elements: Spring scale under turntable linked to timer cam (Dish weight compresses a spring that mechanically presets cooking time.)
rationale: Placing the food is the only input; the oven sets its own time without any user settings.
judge_comment: Setting time by weight with no user input is appealing, but weight does not reliably indicate heating needs (a heavy dish vs. its contents), so a mechanical spring scale would be inaccurate.

title: Steam-Stop Cooking
new_elements: Vent humidity sensing (capacitive polymer sensor) (Detects steam burst from food reaching ~100 °C and stops the cycle.); Humidity auto-stop module (Replaces timer; cooking ends when steam signature appears.)
rationale: No time to set at all: the oven stops itself when the food is hot.
judge_comment: Automatic stopping on a steam signal removes all settings and is plausible, though sensor cook exists in premium models and it fails for dry foods or covered dishes.

title: Target-Temperature Knob
new_elements: IR thermopile food-surface sensing (Non-contact thermometer through a mesh port reads food temperature.); Doneness dial (warm / hot / boiling) (Single knob sets target temperature; magnetron cuts off when reached.)
rationale: Users state the outcome they want rather than guessing time and power.
judge_comment: Outcome-based control removes guesswork and is highly intuitive, though IR sensing of surface temperature in a microwave cavity is tricky and accuracy is limited.

title: Dead-Man's Heat Button
new_elements: Hold-to-heat momentary button (Microwaves run only while the button is held, like a hand blender.)
rationale: The most primitive possible control: press to heat, release to stop, nothing to learn or forget.
judge_comment: Extremely simple with zero learning, but holding a button for minutes is impractical and it is a regression in convenience.

title: Cooking Coins
new_elements: Token-slot timer (1 token = 1 minute) (Reusable plastic tokens dropped in a slot advance a mechanical escapement.)
rationale: Counting tokens is a tangible, child-and-elder-friendly way to set time without reading a dial.
judge_comment: Tangible and quirky, but tokens can be lost and users still must know how many minutes to use.

title: Punch-Card Recipes
new_elements: Mechanical punched-card program reader (Card notches depress follower pins that set time cam and power cam.); Recipe card slot (Insert a food card (soup, popcorn, milk) and the oven is fully set.)
rationale: Choosing a card is a single physical act that replaces all numeric setting.
judge_comment: Mechanical cam-based card reader is concrete and removes numeric entry, but cards are limiting and costly to produce and manage.

title: Packaging-Tag Auto-Set
new_elements: Passive NFC/RFID tag reading (Reader in fascia decodes heating instructions printed into food packaging tags.); Tap-to-cook tag reader (Tap the package, close the door, done.)
rationale: The package tells the oven what to do, so the user never reads instructions.
judge_comment: Tap-to-cook is effortless for users but depends on industry adoption of tags, so it only works with compatible packaged foods.

title: Hot / Gentle Two-Button Power
new_elements: Two-button power selector (Hot, Gentle) (Full power or 30 % duty for defrost/melt; five steps collapsed to two.)
rationale: A binary choice is understood instantly; most users never use intermediate levels anyway.
judge_comment: Simple and highly feasible, but it is a modest simplification and not a radical one.

title: Spiral One-Knob Time+Power
new_elements: Single spiral-track knob (One rotary control: first sector gentle long cycles (defrost), then full-power minutes.)
rationale: One knob means there is only one thing to turn, eliminating the time-vs-power confusion.
judge_comment: A single knob combining time and power is intuitive and mechanically plausible, though the spiral mapping is only loosely defined.

title: Passive Defrost Plate
new_elements: Lossy-dielectric attenuator lid (Silicone-carbide-loaded cover absorbs ~70 % of RF, giving gentle heating with no electronics.); Snap-on defrost dome (Place dome over food for defrost/melt; oven itself has only one power.)
rationale: Power selection becomes a physical object you can see, not a setting you must remember.
judge_comment: A passive attenuator dome is creative and substitutes hardware for settings, but a lossy lid would heat up, wastes energy, and adds a separate accessory to manage.

title: Solid-State Continuous Power Dial
new_elements: GaN solid-state 2.45 GHz power amplifier (Low-voltage RF source with truly continuous power control, no HV or filament.); Solid-state RF module with linear power dial (Replaces magnetron, HV transformer, capacitor and diode.)
rationale: Power behaves like a stove knob (smooth, immediate), matching users' existing mental model.
judge_comment: A solid-state RF source with a linear dial is technically real and gives an intuitive stove-like model, but it is costly and doesn't substitute something cheaper.

title: Door Pops Open at End
new_elements: Timer-released door latch (Timer cam trips the latch so the door swings ajar at zero, replacing the bell.)
rationale: An open door is an unmistakable, universal signal that the food is ready.
judge_comment: A door that pops ajar at the end is a clear and quirky signal that is easy to build, though it only addresses the done-alert and not operation.

title: Steam Whistle Finish
new_elements: Airflow-driven whistle on vent (Timer shutter diverts fan air through a kettle-style whistle for a few seconds.); Vent whistle (Replaces bell striker; uses existing fan airflow.)
rationale: A kettle whistle is a sound every household already associates with 'hot and ready'.
judge_comment: Using existing fan airflow for a kettle-style whistle is a clever and intuitive cue, though it only signals the end and a shutter adds some complexity.

title: Spoken 'Ready'
new_elements: Voice-chip announcer (Cheap sound IC says 'Ready' and 'Door open' instead of a bell.)
rationale: Plain words need no interpretation, especially for elderly or visually impaired users.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap, clear and accessible, but talking appliances already exist and it covers only the end-of-cycle cue.

title: Thermochromic Window
new_elements: Thermochromic ink on door glass (Window tint shifts colour as cavity air warms, showing 'hot' state passively.); Colour-changing door pane (Visual doneness/hot indicator with no bulb or electronics.)
rationale: Colour is read at a glance from across the room without learning any indicator.
judge_comment: A passive colour cue is intuitive, but thermochromic ink on a door pane facing microwave heat and food splatter is dubious, and cavity air temperature is a poor proxy for doneness.

title: Music-Box Timer
new_elements: Clockwork music-box timer (Wound timer plays a tune as it unwinds; silence plus final chord marks the end.)
rationale: Continuous audible progress tells the user where they are without reading a dial.
judge_comment: A wind-up music-box timer is charming, mechanically simple and gives continuous progress feedback, though a tune may annoy and it does not simplify setting the time.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Sand-flow timing with weight-tilt switch (Door closure flips a sealed hourglass; emptied bulb tilts a lever opening the circuit.); Visible hourglass timer (Swap-in glasses of 1, 3, 5 min; remaining time is literally visible.)
rationale: An hourglass is the oldest, most intuitive time display—no numbers, no dial.
judge_comment: A visible hourglass with fixed durations is very intuitive and needs no learning, but a tilt switch, sand-timing accuracy and fixed times limit its practicality.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord retracting timer (Pull the cord out; length pulled equals minutes; it retracts as time elapses.)
rationale: Length is a direct, body-scaled metaphor for duration, easier to judge than a small dial.
judge_comment: An intuitive length-equals-time metaphor with visible countdown by retraction, though a mechanical cord timer is imprecise and needs a way to adjust or cancel.

title: Door Handle Is the Timer
new_elements: Rotating door-handle timer (Twist the handle on closing to set minutes; one gesture closes and starts.)
rationale: Closing and setting merge into one motion, halving the steps to operate.
judge_comment: Merging closing and time setting into one gesture cuts steps, and a rotary handle linked to a timer is simple to build, but twisting a handle may not be obvious to first-time users.

title: Close-to-Start Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity with auto-start (Slide the drawer shut and a default 1-minute cycle begins; pull open to stop.)
rationale: Loading the food is the only action; there is no separate start step to learn.
judge_comment: Close-to-start removes the start step entirely, and the open-to-stop behavior is intuitive, though a fixed 1-minute default limits flexibility.

title: Top-Loading Lid Oven
new_elements: Rice-cooker-style hinged lid cavity (Drop mug or bowl in from above; lid closure engages interlocks and starts.)
rationale: Putting a cup into a pot-like opening is more natural than sliding plates into a box.
judge_comment: The top-loading pot-like format is a natural fit for mugs, but it does not directly simplify time or power setting and raises spill and cavity-geometry issues.

title: Magnetic Fridge-Style Door
new_elements: Magnetic gasket latch with reed-switch interlock (Door held by magnets; pull to open, reed switches sense closure.); Button-less magnetic door (No push button or latch lever.)
rationale: Users open it like a fridge—no hunting for the release button.
judge_comment: A magnetic door with reed-switch interlock is easy to build and removes the release button, but it only simplifies opening, and safety interlock redundancy needs care.

title: Foot-Pedal Door
new_elements: Bin-style foot pedal door opener (Step on pedal to pop door; hands stay free for the hot dish.)
rationale: Opening with a foot is already learned from kitchen bins and removes a fiddly button.
judge_comment: Practical and familiar, but it only simplifies door opening and is not radical; the foot pedal could be awkward with a low-mounted or countertop unit.

title: Tray Ejects at End
new_elements: CD-style sliding tray with auto-eject (At zero the door drops and the tray slides forward presenting the food.)
rationale: The oven hands you the food—no signal to decode and no door to open.
judge_comment: Auto-eject presenting the food is an intuitive finish cue, but a tray mechanism adds cost and spill risk, and it does little for the start-up interaction.

title: Transparent ITO Cavity Walls
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide (ITO) coated glass shielding (Conductive transparent film reflects 2.45 GHz while passing light.); Glass-walled see-through cavity (Ambient kitchen light illuminates food; no lamp, no mesh.)
rationale: Seeing food plainly from any angle removes the need for indicators or guesswork.
judge_comment: A transparent conductive glass cavity is a bold substitution for mesh and lamp, but durability, cost, and RF leakage at seams are serious concerns, and the link to simple operation is indirect.

title: RF-Harvesting Cavity Lamp
new_elements: Rectenna-powered LED (Small antenna-diode-LED puck inside cavity lights from stray field only when RF is on.); Wireless RF-powered indicator LED (No wiring, no lamp holder; doubles as 'microwaves active' indicator.)
rationale: Light-on means heating-on, an unambiguous status cue with nothing to configure.
judge_comment: A rectenna-powered LED is a clever, self-explanatory heating indicator and truly simplifies wiring, though its benefit for ease of use is modest and the light output is limited.

title: External Light-Guide Illumination
new_elements: Door-edge LED light guide (LEDs in the fascia shine through the mesh via an acrylic light pipe; user-replaceable.)
rationale: A lamp that never leaves the user in the dark keeps the simplest feedback channel working.
judge_comment: Feasible and easy to service, but it is an incremental lighting tweak with little effect on learning-free operation.

title: Webcam Doneness Viewer
new_elements: Cavity camera with front display (Tiny camera shows magnified food on a fascia screen, optionally to a phone.)
rationale: A big clear image of the food needs no interpretation compared with squinting through a mesh.
judge_comment: A camera helps judge doneness but adds cost and a screen, and it barely simplifies operation, so it doesn't fit SUBSTITUTE or the no-learning-curve need well.

title: Fan-Driven Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Airflow-spun metal mode stirrer (Cooling exhaust spins a reflector fan in the waveguide, scrambling standing waves.); Flat fixed cavity floor (No turntable, roller ring or motor; plates never catch or tilt.)
rationale: Nothing to align or reseat—just put the plate anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are real and used in many microwaves, and removing the turntable eliminates reseating, though the airflow-driven version is only a modest change.

title: Rotating Underfloor Antenna
new_elements: Flatbed rotating feed antenna (Motor rotates the RF antenna under a ceramic floor instead of rotating the food.)
rationale: Removes the most common user error (misplaced turntable) from the product.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas under a ceramic floor exist in commercial units, and they plausibly remove the turntable-placement error.

title: Convection-Spun Tray
new_elements: Thermal updraft turbine (Hot cavity air rising through angled vanes spins the tray like a candle carousel.); Motorless heat-spun turntable (Tray spins only when food is hot; no motor, no wiring.)
rationale: Visible spinning doubles as a 'heating is happening' cue with zero controls.
judge_comment: A heat-driven turntable is radical and clever, but microwave cavity air is barely hot, so the updraft would likely be too weak and unreliable to spin a loaded tray.

title: Silicone Mat Instead of Glass Tray
new_elements: Dishwasher-safe silicone cavity mat (Soft mat on a fixed floor; nothing to break, slip, or reinstall wrongly.)
rationale: Eliminates the puzzle of reseating a glass tray on a roller ring after cleaning.
judge_comment: A silicone mat fixes reseating but food would not be stirred or heated evenly without rotation, and silicone could deform or sag, so the substitution is weak.

title: Cylindrical Bowl Cavity
new_elements: Round ceramic-lined cavity (Cylindrical cavity with top feed averages field modes; no corners, no tray.)
rationale: A bowl-shaped interior tells users exactly where food goes and wipes clean with one motion.
judge_comment: A round cavity without a tray is novel and makes the loading position clear, but it only indirectly reduces the learning curve and the claim of an averaged field is optimistic.

title: Hinge-Integrated Interlock
new_elements: Contact-bearing door hinge (Hinge pin carries redundant contacts closed only when door is fully seated.)
rationale: Fewer hidden switches means fewer 'why won't it start' failures for the user.
judge_comment: A concrete and plausible hinge-based interlock, but users never see the interlock, so it barely affects ease of learning and is not radical.

title: Food-Present Start Switch
new_elements: Tray weight-switch gating start (Oven only runs when something rests on the floor; empty-run and forgetting-to-load impossible.)
rationale: Removes a whole class of user mistakes without adding anything the user must learn.
judge_comment: A weight switch prevents empty runs and needs no learning, but it can misfire with light foods and does not simplify the controls.

title: Tactile Embossed Fascia
new_elements: Raised-icon tactile fascia (Moulded raised food shapes and notches replace printed numerals.)
rationale: Shapes you can feel work in the dark and without reading glasses.
judge_comment: Tactile raised icons are cheap, easy to make and accessible, and they replace printed numerals, but they are only a modest change.

title: Traffic-Light Dial Zones
new_elements: Colour-zoned single dial (Green (warm drink), amber (plate), red (frozen) sectors instead of minutes and watts.)
rationale: Colour categories are grasped faster than numeric scales.
judge_comment: A colour-zoned single dial replaces numeric settings with intuitive categories, which directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build.

title: Slider with Life-Size Marks
new_elements: Linear slider marked with cup / bowl / plate silhouettes (Slide to the picture matching your dish; slider returns as time elapses.)
rationale: Matching a picture to the dish in your hand needs no knowledge of cooking times.
judge_comment: A picture-matching slider directly removes the need to know cooking times, though the mapping of dish silhouette to power and time is somewhat vague.

title: Shared-Motor Timer and Turntable
new_elements: Single motor driving timer cam and turntable via gear train (One synchronous motor replaces two; tray stops exactly when timer ends.)
rationale: A visibly spinning tray becomes the timer display itself—motion equals time left.
judge_comment: A visible spinning tray as the timer is intuitive and mechanically plausible, but it offers only a modest gain in operating simplicity.

title: Glass-Ceramic Waveguide Cover
new_elements: Wipe-clean glass-ceramic waveguide window (Replaces fragile mica with a durable sealed pane; no user maintenance.)
rationale: Users never need to learn about or replace a burnt mica sheet.
judge_comment: This is a maintenance improvement that barely touches the need for simple operation.

title: Roll-Up Tambour Door
new_elements: Metallised slat tambour with choke edges (Interlocking conductive slats roll up into the cabinet top.); Garage-style roll-up shutter door (Push up to open, pull down to close and start; no swing clearance.)
rationale: A single up/down gesture replaces button, latch and swing path.
judge_comment: A single-gesture roll-up door is a radical and intuitive idea, but sealing microwaves with a slat tambour is difficult and cost is high.

title: Autoranging Universal Supply
new_elements: Universal-input inverter supply with crystal-timed controller (Works on any mains; timer no longer depends on mains frequency.)
rationale: One identical product everywhere means instructions and behaviour never vary by region.
judge_comment: A universal supply with a crystal-timed controller gives consistent behavior but does little for the user's learning curve.

title: Distributed Low-Power RF Sources
new_elements: Four wall-mounted 200 W solid-state emitters (Phase-staggered sources give uniform field; turntable and waveguide removed.)
rationale: Even heating means no stirring, flipping or 'let stand' rituals for the user to learn.
judge_comment: Even heating removes stirring rituals, but it's only indirectly tied to operation simplicity and solid-state RF at 4x200W is costly, not a cheaper substitute.

title: Thermal Cutouts as the Only Timer
new_elements: Cavity-air snap-disc stop (no timer) (Oven runs until cavity air reaches a set temperature from food steam, then opens; single 'Go' button.)
rationale: Reuses a part already in the oven to make time-setting disappear entirely.
judge_comment: A single Go button with auto-stop is very simple to use, but cavity air temperature is a poor proxy for doneness and risks overheating or underheating food, plus it can't handle dry or sealed items.

title: Glowing Progress Ring Around Door
new_elements: LED ring around door that shrinks with remaining time (Lit arc length shows time left and flashes green at end; replaces bell and interior lamp.)
rationale: Progress is readable from across the room with no numbers or sounds to interpret.
judge_comment: An LED ring is a plausible, cheap replacement for the bell and lamp, but it only improves feedback and does not remove the need to set the time.

title: Pressure-Pad Floor Start
new_elements: Press-down cavity floor plate (Pressing the dish down onto the sprung floor arms a 1-minute cycle; door close starts it.)
rationale: The fascia disappears; the only control is where the food already goes.
judge_comment: Removing the fascia is bold, but a fixed 1-minute cycle and the odd press-to-arm interaction add confusion and weigh-sensing is unreliable.

title: Door Window as Big Countdown
new_elements: Transparent e-paper laminated on door glass (Bistable display shows huge remaining-minutes digit over the view of the food.); E-paper countdown door (Fascia reduced to one knob; the door itself is the display.)
rationale: One giant number where the user is already looking removes any need to find or read a panel.
judge_comment: A big countdown on the door is readable, but transparent e-paper is immature and costly, and a knob still needs the user to set a time.

title: Weigh-to-cook timer
new_elements: Spring scale under turntable (Food weight compresses a spring that mechanically sets the timer cam travel); Mass-proportional cam timing (Cooking time derived from load mass, no user dial)
rationale: Nothing to set: put food in, close door, the weight picks the time.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is ideal for the need, but mass is a poor proxy for the right cook time (food type and starting temperature vary), and a mechanical spring-cam linkage under a rotating turntable is awkward.

title: Hourglass sand timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand timer switch (User flips a visible hourglass; falling sand tilts a balance that opens the magnetron contact)
rationale: Universally understood gesture; the remaining sand shows time left without reading a scale.
judge_comment: The flip gesture is intuitive and the visible time remaining helps, but fixed sand durations offer little flexibility and a sand-driven balance that switches the magnetron is a fiddly mechanism.

title: Single doneness dial
new_elements: Combined cold-to-hot dial (One knob with a thermometer-style icon scale drives both time cam and duty cam via a compound cam)
rationale: Two abstract settings collapse into one intuitive 'how hot do you want it' choice.
judge_comment: One intuitive dial that merges time and power is plausible with a compound cam and simplifies the interface, though it is less radical and still requires a choice.

title: One-minute button
new_elements: Single big 'GO' button (Each press winds a fixed 60 s of clockwork; power fixed at full)
rationale: The whole interface is one button; press more for more.
judge_comment: One button is very simple and easy to build, but it resembles existing quick-start buttons, so novelty is low, and the fixed 60 s steps and fixed full power limit control.

title: Cook-until-steam
new_elements: Bimetal steam sensor in vent (Steam in the exhaust flow warms a bimetal strip that trips the circuit); Stops heating automatically when food steams (Closed-loop end condition with no user input)
rationale: Zero settings: the oven stops itself when the food is hot.
judge_comment: A closed-loop steam sensor needs no settings and is radical, but bimetal response is slow and unreliable across foods, including dry foods that don't steam, and carries overheating risk.

title: Punch-card recipes
new_elements: Food punch-card slot (Inserting a notched card for 'soup', 'milk', 'defrost' mechanically positions time and power cams)
rationale: Pick the picture card that matches your food; no numbers at all.
judge_comment: Picture-card cams remove numbers entirely and are mechanically plausible, though card variety and food-weight variation limit accuracy.

title: Icon selector instead of power knob
new_elements: Pictogram power selector (Positions labelled mug, plate, snowflake, butter instead of 1-5)
rationale: Users choose a food, not a percentage, removing the need to understand duty cycles.
judge_comment: Easy and effective pictogram substitution, but it is an incremental, already-seen idea and not very radical.

title: Delete the power knob
new_elements: Fixed full-power link (Hard-wired full power; defrost done by a separate low-power cam built into the timer's first minutes)
rationale: One fewer decision and one fewer part; most users never change power anyway.
judge_comment: Removing a decision simplifies operation, but a defrost cam in the timer is vague and reduces flexibility.

title: Pull-handle magnetic door
new_elements: Magnetic catch and grab handle (Fridge-style magnetic strip replaces hooks, lever and push button)
rationale: Opening a fridge is a motion everyone already knows; no hidden button to find.
judge_comment: A familiar fridge-style pull door is intuitive, but magnetic catches need safety interlocks and RF seal compliance.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Sliding cavity drawer (Whole cavity floor slides out like a drawer; closing it is the only action, which also starts the timer)
rationale: Loading from above with no swinging door removes door handling and reaching into a hot box.
judge_comment: A drawer with auto-start on close is very simple to use, but sealing the cavity against leakage and handling spills is hard, and auto-start raises safety concerns.

title: Roll-top tambour door
new_elements: Interlocking metal tambour shutter (Bread-bin style roll-up door made of conductive slats with overlapping choke edges)
rationale: No swing clearance, no latch button; push up to open, pull down to start.
judge_comment: A bread-bin tambour door removes the latch and swing, but RF choke sealing along slat gaps and guide rails is very hard, and a door that is merely pulled down to start is a questionable safety interlock.

title: Foot-pedal door
new_elements: Pedal-bin style foot pedal (Bowden cable from a floor pedal lifts the door hooks)
rationale: Hands-full users open the door with a familiar bin-pedal gesture.
judge_comment: A pedal-bin gesture is familiar, but it only helps the hands-full case, adds floor clutter and a mechanical linkage, and barely reduces the learning curve.

title: Conductive-glass window, no mesh
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide coated glass (ITO/FTO film reflects 2.45 GHz while passing visible light); Clear shielded door pane (Full-clarity window without perforated metal)
rationale: Seeing food clearly makes 'is it done?' obvious without reading any indicator.
judge_comment: A conductive oxide pane is technically plausible for RF shielding and gives a clear view, but it only loosely serves simple operation and edge sealing and durability are concerns.

title: Phosphorescent cavity instead of lamp
new_elements: Glow-in-the-dark enamel liner (Strontium aluminate pigment in the cavity enamel charged by kitchen light)
rationale: No bulb to burn out or replace; the appliance never needs a maintenance step.
judge_comment: A phosphorescent liner removes bulb maintenance but does not help operation, and it would glow too dimly and fade quickly, leaving the interior hard to see.

title: Thermochromic door panel
new_elements: Colour-changing door skin (Thermochromic film goes from blue to red as cavity air heats, fading back when food is cooling)
rationale: Hot-or-not is read at a glance from across the room with no display to interpret.
judge_comment: A thermochromic door skin gives an intuitive, display-free status cue, although air temperature does not reflect food state and the film must withstand heat and cycling.

title: Fan-air whistle alert
new_elements: Exhaust whistle flap (Timer cam diverts fan exhaust through a kettle-style whistle for a few seconds at zero)
rationale: A kettle whistle is a sound everyone already associates with 'hot and ready'.
judge_comment: Familiar kettle whistle is an intuitive done signal, but it only replaces the beep and does little to simplify operation.

title: Door pops open at zero
new_elements: Timer-released door spring (At zero the cam trips the latch and a spring cracks the door open a few cm)
rationale: The open door is the signal and the next step at once; nothing to hear, press or remember.
judge_comment: Door cracking open at zero is a clear, intuitive cue that doubles as the next step, and it is mechanically simple, though it may startle users or hit safety or hygiene constraints.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Waveguide mode-stirrer paddle (Fan-driven metal paddle scatters the field; flat ceramic floor, no moving tray)
rationale: No tray to centre, knock off its ring or wash; just set the plate anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many real microwaves, so this is feasible and removes tray handling but is not radical.

title: Rotating antenna under flat floor
new_elements: Sub-floor rotating feed antenna (The turntable motor spins the waveguide antenna instead of the food)
rationale: Oversized dishes stop jamming; users never think about fit or alignment.
judge_comment: A rotating antenna is a real existing approach that removes fit concerns, but it only indirectly helps with ease of operation.

title: Air-jet spun tray
new_elements: Fan-exhaust turbine turntable (Cooling air is ducted onto vanes under the tray, spinning it with no second motor)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail means fewer confusing failure modes for the user.
judge_comment: Spinning the tray with exhaust air is clever but weakly linked to the need and impractical given low airflow torque and heavy loads.

title: Turntable motor as the timer
new_elements: Revolution-counting trip wheel (Turntable shaft drives a ratchet that opens the circuit after N revolutions set by the knob)
rationale: Time is shown as visible spins of the plate, a concrete cue rather than an abstract clock.
judge_comment: Counting plate revolutions is a clever, visible timer, but it fails if the plate is stalled or the motor speed varies, and it does little to remove the need to learn how long to heat.

title: Bimetal thermal timer
new_elements: Self-heated bimetal delay switch (A small heater warms a bimetal strip; knob sets the gap, so bending time equals cooking time)
rationale: A silent, motorless timer with the same single-knob simplicity at lower cost.
judge_comment: Bimetal delay switches are proven and cheap, but the timing drifts with ambient temperature, and the knob still sets a number rather than simplifying the operation.

title: Wind-up crank timer
new_elements: Hand-wound mainspring escapement (Crank turns equal minutes; a toy-style escapement runs the time down and trips the switch)
rationale: The physical effort of winding gives tactile, unmistakable feedback of how much time was set.
judge_comment: Wind-up timers are the classic mechanical design and are easy to build, but they are not new and the cranking adds effort for users.

title: Food-pictogram time scale
new_elements: Picture-scaled timer bezel (Dial marked with mug, bowl, plate, frozen-block icons at their typical durations instead of minutes)
rationale: Users point the knob at what they are heating rather than guessing a number.
judge_comment: Pictogram icons directly remove the need to know a time and cost almost nothing to print, though the gain is mostly a relabelling rather than a radical rethink.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pull a cord out; its slow spring retraction runs the timer and the stop at the end trips the switch)
rationale: Cord length shows remaining time at a glance and needs no grip strength or fine motor skill.
judge_comment: A pull cord is an intuitive way to set time and shows what remains, and it is easy for users with limited dexterity, but it needs a damped retraction mechanism that keeps accurate time.

title: Door-close auto-start
new_elements: Hinge ratchet starter (Closing the door advances a ratchet that winds a fixed 60 s; close again to add another minute)
rationale: Shutting the door is the start command, so there is literally no control panel.
judge_comment: Closing the door as the start command removes the control panel and is easy to learn, though a fixed 60 s step is crude and a mechanical ratchet adds wear.

title: Shelf slots as the selector
new_elements: Labelled rack positions with position switches (Placing the rack in the 'drink', 'plate' or 'defrost' slot presses a switch that sets time and power)
rationale: Where you put the food is the setting; the oven has no knobs to learn.
judge_comment: Position-as-setting is intuitive, but the rack position would have to be physically recognized, and a rack in the cavity is awkward in a microwave.

title: Sliding mesh attenuator for power
new_elements: Pull-out waveguide shutter (A perforated metal slide across the waveguide mouth continuously reduces coupled power)
rationale: Power becomes a visible 'how open is the gate' slider instead of a hidden on/off rhythm.
judge_comment: A mechanical waveguide shutter is a visible power control, but it risks arcing and leakage, and the user still has to choose a power level.

title: Embossed relief fascia
new_elements: Moulded tactile fascia (Icons and scale moulded as raised relief instead of printed, readable by touch)
rationale: Legends never wear off and can be read by feel, so operation stays obvious for life.
judge_comment: Raised relief is easy to make and helps with legibility and accessibility, but it does not simplify the operation itself.

title: Solid-state RF with reflection auto-stop
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF power amplifier (Low-voltage transistor source with built-in forward/reflected power sensing); Stops when food absorption changes (Reflected-power signature indicates thawed or boiling food)
rationale: The generator itself senses doneness, removing timer and power decisions.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing could make cooking fully automatic with no inputs, but reliable doneness detection is still hard and the parts are costly.

title: Hinge as the mains switch
new_elements: Rotary hinge contact block (Door hinge pin carries redundant wiping contacts that close only when fully shut)
rationale: One fewer misalignable mechanism means fewer 'why won't it start' moments.
judge_comment: Hinge contacts are an internal swap that users never notice, so it barely helps learning-free operation, and microwaves already use door interlocks.

title: Toaster-lever start
new_elements: Push-down cooking lever (Pressing the lever down starts a fixed cycle; it pops up with a click when done)
rationale: Borrows the toaster, the most learned-already kitchen interface.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster lever with a fixed cycle removes the learning curve, though a fixed cycle limits flexibility.

title: Pop-up done flag
new_elements: Spring pop-up flag (Timer cam releases a bright flag on top of the cabinet, like a roast thermometer pop-up)
rationale: A silent visual 'done' that stays up until reset, so you never miss or misread it.
judge_comment: A mechanical pop-up flag is simple and clear, but it only covers the done signal rather than operation.

title: Package tells the oven
new_elements: Cavity RFID reader (Reads a tag printed on the food package that encodes time and power); Printed conductive-ink RFID tags (Microwave-safe low-cost tags on ready-meal packaging)
rationale: No reading instructions, no dialling: the meal programmes the oven.
judge_comment: Packages that program the oven eliminate input, but they need ecosystem adoption and RFID-safe tags in a microwave field.

title: Dedicated mug port
new_elements: Side mug-sized mini cavity (Inserting a mug closes a switch for a fixed drink cycle; main cavity untouched)
rationale: The most common task becomes a single insert-and-wait action.
judge_comment: A dedicated mug port makes the most common task one step, though a second cavity adds cost and complexity.

title: Resettable breaker for the fuse
new_elements: Push-to-reset thermal breaker (User-accessible breaker button replaces the internal ceramic fuse)
rationale: A dead oven is fixed by one obvious button, not a technician visit.
judge_comment: A user-resettable breaker helps with repair, not with everyday operation, so it barely addresses the no-learning-curve need.

title: Short-range precision dial
new_elements: 0-6 minute wide-arc timer (Same clockwork re-geared so 10 s steps are finger-sized on the dial)
rationale: Real tasks are 30 s to 5 min; a readable scale there prevents guesswork and overcooking.
judge_comment: A finger-sized dial scale matched to real cooking times is simple and intuitive, but it is an incremental tweak rather than a radical one.

title: Set the temperature, not the time
