new_elements: IR thermopile with target dial (User dials 'warm' or 'hot'; a thermopile watching the food stops heating at that surface temperature)
rationale: People know how hot they want soup, not how many minutes it takes.
judge_comment: Dialing 'warm' or 'hot' matches how people think about heating food, though an IR thermopile only reads the surface temperature and can be inaccurate.

title: One-word voice start
new_elements: Offline single-keyword voice chip (Recognises only 'heat' and 'stop'; each 'heat' adds a minute)
rationale: No panel to see or reach; the vocabulary is two words.
judge_comment: Two spoken words need almost no learning and offline keyword chips are cheap, but noisy kitchens and the lack of any visible feedback are drawbacks.

title: Push-push soft door
new_elements: Push-to-open cabinet latch (Press anywhere on the door to pop it; press again to close with damped soft-close)
rationale: No button to locate; the whole door is the button.
judge_comment: Making the whole door the button removes the need to find a control, and push-latches and soft-close hardware are proven, though it only covers opening and closing.

title: Daylight fibre lighting
new_elements: Fibre-optic light pipe from the fascia (Acrylic light guide pipes ambient kitchen light into the cavity through a choke-sealed port)
rationale: Nothing to burn out, so the 'look inside' check always works.
judge_comment: Clever substitution of the bulb, but it only marginally helps operation simplicity and a dim cavity may undercut the 'look inside' check.

title: LED strip for the lamp
new_elements: Mains-driven LED bar behind door frame (Lifetime LEDs doubling as a bright 'cooking' ring around the window)
rationale: A glowing door ring makes 'it is running' unambiguous from any angle.
judge_comment: Feasible and gives clear running feedback, but it is an incremental lighting tweak rather than a radical idea.

title: Add-30-seconds rocker
new_elements: Single 'a bit more' rocker (One oversized rocker: each tap adds 30 s of full power; auto-starts on door close)
rationale: Mirrors how people actually use microwaves: start, check, add a bit.
judge_comment: A single rocker with auto-start on door close removes nearly all learning and matches real behaviour, though the idea itself is not very wild.

title: Passive chimney cooling
new_elements: Heat-pipe and chimney stack (Magnetron heat conducted to a rear fin chimney; natural draught replaces the fan)
rationale: A silent, fanless oven gives one clear sound (the done signal) and no noise to misinterpret as a fault.
judge_comment: A fanless magnetron is bold, but passive cooling is likely inadequate and the link to operation simplicity is indirect.

title: Vibrating pager puck
new_elements: Detachable vibrating coaster (Restaurant-pager style puck buzzes when the timer trips; sits on the oven top when not carried)
rationale: You feel 'done' in your pocket; no need to watch or listen to the appliance.
judge_comment: A vibrating pager is easy to build and understand, but it adds an accessory instead of simplifying the controls.

title: Weight-sensing defrost
new_elements: Frozen-mass defrost cam (Spring scale under the tray plus a 'frozen' flip switch picks a defrost duty and duration automatically)
rationale: Defrosting, the most confusing task, becomes 'flip one switch'.
judge_comment: Directly removes the most confusing task with a mechanical scale and one switch, though it is a fairly sensible rather than radical substitution.

title: Removable silicone floor mat
new_elements: Dishwasher-safe silicone cavity mat (Non-slip mat replaces the glass tray on a flat floor; lifts out to wash)
rationale: No breakable tray to re-seat on its ring; cleaning is lift, rinse, drop back.
judge_comment: Practical and easy to clean, but it addresses cleaning more than operation, and silicone mats may affect heating and the turntable's evenness function.

title: Overlapping lip seal instead of choke
new_elements: Conductive elastomer gasket (Metal-filled silicone gasket seals RF by contact, tolerating a slightly misaligned door)
rationale: A door that seals even when shut casually removes 'slam it harder' learning.
judge_comment: Conductive gaskets exist and are plausible, but the link to no-learning-curve operation is weak and leakage safety is a concern.

title: Rotating cavity, fixed food
new_elements: Slowly rotating waveguide feed ring (The feed port orbits around the cavity wall so the field sweeps the food)
rationale: Food stays where you put it, so handles and cups never spin out of reach.
judge_comment: A radical idea that keeps food stationary, but a rotating feed ring is mechanically complex and its field-sweeping effect is unproven.

title: Shadow-clock timer window
new_elements: Large mechanical countdown drum (Timer cam drives a drum with huge numerals and a shrinking colour bar visible from across the room)
rationale: Remaining time is read like a traffic light, not a tiny dial scale.
judge_comment: A large visible countdown drum makes the remaining time instantly readable and is mechanically simple, though it is incremental.

title: Single Big Button
new_elements: One-touch start/stop button (Replaces timer and power knobs with one button; each press adds 30 s at full power); Single-action cooking start (User starts heating with one press, no settings)
rationale: Removes all choices so anyone can operate it instantly.
judge_comment: Very simple and workable (similar to existing +30s buttons), but not radical and the user still has to judge how long to run it.

title: Weight-Sensing Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Weighs the food and sets time automatically); Automatic time setting by mass (No timer input needed)
rationale: The food itself tells the oven how long to run, eliminating the timer knob.
judge_comment: Weight alone is a poor predictor of heating time since food type matters, but it removes timer input and the load cell is plausible.

title: Steam-Stop Sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor auto-stop (Stops heating when steam burst indicates food is hot); Capacitive humidity sensing (Low-cost MEMS sensor)
rationale: Replaces timer with doneness detection so users never set a time.
judge_comment: Humidity or steam sensing for auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, yet it truly removes the need to set anything and uses a named low-cost sensor.

title: Door-Is-The-Switch
new_elements: Door-closure start interlock (Closing the door starts heating; opening stops it); Zero-control operation (Only action is door open/close)
rationale: No buttons or knobs at all; the door is the entire interface.
judge_comment: Radical zero-control interface, but the duration is undefined and starting on door close risks accidental or empty operation, which is a safety problem.

title: Egg-Timer Style Dial Only
new_elements: Single 0-10 min dial (Replaces both knobs; power fixed at full)
rationale: One familiar kitchen-timer gesture is all that is needed.
judge_comment: Mechanical timer dials are already common on microwaves, so this is familiar and easy but not novel.

title: Food-Picture Buttons
new_elements: Icon preset keypad (Buttons show cup, plate, popcorn, bowl; each runs a fixed program); Picture-based selection (No numbers or reading required)
rationale: Users match food to picture, no mental arithmetic on wattage or minutes.
judge_comment: Highly intuitive and easy to build, but picture presets are already common and not radical.

title: Voice Command Module
new_elements: Offline voice recogniser (Replaces knobs with spoken commands like 'two minutes'); Keyword-spotting ASR chip (No internet needed)
rationale: Talking is the most natural interface with zero learning.
judge_comment: Natural interface and feasible with offline keyword spotting, though noisy kitchens and existing products limit novelty.

title: IR Thermometer Auto-Stop
new_elements: Infrared surface-temperature sensor (Stops when food reaches 70 °C); Target-temperature cooking (Doneness replaces duration)
rationale: User never guesses time; oven stops when food is hot.
judge_comment: Doneness-based stopping removes time guessing, but IR only reads surface temperature and accuracy through a door is difficult.

title: Barcode Reader Door
new_elements: Package barcode scanner (Reads ready-meal code and sets program automatically); 1D barcode camera scanning (Low-cost CMOS camera)
rationale: Scanning the package removes all manual settings.
judge_comment: Scanning removes settings for packaged meals, but it only works for foods with compatible barcodes and instructions.

title: Foot Pedal Start
new_elements: Foot-pedal run switch (Oven heats only while pedal pressed, like a sewing machine)
rationale: Intuitive hold-to-run control with no timing decisions.
judge_comment: Hold-to-run is intuitive and wild, but it is tiring for long cooks and raises safety concerns around unattended operation and the door.

title: Hold-To-Heat Button
new_elements: Momentary dead-man heat button (Magnetron runs only while finger holds button); Direct manual duration control (User feels the duration, no counting)
rationale: Simplest possible control metaphor: press to heat, release to stop.
judge_comment: Press-and-hold control is instantly understood and substitutes the keypad and timer, though it is tiring for long heats and the dead-man switch is not very radical.

title: Sand Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Flip hourglass with optical end sensor (User flips hourglass; sensor stops oven when sand runs out)
rationale: Universally understood timing object replaces numbered dial.
judge_comment: A familiar hourglass metaphor requires no learning, but flipping it for each duration is fiddly, fixed durations are limiting, and the optical sensor adds complexity.

title: Colour-Change Window
new_elements: Thermochromic door panel (Glass turns from blue to red as cavity warms, no lamp needed); Thermochromic ink film (Passive, no power)
rationale: Status is read at a glance by colour with no display to learn.
judge_comment: It is a clever passive status cue, but it covers only status rather than operation, and a thermochromic door panel would be slow, unreliable and hard to keep shielded and safe.

title: LED Ring Progress
new_elements: LED ring around door (Fills as cooking proceeds, replaces bell and lamp)
rationale: Progress is visible from across the room without reading anything.
judge_comment: It is easy to build and intuitive for progress, but it is not very radical and does not simplify input controls.

title: Smartphone Camera Lens
new_elements: Phone cradle with mesh window (User's phone camera replaces lamp and viewing window)
rationale: Uses device users already know to monitor food.
judge_comment: Using the phone adds a dependency and extra steps that work against a no-learning-curve goal, and it raises safety and RF-mesh concerns.

title: Glass-Only Cavity
new_elements: Transparent mesh-laminated glass casing (Whole oven is see-through, no lamp or window holes)
rationale: What you see is what is happening; nothing hidden to understand.
judge_comment: A see-through cavity is physically implausible because microwaves need shielding, and visibility does little to simplify operation.

title: Rotating Drum Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Mode-stirrer fan (Replaces glass turntable with metal stirrer for even heating)
rationale: No turntable to remove, clean or misalign, so nothing to get wrong.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are an existing technology and removing the turntable helps a little, but it does nothing for the controls.

title: Flat-Bed Ceramic Floor
new_elements: Fixed ceramic floor with bottom antenna (Flat floor, no moving parts)
rationale: Any dish fits anywhere; no fitting a plate to a ring.
judge_comment: Flat-bed microwaves already exist and make loading easier, but the operating interface is unchanged.

title: Pull-Handle Door
new_elements: Magnetic-latch pull handle (Replaces push-release button with a fridge-style pull)
rationale: Everyone knows how to pull a handle; no hunting for a button.
judge_comment: Pull handles are common and intuitive, but they only affect opening the door, not operation.

title: Drawer Oven
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Food sits in a drawer; pushing it shut starts heating)
rationale: Drawer metaphor is familiar and closing it is the only action.
judge_comment: Closing the drawer to start heating is an intuitive single action, though it needs safe defaults for time and power, and the shielding is harder to engineer.

title: Auto-Open Door
new_elements: Spring auto-opening door at end (Door pops open when done, replacing bell)
rationale: End-of-cook is unmistakable and food is already accessible.
judge_comment: Easy and feasible, but it only addresses end-of-cook signaling and leaves the start and setup steps unchanged.

title: Toaster Lever
new_elements: Push-down toaster lever (Lever starts cooking and pops up when done)
rationale: Borrows the universally understood toaster gesture.
judge_comment: A toaster lever is an intuitive gesture that removes the learning curve, though it needs a fixed time or auto duration to work.

title: Two-Position Slider
new_elements: Warm/Cook slider (Replaces 5-step power cam with two settings)
rationale: Two obvious choices instead of five abstract power levels.
judge_comment: Simplifies the power choice with a cheap, workable substitution, but it is incremental rather than radical.

title: No Power Knob, Inverter Auto-Taper
new_elements: Inverter supply with automatic power taper (Starts full, reduces automatically as food warms); Inverter magnetron drive (Continuous power control)
rationale: Oven manages power itself so user never picks a level.
judge_comment: Removes the power decision through inverter control that already exists in the market, although cook time is still unaddressed.

title: Dish-Recognising Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera with food classifier (Identifies food type and sets program); Edge image classification (Tiny neural net on microcontroller)
rationale: Put food in, close door, done—no settings.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation fits the need well, but a camera and classifier is costly and not a simpler substitute, and classification can be unreliable.

title: RFID Container Tags
new_elements: RFID reader for tagged containers (Supplied containers carry program tags)
rationale: Container choice replaces settings; user learns nothing.
judge_comment: Tagged containers auto-select programs, so users set nothing, but they must use proprietary containers and the idea only loosely fits the substitute operator.

title: Reflected-Power Doneness
new_elements: Directional coupler load monitor (Detects change in absorbed microwave power to stop automatically); RF reflectometry (Senses food state via impedance)
rationale: Oven senses doneness electrically, removing timing from the user.
judge_comment: Reflected-power sensing could remove timing from the user and is plausible, but reliably detecting doneness across foods is hard.

title: Cup-Shaped Cavity
new_elements: Mug-only cylindrical cavity (Fits one mug; fixed program for drinks)
rationale: Single-purpose shape means there is only one way to use it.
judge_comment: A mug-only cavity is simple and radical in its constraint, but it is too limited for general microwave use.

title: Tactile Braille-Free Knob with Clicks
new_elements: Detent knob with one-minute haptic clicks (Each click equals one minute, no scale to read)
rationale: Counting clicks by feel replaces reading a dial.
judge_comment: A click-per-minute detent knob is easy to build and intuitive, but it is an incremental tweak to existing dials.

title: Gesture Wave Start
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (Wave hand to add 30 s)
rationale: Touch-free, no buttons, works with messy hands.
judge_comment: Wave-to-add-time is hands-free and feasible, but gestures may need some learning and it still requires timing decisions.

title: Spoken Progress Instead of Bell
new_elements: Speech synthesis speaker (Says 'your food is ready' instead of bell)
rationale: Plain language feedback needs no interpretation.
judge_comment: Voice feedback is clear and easy to build, but it only replaces the bell and doesn't simplify operation much; it is also a fairly common idea.

title: Transparent Turntable With Minute Marks
new_elements: Turntable as clock face (Turntable rotation itself shows elapsed time; no lamp or display)
rationale: Existing motion doubles as timer display, removing a control.
judge_comment: Using the turntable rotation as a timer display is a clever concept, but the rotation is hard to read as elapsed time and it doesn't help the user set anything.

title: Glow Door Instead of Lamp
new_elements: Edge-lit LED door glass (Door itself glows, replacing interior bulb)
rationale: Obvious on/off state visible from anywhere, nothing to learn.
judge_comment: An edge-lit door is feasible and makes the on/off state obvious, but it is a minor change with little effect on learning the operation.

title: Plate Clip Sensor
new_elements: Dish-presence switch (Oven refuses to start empty and auto-starts a default when dish placed)
rationale: Prevents the common mistake of running empty without any instructions.
judge_comment: Presence detection with an automatic default start removes the need for any controls and prevents running empty, though a default program can heat food wrongly.

title: Water Reservoir Steam Oven Hybrid
new_elements: Auto-fill steam cup (Replaces power-level knob; steam prevents drying so full power is always safe)
rationale: Always-full-power becomes forgiving, so no power choice is needed.
judge_comment: Always-safe steam heating removes the power-level choice and is bold, but the plumbing, cleaning and reliability burdens are heavy and the claim that full power is always safe is doubtful.

title: Doorbell Chime Replacement
new_elements: Pleasant wireless chime relay (Rings existing home doorbell receiver when done)
rationale: Reuses a sound users already associate with attention.
judge_comment: Done-alert via the existing doorbell is feasible but only addresses completion notification, not operation, and is not really a substitution that simplifies use.

title: Coin-Slot Style Token Timer
new_elements: Minute token slot (Drop one token per minute into slot; mechanical count sets time)
rationale: Physical counting is intuitive for children and elderly.
judge_comment: A token-per-minute mechanical timer is intuitive, zero-learning and cheap, and replaces the keypad in a playful, concrete way.

title: Wall-Plug Timer Removal
new_elements: Smart plug controlling magnetron power (Oven has no controls; external plug app or button starts it)
rationale: Oven becomes a dumb appliance; control lives where user already is.
judge_comment: Moving control to a smart plug adds an app and is hazardous or impractical since power cycling does not set time or power, making it less simple.

title: Weight-Gradient Floor
new_elements: Pressure-mat floor (Cheap resistive mat under ceramic floor senses load for auto-time); Force-sensitive resistor (Printed sensor)
rationale: Cheaper than load cell, still removes timer decision.
judge_comment: A force-sensitive mat could estimate load for automatic timing, but weight is a poor proxy for food heating needs and a ceramic floor complicates it.

title: Acoustic Popcorn Sensor
new_elements: Cavity microphone (Stops when popping or boiling sounds change)
rationale: Oven listens so user does not have to.
judge_comment: A cavity microphone that auto-stops removes the timing decision, but a microphone in a microwave cavity faces heat and noise issues and works only for certain foods.

title: Colour-Coded Dial Zones
new_elements: Three-colour dial (Green drink, yellow plate, red frozen; no numbers)
rationale: Colour zones map directly to tasks instead of minutes.
judge_comment: Intuitive and easy to build, but colour-coded presets are a fairly familiar idea and the substitution is mild.

title: Magnetron Replaced by Induction Plate
new_elements: Induction-heated ferrite dish (Dish heats by induction; simpler safety and no interlock door); Induction heating (Coil under floor)
rationale: Open-top design removes door and interlock complexity entirely.
judge_comment: Radical swap that removes the door, but it is no longer really a microwave, induction heating needs a ferrite dish, and an open top raises heat and safety problems, so the fit with simplicity is indirect.

title: Fixed-Time Capsule Oven
new_elements: Single fixed 90-second program (Only one program; repeat if needed)
rationale: Zero parameters; the only decision is whether to run again.
judge_comment: Zero learning curve and trivially feasible, but one 90-second program is too limiting for many foods.

title: Analog Clock-Hand Timer
new_elements: Large clock-face hand timer (Hand set to minute like a wall clock, visible from afar)
rationale: Leverages clock literacy everyone already has.
judge_comment: Uses familiar clock literacy and is easy to build, but it resembles old mechanical timers.

title: String-Pull Starter
new_elements: Pull-cord timer (Pull cord length sets time, like a bath-light cord)
rationale: Single gross motor action, usable with wet or gloved hands.
judge_comment: Quirky pull-cord input is easy to use with wet or gloved hands, but setting the time by cord length is imprecise and feels odd on a microwave.

title: Door Window Projection
new_elements: Pico-projector on door (Projects remaining time onto the food itself, replaces lamp)
rationale: Information appears where the user is already looking.
judge_comment: Projecting time onto the food is a neat display swap, but it doesn't simplify operation, and a projector is neither cheaper nor simpler than the lamp it replaces.

title: Self-Resetting Mechanical Bell Door
new_elements: Door-wound spring timer (Opening door winds timer; closing releases it for fixed run)
rationale: Energy and intent come from the one action users must do anyway.
judge_comment: A door-wound spring timer makes operation fully automatic with zero learning, though a fixed run time limits flexibility and the mechanism is somewhat awkward.

title: Scale-Free Portion Cups
new_elements: Marked portion container set (Fill-line containers map to the fixed program; no settings)
rationale: Standardised portions make a single program always correct.
judge_comment: Standardised portion cups make a single program workable, but they add accessories and only suit certain foods.

title: Thermal-Fuse Overcook Guard
new_elements: Resettable cavity thermostat cutoff (Stops oven if cavity air overheats, forgiving timer mistakes)
rationale: Errors become harmless so there is nothing to learn to avoid.
judge_comment: A thermostat cutoff is plausible and forgives mistakes, but it is a safety feature that does little to simplify operation and isn't very radical.

title: Lid Instead of Door
new_elements: Top-opening hinged lid (Chest-style lid replaces front door and release button)
rationale: Lifting a lid is universal; gravity keeps it closed, no latch to operate.
judge_comment: A top-opening lid is an intuitive opening action that removes the latch, but it does nothing for the controls and raises ergonomic and spill issues.

title: Food-pictogram dial replaces power knob
new_elements: Pictogram preset dial (Single dial with icons (soup, pizza, mug) that sets power and time together via a fixed cam.)
rationale: User picks a picture instead of understanding watts and minutes.
judge_comment: Icon-based presets are intuitive and mechanically plausible with a cam, though presets are somewhat common and fixed amounts limit accuracy.

title: Fixed-power oven, delete the power knob
new_elements: Single full-power operation (Remove the duty-cycle cam entirely; only a timer remains.)
rationale: One control is the shortest possible learning curve.
judge_comment: Removing the power control is very simple and cheap, but reduces function (defrosting, delicate food) and is not very radical.

title: 30-second tap button replaces clockwork timer
new_elements: Add-30s pushbutton (Each press adds 30 s; press starts immediately.)
rationale: No dial to read; tapping is self-explanatory and precise for short runs.
judge_comment: A tap-to-add-30s button is already common on microwaves, easy to understand and feasible, with a clear mechanism.

title: Hold-to-heat deadman button
new_elements: Momentary hold-to-cook switch (Magnetron runs only while the big front pad is held; release stops.)
rationale: Nothing to set; the user simply holds until the food looks ready.
judge_comment: Hold-to-cook is radical and needs no settings, but is tiring for long cooks and has safety/interlock design concerns.

title: IR surface thermometer replaces timer
new_elements: Thermopile IR food sensing (Non-contact sensor in cavity ceiling stops heating at a target temperature.); Cook-until-hot button (Single button; oven stops at 70 °C surface.)
rationale: Removes guessing of time and power altogether.
judge_comment: One-button cook-until-hot is ideal for no learning, but IR measures only surface temperature, giving unreliable results with uneven heating, and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Humidity-sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Steam exhaust humidity sensor (Detects vapour surge and ends the cycle.)
rationale: Press start once; the oven decides when it is done.
judge_comment: Humidity sensors already exist in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is plausible and helpful but not radical, and it does not remove the need to start the oven.

title: Weighing turntable sets the time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (Food mass read at door close; time derived automatically.)
rationale: Weight does the arithmetic so the user never does.
judge_comment: Automatic time from weight removes the main decision, and a load cell in the turntable hub is workable, though mass alone is a weak proxy for the right heating time.

title: Magnetic door replaces lever latch
new_elements: Magnetic door retention (Ferrite strip holds door; simple pull opens it, no button or hooks.)
rationale: Opening like a fridge needs no instruction.
judge_comment: Opening like a fridge is intuitive, but a weak magnetic hold is hard to square with the microwave safety interlock requirements, and the door is a small part of the learning curve.

title: Drawer-style cavity
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Cavity slides out on rails; closing it is the only action.)
rationale: Loading a drawer is universally understood and needs no latch button.
judge_comment: A drawer is familiar and distinctive, but sealing microwave leakage around a sliding cavity is very hard, and it is not cheaper or simpler.

title: Top-loading lid oven
new_elements: Hinged top lid cavity (Bread-bin style lid; gravity seals it, no latch mechanism.)
rationale: Drop food in, shut lid, done—no handles or buttons to learn.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid is a bold change, but gravity alone cannot meet the sealing and interlock requirements, and spills and visibility become problems.

title: Hall-effect door sensing replaces three microswitches
new_elements: Solid-state magnetic interlock (Hall sensors plus a single monitored relay perform redundant logic.)
rationale: Fewer wearing parts means the door always behaves the same, so users never meet odd failure modes.
judge_comment: Plausible solid-state interlock substitute, but the benefit to user operation or learning curve is indirect and the idea is not very radical.

title: Door hook is the HV plug
new_elements: Door-hook contact interlock (The door hook itself closes a mains contact; no separate switches.)
rationale: Door closed equals power present, an inherently obvious rule.
judge_comment: Using the door hook as a mains contact is a bold substitution, but it raises serious safety and regulatory problems and barely changes the user's learning curve.

title: Conductive elastomer gasket replaces choke seal
new_elements: Silver-loaded silicone RF gasket (Compressible conductive seal tolerant of misalignment.)
rationale: Door closes securely however casually it is pushed.
judge_comment: A conductive gasket could forgive sloppy door closing, though RF leakage and wear are real concerns, and the link to operation is modest.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Rotating metal stirrer blade (Fan in waveguide scatters field; flat fixed floor.)
rationale: No plate to seat, nothing to knock off the track.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves, so this is feasible and removes the plate-seating step, though it is not very novel.

title: Door-wound spring drives turntable
new_elements: Clockwork turntable wound by door (Closing the door winds a spring that rotates the plate for 10 min.)
rationale: Removes a motor and wiring with zero change in user behaviour.
judge_comment: A clockwork turntable wound by the door is a creative substitute, but a spring giving 10 minutes of rotation is impractical and the user benefit is small.

title: Under-floor rotating antenna
new_elements: Rotating feed antenna beneath ceramic floor (Antenna spins instead of food; floor is flat and wipeable.)
rationale: Any dish fits anywhere; no instructions about centring.
judge_comment: Rotating antenna under a flat floor (used in some commercial ovens) removes turntable and centring concerns, though the learning-curve benefit is modest.

title: Microtextured floor plate prevents superheating
new_elements: Laser-etched nucleation ceramic (Surface pits seed gentle boiling in mugs.)
rationale: Users need not learn the 'put a spoon in' rule.
judge_comment: Nucleation-site floor is clever for removing a safety rule, but it is unlikely to reliably prevent superheating in a mug sitting on the floor.

title: Inverter supply replaces diode-capacitor doubler
new_elements: Switch-mode HV inverter (Continuous true power control without stored HV capacitor.)
rationale: Enables a smooth 'gentle–fast' slider instead of a stepped cam the user must interpret.
judge_comment: Inverter power control already exists in consumer microwaves, and a slider is simpler than a stepped power menu, but it is not very radical.

title: Solid-state GaN RF source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Reflected-power sensing gives automatic doneness detection.)
rationale: Oven self-adjusts, leaving a single start button.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with feedback sensing could enable one-button autonomous cooking, which fits the need well, though cost and doneness accuracy remain challenges.

title: Neon charge indicator replaces bleeder resistor
new_elements: Neon HV-live lamp (Glows while capacitor holds charge, discharging it meanwhile.)
rationale: A visible 'still hot' cue needs no manual.
judge_comment: A neon indicator offers little for everyday operation and a lamp cannot safely replace a bleeder resistor's discharge function.

title: Electroluminescent cavity wall
new_elements: EL-coated cavity liner (Whole wall glows; no bulb socket or replacement.)
rationale: Nothing ever needs replacing or switching on.
judge_comment: Interesting substitute for the bulb, but it barely affects operational simplicity and EL panels have short lifespans and microwave-compatibility issues.

title: Transparent ITO-coated glass door, no mesh, no lamp
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide shielding glass (ITO layer blocks microwaves while fully clear.)
rationale: Seeing food clearly replaces any need for status indicators.
judge_comment: Clear visibility aids understanding, but ITO shielding at microwave frequencies with full transparency is technically doubtful, and the idea only loosely addresses the learning curve.

title: Ambient-light pipe replaces bulb
new_elements: Acrylic light pipe from front bezel (Pipes kitchen light into the cavity.)
rationale: Removes a bulb and a switch; illumination just happens.
judge_comment: Simple and cheap in principle, but ambient light is unreliable and it hardly improves ease of operation.

title: Door pops ajar at end instead of bell
new_elements: Spring door-release at timer zero (Timer cam releases latch; door cracks open as the 'done' signal.)
rationale: Open door is the most intuitive 'ready' signal possible.
judge_comment: Door opening as the done signal is intuitive and mechanically simple, replacing the buzzer, though it could release hot food unexpectedly.

title: Toaster-style pop-up tray
new_elements: Spring-lifted food tray (Tray rises to the opening when cooking finishes.)
rationale: Borrows a gesture everyone already knows from toasters.
judge_comment: Familiar toaster gesture is intuitive, but a moving tray in a microwave cavity is awkward and unsafe with liquids and plates.

title: Glass-ceramic waveguide cover
new_elements: Glass-ceramic (LAS) waveguide window (Dishwasher-safe rigid plate replaces mica.)
rationale: Wipe-clean interior means no maintenance rules to learn.
judge_comment: Practical substitution of mica, but only tangentially tied to learning-free operation.

title: Integrated molded ceramic cavity ceiling
new_elements: One-piece ceramic cavity top with feed window (Waveguide cover molded into the liner.)
rationale: No removable cover for users to lose or misfit.
judge_comment: Removes a user-facing part, though the link to operation simplicity is weak and ceramic molding is costly.

title: Voice duration input
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognition (Say 'two minutes' to start.)
rationale: Speaking a time requires no understanding of the interface.
judge_comment: Voice input is intuitive and feasible offline, though it adds components rather than substituting cheaper ones and is not very radical.

title: Gentle/Fast rocker replaces 5-step knob
new_elements: Two-position power rocker (Gentle (defrost/reheat) or Fast.)
rationale: Binary choice beats five numbered steps.
judge_comment: Directly cuts complexity with a cheap simple binary control, though the coarse choice limits flexibility.

title: Quartz escapement behind the same knob
new_elements: Quartz-timed knob with stepper return (Mechanical feel retained, electronic accuracy.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar twist gesture while fixing short-time error.
judge_comment: Retains the familiar twist gesture while improving accuracy, though the stepper adds cost and complexity.

title: 'A little – a lot' slider
new_elements: Linear fader labelled little/lot (Single slider maps to combined time and power curve.)
rationale: Qualitative scale removes numeracy from the task.
judge_comment: A single qualitative slider replaces numeric entry and is intuitive, though the combined time/power mapping is vague and imprecise for varied foods.

title: Door is the start switch
new_elements: Close-to-start, open-to-stop (Closing the door starts a fixed 1-min burst; reopen to stop.)
rationale: Zero buttons; the only control is the door.
judge_comment: The door as the only control is radical and needs no learning, but a fixed 1-minute burst is inflexible, and reopening to stop is already standard.

title: Packaging-code reader sets program
new_elements: Cavity-mounted barcode reader (Reads ready-meal code; sets time and power.)
rationale: Ready-meal eaters never read instructions again.
judge_comment: A barcode reader removes the need to read instructions for ready meals, but it only works for coded packaged food and adds cost and cavity-contamination issues.

title: Toe-kick door opener
new_elements: Foot-operated latch release (Pedal at base opens door for hands-full users.)
rationale: Opening with a foot is discoverable and hands-free.
judge_comment: A foot pedal helps hands-full users, but it does little for the operation-without-learning need, and it is not really a substitution.

title: Metallised polymer cavity
new_elements: Vacuum-metallised PPS cavity molding (Lightweight one-shot cavity with conductive coating.)
rationale: Lighter, cheaper oven for students; fewer seams to confuse cleaning.
judge_comment: A metallised polymer cavity is a material swap with almost no link to simple operation, and its thermal and RF durability is doubtful.

title: Metal-detect refusal replaces the 'no metal' rule
new_elements: Floor eddy-current metal sensor (Oven simply won't start with metal inside.)
rationale: Substitutes a user rule with a machine rule.
judge_comment: Removes the need to learn the no-metal rule, though reliable detection of foil or metal trim is hard and false refusals could frustrate users.

title: Thermal-feedback 'warm/hot' knob
new_elements: Target-temperature knob (Knob sets desired food temperature; power modulates to reach it.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not in watts.
judge_comment: Setting a target temperature matches how people think and removes power and time guesswork, but it needs reliable food temperature sensing, such as IR, which is tricky.

title: Lamp stays on as the done signal
new_elements: Light-until-opened completion cue (Cavity lamp remains lit after cycle until door opens; bell removed.)
rationale: Silent, obvious, and needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive as a done cue, but it is a minor change and not radical.

title: Light-bar countdown replaces dial pointer
new_elements: Shrinking LED time bar (Bar length equals remaining time; no numbers.)
rationale: Remaining time is read at a glance like a progress bar.
judge_comment: A progress-bar countdown is instantly understood and cheap to build, though it is only modestly novel.

title: Hand-crank timer
new_elements: Crank-wound escapement timer (One crank turn equals one minute; unwinds visibly.)
rationale: Physical effort maps directly to cooking time.
judge_comment: A wind-up crank timer is tactile and needs no learning, and it is mechanically plausible, but it is limited in precision and a little gimmicky.

title: Tactile-notch blind dial
new_elements: Detented knob with raised minute bumps (Each click is 15 s; feelable without looking.)
rationale: Usable in dim dorm kitchens or by visually impaired users.
judge_comment: A detented tactile dial is easy to use without learning and simple to build, but it is an incremental substitution rather than a radical one.

title: Gravity drop door
new_elements: Lift-up counterweighted door (Lift to open, let go to close; no latch, no button.)
rationale: Letting go always leaves the oven in the safe closed state.
judge_comment: A lift-up counterweighted door removes the latch and button, but the door-safety interlock is hard to get right and the effect on operation is modest.

title: Defrost-only toggle
new_elements: Snowflake toggle switch (Only alternative to full power is a 30% defrost mode.)
rationale: Covers the single real-world use of low power with one icon.
judge_comment: Limiting power choices to full or defrost cuts complexity, but it covers only part of the operation and removes flexibility.

title: Cordless kettle-style docking base
new_elements: Contact-ring docking base (Oven lifts off a powered base; no plug handling.)
rationale: Plugging-in disappears as a step for dorm movers.
judge_comment: A cordless docking base removes the plug step, but a microwave draws high power through contact rings, which is a safety and cost problem, and the idea has little to do with operating the oven.

title: Magnetic breakaway mains connector
new_elements: Magnetic mains coupler (Snaps onto the oven; detaches safely if pulled.)
rationale: Connection is self-aligning and foolproof.
judge_comment: A magnetic breakaway mains connector is plausible, as on some appliances, but plugging in is a one-time step and the idea does not help everyday operation.

title: PTC self-limiting magnetron cooling
new_elements: PTC thermistor current limiting (Inherent resistance rise throttles power when hot; no snap disc.)
rationale: Oven never abruptly trips, so users never puzzle over a dead unit.
judge_comment: PTC limiting is plausible but oddly applied to a magnetron and only loosely tied to operating simplicity.

title: Wax-motor overheat vent
new_elements: Wax-actuator vent flap (Thermal wax opens extra airflow before shutdown is needed.)
rationale: Passive self-care removes a failure mode the user would have to understand.
judge_comment: A wax actuator is feasible and concrete, but it addresses a failure mode users rarely face and barely helps operation.

title: Rocking-floor instead of turntable
new_elements: Cam-rocked ceramic floor (Floor tilts slowly to shift standing-wave pattern.)
rationale: Square dishes fit; nothing to align.
judge_comment: A rocking floor is novel and removes the need to align dishes, but a tilting floor risks spills and its effect on heating evenness is doubtful.

title: Single dial for both time and power
new_elements: Dual-cam combined dial (Early rotation = defrost region, later rotation = full power minutes.)
rationale: Two knobs collapse into one twist.
judge_comment: One dial that combines time and power directly cuts operating steps and is easy to build with cams, though it is not very radical.

title: Cup-shaped cavity for the mug use-case
new_elements: Mug-sized mini cavity with lid (Tiny oven sized for one mug or bowl; fixed 90 s burst on lid close.)
rationale: A product with one purpose needs no settings at all.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug oven that runs a fixed burst when the lid closes removes settings entirely and is realistic, though it narrows the product's use.

title: Self-locking door latch replaces monitor switch
new_elements: Solenoid-locked door during RF (Door physically cannot open while magnetron runs; interlock chain shrinks to one switch.)
rationale: User can never do the wrong thing, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A solenoid door lock during RF does simplify the interlock chain, but it barely addresses learning curve (users already know to open the door), and it frustrates users who want to pause mid-cycle, plus safety regulations still require redundant interlocks, so it's not very radical or wholly on-need.

title: Single combined time-and-dish dial
new_elements: Single dish-pictogram dial (one knob sets time and power together) (One cam knob with icons (mug, plate, soup, defrost) that sets a paired time/duty-cycle profile.)
rationale: Two knobs become one; the user chooses what they are heating, not minutes or watts.
judge_comment: Dish-icon dial simplifies to one control, though similar preset dials already exist and it is not very radical.

title: Toaster-style pop-up lever
new_elements: Push-down spring lever timer (Pressing the lever down starts cooking; lever position = duration; it pops up with a click when done.); Bimetal/spring escapement timer (Toaster-grade mechanism, no synchronous motor, mains-frequency independent.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster lever works; zero instructions needed.
judge_comment: Toaster lever is a familiar metaphor that needs no learning, and a mechanical timer is plausible, though the pop-up lever must be adapted to a door-interlocked microwave.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Large hold-to-heat button (Magnetron runs only while the single big button is held; release stops heating instantly.)
rationale: No timer to understand at all; heating is as direct as holding a tap open.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive and simple to build, but holding it for minutes is tiring and impractical.

title: Weight-sets-time turntable scale
new_elements: Spring scale under turntable (Food weight mechanically sets the cam timer; heavier load = longer run.); Mechanical load-cell linkage (Spring-plate deflection drives timer cam position.)
rationale: User places food and presses start; the machine decides duration from mass.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing removes decisions, but mass poorly predicts heating time, so it is unreliable and mechanically fiddly.

title: Steam-stop sensor replaces timer
new_elements: Humidity sensor auto-stop (Cheap humidity sensor in the vent cuts power when steam burst indicates food is hot.)
rationale: No duration decision needed; closed-loop stopping removes the main guesswork.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on steam removes duration guesswork entirely, though sensor-cook exists already and works poorly for dry or covered foods.

title: Target-temperature dial (warm / hot / boiling)
new_elements: IR thermometer with 3-position temperature dial (Non-contact IR sensor stops heating when food surface reaches the chosen temperature.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not minutes and watts; the dial speaks their language.
judge_comment: A temperature dial matches how people think and removes time/power guessing, though IR surface sensing is imperfect and the part is not cheaper.

title: Fixed single power, no power knob
new_elements: Hard-wired 100% power (knob deleted) (Remove the duty-cycle cam entirely; defrost handled by shorter timer scale markings.)
rationale: One fewer control eliminates the most misunderstood setting on a microwave.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob is simple and cheap, but defrosting and delicate foods become harder and the idea isn't radical.

title: Preset physical buttons instead of dials
new_elements: Three big mechanical preset buttons (Mug / Plate / Defrost) (Each button mechanically winds a fixed cam position; no numbers anywhere.)
rationale: Pressing the picture of what you have is a zero-learning interaction.
judge_comment: Pictorial preset buttons driving a mechanical cam are easy to understand and build, but similar presets already exist.

title: Capsule-pod microwave
new_elements: Keyed food pod with mechanical time/power code (Pod ribs push pins that set timer and duty cycle, like a coffee capsule machine.); Ready-meal convenience (Pre-portioned meals that cook correctly without settings.)
rationale: Insert pod, press go; the packaging carries the knowledge, not the user.
judge_comment: A keyed pod that sets time and power mechanically is wild and zero-learning, but it needs a pod ecosystem and limits what can be cooked.

title: Package-barcode reader sets cooking
new_elements: Cavity camera reading package cook codes (Low-cost camera reads a printed code on the packaging and loads time/power automatically.); 2D barcode optical recognition (Commodity QR decoding on a microcontroller.)
rationale: Reading the instructions is done by the oven, not the user.
judge_comment: Reading package codes automatically is workable with commodity QR decoding, though it depends on packaging adoption and does nothing for non-packaged food.

title: Drawer cavity replaces hinged door
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Whole cavity floor slides out on rails; choke seal at drawer face replaces hinges, latch and button.)
rationale: A drawer is the most familiar kitchen gesture and needs no button to find.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist but are rare, and the drawer removes the door button; it doesn't address timer or power controls, so the learning curve only shrinks a little.

title: Top-loading lid oven
new_elements: Top-loading hinged lid with choke rim (Slow-cooker style lid; gravity keeps it closed, no latch lever needed.)
rationale: Lifting a lid and dropping a bowl in is instinctive, especially for elderly users.
judge_comment: The top-loading lid is intuitive and unusual, but a gravity-closed lid raises RF safety and interlock concerns and it only addresses door opening.

title: Magnetic pull-handle door, no release button
new_elements: Magnetic gasket door with handle (Fridge-style magnetic strip holds door; pulling the handle opens it and trips interlock.)
rationale: No hidden button to locate; the door opens like every other door in the home.
judge_comment: A pull handle removes the hidden button, but the magnetic seal must hold RF containment and many microwaves already use handles.

title: Door-handle twist is the timer
new_elements: Rotary door handle that winds the timer (Closing the door and twisting the handle sets minutes; untwisting stops.)
rationale: One gesture closes, locks and starts; there is nothing else to operate.
judge_comment: Combining close, lock, set time and start into one twist gesture directly removes the learning curve, though the mechanical timer and interlock need engineering.

title: Sliding pocket door
new_elements: Side-sliding mesh door on rails (Door slides into a side pocket; no hinge, no swing clearance, no release button.)
rationale: A one-direction slide is simpler for weak hands than button-plus-swing.
judge_comment: A sliding mesh door is easy to operate, but a sliding seal with mesh is hard to make RF-tight and it leaves the controls unchanged.

title: Open-ended tunnel cavity, no door at all
new_elements: Doorless cut-off waveguide tunnel cavity (Long below-cutoff entry tube with absorbing chokes, as in industrial conveyor ovens.); Below-cutoff waveguide attenuation (Tube narrower than cutoff size attenuates 2.45 GHz exponentially.)
rationale: Nothing to open or close; slide food in and out like a bread box.
judge_comment: Radical and grounded in real industrial conveyor-oven chokes, but a doorless home cavity is hard to make safe and compact, and it only loosely helps ease of use.

title: Transparent conductive-film window
new_elements: Clear ITO/metal-mesh coated glass door (Invisible conductive coating shields RF while giving an unobstructed view.)
rationale: Seeing food clearly lets users judge doneness without understanding timers.
judge_comment: Conductive-film windows are plausible, but a clearer view barely reduces the learning curve, and metal mesh already exists in microwave doors.

title: One 'Go' button, each press adds a minute
new_elements: Single +1 min start button with tally lights (Press starts 1 minute at full power; each extra press adds one more; nothing else on the panel.)
rationale: A single control with one obvious rule is the minimum possible learning curve.
judge_comment: A single-button interface is very easy to use and cheap to build, though a similar one-touch +30s function already exists.

title: Linear slider instead of rotary timer
new_elements: Horizontal slide timer with large print scale (Slider rack drives the cam; position is readable at a glance from across the room.)
rationale: Left-to-right 'more' maps to intuition and is easier for arthritic hands than twisting.
judge_comment: A slider is more intuitive and accessible than a twist knob and is mechanically workable, though it is only an incremental change.

title: Gravity weight-drop timer
new_elements: Weight-driven escapement timer (A lifted weight descends through an escapement; no motor, no mains frequency dependence.)
rationale: Lift the weight, let go: a cuckoo-clock gesture that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: The weight-drop timer is a charming, intuitive gesture, but it is awkward in a kitchen appliance and has limited practical value.

title: Hourglass sand timer window
new_elements: Flip hourglass with optical end sensor (User flips a 2-minute hourglass; photodiode cuts power when sand finishes.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible as sand; the concept is understood by every age.
judge_comment: Intuitive visible timer, but a fixed 2-minute duration limits flexibility and a mechanical hourglass is awkward inside a microwave interface.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Pull-string spring timer (Pull a cord like a toy; length pulled sets duration, cord rewinds as it counts down.)
rationale: A single tug is a gross-motor action that is impossible to do wrong.
judge_comment: A mechanical pull timer is intuitive and cheap, much like classic dial timers, and has no learning curve.

title: Foot-pedal start
new_elements: Floor pedal start/stop (Hands-free pedal runs the oven while pressed, for users carrying dishes.)
rationale: No panel to read; press foot, food heats.
judge_comment: Simple, but holding a pedal for the entire heating time is tiring and awkward, and it may raise safety concerns.

title: Voice command instead of knobs
new_elements: Offline keyword voice module (Recognises 'one minute', 'defrost', 'stop' locally without cloud.); Edge speech recognition (Small-vocabulary keyword spotting on a low-cost MCU.)
rationale: Speaking what you want removes any interface to learn.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is practical and learning-free, but voice control on appliances is already common and it does not replace anything cheaper or simpler.

title: Door-close equals start
new_elements: Close-to-start door switch with fixed 60 s cycle (Shutting the door starts a 1-minute run; opening stops; repeat as needed.)
rationale: The only action is closing the door, which the user must do anyway.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is extremely simple and cheap, but the fixed 60 s cycle limits control and risks accidental starts.

title: Shelf height sets power
new_elements: Multi-level rack where height sets field intensity (Lower rack = strong field node, upper rack = weak; power chosen by where you put the dish.)
rationale: Power becomes a physical placement decision instead of an abstract number.
judge_comment: Creative physical-placement metaphor, but standing-wave nodes are unstable and depend on load, so power-by-height would be unreliable and arguably adds a new thing to learn.

title: Reflected-power auto power level
new_elements: Reflected-power sensor auto duty cycle (Directional coupler measures load absorption and sets on/off ratio automatically.)
rationale: The oven picks the power itself, so the knob and its confusion disappear.
judge_comment: Auto power selection from reflected-power sensing removes a whole decision, though it is a sensor addition rather than a cheap substitution, and the sensing is difficult to do well.

title: Triac phase control replaces cam power switch
new_elements: Continuous inverter power control (Switch-mode supply varies magnetron anode current for true continuous power.)
rationale: 'Low' actually means gentle, so results match expectation without learning quirks.
judge_comment: Inverter control already exists in commercial ovens; it makes low power behave better but the user still has to choose a setting, and the title (triac) contradicts the described switch-mode supply.

title: Thermochromic plate tells you when to stop
new_elements: Colour-changing turntable plate (Plate turns from blue to red at serving temperature; visible through the window.)
rationale: A colour cue replaces mental arithmetic about minutes.
judge_comment: An intuitive visual doneness cue needs no learning, but plate color reflects plate temperature rather than food temperature, and it only tells you when to stop and doesn't help with starting.

title: Big-button wired remote for elderly
new_elements: Tethered two-button remote (Go / Stop) (Oversized tactile buttons on a cord so controls sit at hand or lap height.)
rationale: Two large buttons anywhere you like is simpler than knobs on a high counter.
judge_comment: A two-button Go/Stop remote is very simple and easy to build, but it only moves the controls and hides the time and power decisions.

title: Water-cup dosing timer
new_elements: Drip reservoir timer (Pour water into a cup; it drains through an orifice and a float switch stops heating when empty.)
rationale: More water = more time is a tangible, self-explaining measure.
judge_comment: Wildly novel and tangible water-to-time mapping, but it's irrelevant for most foods and adds plumbing and spill and safety issues.

title: Mug-detect automatic beverage mode
new_elements: Turntable mug-ring sensor (A reed/pressure ring detects a cup footprint and runs a fixed beverage cycle on close.)
rationale: The most common task (reheating a drink) needs zero settings.
judge_comment: Zero-setting for the most common task is plausible with a simple sensor, though it covers just one use case.

title: Light-bar progress replaces clockwork dial
new_elements: Touch-length LED bar timer (Swipe along a strip to light minutes; LEDs extinguish as time elapses.)
rationale: Remaining time is a shrinking bar, legible without reading numbers.
judge_comment: An LED bar with swipe input is cheap, intuitive and easy to build, but it's an incremental change from existing touch interfaces.

title: Repeat-last-run single key
new_elements: Mechanical memory stop on timer cam (A sliding stop remembers last setting so one press re-runs the same cook.)
rationale: Most households repeat the same few cooks; one press reproduces them.
judge_comment: One-press repeat is simple and useful, but it is not radical and the mechanical memory stop is vaguely described.

title: RFID dish tags set the cycle
new_elements: RFID reader under turntable with tagged containers (Microwave-safe containers carry a tag encoding their contents' cook profile.)
rationale: The container knows the recipe; the user only has to put it in.
judge_comment: The container-as-recipe idea is radical and needs no user input, but it requires a tagged-container ecosystem and is impractical for ordinary dishes.

title: Tactile high-contrast rotary timer
new_elements: Oversized ridged knob with raised numerals and detents (Each minute is a click; 1-minute increments felt and heard, braille-style markings.)
rationale: Same mechanism, but settable by feel and audible clicks for low-vision users.
judge_comment: Detented tactile knobs are already common on microwaves, so this is helpful for simple operation but not radical.

title: Talking timer bell
new_elements: Voice-announcing end chime (Replaces mechanical bell with a sound chip saying 'your food is ready' and the minutes set.)
rationale: Spoken feedback confirms what the user did, removing uncertainty.
judge_comment: A voice confirmation is cheap and feasible and reduces uncertainty, but it is incremental and only indirectly cuts the learning curve.

title: Door-edge pull tab, no latch lever
new_elements: Full-width finger lip on door edge (Snap-fit plastic detent holds door; a gentle pull anywhere along the lip opens it.)
rationale: No small button to hunt for; the whole edge is the handle.
judge_comment: A full-width pull lip removes the need to find a button, though door-handle microwaves already exist.

title: Motorised auto-closing door
new_elements: Motor-driven door that closes when start is pressed (Pressing Go swings the door shut and locks; stop re-opens it.)
rationale: Forgetting to close the door is no longer an error the user can make.
judge_comment: An auto-closing door removes one error, but the motor and lock add cost and complexity, which runs against SUBSTITUTE's aim of cheaper and simpler.

title: Roll-up shutter door
new_elements: Tambour conductive shutter (Interlocked metal slats roll up into the top; overlapping slats form the RF seal.)
rationale: Push up to open, pull down to close: a bread-bin gesture with no button.
judge_comment: A roll-up conductive shutter is a radical, intuitive bread-bin gesture, but it is hard to make a reliable RF seal and keep the slats clean.

title: Soft-close damped door with auto-latch
new_elements: Damped self-latching hinge (Hydraulic hinge pulls the door shut from any angle under ~20°, no slam, no button.)
rationale: A nudge is enough to close properly, so 'door not closed' confusion vanishes.
judge_comment: Practical and feasible, but it fixes a minor confusion and is a modest substitution of the latch rather than a radical idea.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Flat ceramic floor with rotating stirrer fan (No glass plate to align or break; any dish shape fits on a flat floor.); Rotating metal mode stirrer (Fan blades in the waveguide scramble standing-wave patterns for even heating.)
rationale: Removes the turntable alignment and cleaning puzzle that confuses new users.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers and flat floors already exist in many ovens, so it is feasible but not novel, and it only mildly reduces the learning curve.

title: Camera-in-cavity doneness stop
new_elements: Cavity camera detecting bubbling/steam (Low-cost camera watches for boil onset or fog and stops heating; also streams to front display.)
rationale: The oven watches the food so the user does not have to set or supervise time.
judge_comment: Camera-based auto-stop removes time setting entirely, but steam fogging and reliable detection across foods are hard.

title: Bimetal cavity thermostat timer
new_elements: Cavity-air bimetal thermostat cut-out (Simple bimetal strip in exhaust air opens the circuit once outgoing air reaches a set temperature.)
rationale: A kettle-style thermostat is cheaper than clockwork and needs no setting.
judge_comment: A cheap thermostat that needs no setting is a clever substitution, but exhaust air temperature is a poor proxy for doneness and varies with food and quantity.

title: Gesture wave start/stop
new_elements: IR proximity wave sensor (Wave once to start a minute, wave again to stop; no touch, no knobs.)
rationale: A single wave is universally understood and works with messy hands.
judge_comment: A wave gesture is intuitive and easy to build, but a fixed one-minute run does not adapt to different foods.

title: Dish-type colour-coded plates
new_elements: Optical colour sensor reading coloured bundled plates (Red plate = dinner, blue = drink, green = defrost; sensor sets cycle automatically.)
rationale: Choosing a coloured plate replaces choosing time and power.
judge_comment: Color-coded plates make the cycle choice automatic and need no learning, but they lock users into proprietary plates and offer little flexibility.

title: Volume-based time: dish footprint sensor
new_elements: Capacitive floor grid measuring dish footprint (Covered area of the cavity floor sets duration proportionally.)
rationale: Bigger dish automatically means longer heating with no input required.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is appealing, but dish footprint is a poor proxy for food mass or type, and a capacitive floor grid is unreliable under a glass plate.

title: Microcontroller + encoder in place of cam timer
new_elements: Low-cost MCU with rotary encoder and buzzer (Replaces synchronous motor, cams and bell; seconds-accurate and mains-frequency independent.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar knob feel while making short durations exact, so results match intent.
judge_comment: A cheap, practical swap that keeps the familiar knob, though it is incremental and not radical, and it adds little simplicity beyond accuracy.

title: NFC phone-tap preset
new_elements: NFC pad accepting phone or card taps (Tap a fridge-magnet card ('soup', 'tea') or a phone to load the cycle.)
rationale: Tapping a labelled card is as simple as a transit gate.
judge_comment: Tap-to-load presets are easy to build and simple to use, but they require cards or a phone, which adds steps for some users.

title: Movable wall sets power by cavity size
new_elements: Sliding rear cavity wall (User pushes the back wall in or out; cavity Q and field density change heating intensity.)
rationale: 'Small space heats fast, big space heats gently' is intuitive physical reasoning.
judge_comment: The idea is wildly original, but a moving wall is mechanically complex, the physics is unpredictable, and manual positioning is not intuitive for heating.

title: Honeycomb-free solid metallised window with outside mirror view
new_elements: Solid steel door with periscope mirror viewer (Door is plain stamped steel; a small choked periscope slot and mirrors show the cavity interior.)
rationale: Cheaper door still lets users check food visually, keeping operation guess-free.
judge_comment: A periscope viewer in a solid steel door is a creative substitution for the perforated glass window, but it mainly cuts cost and only weakly serves a no-learning-curve operation, and a tiny slot with mirrors would give poor, dim visibility while adding grease and cleaning problems.

title: Single big dial replaces timer + power knobs
new_elements: Mechanical timer knob + power knob (Two legacy knobs the user must coordinate); One-dial heat-amount knob (Single knob scaled in 'cups of soup' / 'plates' that sets time and power jointly via a cam); Set heating with one gesture (User turns one thing and walks away)
rationale: Removes the two-variable mental model so nothing has to be learned.
judge_comment: A single dial scaled in portions that sets time and power through a cam is plausible and simple, but it is only a modest step beyond existing dials.

title: Weighing turntable replaces timer knob
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer (User guesses minutes); Spring-scale turntable (Food weight compresses a spring that mechanically winds the timer proportionally); Auto-set time by weight (Heavier food gets longer heating without any input)
rationale: User never chooses a duration; put food in, press start.
judge_comment: A spring-scale turntable that winds the timer by weight needs no user input, though weight correlates imperfectly with heating time and the mechanism has to be built robustly.

title: Steam-sensor cutoff replaces timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer bell (Fixed-duration stop); Humidity sensor stop (Cheap hygristor in exhaust cuts power when food steams); Stop when food is hot (Done means done, not minutes elapsed)
rationale: Zero settings: the oven itself knows when to stop.
judge_comment: A humidity sensor that stops heating is a proven approach (sensor-cook) and gives zero settings, but it is not very radical and it works poorly for dry foods.

title: IR thermometer replaces power knob
new_elements: 5-step duty-cycle power cam (Abstract power levels); IR food-temperature thermostat (Thermopile aimed at food, magnetron cycles until surface reaches eating temperature); Heat to eating temperature (Target outcome, not wattage)
rationale: Power levels disappear; the only concept is 'warm'.
judge_comment: A thermopile that cycles the magnetron until the food reaches eating temperature is conceptually clean, but it reads only surface temperature and adds cost over the basic design.

title: Single START button only
new_elements: Timer + power knobs (Legacy controls); One hard button (Press once = 1 min full power; press again adds a minute; hold = stop); Count presses as minutes (Vending-machine simplicity)
rationale: A single affordance cannot be misused.
judge_comment: One button that adds a minute per press is very simple and easy to build, but it is a common idea and gives little control over time or power.

title: Door-close starts the oven
new_elements: Start action via knob twist (Separate start step); Door-latch start switch (Closing the door begins heating; opening stops it); Start by closing door (No start control at all)
rationale: The only act the user already knows how to do starts the process.
judge_comment: Close-to-start is simple and intuitive, but it still needs a way to set the time, and accidental starts with an empty cavity are a safety risk.

title: Foot pedal replaces knobs
new_elements: Front-panel knobs (Hands-busy users struggle); Foot pedal timer (Press pedal with foot while holding plate; heating runs as long as pedal held or per stomp); Hands-free control (Like a bin lid)
rationale: Universally understood pedal gesture, no panel to read.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is novel and hands-free, but it is awkward to hold for long heating times and a pedal-held microwave raises ergonomic and safety questions.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Clockwork dial timer (Numbers to read); Flip sand-glass timer (Flip the glass to start; a float switch stops heating when sand runs out); Visible analog countdown (Everyone understands sand running)
rationale: Pre-literate, pre-numeric time setting.
judge_comment: A sand-glass timer is charming and needs no numbers, but a float switch driven by sand is imprecise and impractical, and the fixed durations are limiting.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Rotary timer knob (Requires grip and reading); Pull-string wind-up (Pull cord like a toy; the further pulled, the longer it runs, retracting as it counts); Length-as-time setting (Direct physical mapping)
rationale: Pulling harder = heating longer is intuitive to a toddler.
judge_comment: A pull-cord has a direct length-to-time mapping that anyone grasps, and a retracting spring timer is plausible mechanically, though precision and wear are concerns.

title: Slider with food pictograms
new_elements: Numbered time knob (Minutes are abstract); Pictogram slider (Slider stops at icons: mug, plate, frozen box, popcorn; each is a fixed cam program); Select by picture (Language-free)
rationale: Users match food to picture instead of computing time.
judge_comment: A pictogram slider with cam programs is cheap, language-free and needs no learning, though it is less radical and less flexible than the other ideas.

title: Barcode-reading door
new_elements: Manual time/power entry (User reads package and transcribes); Barcode scanner in door frame (Pass the package past the door; oven looks up heating instructions); Auto-program from packaging (Package tells the oven)
rationale: Instructions are already on the box; the oven reads them so the user doesn't.
judge_comment: Scanning the package removes manual entry and learning, but it needs a barcode-to-instructions database that barely exists, and the substitution is more of an addition.

title: RFID smart dishes
new_elements: Power/time controls (Set per use); RFID-tagged bowls and turntable reader (Each household dish carries a tag encoding its default program); Dish selects program (Soup bowl always does soup)
rationale: Choosing a bowl is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Choosing the dish becomes the interface, which is intuitive, but it needs special tagged dishes and the tags must survive microwaving.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Human setting choice (Guesswork); Cavity camera + food classifier (Tiny camera identifies pizza/soup/frozen and picks program); Recognize food and heat (No input)
rationale: The oven does the thinking the user used to do.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation fits the need well, and cavity cameras with classifiers already exist, though recognition is imperfect and not cheap.

title: Voice command replaces panel
new_elements: Knobs and buttons (Must be found and interpreted); Offline voice module (Say 'warm my coffee'; cheap keyword chip, no cloud); Speak the goal (Natural language)
rationale: Talking needs no instruction manual.
judge_comment: Voice control is easy to use and feasible with offline chips, but it is a common idea with limited vocabulary and little novelty.

title: Thermochromic bell replacement
new_elements: Mechanical end bell (Audible only, missed when away); Thermochromic turntable (Glass changes colour when food above it is hot; readout is the food itself); Show doneness by colour (Glance tells state)
rationale: Red means hot, universally understood, no clock reading.
judge_comment: A thermochromic turntable that shows food heat is a creative substitute for the bell, but it only displays state and does not simplify setting up, and turntable glass colour tied to food temperature is physically doubtful.

title: Door pops open at end
new_elements: Bell + push-release button (Two things to notice and operate); Spring auto-open latch (Timer release lets the door swing ajar like a toaster pop); Signal and release in one (Open door = done)
rationale: Toaster logic: nothing to press, the oven hands the food back.
judge_comment: Spring-ajar door replaces bell plus button; simple and plausible, though some microwaves already have similar pop-open doors, and it only partly addresses starting the cook.

title: Drawer replaces hinged door
new_elements: Hinged door + release button (Button hunting); Pull-out drawer cavity (Food sits on a drawer; push shut to start, pull to stop); Load like a drawer (Familiar kitchen gesture)
rationale: Drawers need no instructions.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive gesture and exists in commercial drawer microwaves, but RF sealing and push-to-start are harder and the swap isn't clearly cheaper.

title: Top-loading lid
new_elements: Front door with button (Side access and latch); Pot-style hinged lid (Lift lid, drop food, close lid starts; looks like a saucepan); Cook-pot metaphor (Behaves like cookware)
rationale: Borrows a mental model everyone already owns.
judge_comment: The pot-lid metaphor is familiar, but top-loading microwaves are awkward for ergonomics and spills, and the start/time input still isn't addressed.

title: Transparent casing, no lamp
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp + mesh window (Dim, bulb fails); ITO-coated glass cavity (Fully transparent conductive glass shields RF while ambient light shows food); See food directly (No window, no bulb)
rationale: Checking progress needs no learned window-peering.
judge_comment: An ITO glass cavity is radical and removes the lamp, but it is costly and has serious RF and heat problems, and it only loosely serves a no-learning-curve operation.

title: Webcam view on fridge/phone
new_elements: Incandescent lamp + door mesh (Must stand at the oven); Cavity webcam (Streams food view to any screen); Remote glance (Check from the sofa)
rationale: Monitoring becomes passive.
judge_comment: A webcam is feasible but adds complexity and cost, so it runs against simplicity and mostly serves remote monitoring rather than ease of operation.

title: Projected countdown on the food
new_elements: Small dial scale (Hard to read remaining time); Mini projector in lamp socket (Replaces bulb; projects shrinking light ring onto the plate); Light = time left (Readable from across room)
rationale: Status shown where the eye already looks.
judge_comment: Projected countdown is clever and intuitive for reading status, but it doesn't remove the need to set time, so it only partly addresses zero learning curve.

title: Colour-changing cavity light
new_elements: White incandescent lamp (Only illuminates); RGB LED cavity light (Blue while heating, green when done, red if too hot); Encode state in light (Traffic-light semantics)
rationale: Same lamp, now also the display.
judge_comment: Easy, cheap and intuitive status feedback, but it is incremental and does not simplify input; heat-state colors are also hard to sense accurately.

title: Fixed-food cavity sized for one mug
new_elements: 20 L general cavity + controls (Generality demands settings); Mug-only cavity (Hole exactly fits a mug; one wattage, one time; cup detected by weight); Do one thing (Single-purpose appliance)
rationale: Constraining the task eliminates all decisions.
judge_comment: Removes all decisions via a single-purpose mug cavity with weight detection; highly relevant though limited in versatility.

title: Solid-state RF replaces magnetron + power cam
new_elements: Magnetron + duty-cycle cam (Uneven heating, cold spots cause misuse); Solid-state RF amplifier array (Feedback via reflected power finds food and heats evenly); Self-adaptive even heating (No stirring, no turning)
rationale: Removes the learned rituals of stirring and half-time turning.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and removes stirring rituals, but is costly rather than cheaper and does not directly simplify the controls.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Glass turntable + roller ring (Must be seated correctly, breaks); Fan-blade mode stirrer (Rotating metal blades in roof spread the field; flat fixed floor); Even field with flat floor (Nothing to align)
rationale: No turntable to misplace or jam.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are existing tech and remove a minor misplacement issue, with limited effect on operational learning.

title: Sliding shelf conveyor
new_elements: Turntable (Rotation only); Belt-fed tunnel oven (Place plate on belt; it rides through the field and exits warm); Walk-through heating (No door, no timer)
rationale: Belt speed fixes dose; the user only places and collects.
judge_comment: Place-and-collect operation is very simple, but a walk-through microwave tunnel needs heavy RF choking and suits a commercial setting more than a home, and the belt speed can't adapt to different foods.

title: Smartphone as the control panel
new_elements: Physical control panel (Fixed, cryptic); NFC tap + phone UI (Oven has no controls; tap phone, pick big picture buttons); Familiar touchscreen UI (Interface users already know)
rationale: Leverages the one UI people have already learned.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but it's already common in smart appliances, and needing a phone and app adds friction rather than removing it.

title: Big tactile e-ink dial
new_elements: Printed dial markings (Fixed minute numbers); E-ink knob face (Knob face shows plain words 'warm / hot / boil' that update as you turn); Plain-language setting (Words not numbers)
rationale: Describes outcomes instead of parameters.
judge_comment: A plain-word e-ink dial is practical and cheap and lowers the learning burden, though it remains a conventional control with vague outcome settings.

title: Pressure-mat plate detector
new_elements: Start step + turntable (Separate actions); Pressure-mat floor (Placing food on floor pad starts a default cycle; lifting it stops); Presence-triggered heating (Like an escalator)
rationale: Zero controls; the food's presence is the command.
judge_comment: Presence-triggered heating removes controls entirely, but a default cycle fits few foods and a floor pad inside a cavity is hard to engineer.

title: Induction-coupled heating plate
new_elements: Magnetron + cavity door (Shielding dictates enclosed box); Open induction warming pad (Set ferrous-base plate anywhere on pad; heats contents by conduction); Open-air reheating (No door, no cavity)
rationale: Put plate down, it warms: coaster-level simplicity.
judge_comment: An induction pad is simple to use, but it needs ferrous plates, heats by conduction rather than microwaves, and won't behave like a microwave on typical food.

title: Thermal-fuse style one-shot timer
new_elements: Adjustable clockwork timer (Infinite settings); Bimetal fixed-time snap switch (Heats to trip after ~90 s, auto resets; one dose per press); Fixed dose heating (Repeat presses for more)
rationale: Dosing is additive and obvious; cheaper than clockwork.
judge_comment: A bimetal fixed-dose switch with one press per dose is simple and cheap, though repeated presses add a small learning step and the resolution is coarse.

title: Coin-op style lever
new_elements: Rotary knobs (Fine adjustment); Pull-down slot-machine lever (One pull = one cycle; spring returns); Single pull start (Gross motor, no precision)
rationale: Satisfying, unambiguous, accessible to arthritic hands.
judge_comment: A lever is accessible and unambiguous, but a single fixed cycle per pull doesn't solve how long to heat, and it adds mechanical cost.

title: Gesture wave start/stop
new_elements: Push button and knobs (Need touch with dirty hands); IR proximity gesture sensor (Wave once to start, wave to stop); Touchless control (Like a tap)
rationale: Known from automatic taps and soap dispensers.
judge_comment: Gesture control is plausible and touchless, but it only replaces the start button and leaves time-setting unsolved. Gestures can also be ambiguous.

title: Graduated dose cup replaces time knob
new_elements: Minutes scale (Abstract units); Water-clock timer (Fill a little reservoir to the mark for your food; drain rate times the heat); Volume-as-time (Pour and go)
rationale: Analog, visible, needs no numeracy.
judge_comment: A water-clock dose cup is wildly original and needs no numeracy, but it risks spills, water near electronics, and inaccurate timing, and it is hard to reconcile with a microwave.

title: Door-handle twist as the only control
