judge_comment: A projected heat map is a striking idea, but it adds complexity and cost rather than substituting a part, and it only partly reduces the learning curve.

title: Tactile embossed controls
new_elements: Embossed tactile icons and detents (Controls readable by touch and sight.)
rationale: Universal design widens who can operate it without help.
judge_comment: Tactile controls are easy to build and aid usability, but they are an incremental change and not radical.

title: Mirror cavity using room light
new_elements: Polished reflective cavity walls (Room light through the window lights the food; no lamp.)
rationale: Passive viewing with one fewer part to fail.
judge_comment: Replacing the lamp with a mirrored cavity is a simple substitution, but dim room light makes it a poor fit, and it does little for ease of operation.

title: Door-as-switch start
new_elements: Closing the door starts heating (Interlock closure doubles as start command.)
rationale: Eliminates the start step entirely.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start heating removes a step and is intuitive, though it needs a default time and raises safety and accidental-start concerns.

title: Ultrasonic vibrating floor
new_elements: Piezo-vibrated cavity floor (Micro-shuffles food through the field without rotation.)
rationale: No turntable to misplace, dish can be any size.
judge_comment: Piezo vibration in place of a turntable is inventive, but it is doubtful for heavy loads and does little to simplify operation.

title: Integrated power module
new_elements: Sealed potted HV power block (Diode, capacitor and bleeder in one replaceable brick.)
rationale: Simplifies service so the appliance stays trouble-free for novices.
judge_comment: A service-oriented component change that does little for operational simplicity, and the user never notices it.

title: Gentle chime plus door pop
new_elements: Three-note chime with latch release (Replaces harsh bell.)
rationale: Two redundant, obvious done-cues.
judge_comment: Clear end-of-cycle cues are helpful, but it is an incremental tweak and does not remove any learning.

title: Temperature probe instead of timer
new_elements: Plug-in food probe with target-temp dial (Set 'hot' not 'minutes'.)
rationale: Users specify the outcome they care about.
judge_comment: Setting a target temperature instead of time matches the user's goal and is feasible, though it adds a probe to handle.

title: Single-button mug microwave
new_elements: Mug-sized cavity with one preset button (Fixed 90 s full power; nothing else.)
rationale: A one-function appliance has literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A one-button, fixed-function appliance has essentially no learning curve and is easy to build, though it is limited in scope.

title: Nucleation-textured floor
new_elements: Micro-textured ceramic floor plate (Promotes safe boiling, replacing smooth glass turntable.)
rationale: Removes a hidden hazard that otherwise requires user knowledge.
judge_comment: A clever safety substitution that removes a hidden hazard, but only indirectly serves simple operation and its efficacy is uncertain.

title: Toaster-style push-down start lever
new_elements: Spring-loaded push-down lever timer (Push lever down to start fixed reheating cycle; it pops up and stops RF when done, like a toaster.); Thermally-released latch with spring return (Simple escapement/bimetal release holds the lever for a preset duration.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster works, so a single push lever removes any dial reading or setting.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever is instantly familiar and zero-learning, though a fixed cycle suits only some foods and a bimetal timer is imprecise.

title: Single doneness slider replaces both knobs
new_elements: One-axis 'cold→piping hot' slider (A single slider sets a combined time/power profile; no separate power knob.)
rationale: Two interacting controls collapse into one intuitive 'how hot' choice.
judge_comment: A single slider is simple and feasible, but it is an incremental simplification with few concrete mechanisms.

title: Food pictogram dial instead of minutes
new_elements: Pictogram program dial (mug, soup, plate, snowflake) (Each icon position maps to a fixed cam time and duty cycle.)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating rather than translating it into minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Pictogram dials already exist on many microwaves, but they are intuitive and easy to build with a cam.

title: Purely mechanical weighing-pan timer
new_elements: Spring-scale-to-cam linkage (Food weight compresses a spring under the tray; the deflection mechanically presets the timer cam.); Weight-set turntable support (Roller ring on a calibrated spring pan that winds the timer proportional to load.)
rationale: Placing the food sets the time, so the user never touches a timer.
judge_comment: Placing the food sets the timer mechanically with no interaction, which is radical, but calibrating a spring scale to cook time across foods is hard.

title: Load-cell auto-time turntable
new_elements: Strain-gauge turntable coupler (Cheap load cell in the coupler weighs food and sets cook time automatically.)
rationale: Weight substitutes for the user's time estimate, leaving just a start button.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-time leaves only a start button, but weight alone is a poor predictor of heating time and a load cell in a rotating coupler is awkward.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop replaces timer
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent (Detects steam burst from food and ends the cycle shortly after.); Capacitive humidity sensing (Low-cost polymer humidity sensor reads cavity exhaust moisture.)
rationale: The food itself tells the oven when it is hot, so there is nothing to set.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop removes the need to set anything, though steam-sensing is already used in sensor-cook microwaves and fails for dry foods.

title: Temperature dial instead of time dial
new_elements: IR thermopile with 'warm/hot/boiling' knob (User selects a target food temperature; a ceiling IR sensor stops RF when reached.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not minutes, so the setting becomes self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A temperature-based knob is intuitive and plausible with an IR thermopile, but it still requires a setting and surface IR readings can be inaccurate.

title: Door closing starts cooking
new_elements: Door-triggered fixed cycle (Closing the door starts a 1-minute cycle; opening cancels; repeat for more.)
rationale: The only action needed is the one users already perform: shutting the door.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is very simple, but it risks accidental starts and a fixed 1-minute cycle is crude.

title: Auto-popping door replaces bell
new_elements: Timer-released spring door (Timer cam trips the latch so the door swings ajar at end; lets steam out and signals done.)
rationale: An open door is unmistakable feedback and removes the step of pressing a release button.
judge_comment: A spring door that pops open at the end gives unmistakable feedback and is mechanically simple, but it only addresses the end of the cycle and not the setup.

title: Magnetic fridge-style door, no button
new_elements: Magnetic gasket pull-door (Flexible magnetic strip holds door shut; user simply pulls the handle.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is universal; no hunting for a release button.
judge_comment: A magnetic pull door is intuitive, but the microwave's safety interlocks and RF sealing make it a small, familiar change that doesn't tackle operation complexity.

title: Pull-out drawer cavity
new_elements: Drawer-type cooking cavity (Cavity slides out like a drawer on rails; closing it completes the choke seal and interlock.)
rationale: Drawers need no instructions and avoid door/button confusion for children and the elderly.
judge_comment: A drawer is intuitive, but it adds little over a door for simple operation, and sealing a sliding cavity against microwave leakage is hard and costly.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable set
new_elements: Rotating metal mode stirrer behind ceiling (Fan-driven paddle scrambles the field; flat fixed cavity floor.)
rationale: No tray to seat, align or knock off its ring—just put the plate anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are well-proven and remove the tray-seating step, but the change is only an indirect help to operation and is not radical.

title: Rotating antenna under ceramic floor
new_elements: Rotating feed antenna under flat ceramic base (Waveguide feeds a slowly spinning antenna below a flat, fixed floor.)
rationale: A flat floor removes the 'did I put the tray back correctly?' failure mode.
judge_comment: A rotating antenna under a ceramic floor already exists commercially, and it removes the tray error mode, though it doesn't simplify the controls.

title: Solid-state RC timer with 0-5 min scale
new_elements: Analog RC timer with triac (Potentiometer-set RC delay drives a triac; full dial sweep covers 0-5 min.)
rationale: A wide, precise short-time scale matches real use so users hit the right time first try.
judge_comment: An analog RC timer is simple and cheap, and the 0-5 min scale suits real use, but it is a minor tweak that gives limited precision.

title: Wind-up spring egg-timer mechanism
new_elements: Mainspring clockwork escapement (Turning the knob winds a spring; no synchronous motor, frequency-independent.)
rationale: Identical kitchen-egg-timer feel with tactile winding that users already understand.
judge_comment: A wind-up egg-timer knob is instantly familiar with zero learning curve, and it replaces the motor and electronics, as old microwaves did.

title: Two-position cook/defrost switch
new_elements: Rocker switch: Cook / Defrost (Replaces 5-step cam with a two-state duty-cycle selector.)
rationale: Five abstract power levels become one obvious binary choice.
judge_comment: Simple binary choice cuts complexity and is easy to build, but it is an incremental, fairly obvious simplification.

title: Push-and-turn single knob
new_elements: Combined rotary encoder knob (Turn to set time; press-and-turn to toggle defrost; one control on fascia.)
rationale: One physical object to learn instead of two.
judge_comment: A single combined knob is concrete and workable, though press-and-turn is a hidden gesture that adds some learning.

title: Colour-zoned dial replaces numbers
new_elements: Colour-band fascia (blue/green/orange/red) (Dial scale printed as colour zones meaning drink/plate/meal/defrost instead of minutes.)
rationale: Colour cues are read faster and more reliably than small numerals.
judge_comment: Colour zones that map to food types remove the need to think in minutes, but the meanings must be learned and are imprecise.

title: Tactile detents and braille scale
new_elements: Detented knob with raised braille/pips (Each 30 s is a felt click and a raised dot; numbers embossed.)
rationale: Setting time by feel removes the need to read anything at all.
judge_comment: Tactile detents and raised pips improve accessibility and eyes-free use, though they add little for ordinary users and mostly add features.

title: Audible click-per-30s knob
new_elements: Ratchet knob with audible clicks (Each click heard while turning equals 30 s; no label reading required.)
rationale: Counting clicks is simpler than reading a dial for anyone, sighted or not.
judge_comment: Audible clicks per 30 s are simple and cheap, but counting clicks is not obviously easier than reading a dial, and the idea overlaps with idea 4.

title: Token-slot timer (one token = one minute)
new_elements: Coin/token drop timer (Reusable tokens dropped in a slot each add one minute; mechanically advances the cam.)
rationale: Counting physical tokens is a concrete, zero-learning way to set time.
judge_comment: Playful and concrete, but tokens can be lost and it is arguably less simple than a single dial or start button.

title: NFC packaging sets the program
new_elements: NFC reader in fascia (Tap ready-meal pack; its tag preloads time and power, start is automatic.); Passive NFC tag reading (13.56 MHz reader IC reads cook parameters from food packaging.)
rationale: The packaging does the thinking so the user only taps and waits.
judge_comment: Tap-and-go removes setting entirely for packaged meals, though it needs packaging ecosystem adoption and offers no help for non-packaged food.

title: Camera food-recognition auto-cook
new_elements: Ceiling camera with on-device classifier (Recognises mug, plate, frozen block and picks time/power; doubles as viewing camera.)
rationale: Zero settings: the oven sees what you put in and heats accordingly.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking fits the need well, but recognition accuracy and safety for varied foods are uncertain, and the idea is not very radical.

title: Offline voice chip replaces control panel
new_elements: Keyword speech module (Low-cost offline recogniser accepts 'two minutes', 'defrost', 'stop'.)
rationale: Speaking a request needs no manual and no dexterity.
judge_comment: Voice control is accessible but already common, and noise, accents, and discoverability of commands can create a learning curve.

title: Foot pedal door opener
new_elements: Pedal-cable door release (Bin-style foot pedal pulls the latch lever via Bowden cable.)
rationale: Opening with hands full of plates becomes effortless and obvious.
judge_comment: A mechanically simple foot pedal is feasible but only addresses door opening, not operation or learning.

title: Roll-top tambour door
new_elements: Metal-slat tambour shutter (Shutter rolls up into the roof; overlapping conductive slats form the shield.)
rationale: Push up / pull down is a single obvious gesture with no swing clearance.
judge_comment: A tambour door is a clear single gesture, but a conductive slat shutter would struggle with RF leakage at the gaps, and it adds cost and hygiene problems.

title: Low-voltage LED replaces incandescent lamp
new_elements: LED lamp fed from transformer filament tap (3 V LED strip on the cavity ceiling; lifetime exceeds the oven.)
rationale: A light that never fails keeps the 'look inside to check' habit reliable.
judge_comment: An LED swap is plausible and concrete, but it is an obvious change that barely affects operational simplicity.

title: Light pipe brings in kitchen light
new_elements: Acrylic light pipe from top panel (Ambient room light guided into the cavity through RF-safe aperture; no lamp.)
rationale: Nothing to switch on or replace; the cavity is simply always visible.
judge_comment: A lamp-free light pipe is a creative idea, but it depends on ambient light and an RF-safe aperture, and it does little for ease of use.

title: Electroluminescent cavity ceiling
new_elements: EL phosphor panel (Thin EL sheet behind mica ceiling glows uniformly; no bulb socket.)
rationale: Shadow-free view of the food makes 'is it done?' checks easier.
judge_comment: An EL panel gives even lighting, but it would be hard to make it survive the heat, steam and RF in the cavity, and it adds little to operation.

title: Light colour counts down remaining time
new_elements: RGB cavity light tied to timer (Light shifts blue→amber→green as the cycle progresses; green = done.)
rationale: Progress is visible at a glance across the room without reading a dial.
judge_comment: A color-coded light for progress is intuitive and needs no learning, and it is easy to build with an RGB LED tied to the timer.

title: Fan-driven exhaust whistle replaces bell
new_elements: Timer-flap exhaust whistle (At end of cycle the cam opens a flap routing fan air through a kettle whistle.)
rationale: The familiar kettle whistle is an instantly understood 'ready' cue.
judge_comment: A whistle is an intuitive ready cue, but it only replaces the bell and the fan-air routing is a bit contrived.

title: Repeating piezo reminder replaces bell
new_elements: Piezo buzzer with repeat-until-opened (Chirps every 30 s until the door is opened; cheaper than striker and bell.)
rationale: Users never need to remember or watch the clock; the oven nags for them.
judge_comment: A repeating buzzer is cheap and easy to understand, but it is a very obvious substitution and not radical.

title: Pop-up flag indicator
new_elements: Spring pop-up 'READY' flag (Cam releases a bright flag on top of the cabinet at cycle end; silent and visible.)
rationale: A visible status flag needs no interpretation and works in noisy shared kitchens.
judge_comment: A mechanical pop-up flag is simple, silent, and clear, but it only signals completion and adds little to operation.

title: Thermochromic door window
new_elements: Thermochromic film on door glass (Inner glass tint changes colour as cavity air passes ~60 °C, showing food is hot.)
rationale: The window itself says 'hot' so the user needs no timing skill.
judge_comment: Thermochromic glass could show that food is hot, but it does not help control operation, and film near microwaves and food heat is questionable.

title: Zoned cavity: position sets power
new_elements: Two-zone cavity floor (mug ring / plate area) (Field is shaped so the small mug ring gets gentle heating, plate area full power; no power knob.)
rationale: Where you put the food replaces a power setting.
judge_comment: Placement-based power selection removes a control entirely and is radical, but shaping the microwave field into zones is technically hard.

title: Dedicated mug microwave, one button
new_elements: Mug-sized cavity with single Go button (~1.5 L cavity, fixed 90 s / 500 W cycle tuned for a drink; no turntable.)
rationale: One product, one job, one button—nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug oven with one button is plausible and truly zero-learning, though it is narrow in use and only loosely a substitution.

title: Big single Go button, press again for more
new_elements: Single large start button (+30 s per press) (Each press adds 30 s to a solid-state counter; no knobs at all.)
rationale: A lone button cannot be misused and matches how most people already use microwaves.
judge_comment: A one-button +30 s design is simple and easy to build, but it is already common and not radical.

title: Quantity dial marked in cups and plates
new_elements: Portion-count dial (1 cup…3 plates) (Scale shows portions instead of minutes; cam gearing maps portion to time.)
rationale: Users know how much food they have, not how many minutes it needs.
judge_comment: Using portions instead of minutes is intuitive and the cam-gearing mechanism is concrete, though mapping food types to time is imprecise.

title: Inverter supply replaces transformer, cap and diode
new_elements: Switch-mode inverter HV supply (Lightweight resonant inverter gives continuously variable true power.)
rationale: Gentle, continuous power means defrost 'just works' without choosing cycle levels.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies already exist and mainly improve power control, so the link to a zero-learning interface is indirect.

title: Solid-state GaN RF source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier with reflected-power sensing (Replaces magnetron and HV chain; reflected power indicates food state for auto-stop.)
rationale: Built-in sensing lets the oven stop itself, removing the need for any settings.
judge_comment: A GaN solid-state source with reflected-power sensing could enable auto-stop and no settings, but cost and the reliability of food-state detection are still challenges.

title: Hall-sensor door detection
new_elements: Redundant Hall/reed door sensors (Contactless magnets replace mechanical microswitches; no latch alignment fuss.)
rationale: Door never needs to be 'slammed just right' to start, removing a hidden learning step.
judge_comment: Feasible and a legitimate substitution, but it addresses a minor pain point and does little for operational simplicity.

title: Door handle doubles as timer lever
new_elements: Handle-slide timer (After closing, slide the door handle sideways; distance sets time and starts the cycle.)
rationale: The hand is already on the handle, so closing and setting become one continuous motion.
judge_comment: Merging closing, timing and starting into one gesture is intuitive and fairly novel, though the mechanical and sensing design needs work.

title: Hourglass visual timer
new_elements: Rotatable sand hourglass with optical end-sensor (Flip the glass to start; sand level shows time left; photo-gate stops RF when empty.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible as a physical quantity anyone understands.
judge_comment: An intuitive and charming physical timer, but fixed sand durations limit flexibility and the sand adds mechanical complexity.

title: Three-button fascia: Drink / Meal / Defrost
new_elements: Three preset membrane buttons (Each button fires a fixed time/power program; nothing else on the panel.)
rationale: Choosing one of three labelled buttons is the lowest possible cognitive load.
judge_comment: Very simple and immediately usable, but presets are a common approach and not very radical.

title: Weight-plus-IR closed-loop with no controls
new_elements: Controller fusing load cell and IR sensor (Weighs food, heats until surface reaches 70 °C, stops; fascia has only Start.)
rationale: Sensors replace all user judgment, leaving a single start action.
judge_comment: A single Start button gives zero learning curve, but reliable IR surface sensing in a microwave and heating uneven foods are technically hard.

title: Cheap microwave stop/start by lid pressure
new_elements: Press-to-run top lid (Toaster-oven-style lid; RF runs only while a weighted lid is down, lid springs up at timer end.)
rationale: Open means off, down means cooking—a state anyone can read at a glance.
judge_comment: Lid-down-means-cooking is an intuitive state, but a top lid with RF sealing and safety interlocks is awkward and replaces a front door, so it is hard to realize.

title: Printed cook-chart lid replaces manual
new_elements: Embossed quick-chart on top panel (Durable pictorial chart (food → dial position) moulded into the cabinet top.)
rationale: Guidance lives on the product itself so no manual is ever needed.
judge_comment: Practical and cheap, but a printed chart is an obvious idea and only shifts guidance onto the product rather than simplifying operation.

title: Self-centering silicone mat replaces glass tray
new_elements: Keyed silicone turntable mat (Flexible mat drops onto the coupler in any orientation; dishwasher-safe, unbreakable.)
rationale: Removes the fiddly tray-and-ring reassembly that confuses users after cleaning.
judge_comment: A silicone mat could simplify reassembly, but it must withstand heat and sit flat under load, and it addresses only a minor confusion.

title: Bimetal food-contact probe dial
new_elements: Snap-disc probe on flexible lead (User clips a bimetal probe into the food; the disc opens the RF circuit at eating temperature.)
rationale: A purely mechanical probe ends cooking at the right moment with no settings.
judge_comment: A mechanical snap-disc probe gives setting-free doneness, but a metal probe inside a microwave cavity risks arcing and the cutoff temperature is fixed.

title: Bluetooth-free beeper in a magnet fob
new_elements: Detachable wireless beeper fob (Low-power 433 MHz fob on the fridge-magnet style; chirps when the cycle ends.)
rationale: No app or pairing: carry the fob and the oven simply finds you.
judge_comment: A fob that chirps at cycle end is feasible and needs no pairing, but it adds a device and does little for operating simplicity.

title: Transparent mesh-free door with embedded ITO shield
new_elements: Transparent conductive (ITO) coated glass shielding (Conductive transparent coating blocks 2.45 GHz without a perforated mesh.)
rationale: A clear, unobstructed view lets users judge doneness by eye without guesswork.
judge_comment: A transparent ITO-coated door shield is a plausible substitution for the perforated mesh, but it only loosely serves 'no learning curve' (better visibility of doneness), isn't very radical, and has real challenges with RF attenuation, durability and cost.

title: Hourglass visual timer
new_elements: Rotating coloured-disc countdown window (Timer cam drives a painted disc; red area shrinks to zero behind a window, no numbers.)
rationale: Time remaining is read at a glance as a shrinking colour patch, so no numerals or clock-reading skill are needed.
judge_comment: Easy to read countdown, but the user still has to set a time, so the learning curve is only partly removed.

title: Weigh-and-go
new_elements: Load cell under turntable (Weight of dish sets cooking duration automatically; user only presses start.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost load cell as used in kitchen scales.)
rationale: The user never chooses a time; mass alone decides it.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing removes the time decision, but weight is a poor proxy for heating needs, which depend on food type and starting temperature.

title: Steam-stop cooking
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent (Heating runs until a steam burst signals the food is hot, then stops.)
rationale: Replaces timing with a single 'heat until done' button, eliminating guesswork.
judge_comment: A single 'heat until done' button is very simple, and humidity sensing is already used in sensor-cook microwaves, though it works poorly for dry or covered foods.

title: Infrared done-detector
new_elements: IR thermopile aimed at food surface (Cooks until surface reaches ~70°C; no time or power knob.)
rationale: Target temperature replaces both time and power decisions.
judge_comment: A target temperature removes both time and power decisions, but IR only reads the surface and its accuracy is limited through steam and containers.

title: Pictogram preset buttons
new_elements: Four large picture buttons (mug, plate, bowl, snowflake) (Each button hard-wires a fixed time/power cam combination.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of what you are heating needs no reading or numeracy.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are simple and cheap, but similar presets are common and the fixed settings are inflexible.

title: Picture slider
new_elements: Linear slide lever with food icons (Slide the pointer to the icon; lever position sets cam timer.)
rationale: A single linear motion to an icon is more intuitive than rotating to minutes.
judge_comment: A simple mechanical slider with icons is intuitive and cheap, though food icons give coarse control and it's an incremental substitution.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline keyword microphone module (Says 'heat', 'defrost', 'stop', 'open'; no knobs or buttons at all.); Edge speech recognition (On-chip keyword spotting, no cloud.)
rationale: Speaking is the most universal interface with zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is feasible and needs no learning, but it gives no time/power control and noisy kitchens and accents hurt reliability.

title: Package-scanning cook
new_elements: Barcode/OCR camera at door (Reads the heating instructions printed on the package and sets time/power itself.)
rationale: Show the box to the oven and press start; no instructions to interpret.
judge_comment: Reading package instructions is a clever zero-learning flow, but OCR of varied packaging is unreliable and costly, and it can't help with non-packaged food.

title: NFC meal tags
new_elements: NFC reader in cavity floor (Tagged ready-meals program the oven on contact.)
rationale: Placing food in the oven is the whole user interaction.
judge_comment: Placing a tagged meal and nothing else is the ultimate no-learning interaction, but it depends on ecosystem adoption and excludes untagged food.

title: Single doneness dial
new_elements: One 'cold-to-hot' knob (Combined cam sets time and duty cycle together along one curve.)
rationale: Two knobs become one, halving the decisions and the parts.
judge_comment: Consolidating to a single knob is simple and highly feasible, but it is incremental and the combined curve may be unclear and not radical.

title: No power knob at all
new_elements: Fixed-power magnetron feed (Power knob deleted; defrost handled by lengthening time via timer scale.)
rationale: Removing a control removes a decision and a mistake source.
judge_comment: Deleting the power knob is simple and effective, but it is an obvious subtraction, and it leaves defrost to be handled awkwardly through timing.

title: Inverter auto-power
new_elements: Inverter power supply with automatic ramp (Continuous power follows a built-in gentle profile; no user setting.); Switch-mode inverter magnetron drive (Replaces duty-cycle cam.)
rationale: Power becomes invisible to the user yet gentler on food.
judge_comment: Inverter drive with an automatic gentle ramp removes the power decision and is real technology, though not very radical and it is not cheaper.

title: Gentle/Normal rocker
new_elements: Two-position rocker switch (Replaces 5-step cam with 30%/100% selection.)
rationale: A binary choice is instantly understood by anyone.
judge_comment: A two-position rocker is easy to understand and cheap, but it is an incremental simplification.

title: Weight-set power
new_elements: Weight-indexed duty-cycle cam (Load cell shifts the cam; heavier dishes get fuller power.)
rationale: Power is chosen by the food, not by the user.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic power eliminates user choice entirely and is fairly novel, but a load cell and a mechanical cam shifter add cost and complexity, and weight is a weak proxy for food type.

title: Snowflake/flame switch
new_elements: Defrost/Cook icon toggle (Large tactile toggle with only two universally understood icons.)
rationale: Icons replace numeric power percentages.
judge_comment: Universally understood icons on a tactile toggle are intuitive and easy to build, but this is a common idea.

title: Plain pull handle
new_elements: Pull-handle door with friction catch (No button, no latch lever; magnet/friction holds door and interlock closes on contact.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is a universally known gesture; no hidden button to find.
judge_comment: Intuitive and simple, but a pull handle is already common and not radical; friction catch must still satisfy safety interlock requirements.

title: Foot-pedal door
new_elements: Floor pedal cable release (Like a pedal bin: step to open with full hands.)
rationale: Borrowing the pedal-bin idiom gives hands-free opening with no explanation.
judge_comment: Pedal-bin idiom is clear, but it addresses only door opening, adds a cable mechanism, and is awkward on a countertop unit.

title: Pops open when done
new_elements: Spring door-ejector tripped by timer cam (Bell cam also releases latch so door springs ajar at zero.)
rationale: 'Done' is signalled by the door itself opening, like a toaster popping.
judge_comment: Toaster-style pop-open gives a clear done signal and is mechanically plausible with a timer cam, though it does not simplify the rest of operation.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Whole cavity floor slides out on rails; closing the drawer seals the choke.)
rationale: Drawers need no instruction and keep food level while loading.
judge_comment: Drawer is intuitive and novel, but sealing the microwave choke on a sliding cavity is difficult, and spills are a concern.

title: Roll-up door
new_elements: Vertical tambour shutter of conductive slats (Door rolls up into the top like a bread-bin lid.)
rationale: No swing clearance and a familiar bread-bin gesture.
judge_comment: Bread-bin roll-up is a familiar gesture and quirky, but conductive slat gaps would leak RF and make the seal difficult.

title: Magnetic no-latch door
new_elements: Magnet strip seal with reed interlock (Fridge-style magnetic closure replaces hooks, lever and button.)
rationale: Opens like a fridge, the most familiar kitchen door.
judge_comment: Fridge-style magnetic door is familiar, but microwave RF leakage and safety interlock standards make a weak magnetic seal risky, and it only addresses door opening, not operation.

title: Nudge-open soft door
new_elements: Push-push latch with damped spring (Press the door panel anywhere; it clicks open gently.)
rationale: Whole door is the button; nothing to locate.
judge_comment: Push-push latch is a proven, cheap mechanism that simplifies opening, though it leaves start and time controls unaddressed.

title: Carousel cavity
new_elements: Rotating half-cylinder cavity (Spin the drum to expose the shelf; metal drum wall doubles as door.)
rationale: One rotation both opens and closes; no handles, hinges or buttons.
judge_comment: Rotating drum cavity is highly radical but has serious RF sealing, turntable and cost challenges, and it adds a new learning curve.

title: Top-loading chest
new_elements: Lift-up lid cavity (Like a slow-cooker; gravity keeps lid shut, lifting it stops cooking.)
rationale: Pot-with-lid is the oldest kitchen idiom.
judge_comment: Top-loading lid with a familiar slow-cooker metaphor is intuitive and feasible, though spills, choke seals and ergonomics are concerns.

title: Clear conductive window
new_elements: ITO/metal-mesh film laminated glass (Optically clear shielding film replaces perforated steel.); Transparent conductive coatings (Sputtered ITO or fine wire mesh.)
rationale: Full visibility lets users judge doneness without any readout.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive film is a plausible, concrete substitution, but it has little effect on operation simplicity.

title: Hand-wave door
new_elements: Proximity sensor + motorised door (Wave in front of the oven; door opens, like an automatic shop door.)
rationale: No button, handle or grip strength required.
judge_comment: Opening the door touchlessly is easy, but it only covers one step and adds cost and a motor rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Big-detent minute dial
new_elements: Ratchet dial with 30-second clicks (Coarse, audible detents replace continuous imprecise scale.)
rationale: Counting clicks is easier than reading a fine scale.
judge_comment: Coarse detents simplify time setting and are very feasible, but similar mechanical dials already exist.

title: Glowing time ring
new_elements: LED arc around the dial (Lit arc shrinks as timer runs; same cam, added ring.)
rationale: Progress visible from across the room without a display.
judge_comment: The ring is a helpful glanceable cue, but it adds a component and does not simplify operation itself.

title: Detachable egg timer
new_elements: Removable spring egg-timer that docks as the knob (Docked it runs the oven; undocked it is an ordinary kitchen timer.)
rationale: Uses an object people already know how to use.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer used as the control has essentially no learning curve and is a clever dual-purpose substitution.

title: Punch-card programs
new_elements: Slot for mechanical program cards (Notched card physically sets time and power cams, like a jukebox.)
rationale: Insert the 'soup' card: tangible, no settings to remember.
judge_comment: Physical cards make programs tangible, but needing a card library and cams adds complexity and limits flexibility.

title: Gravity clock timer
new_elements: Weight-driven escapement timer (Lift the knob to wind; descending weight runs the clock independent of mains frequency.)
rationale: Lifting to wind is intuitive and works identically in every region.
judge_comment: A weight-driven escapement timer is novel and intuitive to wind, but it is clunky, imprecise and not clearly simpler than a standard mechanical timer.

title: Portions dial
new_elements: Knob marked 1-4 plates (Portion count sets both time and power via one cam.)
rationale: People know how many portions they have; they don't know wattage.
judge_comment: Portion-based dial maps to what users know and removes wattage and time guesswork, using a plausible cam mechanism.

title: One big start button
new_elements: Single illuminated start/stop pad (All timing by sensors; one button only.)
rationale: The smallest possible interface: one button.
judge_comment: One button is minimal, but fully sensor-based timing is already known and often unreliable, and the idea lacks mechanism detail.

title: Close-to-start door
new_elements: Door-latch-triggered start (Closing the door starts a fixed cook; opening stops it.)
rationale: Loading the oven is the only action required.
judge_comment: Zero-step operation is simple, but a fixed cook time suits few foods and risks accidental starts.

title: Hold-to-heat button
new_elements: Dead-man heating button (Magnetron runs only while the pad is pressed; release stops.)
rationale: Like a kettle switch held down: direct, immediate, impossible to over-set.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is immediately understandable and safe from over-setting, though tiring for long cooks and offers little control.

title: Tactile raised dial
new_elements: Knob with raised bumps and Braille minutes (Same cam, tactile overlay for low-vision users.)
rationale: Operable by feel without reading.
judge_comment: Helps low-vision users but is a minor accessibility tweak that doesn't remove the learning curve or count as radical.

title: Thermochromic plate
new_elements: Turntable with colour-change glaze (Plate turns red at 60°C; user stops when colour appears.); Thermochromic ceramic pigments (Reversible colour-shift glaze.)
rationale: Doneness is shown as a colour, no timing judgement needed.
judge_comment: Colour feedback is intuitive, but a plate at 60°C doesn't reflect food temperature and the user still has to stop the oven manually.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable
new_elements: Rotating metal fan stirrer in waveguide (Flat fixed floor; no glass plate to position or break.)
rationale: Removes the 'is the plate seated right?' failure mode.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in commercial ovens and simplify the floor, but they do little for operational simplicity.

title: Solid-state PWM power
new_elements: Triac phase-controlled transformer (Smooth power via triac replaces mechanical duty cam.)
rationale: Enables one smooth, intuitive slider instead of five discrete steps.
judge_comment: A smooth slider is somewhat simpler, but the triac on a transformer is technically questionable and inverter power already exists.

title: Evaporation-stop
new_elements: Weight-loss cutoff (Load cell stops heating once a few grams of water have steamed off.)
rationale: Physics decides when it's hot; the user decides nothing.
judge_comment: Automatic stop via load-cell weight loss removes user decisions entirely, though accuracy varies by food and a load cell adds cost.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Pull-cord retracting timer (Pull the cord out; it retracts over minutes, like a talking-doll string.)
rationale: Pull length maps to time in the most physical way possible.
judge_comment: Pull length mapping to time is intuitive and mechanically simple, though it is imprecise for short or long times and says nothing about power level.

title: Twist-handle timer
new_elements: Door handle that twists to set minutes (Handle doubles as timer knob; one hand, one gesture.)
rationale: Open, load, twist, close: controls live where the hand already is.
judge_comment: Combining the handle and timer is intuitive, but the interlock and door-latch mechanics and the safety implications are unresolved.

title: Camera door
new_elements: Solid steel door with internal camera and front screen (Live view replaces mesh window; screen also shows a big countdown.)
rationale: Brighter, larger view of the food than a dim mesh window.
judge_comment: A camera and screen is feasible but adds complexity and cost, and it barely addresses operation simplicity.

title: Conductive curtain door
new_elements: Metallised-fabric roller blind with choke rail (Soft blind drops to seal; lift it to reach in.); Metallised textile RF shielding (Silver-coated nylon fabric.)
rationale: A curtain you push aside needs zero explanation.
judge_comment: A fabric door is very radical and intuitive to use, but reliably sealing RF leakage with soft fabric is a serious safety challenge.

title: Doorless choke tunnel
new_elements: Open cut-off waveguide access tunnel (Long narrow metal entry tunnel attenuates 2.45 GHz below leakage limit; no door at all.); Below-cutoff waveguide attenuation (Aperture smaller than half wavelength over sufficient length.)
rationale: Nothing to open or close: just slide the dish in.
judge_comment: A doorless cut-off waveguide tunnel is radical and physically grounded, but the tunnel would need to be long, which limits the dish size and makes the cavity awkward to use.

title: Joystick control
new_elements: Single 2-axis lever (Push forward for longer, sideways for stronger; both cams driven by one stick.)
rationale: One gestural control instead of two scales to read.
judge_comment: A single lever merges time and power, but the 2-axis mapping is itself something users must learn, and cam-driven timing is mechanically awkward.

title: Lift-to-stop plate
new_elements: Turntable presence switch (Heating only while a dish rests on the plate; lifting the dish ends the cook.)
rationale: Taking the food out is the stop command.
judge_comment: Using dish presence as the stop command is intuitive and replaces a button, though a presence switch is hard to make reliable with different dishes and mid-cook checks.

title: Reflected-power auto level
new_elements: Directional coupler sensing reflected RF (Oven lowers power as food's absorption changes; no user power setting.)
rationale: Power self-adjusts to the load so the user never sets it.
judge_comment: Removes the power setting entirely, but it adds cost and complexity instead of substituting something simpler, and it doesn't tell the user how long to cook.

title: Living-hinge door
new_elements: Polymer living hinge with metal choke insert (One moulded flexure replaces stamped hinges and pins.)
rationale: Lighter, self-centring door that swings effortlessly for elderly users.
judge_comment: It eases door handling, but it does little for operation with no learning curve, and a polymer hinge near the RF choke and heat is questionable.

title: Audible tick countdown
new_elements: Escapement tick that speeds up near zero (Timer ticks louder and faster in the last 30 s; bell at end.)
rationale: Remaining time is communicated by sound, no need to look or read.
judge_comment: A mechanical ticking timer is simple and familiar and gives sound-based feedback, but it only conveys remaining time and is not radical.

title: Hold-to-Cook dead-man button
new_elements: Momentary hold-to-cook button (Magnetron runs only while the big button is pressed; release = stop.)
rationale: No duration to set or read: you hold it until the food looks done, zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Hold-to-cook removes timer entirely and is instantly understandable, though holding a button for minutes is tiring and a safety/ergonomics tradeoff.

title: Toaster-style push-down lever
new_elements: Spring lever with pop-up release (Push lever down to start a fixed run; it pops up with a clack when done, like a toaster.)
rationale: Borrows a universally understood toaster gesture instead of a numeric timer.
judge_comment: A toaster lever is a familiar gesture and easy to build, but a fixed run time limits flexibility and it's not very radical.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Pull-cord clockwork timer (Pull the cord out; its slow spring retraction keeps the circuit closed, length = time.)
rationale: A single intuitive physical gesture (pull more = cook more) with no dial markings to interpret.
judge_comment: Pull-cord clockwork timer is intuitive and mechanical, replacing electronics cheaply, though precision and cord wear are concerns.

title: Hourglass sand timer switch
new_elements: Sand-flow optical interruption (Flipping a visible hourglass closes an optical switch until sand runs out.); Flip-hourglass cooking timer (Hourglass module on the front panel; flip to start, empty = stop.)
rationale: The remaining time is literally visible as sand, understood by children and elderly alike.
judge_comment: Visible hourglass is charming and understandable, but fixed durations and sand-based optical switching are clunky and imprecise for varied foods.

title: Three big pictogram buttons
new_elements: Cup / Plate / Snowflake preset buttons (Three oversized buttons each hard-wired to a fixed time-and-power profile.)
rationale: Replaces two knobs with one-press choices described by pictures, not numbers.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are simple and feasible but a common approach with little radical novelty and limited coverage.

title: Weighing turntable sets the time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable auto-timer (Food mass measured on the turntable sets cook duration automatically.)
rationale: User just places food and presses start; time is derived, never chosen.
judge_comment: Mass-based timing removes time entry, but mass alone poorly predicts the needed time (food type, starting temperature), and it adds load-cell cost.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Humidity-burst sensing (Cheap humidity sensor in the vent detects the steam surge when food is hot.); Steam-stop start button (One start button; oven stops itself when steam is detected.)
rationale: Removes the need to estimate time at all: press start, it stops when hot.
judge_comment: Steam sensing is proven (sensor-reheat exists), cheap, and gives true one-button operation, though it is less radical because it is already on the market.

title: Infrared food-surface thermostat
new_elements: IR thermopile stop switch (Non-contact sensor in the cavity roof cuts power when food surface hits ~70 °C.)
rationale: Cooking becomes 'until hot', a concept everyone already has.
judge_comment: 'Cook until hot' is an intuitive model, and an IR thermopile is plausible, but it reads only the surface temperature, and the sensor must work through steam and a shielded cavity.

title: Close-the-door-to-start
new_elements: Door-closure start switch with fixed 60 s run (Shutting the door starts a one-minute burst; reopen to stop, reshut for another minute.)
rationale: Eliminates every control: the only interaction is opening and closing the door.
judge_comment: It is extremely simple and cheap, but the fixed 60 s run is a crude fit for varied foods and risks accidental starts, including an empty oven.

title: Knock-to-add-time casing
new_elements: Piezo knock detection (A piezo disc on the wrapper counts taps.); Tap-counter timer (Each knock on the case adds 30 s; a knock while running stops.)
rationale: No knob, no button labels: tapping is the most primitive interaction there is.
judge_comment: Tapping is novel and needs no labels, but counting taps to set time is itself something to learn, and accidental knocks could trigger it.

title: Rotate the whole oven to set time
new_elements: Turntable base with clockwork return (The oven sits on a wind-up base; twist the oven body, it slowly turns back and stops cooking at zero.)
rationale: The product itself becomes the dial, a giant unmistakable indicator of remaining time.
judge_comment: Wildly radical and intuitive as a time indicator, but rotating a heavy oven with power cables and a clockwork return is impractical and arguably not simpler.

title: Token-slot minute counter
new_elements: Drop-token timer (Each steel token dropped in a slot buys one minute; tokens return to a tray when spent.)
rationale: Counting physical tokens is simpler than reading a scale and gives tangible feedback.
judge_comment: Tangible and easy to grasp, but it adds loose tokens to lose and is arguably more clumsy than a dial.

title: Single slider with cup-to-plate icons
new_elements: One linear slider (sip ↔ feast) (A single slider spans small-cup to full-plate icons, mapping to combined time and power.)
rationale: Collapses two abstract settings into one picture-based choice of 'how much food'.
judge_comment: A single picture-based slider directly removes the learning curve and is readily buildable, though not very radical.

title: Light-is-the-timer
new_elements: Fading-glow bar timer (A row of warm LEDs lights up as you press start repeatedly; they extinguish one by one as time passes.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown as light rather than digits, readable from across the room.
judge_comment: Light bar gives clear remaining-time feedback, but repeated pressing to set time is still a mild learning step.

title: Bimetal cavity-heat timer
new_elements: Bimetallic strip snap switch (A strip warmed by exhaust air bends and opens the circuit when the cavity is hot.); Thermal snap-off switch (Replaces clockwork; cook ends when the exhaust reaches a set temperature.)
rationale: Cheaper than a motor timer and needs no setting: it just stops when things are hot.
judge_comment: Self-stopping thermal switch needs no setting, but exhaust temperature doesn't reliably indicate food doneness across loads and risks overheating or undercooking.

title: Voice stop word
new_elements: Offline single-keyword recognition (Tiny MCU listens only for 'stop' and 'go'.); Spoken start/stop module (Say go to run, say stop to end; no timer hardware.)
rationale: Two words everyone knows replace every control and are usable with full hands.
judge_comment: Two-word voice control is intuitive and feasible with cheap offline keyword chips, but 'no timer hardware' is vague on how cook duration is set and noisy kitchens risk false triggers.

title: Foot pedal cook control
new_elements: Floor pedal run switch (Like a sewing machine: press pedal to cook, lift to stop.)
rationale: Hands-free, no settings, familiar from sewing machines and car accelerators.
judge_comment: Dead-man pedal is very simple conceptually and familiar, but standing and holding a pedal for minutes is impractical and awkward.

title: Pictogram wheel instead of minute dial
new_elements: Food-picture rotary dial (Dial face shows coffee, soup, pizza slice, frozen peas; each detent is a preset time.)
rationale: Keeps the cheap cam timer but removes the need to know how many minutes food takes.
judge_comment: Picture-based preset detents on a cheap cam timer remove the need to know cook times and are easy to build, though the idea is fairly incremental.

title: Door-handle twist timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle wind-up timer (Closing the door and twisting its handle winds the clockwork; it unwinds as it cooks.)
rationale: Merges shutting the door and setting time into one continuous hand motion.
judge_comment: Combining door closing and timer winding into one motion is elegant and intuitive, though mechanical coupling and safety interlock complexity add challenges and cook time is still user-judged.

title: Count-the-door-closes timer
new_elements: Door-bounce minute counter (Each close of the door within 3 s adds one minute; then it starts.)
rationale: Reuses the one action every user already performs; nothing else to find or learn.
judge_comment: Using door slams to count minutes is clever and cheap with a switch, but it is non-obvious to learn, which undermines the no-learning-curve goal, and risks accidental starts and door wear.

title: Fixed-power, time-only oven
new_elements: Deleted power control (single full-power mode) (Power knob removed; defrost achieved by shorter repeated runs.)
rationale: One fewer control means one fewer thing to understand, and lower BOM.
judge_comment: Removing the power control simplifies operation and is trivially feasible, but it is a common, unradical subtraction that makes defrosting awkward.

title: Ice/flame rocker switch
new_elements: Two-position snowflake/flame rocker (Gentle (30 % duty) vs full power, no intermediate steps.)
rationale: Binary choice with self-explanatory icons replaces five abstract numeric levels.
judge_comment: A binary icon rocker is intuitive and easy to build, though it is an incremental simplification rather than a wild one.

title: Shelf height = power
new_elements: Field-intensity gradient positioning (Cavity designed so field strength drops predictably with height above the feed.); Two-level rack (defrost shelf / cook floor) (Place food high for gentle heating, low for full heating.)
rationale: Power becomes a spatial choice with no electrical control at all.
judge_comment: Using shelf height for power is a creative idea, but cavity fields are standing-wave patterns that are not predictably graded, and users may find it less intuitive.

title: Water-cup ballast for gentle mode
new_elements: Built-in ballast water reservoir with lever (Pull a lever to slide a sealed water load into the cavity corner, absorbing part of the power.)
rationale: True continuous gentle heating without duty cycling, via one obvious lever.
judge_comment: A sliding water ballast is wild and concrete, but it is mechanically messy, wasteful, and unreliable in practice, and it adds a lever to learn.

title: Continuous variac power dial
new_elements: Variable-tap anode supply (Tapped transformer plus phase control lowers magnetron drive continuously.); Smooth dim-style power dial (Works like a lamp dimmer: more turn = hotter, no steps or pulsing.)
rationale: Matches the mental model of a light dimmer, which nobody needs to learn.
judge_comment: A dimmer-like continuous power dial is intuitive, but magnetron power control is hard and costly, and it is not a cheaper substitution.

title: Power folded into the far end of the timer
new_elements: Single combined knob with defrost zone (One knob: 0-10 min full power, then a coloured 'thaw' zone that cycles at 30 %.)
rationale: One knob only; defrost is just 'turn it further', no second control to decode.
judge_comment: Simple and practical single-knob design, but it's an incremental merge of controls rather than a radical idea.

title: Container-shape cradle selects power
new_elements: Mug-ring / plate-ring turntable with microswitches (Placing a mug in the small ring triggers low power; a plate on the outer ring triggers full.)
rationale: Where you set the food down is the setting; no control needs to be touched.
judge_comment: Placement-as-setting is intuitive and novel, but it's limited in flexibility and the mapping from container to power is questionable.

title: Weight-derived power level
new_elements: Scale-driven duty controller (Load cell picks duty cycle and time together from food mass; user only presses start.)
rationale: Both knobs vanish; the oven infers settings from the food itself.
judge_comment: Reduces operation to pressing start, but mass alone is a poor predictor of needed heating time or power, so accuracy suffers.

title: Thermochromic 'done' label replaces power logic
new_elements: Colour-change dish set with fixed gentle mode (Oven runs one gentle mode; supplied dishes turn red when contents reach serving temp.)
rationale: User watches a colour instead of choosing a power level.
judge_comment: Colour feedback is intuitive, but the dish dependency and unreliable thermochromic heating in a microwave make it weak, and the user still needs to set time.

title: Drawer instead of hinged door
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (The whole cavity floor slides out on rails; no hinge, latch or button.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to open a drawer, and it brings food to the user at waist height.
judge_comment: Drawer opening is familiar and ergonomic, but it addresses only door opening, not the core operation, and microwave sealing is a challenge.

title: Top-loading chest lid
new_elements: Lift-up lid on gas strut (Food is lowered in from above like a chest freezer; lid rests open by itself.)
rationale: Nothing to latch or push; gravity keeps the door shut and spills stay inside.
judge_comment: Top-loading lid is familiar from chest freezers and removes the latch, but it is awkward for reaching and placing food and it still needs controls and a safety interlock.

title: Tambour roll-top shutter
new_elements: Interlocking conductive slat shutter (Overlapping steel slats form a continuous RF seal when rolled closed.); Roll-up bread-bin door (Slide the shutter up into the housing to open; no swing radius.)
rationale: Familiar bread-bin gesture, no button to find and no door swinging into the user.
judge_comment: The roll-top shutter is a very novel and concrete mechanism, but a reliable RF seal across moving slats is hard and it still needs controls.

title: Magnet-held door, just pull
new_elements: Magnetic gasket closure with finger lip (Fridge-style magnetic strip holds the door; interlock reads a reed switch.)
rationale: Opens like a fridge, the most familiar appliance door, with fewer parts.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic door is intuitive and plausible, but it is not radical, and magnetic seals raise concerns about RF leakage and about child safety.

title: Push the door itself to open (push-push latch)
new_elements: Push-to-open cabinet latch (Press anywhere on the door face and it springs ajar; no separate button.)
rationale: Removes the hunt for a small button; the whole door is the button.
judge_comment: A push-to-open door is simple, cheap and proven in cabinets, and it removes the button hunt, but it is an incremental change.

title: Door auto-ejects when the bell rings
new_elements: Timer-cam-driven door kicker (The same cam that rings the bell releases the latch so the door pops open a few cm.)
rationale: Finished food is announced physically and the door is already open, no button needed.
judge_comment: A door that pops open when the timer ends is clever and removes a step, using a mechanical cam that is plausible, though it does not address how the user sets the time.

title: Foot-bar door release
new_elements: Toe-kick latch bar (Bar along the base; nudge it with a foot to pop the door.)
rationale: Works with both hands full of dishes, like a pedal bin.
judge_comment: A foot-nudged toe-kick latch is practical and intuitive for full hands, but it only simplifies door opening and doesn't really substitute a part, so it only partly serves a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Revolving cylinder cavity
new_elements: Rotating drum with one open sector (Spin the drum so its opening faces you to load; spin away to seal and cook.)
rationale: A single twist both closes the oven and is the obvious way in, like a revolving door.
judge_comment: A revolving drum cavity is very radical and intuitive, but sealing RF, hygiene, cleaning and the loss of usable volume make it hard to build.

title: Living-hinge polymer door frame
new_elements: Polypropylene living hinge with conductive gasket (Door frame molded with integral flex hinge; RF seal via conductive elastomer.); Moulded one-piece hinge-door (No steel hinge, no pins, no screws.)
rationale: Lighter door that swings freely with no stiff detent, easier for elderly hands.
judge_comment: A one-piece polymer hinge is a concrete cost and weight substitution, but it barely affects learning curve, and the durability and RF seal are doubtful.

title: Single pivot pin hinge
new_elements: Vertical pivot rod through door edge (One rod replaces two stamped hinges; door rotates like a saloon door.)
rationale: Fewer parts and a smoother, lighter swing that needs less force.
judge_comment: A single pivot rod is simple and plausible, but it's a minor mechanical tweak with little effect on operational simplicity.

title: ITO-coated glass instead of mesh
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide shielding (Multi-layer ITO/silver coating on glass reflects 2.45 GHz while passing light.); Clear conductive glass door (Door window is plain-looking glass; no perforated sheet.)
rationale: Users see clearly what is happening, reducing mistakes without any interface at all.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive coated glass is a real substitute for mesh and improves visibility, but its link to simple operation is indirect, and heat and shielding performance are uncertain.

title: Door-open-by-default, close is the only action
new_elements: Spring-open door with hold-closed cook cycle (Door rests open; pushing it shut latches and runs a fixed cycle, then it springs open again.)
rationale: The oven's state is always obvious: open means ready, closed means cooking.
judge_comment: Clear state signaling and a single action, though an open door at rest is a bit awkward and the fixed cycle limits flexibility.

title: Fabric mesh curtain door
new_elements: Metallised textile RF curtain (Dense silver-plated fabric with magnetic edge seals blocks microwaves.); Drop-curtain door (Lift the curtain with one finger to load; it falls shut by weight.)
rationale: No mechanism at all to operate; it cannot be opened 'wrong'.
judge_comment: Radical, but a fabric curtain is very unlikely to meet microwave leakage safety standards, and removing the door mechanism doesn't much simplify operation.

title: Timer bell replaced by lamp-off cue
new_elements: Silent timer with cavity-light-as-status (Bell removed; the interior lamp glows while cooking and goes dark when done.)
rationale: Lit means busy, dark means ready — a status language with nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive status cue, but it only covers the done signal, not operation, and the missing bell may cause missed alerts.

title: Big single 'Go' button, 1 min each press
new_elements: One oversized add-a-minute button (Only control on the front; press for each minute, long-press to cancel.)
rationale: A single control with a single meaning is the lowest possible learning curve.
judge_comment: A single add-a-minute button is highly learnable and trivially buildable, though less flexible for varied foods.

title: Mirror periscope window
new_elements: Top-mounted periscope viewport (Angled mirrors in a choke tube let users look down into the cavity from above without a mesh window.)
rationale: Users check food by glancing down naturally, with no door window to peer through.
judge_comment: A periscope is an inventive swap for the window, but it adds little to ease of operation and has RF choke and usability issues.

title: Two-knob swap for a single 'cold → hot' thermostat dial
new_elements: Target-temperature dial with IR feedback (Set desired food temperature; oven runs until an IR sensor confirms it.)
rationale: Replaces time-and-power reasoning with the one thing people actually want: how hot.
judge_comment: A temperature dial matches user intent and removes time and power reasoning, though IR sensing of food temperature is imprecise and it is a fairly modest substitution.

title: Gravity-fall weight timer
new_elements: Escapement-regulated falling weight (A lifted weight descends through a clock escapement; reaching bottom opens the switch.); Lift-the-weight timer (Raise the side weight by hand; its descent is the countdown, visible from afar.)
rationale: No motor, no mains-frequency dependence, and the countdown is a plainly visible object.
judge_comment: A visible falling-weight timer is intuitive and needs no electronics, but it is bulky and has limited precision for a microwave.

title: Handle-pull latch replaces push button
new_elements: Full-width grab handle with integral latch (Pulling the handle lifts the hooks; pushing the door home re-latches.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is the default door gesture; no one must discover a button.
judge_comment: A pull handle is easy and highly feasible, but it only addresses door opening and is not radical.

title: Timer as a sliding cover over the window
new_elements: Window-shutter countdown (Slide an opaque shutter across the door to start; clockwork draws it back, revealing food as time ends.)
rationale: Remaining time equals how much of the window is still covered — instantly readable.
judge_comment: A shutter that shows remaining time is a wild, readable metaphor, but an opaque cover over the window and clockwork integration are awkward, and it has safety and usability issues.

title: Plug-in-to-start, unplug-to-stop
new_elements: Controls-free oven with cord-switch start (No front controls; inserting the magnetic power connector runs at fixed power for a 90 s auto-cycle.)
rationale: A blank front panel is impossible to misuse; the only decision is plug or unplug.
judge_comment: A controls-free, plug-to-start oven is radically simple, but a fixed 90 s cycle fits few foods and plugging in is clumsy as a control.

title: Rubber-band tension timer
new_elements: Elastic-driven air-dashpot timer (Stretched elastomer band relaxes through a pneumatic damper, releasing a switch at the end.); Stretch-band countdown lever (Pull the lever against the band; its slow return is the cook time.)
rationale: Dirt-cheap, motor-free, and the lever position shows remaining time at a glance.
judge_comment: A pull-lever timer that visibly counts down is intuitive with no learning curve, and replacing the electronic timer with a cheap elastic-pneumatic damper fits the substitute operator; however, air dashpot timing accuracy across temperature and a 10-second to 5-minute range is questionable, and mechanical timers already exist in older microwaves, which limits novelty.

title: One-button weigh-and-go
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing two-knob control set); Single START button with load cell (turntable load cell sets time from weight; one button); Auto-set cooking time (time derived from food mass)
rationale: One button and zero settings removes all learning.
judge_comment: Single-button weight-based timing strongly removes learning, though weight is a poor proxy for heating time and the brief's SUBSTITUTE operator is only loosely met.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing 0-30 min spring timer); Flip hourglass trigger (sand glass with optical gate; flip to start, empty = stop)
rationale: Everyone already knows how an hourglass works.
judge_comment: The hourglass is an intuitive metaphor and a fun, radical swap, but fixed durations and flip-to-start are limiting and the optical gate adds complexity.

title: Fixed power, time only
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing duty-cycle cam); Hardwired full-power magnetron (no power selector at all)
rationale: Removing a choice removes a decision the user must learn.
judge_comment: Removing power control is simple and cheap and cuts decisions, but it is an obvious simplification that limits cooking quality.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Retracting pull cord (pull length = minutes; cord reels back as it cooks)
rationale: A visible cord length is a self-explanatory time display.
judge_comment: A pull cord that reels back gives a self-explanatory physical time display, though the mechanism is somewhat fiddly and needs a retract-rate governor.

title: Magnetic pull-open door
new_elements: Door push-release button (existing latch); Magnetic seal door with handle (fridge-style magnetic gasket; pulling the handle cuts power)
rationale: Opening like a fridge needs no button hunting.
judge_comment: Fridge-style opening is familiar and removes button hunting, but magnetic seals are questionable for microwave leakage safety and the need is only marginally improved.

title: Food-pictogram scale
new_elements: Minute scale printing (existing numeric dial legend); Pictogram dial legend (coffee cup, soup bowl, plate, frozen box icons replace minutes)
rationale: User turns to the picture of what is inside, no mental conversion.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is simple and cheap, but it is a labeling change and the icons map to time only loosely.

title: Food card slot
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); Punch-card slot (insert a printed food card whose notches set time and power mechanically)
rationale: Choosing a card is simpler than setting two dials.
judge_comment: A mechanical punch-card is a quirky, concrete substitution that removes dial setting, though handling cards adds its own friction.

title: Mode stirrer instead of turntable
new_elements: Glass turntable (existing rotating plate); Flat floor with rotating stirrer blade (metal stirrer under ceiling evens the field)
rationale: No plate to align, nothing to knock off its track.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves, and the change barely affects operation learning.

title: Spoken 'done'
new_elements: Mechanical bell (existing end bell); Speech chip (says 'your food is ready' in local language)
rationale: No need to learn what the sound means.
judge_comment: A speech chip is cheap and clear, but it addresses only the end signal, which is already intuitive.

title: Stop-when-hot IR sensor
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); IR surface thermometer cutoff (stops when food reaches eating temperature); Doneness-based stop (replaces time as the stop criterion)
rationale: User never estimates time; press start, it stops itself.
judge_comment: Doneness-based auto-stop removes time estimation entirely and matches the need, though IR measures only surface temperature and may be unreliable.

title: Single gentle-to-blast dial
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); Combined intensity dial (one knob where position couples power and time via a single cam)
rationale: Two decisions collapse into one knob turn.
judge_comment: A single coupled dial simplifies operation and is easy to build, but it is an incremental tweak, not a radical one.

title: Foot pedal start
new_elements: Control panel (existing knobs); Foot pedal (hold pedal to cook; release to stop)
rationale: Like a sewing machine: press to go, obvious even hands-full.
judge_comment: The hold-to-cook pedal is intuitive and a safe dead-man switch, but it is awkward for longer cooking and still leaves power and time unaddressed.

title: Drawer that starts on close
new_elements: Hinged door + push button (existing); Sliding drawer cavity (pushing drawer shut starts a fixed cycle; pulling stops)
rationale: Close = cook, open = stop; no separate controls.
judge_comment: Close-to-cook removes controls entirely and is very intuitive, though a fixed cycle limits flexibility and a drawer adds mechanical complexity.

title: RFID container tells the oven
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); RFID reader + tagged containers (bundled bowls/mugs carry their own program)
rationale: The container knows what to do, the user just puts it in.
judge_comment: Tagged containers give true zero-learning operation, but they require bundled proprietary bowls and a program for each one.

title: Steam-sensor stop
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Humidity sensor in vent (stops shortly after steam burst detected)
rationale: Reheating needs only 'start'; the oven senses the rest.
judge_comment: Steam sensing for auto-stop is plausible and already exists in sensor-reheat ovens, and it reduces decisions to just pressing start.

title: Weight-driven power selection
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing); Spring-scale floor switch (light loads mechanically select low duty cycle, heavy loads high)
rationale: Power is chosen by physics, not by the user.
judge_comment: Weight is a poor proxy for the right power (a small frozen item versus a small soup), so it may produce wrong results, though removing a decision is clever.

title: Transparent door, no lamp
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp + mesh window (existing); Fine-mesh clear glass door (room light suffices; nothing to switch or replace)
rationale: Seeing food directly is the most intuitive feedback.
judge_comment: A clear door without a lamp gives intuitive feedback, but the food may be hard to see in dim rooms and it does little for operation simplicity; clear glass also raises RF shielding questions.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Control panel (existing knobs); Offline keyword mic (understands 'heat', 'stop', 'more')
rationale: Talking requires no manual.
judge_comment: Offline keyword voice control is plausible and needs no learning, but it is not much simpler than a knob and is a non-obvious substitution for a cheaper part.

title: Tap-tap +30s only
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); One big tap pad (each tap adds 30 s and starts; hold to cancel)
rationale: A single gesture covers every use case.
judge_comment: One tap pad that adds 30 seconds is simple, cheap, and easy to build, though it is less precise for longer cooking times.

title: Detachable egg timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Magnetic kitchen egg timer dock (wind the familiar egg timer, drop it in the dock, oven runs until it rings)
rationale: Reuses a device people already understand.
judge_comment: A familiar wind-up egg timer as the control is intuitive and cheap, and it is playful, though a detachable dock adds a part that can get lost.

title: Rotating antenna, fixed plate
new_elements: Glass turntable + motor (existing); Rotating waveguide antenna (antenna spins beneath a fixed ceramic floor)
rationale: No turntable to seat correctly; square dishes just fit.
judge_comment: Removes turntable seating, which is a minor part of operation; it only loosely serves the no-learning-curve need, though it is plausible, since stirrer or rotating-antenna designs already exist.

title: Door swings open when done
new_elements: Mechanical bell (existing); Timer-released door spring (end of cycle pops door ajar)
rationale: An open door is unmistakable; no sound to interpret.
judge_comment: A door that pops ajar is a clear, intuitive end signal, but it does not simplify operation itself and could be a nuisance.

title: Colour-change window
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp (existing); Thermochromic door panel (door tints red while hot inside, clear when safe)
rationale: Status shown by colour, understood by anyone.
judge_comment: Colour status is intuitive, but a thermochromic door tracks surface temperature rather than cooking state, and it is difficult to make safe and reliable.

title: Little / Medium / A lot
new_elements: Minute scale printing (existing); Three-word dial legend (only 'a little', 'medium', 'a lot' with detents)
rationale: Plain words replace numeric estimation.
judge_comment: Plain-word dial directly removes numeric guessing and is cheap and simple, though it is imprecise and not very radical.

title: Defrost/Cook toggle
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing); Two-position snowflake/flame switch (30% or 100% duty only)
rationale: Five abstract levels become one binary icon choice.
judge_comment: A binary snowflake/flame switch greatly simplifies power choice and is easy to build, but it limits flexibility.

title: Ratchet click timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing continuous dial); Audible 30 s ratchet dial (each click is 30 s; count clicks, no reading)
rationale: Tactile counting works for all ages and eyesight.
judge_comment: Click-counting dial is simple and tactile, but it's a modest tweak of existing mechanical timers and not very radical.

title: Turntable is the dial
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Hand-wound turntable spring (rotate the plate by hand to wind; it unwinds while cooking)
rationale: Setting the time is part of placing the food.
judge_comment: Winding the turntable by hand to set time is quirky and merges placement with setting, though the wind-to-time mapping and wear are questionable.

title: Close-to-start, open-to-stop
new_elements: Start mechanism in timer knob (existing); Door-switch start (shutting the door starts a 1-minute default; reopen to stop)
rationale: The door is the only control.
judge_comment: Door-as-sole-control is very intuitive, but a fixed 1-minute default limits usefulness and risks accidental starts.

title: Toaster lever
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + bell (existing); Push-down pop-up lever (press down to start, lever pops up when done)
rationale: Borrows the universally understood toaster interaction.
judge_comment: Toaster-style lever leverages a universally known interaction and is easily built with mechanical parts, though time setting still needs a dial.

title: User-stickered dial
new_elements: Minute scale printing (existing); Blank dial + sticker sheet (family writes 'Mum's tea', 'rice' at their own positions)
rationale: Personal labels remove remembering of times.
judge_comment: Customizable sticker labels cut memory load and are cheap, but users must still set up and the dial remains a dial.

title: Periscope mirror view
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp (existing); Top-mounted mirror periscope (daylight channeled into cavity, view from above)
rationale: A clear top-down view of the dish makes checking trivial.
judge_comment: A top-down view helps checking food but does little for operating the microwave, and a daylight periscope is awkward.

title: Dedicated mug button
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); Single 'Mug' button (one fixed 90 s full-power profile; the only control)
rationale: Serves the most common task with zero settings.
judge_comment: A single fixed-profile button needs no learning, but it covers only one task and is not very radical.

title: Pressure-mat auto-run
new_elements: Control panel (existing); Pressure mat floor (placing a dish and shutting the door runs a weight-scaled cycle)
rationale: No control panel exists to learn.
judge_comment: Auto-running by weight removes all controls and learning, but weight is a poor proxy for heating needs and starting unattended is a safety risk.

title: Raised tactile scale
new_elements: Minute scale printing (existing); Embossed bumps dial (one bump per minute, big bump per five)
rationale: Usable by touch alone, in the dark, by anyone.
judge_comment: Tactile bumps improve accessibility of a dial, but the user still has to understand timing, so the learning curve is only partly reduced.

title: Red stop, green go
new_elements: Control panel (existing); Two giant arcade buttons (green runs while held/toggled, red stops)
rationale: Traffic-light colours need no instruction.
judge_comment: Colour-coded go and stop buttons are intuitive and cheap, but the user still has to decide on a time, and the idea is fairly obvious.

title: Bimetal thermal timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing escapement); Bimetallic heater-strip timer (cheaper strip bends to cut power; single slider sets bias)
rationale: Simpler, cheaper mechanism behind the same one-slider interface.
judge_comment: The interface stays the same, so the user gains little. The cheaper bimetal mechanism is a plausible substitution but imprecise, and the benefit is to cost rather than to simplicity.

title: Sun-icon power slider
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing numbered steps); Growing-sun slider (slider with small to large sun icons)
rationale: Icon size intuitively maps to heat intensity.
judge_comment: An intuitive icon slider helps users and is easy to build, but it is an incremental change rather than a radical one.

title: Countertop vibration alert
new_elements: Mechanical bell (existing); Eccentric-mass vibrator in feet (gentle rumble felt through the counter)
rationale: Works for hearing-impaired users with no setup.
judge_comment: A vibration alert is feasible and inclusive, but it has little to do with removing the learning curve.

title: Toy wind-up key
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Oversized wind-up key (turns of a visible key = minutes, key unwinds as it cooks)
rationale: Childhood-familiar winding makes time setting playful and obvious.
judge_comment: A familiar wind-up key makes setting the time obvious and playful, and the visible unwinding gives clear feedback. It is mechanically plausible.

title: Elbow bar door
