new_elements: Door push-release button (existing); Full-width push bar (hospital-style bar, press anywhere with elbow or hip)
rationale: No target to find; any push opens it.
judge_comment: A push bar removes the need to find a release target, so opening the door is easy and needs no learning, and it is easy to build.

title: Rest indicator instead of power levels
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing); Full power + 'wait' lamp (always full power; after cycle a lamp glows 60 s saying 'let it rest')
rationale: Removes the power decision while keeping even heating via resting.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible, but it only removes the power choice and the user still has to set the time and wait.

title: Camera watches the bubbles
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Cavity camera with motion detection (stops when boiling or bubbling motion detected); Low-cost image motion sensing (frame-difference chip)
rationale: The oven watches so the user does not have to.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on boiling motion removes the guesswork about time, but steam, condensation and varied foods make detection unreliable.

title: Built-in bowl cavity
new_elements: Glass turntable (existing); Integrated ceramic bowl floor (cavity floor is a removable bowl; pour food straight in)
rationale: No dish choice, no microwave-safe worries.
judge_comment: It removes the dish decision, but a cavity floor that doubles as a bowl is hard to clean, hygienic, and practical for varied foods.

title: Orientation cube controller
new_elements: Control panel (existing); Tilt-sensing cube (cube on top of oven; whichever picture faces up (mug, soup, pizza) runs)
rationale: Turning a toy block is instantly understood.
judge_comment: A tilt cube with pictures is intuitive and playful, but it needs preset programs and has a limited range of foods.

title: Rotary-phone dial
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Finger-stop rotary dial (dial the digit of minutes, it returns and starts)
rationale: One deliberate digit input, no over/under-turning.
judge_comment: The rotary dial is familiar to older users and mechanically plausible, but it is a retro gimmick that is not clearly simpler than a timer knob.

title: Talking pull-string timer
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + bell (existing); Pull-string voice timer (pull string, it announces the set time and later 'ready!')
rationale: Immediate spoken confirmation prevents mistakes.
judge_comment: Spoken confirmation reduces errors, but a pull-string plus voice module adds components rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Handle extension sets time
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (existing); Telescoping door handle timer (pull the handle out to the minute mark, then shut the door)
rationale: The only thing you touch anyway is the handle.
judge_comment: Setting time by pulling the handle is an intuitive single-gesture interface that replaces the knob, though the mechanics and sealing are tricky.

title: Light goes off when done
new_elements: Mechanical bell (existing); Bright exterior ring lamp (glows during cooking, flashes then off when done)
rationale: Visible from across the room, nothing to listen for.
judge_comment: A ring lamp is easy to build and clear, but it only signals status and does not simplify operation much.

title: Preset food shelf slots
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + power knob (existing); Position-coded shelf (left slot = mug, centre = plate, right = frozen; placement selects program)
rationale: Where you put the food is the only input.
judge_comment: Placement-based program selection removes the controls entirely, but the sensing is unreliable and power and time differ by food quantity.

title: Cat-flap push-through door
new_elements: Hinged door + push button + latch (existing); Self-closing flap door (gravity flap with RF gasket; push food in, flap closes itself)
rationale: No latch, no button, no closing step to remember.
judge_comment: A radical idea that removes the latch and the closing step, but a flap cannot contain microwave radiation safely.

title: Weight-sets-time scale platform
new_elements: Load-cell floor plate (Weighs the food and auto-derives heating time, replacing the clockwork timer knob); Strain-gauge load cell (Low-cost weighing sensor as used in kitchen scales)
rationale: User puts food in and presses nothing; weight alone sets duration, no timer to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-derived timing removes the timer entirely and is radical, though weight correlates imperfectly with heating needs and the load cell must survive heat and RF.

title: Tap-to-add-30s single button
new_elements: Single tap button (+30 s per tap) (Replaces the 0-30 min clockwork dial with one button where each tap adds 30 s)
rationale: One control, one gesture, counting taps is intuitive for everyone.
judge_comment: Very easy to learn and cheap, but it is a common existing pattern and not radical.

title: Two-position Gentle/Full rocker
new_elements: Gentle/Full rocker switch (Replaces the 5-step duty-cycle cam with a two-state switch)
rationale: Binary power choice removes the ambiguity of five unlabeled power steps.
judge_comment: Simplifies power choice but leaves the timer unaddressed and offers limited flexibility.

title: Pictogram single knob (cup, plate, popcorn)
new_elements: Food-icon combination knob (One knob with icon detents that sets both time and duty cycle via a dual cam)
rationale: User matches a picture to their food instead of translating minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Icon detents map directly to user intent and a dual cam is plausible, though food categories are coarse.

title: Airflow-driven mode stirrer replaces turntable motor
new_elements: Fan-driven mode stirrer paddle (Metal paddle spun by magnetron cooling air distributes RF; no turntable or motor)
rationale: Flat floor, nothing to align or reseat; the oven just works with any dish placed anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are real and cheap, but the benefit to operation learning is indirect since the controls are unchanged.

title: Flatbed rotating antenna
new_elements: Under-floor rotating antenna (Slow-spinning antenna beneath a flat ceramic floor replaces glass turntable and roller ring)
rationale: Removes the tray-on-ring puzzle and lets oversized dishes be used without jamming.
judge_comment: A rotating antenna under a flat floor is real, existing tech that removes the turntable puzzle, but it only modestly helps operation simplicity.

title: Magnetic pull door, no button
new_elements: Magnetic door catch with handle (Permanent magnets hold the door shut; pulling the handle opens it, replacing button-lever-hook latch)
rationale: Door behaves like every fridge door the user already knows.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic pull door is intuitive and plausible, though safety interlock requirements and a modest gain in simplicity limit it.

title: Hall-effect solid-state interlock
new_elements: Hall-effect magnetic position sensing (Contactless sensors detect door magnet; solid-state relay cuts HV); Hall-sensor interlock module (Replaces three mechanical microswitches with sealed sensors)
rationale: No worn switches means the door never needs a 'slam it harder' trick.
judge_comment: Hall-effect interlocks are feasible and reliable, but the user sees almost no change in operation.

title: Optical beam-break door check
new_elements: IR beam-break door sensor (Door flange interrupts an IR beam; absence of beam-break disables HV)
rationale: Any door position short of closed is unambiguously off, no half-latched confusion.
judge_comment: An IR beam-break check is plausible but lacks redundancy for safety certification, and it is largely invisible to the user.

title: Inverter supply replaces diode/capacitor doubler
new_elements: High-frequency inverter power supply (Switch-mode converter gives continuous variable magnetron power with small low-energy capacitors); Inverter HV board (Replaces transformer, HV capacitor and rectifier diode)
rationale: Power level becomes true and continuous, so 'medium' actually means medium with no duty-cycle surprises.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies already exist and make power levels truer, which helps a bit with predictability but isn't a radical change in learning curve.

title: Solid-state GaN RF source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Transistor-based 2.45 GHz source with reflected-power sensing replaces magnetron and HV chain); Senses food load via reflected power (Auto-adjusts power and stops when absorption drops)
rationale: The oven senses the food itself, so the user never chooses a power level.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing directly removes the need to choose power levels, and it is real emerging tech, though cost and power level are still hurdles.

title: Thermal fuse replaces bimetal thermostat
new_elements: One-shot thermal fuse on magnetron (Cheaper non-resetting cutoff fulfils overheat protection)
rationale: Fewer parts and no reset behavior the user has to understand.
judge_comment: A one-shot thermal fuse is a plausible cost substitution, but users never see it and it does little for ease of operation, and it makes failures non-resettable.

title: Self-bleeding capacitor
new_elements: HV capacitor with integral bleeder (Film capacitor with molded-in discharge resistor replaces separate bleeder wiring)
rationale: Safety is built in and invisible, so unplugging is always safe without rules to remember.
judge_comment: An integral bleeder is feasible and sensible, but it is an invisible safety tweak that barely touches the learning curve.

title: Battery-powered portable microwave
new_elements: Removable Li-ion pack (1 kWh) (Replaces mains cord; charged from USB-C PD or dock); Lithium-ion battery with DC inverter (Low-voltage DC feeding solid-state RF)
rationale: No outlet hunting; students carry it like a kettle and just press go.
judge_comment: A portable battery microwave is bold, but a 1 kWh pack is heavy and costly, and it serves portability rather than simple operation.

title: Silicone mat instead of glass turntable
new_elements: Food-grade silicone turntable mat (Flexible, unbreakable, dishwasher-safe mat replaces tempered glass tray)
rationale: Nothing to break or misalign; drop it in and it works.
judge_comment: A silicone mat is feasible and cheap, but it is a minor change with limited impact on operational simplicity, and it may heat or sag.

title: Glass-ceramic waveguide tile
new_elements: Glazed glass-ceramic waveguide cover (Wipe-clean non-absorbent tile replaces fragile mica sheet)
rationale: No crumbling mica to replace or arcing to diagnose; care-free ownership.
judge_comment: Practical substitution of the mica cover, but it only tangentially serves the no-learning-curve need by reducing maintenance.

title: PTFE wipe-clean waveguide sheet
new_elements: PTFE waveguide cover sheet (Non-stick polymer sheet, microwave transparent, replaces mica)
rationale: Splatter wipes off instantly, removing maintenance knowledge from the user.
judge_comment: PTFE is microwave transparent and wipeable, but its heat tolerance near the waveguide is questionable, and the link to operational simplicity is weak.

title: LED cavity lighting
new_elements: Low-voltage LED cavity lamp (Replaces 20-25 W incandescent bulb; never needs replacing)
rationale: Lifetime light means no bulb-change procedure to ever learn.
judge_comment: LED lamps are already common and have almost nothing to do with the ease of operating the microwave.

title: Spoken 'done' instead of bell
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (Says 'your food is ready' and 'careful, hot' instead of ringing a bell)
rationale: Plain-language feedback requires zero interpretation.
judge_comment: Spoken feedback is easy to understand and feasible, but it is incremental, not radical, and it only covers output.

title: Heat-until-hot IR sensor
new_elements: IR food thermometer stop sensor (Replaces timer: one button heats until surface reaches eating temperature); Thermopile infrared sensing (Non-contact temperature reading through cavity port)
rationale: The user asks for 'hot', not for minutes.
judge_comment: One-button heat-until-hot removes the need to choose time or power, directly serving zero learning curve, though IR surface sensing is imperfect for uneven heating.

title: Humidity-sensor auto-cook
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects steam release to end cooking, replacing both knobs with one Start button)
rationale: One button, the oven decides when the food is steaming done.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor cooking already exists in sensor-cook modes; a single Start button is a clear simplicity win, but it is not radical and it handles non-steaming foods poorly.

title: Package NFC program scan
new_elements: NFC reader in door frame (Reads cook program from ready-meal packaging tag; replaces timer and power knobs); Zero-decision ready-meal heating (Food tells the oven what to do)
rationale: Hold the package near the door and close it; nothing to read or set.
judge_comment: Package tags that program the oven remove every decision, but this needs packaging-industry adoption and covers only ready meals.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline voice command module (Replaces knobs: 'two minutes', 'defrost', 'stop')
rationale: Speaking a duration needs no instructions.
judge_comment: Voice control needs no learning, but it is already common, it is noisy and awkward in some settings, and the description is vague.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Spring-return pull cord timer (Pull length sets time (marked cord); cord retracts as it counts down, replacing the dial)
rationale: Physical length is a more intuitive quantity than an angle on a tiny dial.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer is a tangible and distinctive mechanism, but the cord and its markings still have to be learned and it is a bit gimmicky for a microwave.

title: Door handle is the timer
new_elements: Twist-handle timer latch (Twisting the door handle sets minutes and locks the door; it unwinds and unlatches at zero)
rationale: Closing and setting become one gesture on one part.
judge_comment: Merging door closing and time setting into one twist gesture is clever and radical, though a mechanical latch that must unwind safely brings safety and precision challenges.

title: Foot pedal door opener
new_elements: Foot pedal door release (Replaces push button; frees hands carrying hot dishes)
rationale: Bin-lid familiarity; no fumbling for a small button.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is easy to use, but it only replaces the door opener and does not remove the learning curve for time and power.

title: Top-loading lid microwave
new_elements: Hinged top lid with gravity seal (Chest-style lid replaces front door, button latch and hooks; lid weight closes the choke seal)
rationale: Drop food in from above like a pot; no spill risk and no latch to learn.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid is a radical change and intuitive to use, but it needs a workable microwave choke seal and still has no simple way to set the cooking time.

title: Drawer microwave, close to start
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Food sits in a pull-out drawer; pushing it shut starts a default cycle)
rationale: Push to start is the only instruction needed.
judge_comment: Pushing the drawer shut to start is intuitive, but a default cycle may not suit every food.

title: Close-to-start one-minute mug oven
new_elements: Door-closure start switch (60 s fixed) (Closing door runs exactly 60 s; opening stops; repeat as needed. No timer at all)
rationale: Zero controls; the door is the only interface.
judge_comment: Closing the door to run a fixed 60 s needs no controls and is easy to build, though it is inflexible for different foods.

title: RFID bowls choose the program
new_elements: Supplied RFID-tagged bowl set (Soup bowl, plate and mug each carry a tag read by the oven to set power and time)
rationale: Choosing a bowl is the whole decision.
judge_comment: Choosing a tagged bowl sets the program with no learning, but the user must use the supplied bowls and RFID adds cost.

title: LED ring countdown around knob
new_elements: Illuminated countdown ring (Ring of LEDs around a single quartz-timed knob shows remaining time, replacing bell-only feedback)
rationale: Glanceable progress needs no reading of numbers.
judge_comment: Glanceable progress helps a bit, but it adds an element rather than substituting a part, and it isn't radical.

title: Liquid detection anti-superheat pulse
new_elements: Liquid-load detector (weight + IR) (Identifies cups of liquid and auto-pulses power, replacing manual power selection)
rationale: Safety behavior is automatic, so the user needs no warnings to learn.
judge_comment: Automating power for liquids removes a safety concern, but reliable detection of liquid and superheat risk is hard and the idea is only loosely tied to simple operation.

title: Arc sensor auto-cutoff
new_elements: Acoustic/optical arc detector (Detects arcing flash or crackle and cuts RF, replacing the 'no metal' rule)
rationale: Forgives the most common user mistake instead of requiring knowledge.
judge_comment: Forgiving the 'no metal' rule removes a learned constraint, and arc detection is plausible though not easy to make reliable.

title: Turntable is the timer dial
new_elements: Hand-rotated minute-marked turntable (User turns the tray to a minute mark; motor unwinds it back to zero as it heats)
rationale: The food's own plate is the control; nothing on the front panel.
judge_comment: Using the turntable as a tactile timer dial is a radical, intuitive substitution that needs no learning, though mechanical complexity and precision are challenges.

title: Current-sensing replaces monitor switch
new_elements: Magnetron current monitor (Electronics detect RF-on with door open and trip; replaces third mechanical monitor switch)
rationale: Fewer mechanical adjustments reduce field faults the user would otherwise have to troubleshoot.
judge_comment: This is an internal safety-component swap that the user never sees, so it does little for no-learning-curve operation.

title: NTC in inverter replaces thermostat
new_elements: NTC thermistor magnetron monitor (Inverter reads temperature and derates power smoothly instead of snapping off)
rationale: No abrupt mid-cook shutoff that puzzles the user.
judge_comment: Technically sound and cheap, but it is an invisible internal change that barely affects the learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Music-box timer
new_elements: Wind-up music-box timer (Winding sets time; a tune plays while cooking and silence signals done, replacing dial and bell)
rationale: Audible progress means the user never wonders how long is left.
judge_comment: A wind-up music-box timer gives intuitive audible progress and a simple operation, though a mechanical timer is imprecise and the tune could annoy.

title: Roller ring takes the user's own plate
new_elements: Universal plate roller ring (Three-arm spring roller grips any plate, eliminating the glass tray)
rationale: One less part to wash, align or break.
judge_comment: A roller ring for any plate removes a part, but uneven plates and microwave heating uniformity make it hard, and it does little for ease of use.

title: Push-the-door-to-open
new_elements: Push-push door latch (Cabinet-style push latch: press the door itself to pop it open, no separate button)
rationale: Whole door is the button, nothing to find.
judge_comment: Pushing the door to open is intuitive and cheap, with some safety and interlock design to handle.

title: Thermochromic door window
new_elements: Thermochromic door film (Window tints from blue to red with cavity heat, replacing the lamp as feedback)
rationale: Color shows hot-or-not at a glance without opening or reading.
judge_comment: Color feedback is intuitive, but a thermochromic film must keep the door's microwave shielding and cavity temperature is a poor proxy for cooking state.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Momentary hold-to-heat button (Heats only while pressed; release stops. Replaces timer for short bursts)
rationale: Perfect 10-second warm-ups with no dial reading.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive with zero learning and feasible via a momentary switch, though it only suits short bursts.

title: Two-detent power cam
new_elements: Two-step duty-cycle cam (Defrost/Cook) (Simplified cam replaces five-step cam)
rationale: Cheaper mechanism and a choice anyone can make.
judge_comment: A simple two-choice cam cuts decisions and cost but is an incremental simplification of existing mechanical designs.

title: Quartz timer in a single knob
new_elements: Quartz-timed rotary knob (Electronic timing behind a classic knob; accurate to the second with no keypad)
rationale: Keeps the familiar twist while fixing short-duration imprecision.
judge_comment: A familiar knob with electronic timing is practical, but it's a common approach and adds little to the no-learning-curve need.

title: Strobe beacon end signal
new_elements: Flashing top beacon (Bright flashing light replaces bell for noisy or hearing-impaired contexts)
rationale: Universally noticed signal, no sound to interpret.
judge_comment: A flashing beacon is easy to build and helps accessibility but barely touches operation simplicity.

title: Tactile braille detent knob
new_elements: Tactile-detent knob with raised icons (Molded tactile markings replace printed scale on knobs)
rationale: Settings can be felt, not read, so operation is learnable in one touch.
judge_comment: Molded tactile detents and icons make settings feelable and easy to learn, and are cheap to produce, though not very radical.

title: Single food-pictogram dial
new_elements: One rotary preset dial with food icons (mug, plate, butter, frozen block) (Each icon position encodes a fixed time+power cam profile; no numbers at all.)
rationale: Two abstract knobs become one picture choice, removing all time/power arithmetic.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are easy to understand and feasible with a cam or electronic profile, though icon-based presets exist and are not very radical.

title: One big +30 s button
new_elements: Single large start button, each press adds 30 s at full power (Mechanical ratchet-stepper advances a cam; no setting phase, just press and go.)
rationale: The only interaction is pushing one button, with zero modes to learn.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is extremely simple and feasible, but it is already common on many microwaves and not radical.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Spring-retracting pull cord with coloured length bands (How far you pull the cord equals cooking time; retraction drives the switch and bell.)
rationale: Pulling a cord is a bodily, obvious gesture needing no instruction.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer is intuitive and mechanically plausible, a playful substitute for the knob, but it offers limited control and has some wear concerns.

title: Weigh-and-go scale floor
new_elements: Load-cell weighing of food mass (Cavity floor weighs the load; time is derived from mass automatically.); Weighing turntable base that sets cook time (Replaces user timer input with a scale.)
rationale: User sets nothing; the appliance weighs the food and decides.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic timing removes all user input, but weight alone is a poor proxy for food type and heating needs, and the load cell has to cope with the turntable and heat.

title: Steam-sensor auto stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent with single Start button (Cooking stops when steam burst indicates food is hot through.)
rationale: Replaces the mental model of minutes with a single Start press.
judge_comment: Steam-sensing auto stop with a single Start is highly relevant and feasible, as sensor cooking exists, though it is not very novel and works unevenly for dry foods.

title: Temperature dial instead of timer
new_elements: Thermopile infrared food surface sensing (Non-contact IR sensor reads food temperature through a mica window.); Target-temperature knob (warm / hot / piping) (Heating runs until the IR reading meets the dial setting.)
rationale: People know how hot they want food, not how many minutes it needs.
judge_comment: A temperature dial matches how people think, but IR sensing through a window in a steamy cavity is tricky and surface readings can mislead.

title: Delete the power knob
new_elements: Fixed full-power operation with defrost handled by a dedicated 'Frozen' button (Power selector removed entirely; one extra button covers the only low-power case.)
rationale: Removing a control is the purest simplification.
judge_comment: Easy to build and simpler to use, but it is a modest change and the extra Frozen button still has to be learned.

title: Two-position Heat/Gentle rocker
new_elements: Rocker switch: Heat or Gentle (Replaces 5-step cam with a binary choice (100% / 30% duty).)
rationale: A binary choice is instantly understood by anyone.
judge_comment: A very feasible binary rocker that is easy to grasp, though it is incremental and limits cooking flexibility.

title: Reflected-power self-setting magnetron
new_elements: Reflected RF power sensing (directional coupler) (Measures how much energy the load absorbs; small/light loads automatically get lower duty.); Auto power module in waveguide (Eliminates the manual power knob.)
rationale: Power level becomes invisible and automatic.
judge_comment: Sensing reflected power to set duty automatically is clever and hides the setting, but its accuracy for judging food needs is uncertain.

title: Solid-state RF with continuous auto-cook
new_elements: GaN/LDMOS solid-state 2.45 GHz amplifier (Low-voltage transistor source with continuously variable power and built-in load feedback.); Solid-state RF source module (Replaces magnetron, HV transformer, capacitor and diode.)
rationale: Closed-loop power lets a single Start button cook correctly without user settings.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with closed-loop control is a radical enabler of one-button cooking; it is technically credible but costly and not a cheaper substitute yet.

title: Inverter supply replaces HV transformer
new_elements: High-frequency switch-mode inverter HV supply (Lighter, continuously adjustable, no 1 µF lethal capacitor.); Inverter board (Substitutes transformer + doubler.)
rationale: Smooth true low power makes 'Gentle' settings behave predictably so users learn by feel.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist and the link to zero learning curve is weak, since users still face power settings.

title: Magnetic soft-close pull door
new_elements: Handle-less door edge held by ferrite magnets (Push to close, pull the lip to open; no release button or latch lever.)
rationale: Opening works like a fridge, which everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A fridge-like magnetic door removes the latch and button, but the magnets must still hold a safe seal and satisfy interlock requirements.

title: Drawer-style cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity on slides (Food is placed from above into a drawer; closing the drawer completes the choke seal.)
rationale: No hinge, no button, no reaching into a hot box—just a drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive interaction and has been done commercially, but sealing the choke and handling spills are challenges.

title: Foot-pedal door opener
new_elements: Bowden-cable foot pedal release (Like a pedal bin: step to open while hands hold the plate.)
rationale: Borrowing the pedal-bin gesture removes the hunt for the button.
judge_comment: A pedal frees the hands but adds a hidden gesture and floor-level hardware, and it does nothing for operating the controls.

title: Top-loading pot microwave
new_elements: Cylindrical top-loading cavity with hinged choke lid (Rice-cooker form factor; lid is the door, gravity keeps food centred.)
rationale: A lidded pot is the most familiar kitchen interaction there is.
judge_comment: The rice-cooker form is familiar and radical, but it limits dish shapes, and the top-loading cavity and its rotation or field uniformity are technically difficult.

title: Door pops open at end
new_elements: Timer-released spring that ejects the door ajar (The open door itself is the 'done' signal and the access gesture.)
rationale: Toaster-style ejection needs no interpretation of sounds.
judge_comment: Toaster-style door ejection makes the finished state and the access gesture one and the same, though it needs care for safety and for hot food spilling.

title: Pop-up flag indicator
new_elements: Spring-loaded red flag released by timer cam (Silent visual 'ready' indicator visible across the room.)
rationale: Unambiguous state display, no sound to miss or misread.
judge_comment: A mechanical flag is a simple, clear signal, but it only reports 'done' and does nothing to simplify operating the oven.

title: Voice chip 'Your food is ready'
new_elements: Pre-recorded voice announcement module (Replaces bell striker with a spoken message in local language.)
rationale: Words need no learning of what a ding means.
judge_comment: Voice chips are cheap and easy to build, but the idea is common and only improves the end alert, not how the user operates the oven.

title: Bluetooth ping to phone
new_elements: BLE beacon notification (Low-cost module broadcasts 'done' to a paired phone.); BLE done-notifier (Substitutes mechanical bell.)
rationale: Feedback follows the user, so they never have to learn to wait near the oven.
judge_comment: It needs pairing and a phone app, which adds learning and cuts against the no-learning-curve goal.

title: Pocket vibrating puck
new_elements: Detachable vibrating coin puck (restaurant-pager style) (Dock on fascia; take it with you; it buzzes at end of cycle.)
rationale: Physical pager metaphor is universally understood without setup.
judge_comment: The restaurant-pager metaphor is familiar and intuitive, but a detachable puck adds a part that can be lost and needs charging.

title: Whole-cabinet colour glow
new_elements: Translucent cabinet panel lit red while cooking, green when done (Cabinet itself becomes the status display; replaces bell and inner lamp.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours require no learning.
judge_comment: Intuitive traffic-light status is easy to understand, but it only addresses feedback and not the actual operation of the controls; a lit translucent cabinet panel also needs RF-safe design.

title: Long-life LED replaces incandescent lamp
new_elements: Mains-driven LED module (Lifetime exceeds product life; cheaper to run.); Sealed LED cavity light (Never needs replacing.)
rationale: Removes a maintenance task the user would otherwise have to learn.
judge_comment: It is very feasible but an obvious swap that barely relates to ease of operation.

title: Transparent conductive glass door
new_elements: ITO / fine-wire-grid transparent conductive glazing (Optically clear glass that still forms a Faraday shield.); Clear shielded door, no mesh (Kitchen light illuminates the food; interior lamp optional.)
rationale: Seeing food clearly lets users judge doneness by eye instead of by rules.
judge_comment: Conductive transparent glazing is plausible and gives a clearer view, but its link to learning-free operation is indirect.

title: Electroluminescent door panel
new_elements: Electroluminescent film laminated on the door glass (Whole window glows softly inward; no bulb cavity, no shadows.)
rationale: Uniform light shows the whole plate at once for instant checking.
judge_comment: An electroluminescent door film is novel, but it would be dim, difficult to combine with RF shielding, and only loosely tied to the need.

title: Mode stirrer instead of turntable
new_elements: Rotating metal mode-stirrer fan in waveguide (Stirs the standing-wave pattern; flat solid cavity floor.); Flat-floor cavity with ceiling stirrer (No tray, ring or coupler to misplace.)
rationale: Nothing to seat correctly—any dish goes anywhere on a flat floor.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, and a flat floor removes parts the user could misplace, which makes this a practical way to cut setup effort.

title: Rotating under-floor antenna
new_elements: Motor-driven rotating feed antenna beneath ceramic floor (Feeds energy from below in a sweeping pattern.)
rationale: Flat floor removes tray handling and misalignment errors.
judge_comment: Rotating antenna under a flat ceramic floor is real tech (used in some commercial models), removes the tray, and mildly helps simplicity, though it is not a radical leap.

title: Use your own plate as the turntable
new_elements: Rotating silicone-rimmed hub that grips any plate (The user's dish sits directly on three soft rollers; no glass tray.)
rationale: One fewer part to clean, lose or reseat.
judge_comment: Rollers that grip any plate remove the tray, but stability with varied dish shapes is questionable and it adds little to ease of operation.

title: Removable dishwasher-safe liner
new_elements: Lift-out ceramic-coated cavity liner (Entire cooking box slides out to the sink; replaces enamel wiping.)
rationale: Cleaning becomes 'put it in the dishwasher', nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A removable cavity liner addresses cleaning rather than operation, and is hard to do with RF containment and sealing.

title: Door-is-the-switch reed interlock
new_elements: Magnet-in-door reed-switch interlock with monitor relay (No levers or microswitch alignment; door position alone gates power.)
rationale: Door can be opened mid-cycle any way the user likes and heating simply stops.
judge_comment: A reed switch interlock is plausible, but users already open doors anyway so the operation benefit is minimal, and safety standards require redundant interlocks.

title: Resettable polyfuse
new_elements: PTC polymer resettable fuse (Self-resets after cooling; no replacement part.); Resettable overcurrent protector (Substitutes ceramic cartridge fuse.)
rationale: Users never have to learn about fuses or service calls.
judge_comment: A resettable polyfuse is technically sound, but it is invisible to the user and only marginally touches the operation need.

title: Self-regulating PTC thermal protection
new_elements: PTC thermistor in series with fan and lamp circuit (Current self-limits with temperature; no snap-disc to trip or reset.)
rationale: Overheat protection becomes invisible and never leaves the user puzzled by a dead oven.
judge_comment: A PTC in series with the fan and lamp is a plausible substitution, but it protects the magnetron poorly and barely affects ease of use.

title: Magnetic breakaway power connector
new_elements: Magnetic quick-release mains coupler (Cord detaches safely if pulled; also lets children's tugs do no harm.)
rationale: Plugging in becomes a snap action with no orientation to figure out.
judge_comment: Magnetic breakaway mains couplers exist on appliances like fryers, but plugging in is not where microwave learning-curve problems arise.

title: Passive chimney cooling
new_elements: Heat-pipe + finned chimney natural convection (Silent cooling of magnetron without a fan.); Fanless heat-pipe stack (Removes fan motor and its noise.)
rationale: Silence makes the one remaining sound—'done'—impossible to confuse.
judge_comment: A fanless heat-pipe chimney is novel and concrete, but a magnetron's heat load makes passive cooling doubtful, and the link to ease of use is tenuous.

title: Hand-wound mainspring timer
new_elements: Hand-wound clockwork timer (no synchronous motor) (Twisting the knob winds a spring escapement; mains-frequency independent.)
rationale: Same egg-timer twist the user already knows, with fewer parts.
judge_comment: A wind-up mechanical timer is familiar, intuitive, and cheap, and it directly serves no-learning-curve operation, though it is a retro idea.

title: RC analog electronic timer
new_elements: Potentiometer-set RC timer driving a relay (Cheap analog circuit gives accurate short times from 10 s upward.)
rationale: A single knob stays, but short reheats now work first time without trial and error.
judge_comment: An RC timer with a relay is feasible and keeps a single knob, but it is a conventional analog design and offers modest gains in usability.

title: Tactile click-per-30 s knob
new_elements: Detented knob with one audible click per 30 s and raised braille marks (Time is counted by clicks rather than read off a scale.)
rationale: Counting clicks works eyes-free and needs no numbers.
judge_comment: Eyes-free and simple, but counting clicks still requires some mental effort, and detented timer knobs are already common.

title: LED countdown bar replaces dial scale
new_elements: Row of ten LEDs that extinguish as time passes (Progress is shown as a shrinking light bar instead of a rotating pointer.)
rationale: A shrinking bar is understood at a glance from across the room.
judge_comment: Easy to read at a glance, but it only displays progress and does not simplify setting the time.

title: Thermochromic window
new_elements: Thermochromic film on door glass shifting colour with cavity heat (Window tint tells you whether the food is warm; no lamp needed to judge.)
rationale: Colour is read intuitively, replacing interpretation of time remaining.
judge_comment: An unusual idea, but thermochromic film on glass is not robust and it does not simplify operation, since cavity air temperature is a poor proxy for food temperature.

title: Mug-slot auto-run
new_elements: Mug-sized recess with microswitch that triggers a fixed 90 s cycle (Place a cup, door closes, it just runs; the plate area keeps a normal dial.)
rationale: The most common task—hot drink—needs no settings at all.
judge_comment: It removes all settings for the most common task with a simple microswitch, though a fixed 90 s cycle is rigid.

title: NFC container tags set the cycle
new_elements: Passive NFC tag reading (Tagged bowls/mugs carry their own time+power recipe.); NFC reader under cavity floor (Replaces manual knob setting for tagged dishware.)
rationale: The dish knows its recipe; the user only closes the door.
judge_comment: A dish that carries its own recipe means zero learning, but it needs special tagged dishware and an NFC reader that must work inside the microwave cavity.

title: Barcode-scan packaging
new_elements: Low-cost barcode window on fascia reading ready-meal instructions (Package code maps to printed microwave time; no manual entry.)
rationale: Replaces reading tiny package text and translating it to knob positions.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning removes manual time entry, but it depends on a code-to-time database and only works for packaged meals.

title: Voice-command start
new_elements: Offline keyword-spotting voice module ('heat two minutes') (Replaces knobs with speech; works without internet.)
rationale: Saying what you want is the zero-learning interface.
judge_comment: Offline voice control is feasible and intuitive, but it is a fairly common idea and is not a cheap substitution.

title: Press-harder-for-longer pad
new_elements: Single force-sensitive pad: light press 30 s, firm press 2 min, hold for 5 min (One surface replaces the fascia controls.)
rationale: Control collapses to a single intuitive gesture with no reading.
judge_comment: A single force-sensitive pad is simple and cheap, though the pressure levels may not be discoverable without some learning.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Large momentary button: heats only while held (with transparent door) (No timer, no bell—user watches and releases when satisfied.)
rationale: Radically simple: the oven does exactly what your finger does, for short reheats.
judge_comment: A hold-to-heat button needs almost no learning and is easy to build, but it is impractical for longer heating times.

title: Revolving-drum door
new_elements: Rotating half-open metal drum cavity (revolving-door principle) (Turn the drum to load; turning it closed starts heating; RF seal is always complete.)
rationale: Load, turn, done—one motion replaces door, button and start.
judge_comment: The revolving-drum door is highly radical and elegant for loading, but it is hard to engineer and the RF seal and cleaning are doubtful.

title: Tambour roll-top door
new_elements: Metal-slat roll-top shutter with conductive brush seals (Slides up like a bread bin; no swing clearance, no latch button.)
rationale: Bread-bin gesture is familiar and works in tight kitchens.
judge_comment: Familiar gesture, but microwave leakage through a roll-up slat door with brush seals is a serious safety and engineering problem, and it does little for operational simplicity.

title: Closing the door starts cooking
new_elements: Door-close switch that auto-starts the preset dial time (No separate start action; opening the door pauses, closing resumes.)
rationale: Eliminates the 'did I press start?' step entirely.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start cooking removes a step and is easy to implement with an interlock switch, though there's some risk of unintended starts.

title: Scented 'done' signal
new_elements: Timer-cam releases a puff of warm-air fragrance (vanilla/coffee) (Olfactory end-of-cycle cue instead of a bell.)
rationale: Smell reaches users anywhere in the home with no device to check or sound to decode.
judge_comment: A scent cue is novel, but it replaces the bell without making operation simpler, and fragrance cartridges add cost and could taint the food.

title: Plate-presenting elevator
new_elements: Timer-released platform that lifts the plate out of a top-opening cavity (The food literally rises to meet you when ready.)
rationale: Signal, access and serving collapse into one self-evident event.
judge_comment: A very radical and intuitive serve-on-completion idea, but a lifting platform in a top-opening cavity is hard to build, a spill risk, and costly.

title: Icon-only fascia, no text
new_elements: Moulded-in pictograms and colour zones replacing printed numbers (Fascia communicates by shape and colour only; one tooling for all regions.)
rationale: No language or numeracy needed to operate.
judge_comment: Pictograms and colour zones are cheap and feasible and cut the learning curve, but this is an incremental change rather than a radical one.

title: Reflected-power arc guard replaces user vigilance
new_elements: Metal-detect/arc sensor that refuses to start with metal inside (Reflected-power spike at start cuts RF and lights a 'metal' icon.)
rationale: Users no longer need to learn the 'no metal' rule—the oven enforces it.
judge_comment: Reflected-power sensing to block starts with metal is plausible and removes one learned rule, but it addresses only a narrow safety aspect of operation, is not very radical, and doesn't clearly follow the SUBSTITUTE operator.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand hourglass with optical empty-sensor (User flips a visible sand glass; a photodiode stops the magnetron when sand runs out.)
rationale: Everyone understands sand running out; no numbers to read.
judge_comment: Intuitive visual timer, but fixed sand volume limits flexibility and flipping adds an action; photodiode sensing is plausible.

title: One big Go button (+30 s per press)
new_elements: Single oversized start button adding 30 s per press (Replaces the 0-30 min dial with one tactile button and a click counter.)
rationale: One control, one gesture, zero learning curve for elderly users.
judge_comment: Very simple and cheap, though many microwaves already have a +30s button so it is not radical.

title: Weigh-and-go turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable auto-setting duration by food mass (Strain gauge under turntable computes time; user only closes door.)
rationale: No input at all; the oven decides the time.
judge_comment: Zero input is ideal, but mass alone poorly predicts the needed time for different foods, risking errors.

title: Pull-cord music-box timer
new_elements: Spring-rewind pull-cord escapement (Pull cord length sets duration; cord retracts and clicks off like a toy.)
rationale: Pulling a cord is intuitive and cheaper than a motor cam.
judge_comment: Mechanical pull-cord timer is intuitive and cheap, and resembles old mechanical timers; it is workable and charming.

title: Drawer instead of door
new_elements: Pull-out shielded drawer cavity (Food sits on a sliding tray; drawer edge forms the choke seal.)
rationale: Pull, place, push: no hinge, no button, no latch logic to learn.
judge_comment: Radical drawer format is intuitive, but it still needs a start control and the choke seal is hard to engineer for safety.

title: Roller-shutter front
new_elements: Mesh roller shutter sliding up into the top (Conductive slat shutter replaces hinged door and latch.)
rationale: Lift to open, drop to close — a garage-door gesture everyone knows.
judge_comment: Radical and intuitive gesture, but RF sealing of a moving mesh shutter and safety certification are very hard, and it doesn't address timing or power controls.

title: Magnetic self-latching door
new_elements: Magnetic edge latch with reed-switch interlock (Permanent magnets hold door; pulling handle opens; reed switches do interlock.)
rationale: Removes the push button: the door works like a fridge.
judge_comment: Easy and plausible, but it only simplifies door opening and is an incremental change, since magnetic latches exist on fridges.

title: Foot-pedal door opener
new_elements: Floor pedal cable release for door (Pedal pulls latch lever so hands-full users open with a foot.)
rationale: Same bin-lid gesture people already use; no fiddly button.
judge_comment: Feasible, but it solves hands-full opening rather than learning-free operation, and a floor pedal is awkward for a countertop microwave.

title: Say-a-number voice timer
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recogniser chip (Recognises 'two minutes', 'defrost', 'stop' with no cloud.)
rationale: Speaking is the most natural interface; nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Offline keyword recognition directly removes the learning curve for setting time and is technically mature, though voice-controlled microwaves already exist.

title: Picture dial of foods
new_elements: Single icon dial (cup, plate, popcorn, frozen block) (Each icon maps to a fixed time/power pair on one cam.)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating, not numbers.
judge_comment: A single icon dial with a cam mapping each food to a fixed time/power pair is cheap, simple and directly serves zero-learning use, though preset limits flexibility.

title: Two-position gentle/full rocker
new_elements: Rocker switch: Full / Gentle (Replaces 5-step cam with a two-state switch and fixed 50 % duty.)
rationale: Binary choice removes ambiguity of 5 levels.
judge_comment: A simple, feasible reduction of power levels, but still leaves a choice and is only an incremental change.

title: No power knob at all
new_elements: Fixed full-power magnetron feed, no power control (Deletes cam switch; time is the only variable.)
rationale: Fewest controls possible; cheaper and nothing to misunderstand.
judge_comment: Removing power control makes operation very simple and cheap, but it is not radical and limits cooking results such as defrosting.

title: Toaster-style lever
new_elements: Push-down lever that pops up when done (Lever travel sets duration; a bimetal or motor releases it.)
rationale: Borrows the toaster mental model everyone already has.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever mental model gives a near-zero learning curve and is plausible with a bimetal or motor release, though setting the duration is unclear.

title: Transparent conductive glass door
new_elements: Indium-tin-oxide / silver-mesh coated glass shielding (Optically clear conductive layer replaces perforated steel mesh.)
rationale: Clear view of food lets users judge doneness without any settings.
judge_comment: Conductive transparent coatings exist and improve visibility, but they do little for operational simplicity and add cost.

title: Lift-off lid like a pot
new_elements: Detachable top lid with choke rim, no hinges (Lid rests by gravity; weight switch confirms seal.)
rationale: Lid on/off is a cooking gesture already known from pots.
judge_comment: A radical pot-lid gesture is intuitive, but a hingeless lid is hard to make leak-safe for RF and raises safety concerns.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor stopping when steam plateaus (Replaces timer with closed-loop 'stop when hot' detection.)
rationale: User presses nothing but start; no duration guessing.
judge_comment: Removes duration guessing entirely, which is ideal for zero learning curve, though humidity sensing exists in some high-end models and is unreliable for dry foods.

title: Temperature dial instead of time dial
new_elements: IR thermopile with 'Warm / Hot / Boiling' dial (Oven runs until food surface hits chosen temperature.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not minutes.
judge_comment: A temperature dial matches how people think, and an IR thermopile is a named component, but surface-only readings and containers limit accuracy.

title: Quartz timer in the same knob
new_elements: Rotary encoder + cheap MCU timer (Keeps the knob feel but counts precisely, independent of mains frequency.)
rationale: Same intuitive knob, now accurate for 20-second tasks.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap, but it is basically a standard digital timer behind a knob and adds little for the learning curve.

title: Draw-an-arc touch ring
new_elements: Capacitive ring: trace arc length = minutes (Sealed, no moving parts; arc lights up as it counts down.)
rationale: Visual, continuous, one gesture; easy to wipe clean.
judge_comment: A visual one-gesture capacitive ring is intuitive and sealed, but arc-to-time mapping still requires some learning and similar touch controls exist.

title: Hand-crank timer
new_elements: Crank handle: each turn = 10 s with a click (Winds a spring escapement; no motor, no mains dependence.)
rationale: Counting turns is simpler than reading a dial scale.
judge_comment: A wind-up crank is quirky and tactile, but the spring escapement is imprecise and slower to use than a dial for longer times.

title: Door-close is the start button
new_elements: Door switch that auto-starts 60 s on closing (Closing door starts; opening stops; no separate controls.)
rationale: Zero controls: the door is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Door-close auto-start removes all controls and is plausible, but a fixed 60 s and the risk of accidental starts limit it; some existing microwaves already do something similar.

title: Shelf height sets power
new_elements: Two-level rack: near/far from waveguide = strong/gentle (Field intensity varies with position, replacing duty-cycle cam.)
rationale: Physical placement replaces an abstract power number.
judge_comment: Using shelf position to set power is clever, but standing-wave patterns are unpredictable and the user still has to learn which level to choose.

title: Water-ballast gentle mode
new_elements: Passive ceramic/water absorber block for defrost (User places absorber beside food to soak up half the energy.)
rationale: Defrost becomes 'add the block', no settings.
judge_comment: A passive absorber block is simple and workable, but it adds an extra object and a step, and the heating is uneven.

title: Attenuating defrost cloche
new_elements: Lossy-dielectric cover lid that halves field at food (Cover tunes effective power continuously by design, not duty cycle.)
rationale: Gentler, continuous heating with a cover instead of a knob.
judge_comment: A lossy cover that reduces power is plausible and replaces a knob, but it is fixed at one level and has heat-safety concerns.

title: Revolving-drum loader
new_elements: Rotating mesh drum with one open sector (Spin the drum to present food to the opening; cavity never 'opens'.)
rationale: Spin to load, spin to seal — one motion.
judge_comment: A rotating drum loader is radical and intuitive, but a mesh drum has major RF-sealing and practicality problems, and it doesn't really remove the need to start or time the cooking.

title: Push-push cabinet latch
new_elements: Push-to-open cabinet latch (Pressing the door itself releases it; no separate button.)
rationale: Any push anywhere on the door opens it.
judge_comment: Push-to-open latch is simple and feasible and eases opening, but it addresses only door opening, not the core cooking operation, and it is a known mechanism.

title: Door pops open when done
new_elements: Timer-cam-triggered spring door ejector (End-of-cycle cam also releases latch so the door swings ajar.)
rationale: Oven announces and opens itself; nothing to press.
judge_comment: A cam-triggered door pop-open at cycle end removes a step and is concrete, but it does not simplify setting up the cook.

title: Three preset buttons 1/2/3 min
new_elements: Three large colour-coded fixed-time buttons (Mechanical latching buttons start fixed cycles; no dial.)
rationale: Choosing among three is faster than setting a continuum.
judge_comment: Three fixed-time colour-coded buttons are very easy to use and cheap, though many microwaves already have preset buttons, so it is not radical.

title: Recipe cards you slot in
new_elements: Punched-card slot reading time/power holes (Food cards carry mechanical codes; slot sets both settings.)
rationale: Insert the 'soup card' — no knowledge needed.
judge_comment: Slot-in punched food cards need no knowledge and are novel, but they require card management and limit flexibility.

title: Doneness dial (rare → well)
new_elements: Single toaster-style doneness knob (One cam couples time and duty into a 'light to strong' scale.)
rationale: One knob, one concept, like the browning dial.
judge_comment: A single doneness knob borrows a familiar toaster mental model, so it needs no learning, and a cam coupling time and power is plausible.

title: Defrost bar only
new_elements: Single 'Defrost' latching bar, else full power (Replaces 5-step cam with one 30 % duty option.)
rationale: Only the one non-full mode people actually use.
judge_comment: Simple and cost-saving, with a clear cut to a single exception mode, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Fading light ring as countdown
new_elements: LED ring on door bezel that drains as time elapses (Replaces dial scale with a glanceable progress ring.)
rationale: Understand remaining time from across the room without reading digits.
judge_comment: A glanceable progress ring is intuitive and feasible, though it adds an LED component rather than substituting something cheaper, and it only addresses feedback.

title: Spoken 'Done' instead of bell
new_elements: Voice/chime module saying 'your food is ready' (Replaces mechanical bell with a clearer spoken cue.)
rationale: Unambiguous feedback helps hearing- or memory-impaired users.
judge_comment: Spoken cues are clear and easy to build, but the idea is common and only marginally improves operation.

title: Hinge-free magnet-hung door
new_elements: Door held by magnetic rails, lifts away completely (No hinges or latch; door snaps onto rails and seals by magnets.)
rationale: Grab and lift — no swing arc, no button.
judge_comment: A radical hinge-free door is highly novel, but microwave RF sealing and safety interlocks make magnetic-only retention doubtful.

title: Wave-to-add-a-minute
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (Each hand wave adds 60 s; cover sensor to stop.)
rationale: Touchless, hygienic, one gesture.
judge_comment: Wave gestures need no learning and are plausible with IR sensors, but accidental triggers and discoverability are concerns.

title: Top-loading lid oven
new_elements: Top-hinged gravity-closing lid (Lid falls shut by weight; seal by its own mass; no latch.)
rationale: Can't be left half-open; drop it and go.
judge_comment: A gravity-closing top lid removes the half-open failure mode, but it doesn't simplify setting time or power, and a lid with no latch is a safety problem for microwave door interlocks.

title: Squeeze-bulb timer
new_elements: Pneumatic squeeze bulb with bleed valve (Number of squeezes inflates bellows; bleed-down time equals cooking time.)
rationale: Tactile, mains-independent, and a child could use it.
judge_comment: A squeeze-bulb pneumatic timer is intuitive and a genuinely radical substitute for a keypad, though bleed-down timing accuracy and power control are open questions.

title: 'Same as last time' button
new_elements: Mechanical detent memory of last knob positions (One big repeat button rewinds cams to last used settings.)
rationale: Repetitive daily use becomes a single press.
judge_comment: A repeat button is plausible and simple, but it only helps repeat use and still needs the initial settings, so it's not zero learning curve.

title: Barcode reads the packet
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode/QR scanner (Package code sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: Show the packet, close the door, done.
judge_comment: Scanning the packet removes all setting decisions, which fits the need well, but it's a known concept and depends on barcodes carrying cooking data.

title: NFC sticker on the bowl
new_elements: NFC reader in turntable hub reading container tags (Reusable bowls carry tags with preferred cycles.)
rationale: The container remembers the setting so the user needn't.
judge_comment: NFC tags on bowls are feasible and automate settings, but they only work with tagged containers and the user must program the tags first.

title: Linear ruler slider
new_elements: Horizontal slide with giant 0-10 min ruler (Slider returns left as time elapses; replaces rotary cam.)
rationale: Linear scales are easier to read than small rotary dials.
judge_comment: A linear slider with a big ruler is intuitive and plausible, but it is an incremental change to existing mechanical timers.

title: Weighted dice timer
new_elements: Cube placed on top with time faces (1,2,3,5,10,Off) (Hall sensors read which face is up; set by turning the cube.)
rationale: Playful, visible setting with big readable numbers.
judge_comment: A playful cube with Hall sensors is concrete and novel, but handling and placing a loose cube is not obviously simpler than a dial.

title: Camera reads a scribbled note
new_elements: Door camera with digit OCR (Write '3' on a sticky note on the plate; oven runs 3 minutes.)
rationale: Writing a number is the lowest-tech instruction possible.
judge_comment: Writing a number is very radical, but needing pen, paper and OCR adds steps and cost, so it is not simpler overall.

title: Rotate the whole oven to set time
new_elements: Turntable base: oven body rotates on a cam ring (Twist the oven like a jar lid; it unwinds back as it cooks.)
rationale: Giant, impossible-to-miss control for low-dexterity users.
judge_comment: Twisting the whole oven is wild and highly visible, but it is impractical given power cords, weight and placement, and it is not really simpler.

title: Bimetal thermal timer
new_elements: Bimetal heater-strip delay switch (A heated bimetal strip bends and cuts the circuit after a set travel; no motor.)
rationale: Cheaper mechanism behind the same simple knob.
judge_comment: A bimetal timer is a plausible, cheap substitute for the motor, but it does little for the user's learning curve and is imprecise for timing.

title: Interlock replaces the door button
new_elements: Door with friction seal and no latch; interlock cuts power on crack (Door swings freely; opening 2 mm kills the magnetron instantly.)
rationale: Door behaves like a cupboard; nothing to unlock.
judge_comment: Latchless door with an interlock is intuitive, but it removes a safety-critical latch, and a door that kills power at 2 mm would be annoying and may not meet safety standards.

title: Power by number of pulses
new_elements: Pedal-tap duty: each tap on start = one 10 s burst (User taps as needed; no stored power level.)
rationale: Gentle heating becomes 'tap, stir, tap' with no settings.
judge_comment: Tap-per-burst control is easy to understand and technically simple, though it requires repeated attention and the 'pedal' wording is vague.

title: Smart-plug outsources the timer
new_elements: Oven always-on; mains smart plug/phone app times it (Timer removed from oven entirely; the plug cuts power.)
rationale: Oven becomes a one-switch appliance; timing lives where the user already is.
judge_comment: An app and smart plug add learning burden and risk, such as unattended operation and the oven being left in a start-ready state, which undermines the no-learning-curve goal.

title: Thermochromic 'done' window
new_elements: Thermochromic strip on turntable visible through door (Strip turns red when plate reaches serving temperature.)
rationale: Users can just watch for the colour instead of estimating time.
judge_comment: A visual done cue is intuitive, but a thermochromic strip on a rotating plate would not reflect food temperature accurately, and it does not replace the controls.

title: Fixed one-minute oven
new_elements: Single start lever: always 60 s, full power (No timer, no power knob; press again for another minute.)
rationale: The absolute minimum interface: one lever, one outcome.
judge_comment: A single-lever fixed 60 s cycle is trivially simple and cheap to build, though it is inflexible for many foods.

title: Single food-icon dial
new_elements: Food-icon selector dial (one knob with pictograms (mug, plate, frozen meal) replacing timer and power knobs); Pick result not parameters (user chooses what, not how long or how strong)
rationale: Replaces two abstract knobs with one concrete choice so no mental model of watts or minutes is needed.
judge_comment: Simple and practical, but icon-based presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.

title: One-button humidity auto-stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor (detects steam burst to stop heating); Single Heat button (the only control); Steam sensing (capacitive humidity sensor in exhaust)
rationale: Timer knob is replaced by the food itself telling the oven when it is done.
judge_comment: A single Heat button with humidity auto-stop closely matches the zero-learning-curve need, and humidity sensors already exist (the 'sensor cook' feature), though results vary for dry foods.

title: Weight-sets-time turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (weighs dish and sets duration automatically); Infer time from mass (heavier load, longer run)
rationale: Substitutes the clockwork timer with a scale the user never has to think about.
judge_comment: Weight is a poor proxy for the heating time needed, since food type matters, but a load cell is cheap and the idea is concrete.

title: IR thermometer closed loop
new_elements: IR surface thermometer (reads food temperature and stops at target); Thermopile sensing (non-contact temperature measurement)
rationale: Power-cycle knob replaced by a sensor so the user never guesses duty cycle.
judge_comment: An IR sensor measures only surface temperature, and containers and steam interfere, but it directly removes the guesswork.

title: Door is the start button
new_elements: Door-triggered start switch (closing door starts, opening stops; no separate button)
rationale: Removes a whole control; the gesture everyone already does becomes the command.
judge_comment: Very feasible and intuitive, but it only removes the start button and still leaves the time to be set, and it risks accidental starts with an empty cavity.

title: Toaster-style pull lever
new_elements: Spring lever timer (push lever down like a toaster; pops when done); Toaster latch mechanism (bimetal or spring escapement)
rationale: Borrows an interface everyone learned as a child, replacing the numbered dial.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster-style lever is intuitive and mechanically plausible, though a lever timer's fixed duration limits flexibility.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline voice module ('heat my coffee' replaces both knobs); Keyword speech recognition (small on-device model)
rationale: Spoken intent needs no learning of knob semantics.
judge_comment: Offline voice control removes the need to learn knobs, but it is not cheaper or simpler and the brief's substitution angle is weak; noisy kitchens and ambiguous commands are risks.

title: Room-visible colour beacon
new_elements: Colour status lamp (whole front glows amber while heating, green when done); Signal done at a glance (replaces bell)
rationale: Replaces the ambiguous bell with a universally understood traffic-light cue.
judge_comment: A colour beacon helps with status clarity but does not address operating the controls, and it is easy to implement but incremental.

title: Fully glass cavity, no lamp
new_elements: Transparent metallised-mesh cavity (ITO-coated glass walls, lit by room light); Transparent conductive coating (RF shielding via ITO)
rationale: Removes the lamp and the need to peer through a mesh; the user simply sees the food.
judge_comment: A radical transparent ITO cavity is novel, but it only tangentially helps ease of operation, and RF shielding, durability, and cost are serious obstacles.

title: Two-position gentle/hot rocker
new_elements: Gentle/Hot rocker switch (replaces 5-step power cam)
rationale: Binary choice is instantly understood where five power steps are not.
judge_comment: A binary rocker simplifies power choice and is trivially feasible, but it is a modest, fairly obvious simplification.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip hourglass with optical end-sensor (flip the sand timer; when sand runs out magnetron stops)
rationale: A timer whose meaning is obvious to anyone, zero numbers.
judge_comment: Intuitive flip-to-start interaction with no numbers, but a fixed-duration hourglass limits flexibility and the optical sensor adds complexity.

title: Mode stirrer instead of turntable
new_elements: Ceiling mode stirrer (flat cavity floor, nothing to remove or misplace)
rationale: Removes the glass plate the user must place, seat and clean correctly.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common and only indirectly reduce operating complexity, since the user still has to set time and power.

title: Barcode reads cooking time
new_elements: Package barcode scanner (scans pack, sets program); Barcode lookup (local table of packaged meals)
rationale: The packaging replaces the knobs as the input device.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning of packages is already known and works well for packaged meals, but it does nothing for non-packaged food.

title: NFC-tagged containers
new_elements: NFC reader in floor (tagged mug/bowl announces its own program); NFC tagging (passive tags survive microwave when shielded)
rationale: The dish knows the setting, so the user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Containers that declare their own program mean the user sets nothing, but NFC tags inside a microwave raise serious shielding and arcing problems and need special dishes.

title: Photo-tile touch panel
new_elements: Food photo tiles (six printed photos, press the one that looks like your food)
rationale: Visual matching replaces numeric entry.
judge_comment: Pressing a photo of the food is immediately understandable and easy to build, though it is less radical than the other ideas.

title: Stop-when-steaming
new_elements: Window fog sensor (optical sensor detects condensation on door glass)
rationale: Uses a visible natural cue instead of a timer the user must estimate.
judge_comment: Condensation sensing to auto-stop removes timer guessing, though fog varies by food and many foods don't steam.

title: External doneness bar
new_elements: Front progress bar (LED bar fills as food approaches temperature); Show doneness externally (replaces looking through window with lamp)
rationale: Replaces interpreting what you see through the window with one obvious gauge.
judge_comment: A doneness gauge is clear, but non-contact food temperature sensing is hard and it adds parts rather than substituting simpler ones.

title: Spoken 'done'
new_elements: Speech chime (says 'your food is ready' instead of bell)
rationale: Unambiguous meaning versus a generic bell.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but it only changes the end alert and does little for operating the microwave.

title: Popcorn acoustic sensor
new_elements: Microphone pop-rate sensor (stops when popping slows); Acoustic event detection (counts pops per second)
rationale: Replaces timer with listening, the way people already judge popcorn.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop detection is concrete and plausible and removes timer guesswork, though limited to popcorn.

title: Magnetic pull handle
new_elements: Magnetic soft-close handle (no push button; just pull)
rationale: A handle needs no discovery; a release button does.
judge_comment: A pull handle is intuitive and cheap, but it covers only door opening and is incremental.

title: Silicone mat floor
new_elements: Fixed silicone mat (replaces glass turntable; dish slides anywhere)
rationale: Nothing to align, drop or break.
judge_comment: Removes a minor hassle (turntable) but does not simplify operation of controls, and uneven heating without rotation is a concern.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Hold-to-heat paddle (heats only while pressed)
rationale: Zero settings: release when it looks done.
judge_comment: Dead-man paddle needs zero settings and no learning, though holding for minutes is tiring and it is a bit unusual.

title: Only a +30s button
new_elements: Single +30s button (tap once per half minute, full power)
rationale: Replaces both knobs with counting taps.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is very simple and already partly exists, but is limited for different foods and power levels.

title: Push-for-food, twist-for-portion knob
new_elements: Push-twist combo knob (push cycles food type, twist sets small/medium/large)
rationale: One physical object, two intuitive dimensions.
judge_comment: One knob with push and twist is intuitive but still requires learning food categories and sizes.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Cavity camera (recognises dish and chooses program); Edge image classification (tiny CNN on microcontroller)
rationale: The oven does the identifying so the user does nothing.
judge_comment: Automatic recognition would remove all user input and is a strong match to the need, but accurate recognition and safe heating on a microcontroller is hard and costly, and it is not a cheaper substitution.

title: Target-temperature dial
new_elements: Temperature dial (set 'warm/hot/boiling' instead of time and power)
rationale: Users think in how hot they want it, not watts × minutes.
judge_comment: Matches how users think, but without a temperature sensor or knowledge of the food's mass and starting temperature, the dial would be unreliable, and it substitutes a more complex sensing system for a simple timer.

title: Door pops open when done
new_elements: Auto-pop door latch (door springs ajar at end instead of ringing)
rationale: The outcome itself is the signal; nothing to interpret.
judge_comment: A door that springs ajar is simple and feasible and gives an obvious done signal, but it only covers the end of the cycle, not operation.

title: Slide-to-run lever
new_elements: Linear slide lever (slide right, returns left over time)
rationale: A sliding length is more intuitive than a rotating angle.
judge_comment: A slide lever that returns over time is intuitive and mechanically simple, like a toaster, though its precision and range are limited.

title: Scale-shelf start
new_elements: Weighing door shelf (rest cup on shelf before loading; oven preloads time)
rationale: Setting the time becomes a side effect of loading.
judge_comment: Weighing the load to preset the time removes the need for any input and is plausible, though weight is a crude proxy for the right heating time.

title: Photoluminescent cavity
new_elements: Glow-coated cavity walls (phosphor coating charged by kitchen light, no bulb)
rationale: Visibility with no bulb to fail or switch to learn.
judge_comment: A bulb-free glowing cavity is novel, but phosphor glow is dim and fades, and it does little for operation simplicity.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Push-to-start drawer (pull out, place food, push shut and it runs)
rationale: Replaces door, button and start with one push.
judge_comment: Collapsing door, button and start into one push is intuitive, but it needs a drawer mechanism with microwave sealing and has no way to set time or power.

title: Pictogram-only dial
new_elements: Numberless pictogram timer (cup, bowl, plate icons at the right angles)
rationale: Same clockwork, but the scale is pre-translated into meals.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build and removes the need to read numbers, though icon-to-time mapping is vague and the idea is incremental.

title: Snap-on simplicity cap
new_elements: Knob-limiting cap (snap-on cover exposes only one setting for kids/elderly)
rationale: Physically removes all options that could be set wrong.
judge_comment: A simple mechanical cap that limits options is highly feasible, but it is an accessory that locks in one setting and adds a step.

title: Dedicated mug cavity
new_elements: Mug-sized cavity (fits one cup; one button; fixed program)
rationale: Constrains the task until no setting is possible.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug cavity with one button has essentially no learning curve and is easy to build, though it is less versatile.

title: Wave-hand gesture start
new_elements: IR gesture sensor (wave to start/stop with full hands)
rationale: Replaces button with the natural 'go' gesture.
judge_comment: IR gesture start is feasible and handy with full hands, but it still needs time setting and risks false triggers, so it adds little simplicity.

title: Evaporation-loss stop
new_elements: Continuous weight monitor (stops when mass loss indicates boiling)
rationale: Physics replaces user judgement of duration.
judge_comment: Weight-loss detection to stop at boiling removes duration guessing, but it is only useful for liquids and needs a precise load cell in a harsh environment.

title: Cooking capsules
new_elements: Coded meal capsule reader (capsule rim notches set program mechanically)
rationale: Nespresso-style: insert, press, done.
judge_comment: Insert-and-press capsules with mechanical notch coding give essentially zero learning curve, though they are limited to capsule meals and the concept is familiar from coffee machines.

title: Thermochromic plate
new_elements: Colour-changing turntable (plate turns red when food is hot, visible through door)
rationale: Replaces timer reading with a colour anyone understands.
judge_comment: An intuitive color cue for doneness is appealing, but the plate shows food temperature rather than setting the cook time, and thermochromic materials are hard to make durable and food-safe in a microwave.

title: Tap-the-door counter
new_elements: Door knock sensor (each knock adds 30 s)
rationale: No panel at all; the door is the interface.
judge_comment: Knocking on the door to add time is simple and cheap, but it is less discoverable and accidental knocks could cause errors.

title: Periscope window
new_elements: Mirror light pipe (channels room light into cavity, no bulb)
rationale: Seeing inside needs no lamp switch or bulb.
judge_comment: A light pipe replaces the bulb but does little to make operation simpler, and light would be poor in dim rooms.

title: Cold-to-hot slider
new_elements: Single cold→hot slider (maps combined time×power onto one axis)
rationale: One axis of 'more or less' replaces two interacting knobs.
judge_comment: A single cold-to-hot slider simplifies the controls and is easy to build, though mapping one axis onto time and power loses control and is not very radical.

title: Foot-wave door opener
new_elements: Toe-kick door sensor (door opens when foot waved below, hands full)
rationale: Removes the push-release button and its hunt.
judge_comment: A toe-kick sensor is plausible and helps with hands-full use, but it only touches door opening and not the main operation, and it risks false triggers.

title: Reflected-power load sensing
new_elements: Reflected-power detector (magnetron mismatch reveals load size and water content); RF load impedance sensing (directional coupler on waveguide)
rationale: No buttons: the oven senses what is inside electrically.
judge_comment: Sensing the load from reflected power could remove the controls entirely and is radical, but reliably inferring food type and doneness from it is technically hard.

title: Phone notification instead of bell
new_elements: Done-notification radio (pings phone; nothing to set on oven)
rationale: User never misses the end, no bell to learn.
judge_comment: A phone ping is easy to build but adds a pairing step and complexity, so it works against a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Countdown printed on turntable
new_elements: Numbered turntable rim (rotation rate fixed; rim numbers show elapsed time through window)
rationale: Timer display is free and visible without any extra part.
judge_comment: A numbered turntable rim is a clever, cheap, intuitive timer display, but fixed rotation timing is awkward and it only helps with reading time, not with setting it.

title: Steam-whistle end signal
new_elements: Vent whistle (exhaust steam blows a kettle whistle when food steams)
rationale: Replaces timer and bell with a kettle sound everyone recognises.
judge_comment: A whistle is a familiar signal, but it only works for steaming foods and still requires the user to set a time or power, so it only partly meets the need.

title: Spring-wound crank
new_elements: Crank-to-wind timer (each crank turn equals one minute; no scale)
rationale: Counting cranks is more intuitive than reading a dial.
judge_comment: A mechanical wind-up timer is simple and easy to use, though it is a familiar design, and one crank per minute is not very precise.

title: Big Start / Stop only
new_elements: Two giant buttons (Start runs at full power until Stop or sensor end)
rationale: Interface identical to a light switch.
judge_comment: A two-button interface has almost no learning curve and is easy to build, but full power until stop will overcook many foods and the idea is not radical.

title: Dish with built-in thermometer
new_elements: Bimetal pop-up dish (bundled dish pops an indicator like a turkey timer)
rationale: Doneness shown mechanically in the food, replacing timer judgement.
judge_comment: A bimetal pop-up indicator in the dish is concrete and cheap, but it needs a specific dish and does not control the microwave, so the user still has to act.

title: Smell-of-done sensor
new_elements: VOC gas sensor (detects cooked-aroma volatiles and stops); MOX gas sensing (metal-oxide sensor in exhaust)
rationale: The oven 'smells' doneness so the user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Automatic doneness detection with a MOX VOC sensor removes all settings and matches the need well, but it is unreliable across different foods and the sensor drifts.

title: Transparent door with no mesh, no lamp
new_elements: Choke-slot glass door (RF blocked by quarter-wave choke frame, clear pane); Quarter-wave choke sealing (frame-based RF seal)
rationale: Removes mesh and bulb; checking food is as simple as looking.
judge_comment: A clear door without mesh or lamp is a plausible substitution, but it only marginally helps operation simplicity (viewing food was already easy).
