Clear glass alone cannot block microwaves at 2.45 GHz, since a quarter-wave choke only seals the door perimeter, not the viewing area. So feasibility is questionable, and the idea isn't radical.

title: Pictogram food dial replaces power cam
new_elements: Food-type pictogram dial (Single knob with cup/plate/popcorn icons; cam preset couples time and duty cycle)
rationale: User picks a picture instead of reasoning about watts and minutes.
judge_comment: Highly intuitive and very buildable, but similar to existing auto-menu presets, so not radical.

title: Weighing turntable sets time
new_elements: Strain-gauge load cell under turntable hub (Food mass sets cook time automatically); Weight-driven auto-timer (Replaces clockwork knob)
rationale: Place food, press one button; no time estimation needed.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing removes estimation, but mass alone is a poor proxy for cook time (food type, starting temperature), and a load cell adds cost.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Length pulled equals time, cord retracts as it cooks like a toy)
rationale: Physically intuitive remaining-time display with zero markings to read.
judge_comment: Playful and intuitive, but it only simplifies the time input and still requires the user to choose a duration.

title: IR surface thermometer stops cooking
new_elements: Thermopile IR sensor through cavity ceiling (Reads food surface temperature non-contact); Done-when-hot controller (Stops magnetron at eating temperature)
rationale: Only one button: 'heat until hot'.
judge_comment: A single 'heat until hot' button is the ideal no-learning-curve interface, but IR reads only the surface temperature and is inaccurate through steam and with covered dishes.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable motor
new_elements: Rotating mode-stirrer fan in waveguide (Spreads field evenly; flat enamel floor, no glass plate)
rationale: Nothing to seat, misalign or clean; any dish fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, and the change mainly simplifies cleaning rather than operation.

title: Rotating antenna under floor
new_elements: Air-driven rotating feed antenna (Cooling fan airflow spins antenna, no motor)
rationale: Removes the turntable ritual and a motor that can fail.
judge_comment: Clever motorless mode stirring, but airflow-driven antenna is hard to make reliable and barely affects operation simplicity.

title: Magnetic soft-close door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch (Fridge-style magnet seal, pull to open)
rationale: No button to find; door opens like a cupboard.
judge_comment: Pull-to-open is intuitive, but a magnetic catch alone is a weak RF/safety seal and needs interlocks; still a modest simplification.

title: Hall sensor interlock
new_elements: Redundant Hall-effect magnetic door sensors (Solid-state, no mechanical microswitch wear)
rationale: Door always just works; no sticking buttons to confuse users.
judge_comment: Highly feasible and robust, but invisible to the user and does little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: Drawer cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Food sits in a sliding drawer; closing drawer is the only action)
rationale: Load like a kitchen drawer, push shut to start.
judge_comment: Drawer metaphor is very intuitive with close-to-start, though RF sealing of a drawer and start-time control are challenging.

title: Metallized fabric roller shutter door
new_elements: Conductive mesh roller blind with choke rail (Flexible RF-tight shutter replaces hinged door and latch)
rationale: Swipe shutter down to start; no latch, no button.
judge_comment: Radical and intuitive swipe-to-start, but RF-tight flexible shutter is very difficult and safety-sensitive.

title: Voice-chip timer
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognizer (Says 'two minutes' and it runs)
rationale: Talking replaces knob-turning and reading scales.
judge_comment: Offline voice recognition removes the need to learn the controls, though it adds little cost savings and can struggle in noisy kitchens.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust duct (Steam burst signals food is hot); Steam-stop controller (Single 'cook' button, stops on steam)
rationale: User never sets time; oven senses doneness.
judge_comment: A one-button cook that stops on steam removes time-setting entirely, and humidity sensing already exists in sensor-cook ovens, so it is credible.

title: Lamp colour as done signal
new_elements: Colour-shift cavity LED (Red while cooking, green when done, replaces bell)
rationale: Status readable at a glance from across the room.
judge_comment: A colour LED is simple and feasible, but it only signals status and does not make operation itself easier.

title: PTC resettable thermal cutoff
new_elements: PTC ceramic self-resetting thermistor (Limits current when hot, resets when cool)
rationale: Overheating never bricks the oven; no service knowledge needed.
judge_comment: A self-resetting thermal cutoff is a safety and reliability measure that barely touches the simple-operation need.

title: Inverter supply replaces doubler
new_elements: High-frequency inverter HV supply (No large HV capacitor; continuous true power control)
rationale: Even heating without stirring means fewer user interventions.
judge_comment: Inverter power supplies are real and give more even heating, but the link to ease of operation is indirect.

title: Solid-state RF with reflection sensing
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Measures reflected power to detect food state); Self-tuning doneness detection (Stops when absorption curve flattens)
rationale: Oven knows when food is done; user only presses start.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflection sensing directly delivers press-start-only operation and is plausible, though doneness detection across varied foods is hard and GaN is costly (not cheaper).

title: Glazed cavity replaces mica cover
new_elements: Integral glass-ceramic waveguide window (Fused into cavity wall, wipe-clean, never replaced)
rationale: Eliminates a mysterious replaceable part users don't understand.
judge_comment: A sensible simplification, but the user rarely thinks about the mica cover, so it adds little to operational ease.

title: Enamel floor replaces glass turntable
new_elements: Stamped enamelled flat cavity floor (Combined with mode stirrer, no loose glass)
rationale: Nothing to remove, break or reseat.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable lowers handling effort, but uneven heating without rotation needs a stirrer and the benefit to learning is indirect.

title: Three-button mug/plate/bowl
new_elements: Three preset buttons (Only mug, plate, bowl; fixed time and power each)
rationale: Minimal choice set matches real usage.
judge_comment: Three presets are very easy to learn, but this is a familiar preset approach and fixed times may suit food poorly.

title: Detent scenario knob
new_elements: Click-stop scenario knob (Coffee, leftovers, popcorn, defrost detents only)
rationale: Feelable clicks remove fine adjustment anxiety.
judge_comment: A tactile detent knob with scenario labels is intuitive and cheap, but it is an incremental and not radical substitution.

title: Electroluminescent cavity walls
new_elements: EL phosphor coating on cavity walls (Whole interior glows softly, no bulb)
rationale: Shadow-free view lets users check food without opening.
judge_comment: Novel substitution for the bulb, but it only marginally helps operation simplicity, and EL coatings inside a microwave cavity are doubtful.

title: Ferrite absorber gasket
new_elements: Ferrite-loaded silicone RF gasket (Absorbs leakage; door can be thin and light)
rationale: Lighter door is easier to close one-handed.
judge_comment: Concrete material substitution, but it has little connection to learning-free operation and a thinner door is a weak benefit.

title: Door-as-switch contacts
new_elements: Hinge contact pads (Door metal closes redundant low-voltage sense loop)
rationale: Fewer parts to misalign so door always registers closed.
judge_comment: Plausible and cheap, but interlocks already exist and it is mostly invisible to the user.

title: RFID dish tells oven
new_elements: Microwave-safe RFID tags in dishware (Tag encodes time/power for that dish or meal)
rationale: Put dish in, shut door; the dish does the programming.
judge_comment: Dish-encoded programming removes all settings and is workable, though it requires special dishware and RFID-safe tags.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Low-cost camera + tiny vision model (Recognises soup, pizza, mug; sets program)
rationale: Zero settings; the oven sees what you placed.
judge_comment: Camera recognition gives zero-setting operation and is feasible, though similar products exist and accuracy varies.

title: Slider marked in portions
new_elements: Portion-scale slider (Scale reads 'cup, bowl, plate, big plate' not minutes)
rationale: Users know portion size, not minutes.
judge_comment: Portion-based scale directly removes the need to know minutes and is easy to implement with a mechanical timer or lookup, though not very radical.

title: Pop-up done flag
new_elements: Toaster-style mechanical pop-up flag (Spring flag rises at end instead of bell)
rationale: Borrowed toaster metaphor everyone already understands.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster-style pop-up flag is intuitive and simple, but it only covers the end-of-cycle signal rather than the whole operation.

title: Toaster-slot mug microwave
new_elements: Top-loading mug slot with choke collar (Drop mug in, lever down; pops up when hot)
rationale: Student reheats drinks with a single lever push.
judge_comment: A lever-operated top-loading mug slot is very simple to use, but a microwave that pops up and has a choke collar is technically challenging and limited to mugs.

title: Top-loading lid cavity
new_elements: Gravity-closing top lid (Lid falls shut and seals by weight, no latch)
rationale: Loading from above is natural and can't be left ajar.
judge_comment: A gravity-closing top lid removes the latch and is natural to use, but a top-loading design is less practical and the seal and safety interlock are unclear.

title: Fixed anti-superheat pulse replaces power knob
new_elements: Fixed pulse cam (Built-in 70% duty with pauses that let liquids nucleate)
rationale: Removes the power knob entirely while making liquids safer.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob with a fixed duty cycle reduces choices and adds safety, but it limits control and only indirectly serves ease of use.

title: Thermochromic plate
new_elements: Thermochromic glaze on turntable (Plate turns colour at serving temperature)
rationale: Visual doneness cue instead of guessing time.
judge_comment: Visual doneness cue is intuitive, but a turntable glaze only reflects plate temperature, not food, and it doesn't stop the oven or remove timing decisions.

title: Probe-stop cooking
new_elements: Tethered food probe (Stick in food; oven stops at target)
rationale: One target, no time math.
judge_comment: Probe cooking is intuitive, simplifying to one target, but it already exists in some ovens and tethered probes add handling steps.

title: Susceptor turntable
new_elements: Susceptor-coated glass turntable (Metallised film layer browns food bottoms automatically)
rationale: Crisping without a separate mode to learn.
judge_comment: Susceptor browning is feasible and removes a mode, but it has little effect on the core operation and learning of basic heating.

title: RF-leak sensing instead of interlocks
new_elements: Diode RF leakage detector at door rim (Any leak cuts magnetron drive)
rationale: Door tolerance no longer matters; it just works.
judge_comment: An interesting safety substitution, but it is invisible to users and does nothing for ease of operation.

title: Tap door for +30 s
new_elements: Piezo tap sensor on door (Each tap adds 30 s, double tap stops)
rationale: One gesture replaces knob and buttons.
judge_comment: A single tap gesture replaces the controls with zero learning, and it is cheap and plausible, though accidental taps and discoverability are concerns.

title: Door handle is the timer
new_elements: Rotating handle-timer (Twist handle to set minutes, push door shut to start)
rationale: Single touchpoint for open, set and start.
judge_comment: Merging open, set and start into one handle gesture is intuitive and needs no learning, though the mechanical coupling and a door-closure start (safety interlock) need engineering.

title: One knob only
new_elements: Time-only knob with fixed full power (Power knob deleted entirely)
rationale: Halves the controls to learn.
judge_comment: Simple and very feasible, mirroring existing basic microwaves, but it is an incremental step rather than a radical one, and fixed full power limits use cases.

title: Auto-eject drawer at end
new_elements: Spring-eject tray (Food slides out when done; replaces bell)
rationale: The food presents itself; nothing to open.
judge_comment: An ejecting tray removes a step, but hot food sliding out is a safety and spill hazard, and it adds mechanical complexity rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Shrinking glow bar
new_elements: EL strip countdown along door edge (Lit length shrinks to zero)
rationale: Remaining time readable without numbers.
judge_comment: An EL strip countdown is easy to read without numbers and plausible, but it only addresses display and not setting or starting.

title: Piezo walking floor
new_elements: Ultrasonic vibrating cavity floor (Vibration slowly rotates dish, no motor or glass)
rationale: No turntable to position or clean.
judge_comment: Ultrasonic vibration to rotate a dish is highly novel but physically implausible for heavy dishes, and it only loosely serves the no-learning-curve need.

title: Near-field mug heater
new_elements: Evanescent-field open cup well (Shielded well heats only a mug inside; no door at all)
rationale: Set mug down, lift mug up; nothing else.
judge_comment: Radical doorless mug-only heater is very simple to operate, but evanescent-field containment of microwave leakage and safe heating is highly implausible.

title: Resettable monitor fuse
new_elements: Polymer resettable fuse in monitor circuit (Trips on welded switch, resets after cool-down)
rationale: A safety trip doesn't require a repair visit.
judge_comment: A resettable fuse is plausible and concrete but is about maintenance and safety, not operational simplicity.

title: LED lamp
new_elements: Lifetime LED cavity lamp (Replaces incandescent; never changed)
rationale: Removes a maintenance task users must learn.
judge_comment: LED lamps are already standard and have little to do with operating the microwave without learning.

title: Door-open resets timer
new_elements: Latch-coupled timer reset (Opening door zeroes clockwork)
rationale: No surprise restart when the door is closed again.
judge_comment: Resetting the timer on door-open avoids surprise restarts and is mildly helpful, and mechanically easy.

title: Colour-zone timer scale
new_elements: Colour-banded knob scale (Blue=warm, orange=reheat, red=cook zones)
rationale: Colours are faster to use than minute marks.
judge_comment: Color-coded zones on the knob are simple, cheap, and directly reduce the learning needed, though not radical.

title: Keyed meal pods
new_elements: Notched tray edge mechanically sets cam (Nespresso-style tray notch pushes the timer/power cams)
rationale: Packaging programs the oven with zero electronics.
judge_comment: Mechanical notch-coded trays that set the cams are clever and need no learning, but they lock users into proprietary packaging and cover few foods.

title: Inductive floor pad power
new_elements: Wireless counter power pad (Oven draws power inductively; no cord to route)
rationale: Set it anywhere and go; no plugging.
judge_comment: Inductive power for a 1kW+ appliance is inefficient and impractical, and removing the cord does little for operating simplicity.

title: Metal-detect start lockout
new_elements: Low-power RF pre-pulse arc sniffer (Test pulse detects foil/cutlery and refuses to start with a light)
rationale: Users needn't learn the metal rule; the oven enforces it.
judge_comment: The oven enforces the metal rule so users needn't know it, but reliable arc detection is hard and false lockouts could frustrate.

title: Auto nucleation stick
new_elements: Built-in ceramic boiling-chip holder (Porous stick dips into mugs placed under it)
rationale: Removes a hidden hazard the novice can't anticipate.
judge_comment: It addresses superheating safety, but it is tangential to operating simplicity and a stick under the mug is awkward in practice.

title: Dumb oven, smart plug
new_elements: Timer built into wall plug (Oven has only a run switch; plug sets duration by one dial)
rationale: Oven face is blank; all control is one familiar plug dial.
judge_comment: A familiar plug-mounted timer dial with a blank oven face is simple and cheap, though the oven would need a run switch and a safe plug-based timer.

title: Single 'food dial' replaces timer + power knobs
new_elements: Pictogram food dial (one cam encodes duration and duty cycle) (Positions marked mug / plate / bowl / frozen; a dual-track cam sets both time and on/off ratio.); Dual-profile cam encoding (One shaft, two cam lobes: one trips the clockwork, one sets the duty-cycle contact.)
rationale: The user chooses what they are heating, not minutes and watts, so two abstract controls collapse into one obvious choice.
judge_comment: Choosing by food type removes abstract time and power decisions, and a dual-track cam is plausible, though presets may not suit every load.

title: Zero-knob 'close door = start' microwave
new_elements: Door-actuated fixed-burst starter (Closing the door cocks a 60 s spring timer; opening stops it; nothing else on the fascia.); Starts heating automatically on door closure (Door latch doubles as the start switch.)
rationale: There is literally nothing to learn: put food in, shut the door, it heats for a minute.
judge_comment: Truly zero learning, but auto-start on door close risks accidental runs, including with an empty cavity, and a fixed 60 s is inflexible.

title: Tap-to-add-30-seconds ratchet button
new_elements: Single ratchet push button (each press adds 30 s) (A mechanical escapement advances the timer cam one notch per press; no dial to read.); Pawl-and-ratchet increment mechanism (Each press winds the spring one tooth; clockwork returns it.)
rationale: Counting taps is simpler than reading a 0-30 min scale and precise for short tasks like warming milk.
judge_comment: Counting taps is intuitive and mechanically simple, but it closely resembles existing +30 s buttons.

title: Pull-cord timer: pull length = cook time
new_elements: Spring-return pull cord timer (Pulling a cord winds a clockwork; a short tug is 30 s, arm's length is 5 min; cord retracts as it cooks.)
rationale: Remaining time is a physical length anyone can see and feel, with no numbers or motors involved.
judge_comment: The physical pull length is an intuitive, visible metaphor, though cord wear, repeatability, and accuracy are concerns.

title: Hand-wound mainspring timer (no synchronous motor)
new_elements: Mainspring escapement clockwork (Wind-up toy mechanism replaces the mains-frequency motor timer; works on 50 or 60 Hz.)
rationale: A toy-like wind-up is instantly understood, cheaper, and identical across mains regions.
judge_comment: A wind-up timer is familiar and feasible, but it mostly swaps the mechanism and only indirectly simplifies operation.

title: Quartz clock movement drives the timer cam
new_elements: Quartz kitchen-clock movement (A $1 battery quartz movement turns the cam shaft with second-level accuracy.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar knob but makes the short settings reliable so users never need to re-run cycles.
judge_comment: A quartz movement is a plausible cheap substitute, but it barely changes the user experience and is not radical.

title: Bimetal thermal-delay timer
new_elements: Heater-coil bimetal delay switch (Knob sets a contact gap; a heated bimetal strip bends until it opens the circuit, like a turn-signal flasher.)
rationale: Three moving parts replace a clockwork, same one-knob operation at lower cost.
judge_comment: A bimetal delay timer is a cheap and simple one-knob design, but its timing accuracy and repeatability are questionable.

title: Weighing turntable sets the time automatically
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable support (Food weight compresses a spring that mechanically presets the timer cam (mass to minutes).); Derives cooking time from food mass (No user input of duration.)
rationale: The appliance decides duration from the plate's weight; the user just presses go.
judge_comment: Weight-to-time presetting removes the need to choose a duration, but mass alone is a poor predictor of cook time, so it is mechanically crude.

title: Steam-triggered bimetal auto-stop replaces the timer
new_elements: Exhaust-duct bimetal steam switch (When food steams, hot vapour in the vent snaps a bimetal disc that cuts the magnetron.); Stops heating when food is steaming hot (Purely mechanical closed-loop end-point.)
rationale: Users never estimate minutes; the oven stops when the food says it is hot.
judge_comment: A steam-triggered cutoff gives true no-thinking operation and is a plausible mechanical closed loop, though it works poorly for dry foods and reheating.

title: Target-temperature dial with bimetal probe in the tray
new_elements: Bimetal food-contact thermostat under the tray (Dial reads 'warm / hot / piping'; contact thermostat under a thin tray opens at that temperature.)
rationale: People think in 'how hot', not minutes and watts, so one dial expresses the only thing they care about.
judge_comment: A 'how hot' dial is intuitive, but a contact thermostat under the tray is unreliable in a microwave and measures the tray rather than the food.

title: Reflected-power 'cook until done' instead of a timer
new_elements: Waveguide directional coupler end-point sensor (Absorbed vs reflected RF changes as water heats; a threshold comparator stops the cycle.); Reflected-power food-state sensing (Load impedance tracks food temperature and phase change.)
rationale: One 'go' button and the physics itself decides when to stop.
judge_comment: Removes the need to choose a time entirely, but reflected power is a weak, unreliable indicator of doneness across varied foods and the coupler adds cost.

title: Package-instruction camera replaces both knobs
new_elements: Fascia camera reading printed heating instructions (Hold the ready-meal box up; OCR reads '800 W 3 min' and sets the cycle.)
rationale: The packaging already knows the settings; the user never translates them.
judge_comment: Removes translating instructions, but only works for packaged food with readable labels, and a camera plus OCR is not simpler or cheaper.

title: Two-position Heat/Defrost rocker replaces 5-step power knob
new_elements: Heat / Defrost rocker switch (Full duty or 30 % duty; the three middle steps nobody uses are removed.)
rationale: A binary choice with words instead of five unexplained numbers.
judge_comment: Simple, cheap, and feasible, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Push/pull single knob: turn for time, pull for defrost
new_elements: Push-pull timer knob with integrated power selector (Knob pulled out engages the low-duty cam; pushed in is full power.)
rationale: One control, one hand, and the rarely used option is hidden until needed.
judge_comment: One control is simpler, but hiding defrost behind a pull action is not discoverable and so adds a learning step.

title: Defrost accessory tray replaces the power knob
new_elements: Perforated metal attenuator tray (A screened tray that admits ~30 % of the field; put frozen food on it instead of choosing a power level.)
rationale: Power level becomes a physical object you can see rather than a setting you must remember.
judge_comment: A physical, visible power level is intuitive, but a perforated tray attenuating a fixed fraction is uncertain and adds an accessory to manage.

title: Solid-state RF module replaces magnetron + HV chain
new_elements: GaN/LDMOS solid-state 2.45 GHz amplifier (Low-voltage RF source with continuous power control and built-in reflected-power sensing.); Solid-state microwave generation (Transistor amplifier replaces vacuum tube; no 4 kV, no HV capacitor.)
rationale: Self-sensing power source enables true 'press once, it stops when done' operation.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with built-in reflected-power sensing could enable truly automatic, no-learning-curve cooking; it is plausible but costly, and it substitutes an expensive part rather than a cheaper one.

title: Universal-input inverter replaces HV transformer
new_elements: Switch-mode HV inverter (Light ferrite transformer, continuous power, same unit on 120 V/60 Hz and 230 V/50 Hz.)
rationale: Continuous power means 'defrost' behaves predictably instead of pulsing and surprising the user.
judge_comment: Inverter technology is already in market, and the link to simple operation is indirect, though predictable defrost helps somewhat.

title: Door pops open at end of cycle instead of a bell
new_elements: Timer-released door latch (The timer cam trips the latch lever; the door springs ajar with a click and the food is presented.)
rationale: No alert to interpret and no button to find: an open door means 'ready'.
judge_comment: A door that pops open at the end is an intuitive 'ready' signal that replaces the bell cheaply and simply, though it can alarm users and the opening may not be welcome.

title: Pop-up READY flag replaces the bell
new_elements: Spring pop-up indicator flag in the window (Like a turkey timer: a red flag pops up and stays up until the door opens.)
rationale: A persistent visible state removes the 'did I miss the ding?' confusion.
judge_comment: A persistent pop-up flag is simple and cheap, and it clarifies state, but it adds little to the operation itself and the user must still notice it.

title: Steam whistle alert driven by the cooling fan
new_elements: Air-driven whistle in the exhaust path (At cycle end a flap diverts fan air through a kettle-style whistle until the door opens.)
rationale: Everyone already knows what a kettle whistle means, and it keeps sounding until you act.
judge_comment: A whistle driven by fan air is a familiar and quirky alert that persists until acted on, though it is noisy and its relevance to the operation is modest.

title: Music-box chime replaces the bell
new_elements: Pinned-cylinder music box mechanism (Timer cam releases a wound comb-and-cylinder that plays a short tune.)
rationale: A distinctive tune is unmistakable among kitchen beeps, so users never wonder which appliance is calling.
judge_comment: A mechanical music-box chime is charming and distinctive, but it does little to simplify operation and adds mechanical complexity.

title: Lamp stays lit until the door is opened (lamp as 'done' signal)
new_elements: Latching lamp circuit (Timer ends heating but the lamp holds on; the door switch finally turns it off.)
rationale: One existing component gives both viewing and status, with no extra sound or symbol to learn.
judge_comment: A latching lamp that signals 'done' needs no new learning and is trivially implementable, though it is not very radical.

title: Thermochromic tray replaces the lamp as feedback
new_elements: Thermochromic glass-ceramic tray (Tray turns from blue to red as it warms, visible through the window under ambient light.)
rationale: Colour says hot or cold at a glance; no bulb, no interpretation.
judge_comment: A thermochromic tray gives intuitive hot/cold feedback, but it is heated indirectly, may be unreliable, and does not signal cooking state well.

title: External fascia LED with light pipe replaces the interior lamp
new_elements: Fascia LED + acrylic light pipe into cavity (One LED outside the RF field both lights the food and glows on the panel as the 'running' indicator.)
rationale: A single light that is both the window lamp and the only status indicator keeps the interface minimal.
judge_comment: A single LED with a light pipe is feasible and minimal, but the link to zero learning curve is modest and light-pipe leakage is a concern.

title: Transparent-conductor glass door, no mesh and no lamp
new_elements: Fine-wire / ITO transparent RF shielding glass (Sub-wavelength conductive grid so fine it is invisible; kitchen light suffices.)
rationale: Seeing the food plainly, like through a cupboard, needs no instruction at all.
judge_comment: A transparent RF-shielding conductive door is a bold idea that gives a clear view, but achieving adequate shielding with clarity is difficult and it only weakly addresses operation.

title: Mode-stirrer replaces turntable, roller ring and motor
new_elements: Fan-driven metal mode stirrer in the waveguide (A rotating reflector blade scrambles the field; the cavity floor is flat and fixed.)
rationale: No tray to seat, align, knock off or wash; any dish goes anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many commercial microwaves, so it is proven and removes the tray, but it is not radical.

title: Rotating antenna under a flat ceramic floor
new_elements: Bottom-feed rotating antenna beneath glass-ceramic floor (RF enters from below via a spinning antenna; flat sealed floor, no moving parts in the cavity.)
rationale: A smooth empty box with nothing to set up is the simplest possible interior.
judge_comment: Bottom-feed rotating antennas are already on the market; they give a clean flat interior and serve the need well.

title: Magnetic through-floor drive replaces coupler and roller ring
new_elements: Magnetically coupled tray on a sealed floor (Motor magnet under the floor spins a ferrite-ringed tray; tray can be dropped anywhere, no hole, no spindle.)
rationale: Removes the fiddly re-seating of the coupler that confuses first-time users.
judge_comment: A magnetic coupling through the floor is inventive, but ferrite near microwaves raises heating and arcing concerns and the tray is still present.

title: Rocking floor replaces rotation
new_elements: Cam-rocked cavity floor plate (Floor gently tilts a few degrees in a circle, sliding food through hot and cold spots.)
rationale: Large or rectangular dishes no longer jam on rotation, eliminating a common novice failure.
judge_comment: A rocking floor is highly novel, but it risks spilling liquids and is mechanically awkward, and it only loosely serves simplicity.

title: Fan motor also drives the tray (one motor)
new_elements: Belt/worm take-off from the fan motor to the tray spindle (Single AC motor cools and rotates; fewer parts and fewer failure points.)
rationale: A cheaper unit that behaves identically keeps the basic model basic.
judge_comment: Merging the motors cuts cost but does nothing for the user's learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Hand-wound tray: twist the turntable to set time
new_elements: Turntable-wound clockwork (Rotating the tray backwards by hand winds a spring; unwinding both rotates the food and counts down.)
rationale: The only control is the thing you already touch when placing the food.
judge_comment: Merging time-setting into the tray twist removes the controls entirely and is a bold substitution, though the mechanical timer's accuracy and the interaction of the spring with the load are open issues.

title: Pull-handle magnetic door replaces push-button latch
new_elements: Magnetic-gasket door with reed-switch interlocks (Fridge-style magnet strip holds the door shut; just pull to open.)
rationale: Opening works like every other kitchen door, so nobody hunts for the button.
judge_comment: A magnetic gasket door is plausible and makes opening intuitive, but it only touches door opening and the RF seal and safety requirements need care.

title: Foot-pedal door opener
new_elements: Pedal-bar latch release along the plinth (Bowden cable from a toe bar to the latch lever, like a pedal bin.)
rationale: Hands full of hot plate or child, you open it the way you open a bin: no thought needed.
judge_comment: A pedal-bin-style foot release is simple and workable, but it adds a new action to learn and does little for the core operation.

title: Drawer microwave: the cavity slides out, no door
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer with choke lip (The whole cooking box slides forward on rails; pushing it home closes the RF seal and interlocks.)
rationale: Loading from above into an open drawer is more intuitive and spill-proof than reaching into a lit box.
judge_comment: A drawer microwave exists in built-in form, but a sliding cavity with a choke seal is complex and the overall operation is not simpler.

title: Drop-down oven-style door that is also a plate shelf
new_elements: Bottom-hinged drop door with resting ledge (Door folds down flat so the hot plate can be slid out onto it.)
rationale: Mirrors the conventional oven people already know and gives a safe place to park the hot dish.
judge_comment: An oven-style drop door is familiar and easy to build, but it is only a modest change and has little to do with the operating controls.

title: Sliding pocket door
new_elements: Side-sliding shielded panel door (Door slides into the cabinet wall; no swing radius, no latch button.)
rationale: One obvious sliding motion, and it fits in corners where a swing door bangs into things.
judge_comment: Sliding door is plausible and simple, but it's only a modest change and doesn't remove the need to learn the controls.

title: Top-loading lid microwave for mugs and bowls
new_elements: Rice-cooker style hinged top lid over a round cavity (Drop the mug in from above, close the lid; gravity and a choke ring seal it.)
rationale: A lidded pot is the most familiar kitchen object there is; nothing to explain.
judge_comment: A familiar rice-cooker-style top lid is intuitive and workable with a choke seal, though limited to mugs and bowls.

title: Bell-jar microwave: lift the dome over the plate
new_elements: Metallised glass dome on a heated base (The dome is the cavity and the door; lifting it off opens the interlock in the rim.)
rationale: Plate down, dome on, lift off: the cooking gesture is as simple as covering a dish.
judge_comment: The cloche gesture is very intuitive and fresh, but a metallised glass dome with an RF seal and a rim interlock is hard to make safe and efficient.

title: The dish is the cavity: docking microwave pot
new_elements: Shielded lidded cooking pot that docks onto an RF base (You eat from, store, and heat in the same sealed pot; docking it closes the waveguide path.)
rationale: No transferring food between containers and no appliance interior to understand or clean.
judge_comment: A dish that doubles as the cavity is radical and removes steps, but docking a sealed RF path through a pot is difficult and the pots would cost a lot.

title: Door as a waveguide segment replaces interlock switches
new_elements: Door-carried waveguide section (RF path passes through a duct in the door; opening physically breaks the duct so energy cannot reach the cavity.)
rationale: Safety by geometry rather than by three switches means fewer failure modes the user ever meets.
judge_comment: The geometric safety concept is clever and concrete, but users barely notice it, so it does little for ease of use, and regulators would still require redundant interlocks.

title: Hinge pin is the mains switch
new_elements: Rotary-contact hinge interlock (Hinge pin carries the mains contact; door open = circuit mechanically open at the hinge.)
rationale: Removes misaligned-switch 'it won't start' faults that baffle users.
judge_comment: Mechanically interesting, but carrying mains current through a hinge pin is unsafe and bypasses the required redundant interlocks, and it only loosely addresses operation simplicity.

title: Resettable PTC replaces fuse and monitor switch
new_elements: Polymer PTC resettable overcurrent element (Trips on fault, resets when unplugged and cooled; no fuse to find or replace.)
rationale: 'Unplug it and plug it back in' is the only recovery step anyone needs to know.
judge_comment: A resettable PTC is a plausible simplification and gives a simple recovery step, but PTCs are not suited to mains fuse duty or to replacing the monitor switch, and users rarely deal with fuses anyway.

title: Passive chimney cooling replaces fan and motor
new_elements: Natural-convection heat-pipe chimney (Heat pipes from the magnetron to a rear stack create silent draught; no fan.)
rationale: A silent appliance removes the 'is it still running?' ambiguity and one more thing to fail.
judge_comment: Magnetron heat dissipation is too high for passive convection alone, and the idea has little to do with learning curve.

title: Flush glass-ceramic ceiling replaces mica cover
new_elements: Sealed glass-ceramic waveguide window (A flush, non-porous panel that wipes clean and never gets replaced.)
rationale: Users never discover the scary 'burnt cardboard' part or need to know it exists.
judge_comment: Feasible, and glass-ceramic ceilings already exist, but it mainly eases cleaning and does little for operation.

title: Moulded tactile pictograms replace printed fascia legends
new_elements: Embossed icon fascia with detent clicks (Raised mug/plate/snowflake symbols and audible knob detents; no text, no ink to wear off.)
rationale: Language-free and readable by touch, so first use needs no manual and no eyesight.
judge_comment: Tactile, language-free icons with detent knobs directly remove the learning curve and are very manufacturable, though not especially radical.

title: Traffic-light colour zones replace numbered scales
new_elements: Colour-band knob scales (Green = drink, amber = plate, red = long cook; defrost shown as blue band.)
rationale: People match colours faster than they estimate minutes.
judge_comment: Simple and directly lowers the learning curve, but color-coded dials are a fairly incremental and expected change.

title: Thermochromic frosting window as burn warning
new_elements: Thermochromic laminate door glass (Window tints red while contents are hot, clearing as they cool to safe handling temperature.)
rationale: Hot/not-hot is shown without a reading, aimed at children and elderly users.
judge_comment: Creative safety cue, but it addresses hot/cool warning rather than operating simplicity, and thermochromic glass in a microwave door is awkward.

title: Hourglass-style visible countdown replaces the dial scale
new_elements: Rotating coloured-sector time window (A coloured wedge visibly shrinks as time runs out, like a kitchen egg timer, no digits.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood pre-literately as 'how much red is left'.
judge_comment: An intuitive egg-timer-like display of remaining time suits no-learning-curve use and is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Swing-out plate shelf door replaces turntable and door
new_elements: Door-mounted carousel shelf (The food shelf is attached to the door; opening swings the plate out to you, closing swings it in.)
rationale: No reaching into a hot box: the appliance hands the plate to the user.
judge_comment: Wildly different and offers easier loading, but a door-mounted shelf has serious problems with weight, spills, and RF sealing, and it does not simplify the controls.

title: Vibrating floor stirs the field instead of rotating food
new_elements: Low-frequency vibrating cavity floor (An eccentric weight on the fan shaft shimmies a thin floor plate, shifting standing waves and nudging liquids.)
rationale: Nothing to align or remove, and the gentle agitation also prevents superheated-drink surprises.
judge_comment: Removes the turntable, but a vibrating floor is unlikely to even out heating well, and it does little for operation simplicity.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Single hold-to-heat push bar (Magnetron runs only while the bar is held; release = stop, no timer, no power setting)
rationale: Zero settings to learn: you press until the food looks right.
judge_comment: Very intuitive and radical simplification that removes all settings, though holding a button for minutes is tiring and the bar is a minor substitution.

title: Load-cell auto-timer
new_elements: Turntable load cell (Weighs the dish and derives heating time from mass; one Start button); Strain-gauge weighing (Cheap kitchen-scale sensor under turntable motor)
rationale: User never estimates minutes; the oven weighs and decides.
judge_comment: A cheap load cell and a single Start button are concrete, but mass alone is a poor predictor of heating time, so results may be unreliable.

title: Temperature dial instead of time dial
new_elements: IR thermopile with target-temperature knob (Knob labelled Warm/Hot/Boiling; heating stops when surface reaches target)
rationale: 'How hot' is intuitive; 'how many minutes at what power' is not.
judge_comment: Temperature targeting is intuitive and the dial labels are clear, but a surface-only IR reading and its cost reduce accuracy and simplicity.

title: Steam-stop sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust duct (Stops heating when steam burst indicates food is hot throughout)
rationale: Replaces timer guesswork with a single Start press.
judge_comment: A single Start press is ideal, though steam detection fails for covered or low-moisture foods and some sensor-based ovens already do this.

title: Picture-preset buttons only
new_elements: Four pictogram buttons (cup, plate, soup, defrost) (Each button hard-wires a fixed time/power pair; no numbers anywhere)
rationale: Choosing a picture of your food needs no instruction.
judge_comment: Easy to build and to understand, but it is an incremental, familiar preset approach with limited flexibility.

title: One-button +30 s
new_elements: Single '+30 s' button with LED countdown bar (Each press adds 30 s and starts immediately; nothing else on the panel)
rationale: One control, one gesture, learnable in a second.
judge_comment: Very simple and learnable instantly, though quick-start +30 s buttons already exist and it lacks defrost or power options.

title: Door is the switch
new_elements: Door-closed-equals-on interlock with 5 min safety cutoff (Closing the door starts heating; opening stops it; no timer knob)
rationale: The only action is open/close, which everyone already knows.
judge_comment: Radical and intuitive, but heating on door close risks accidental starts with no food or an empty cavity, and there is no duration control beyond the cutoff.

title: Delete the power knob
new_elements: Fixed 500 W single-power magnetron drive (Lower fixed power that is safe for reheat and defrost alike; knob removed)
rationale: Fewer controls equals less to learn.
judge_comment: Removes a control, but one fixed power compromises performance and the idea is a modest, obvious simplification.

title: Gentle/Strong rocker with inverter
new_elements: Inverter continuous-power supply (Switch-mode HV supply gives true continuous power); Two-position Gentle/Strong rocker (Replaces 5-step cam with a binary choice)
rationale: A binary choice is the simplest possible power setting.
judge_comment: A binary power choice is easy to grasp and an inverter makes it feasible, though it adds cost and still needs timer input.

title: Offline voice chip
new_elements: Keyword-spotting voice module ($2 chip understands 'two minutes', 'defrost', 'stop' without cloud)
rationale: Speaking a duration needs no interface literacy.
judge_comment: Voice requires no learning, and offline keyword spotting is plausible, but noisy kitchens and accents cause errors and it is not especially cheap or simple.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pull a cord out marked in minutes; a vacuum-style cord retractor pulls it back and trips the switch at zero)
rationale: Visible cord length is a tangible, obvious representation of remaining time.
judge_comment: A visible, intuitive time representation that replaces the keypad, though the retractor mechanism's reliability and fine accuracy are open questions.

title: Egg-timer drum with braille detents
new_elements: Oversized tactile drum timer (Hand-sized drum with 1-minute clicks and raised numerals)
rationale: Large tactile clicks make setting time unmistakable for elderly users.
judge_comment: Mechanical dial timers are well known and work well, but this is more an incremental than a radical substitution.

title: Tap-the-packet NFC
new_elements: NFC reader on front panel (Tap food packaging; tag carries time and power)
rationale: Packaging knows the recipe so the user needn't.
judge_comment: Tap-to-cook removes settings entirely, but it requires packaging tags across the industry and offers no fallback for untagged food.

title: Magnetic no-button door
new_elements: Magnetic-catch door with pull handle (Magnets hold door shut; pull to open, push to close; interlocks sensed by reed switches)
rationale: Removes the 'which button opens it' question.
judge_comment: Removing the door button is simple and feasible, but it addresses only a minor part of operation and the safety interlocks need care.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Food sits in a sliding drawer; push shut to seal with choke flange)
rationale: Push/pull is a universal gesture with no latch to find.
judge_comment: The drawer gesture is intuitive, but sealing microwave leakage at a sliding drawer is hard, and it doesn't address setting time or power.

title: Top-loading lid
new_elements: Chest-style top lid cavity (Drop food in from above; lid weight closes interlocks)
rationale: Dropping food into a box is the simplest loading motion.
judge_comment: Top-loading chest lid is a clear, plausible change, but it does little to simplify operation beyond loading and makes it harder to see and reach the food.

title: Revolving-carousel cavity
new_elements: Rotating half-drum cavity (Turn the drum to present the shelf outward; turning back seals it)
rationale: No door at all to open or latch.
judge_comment: A rotating half-drum with no door is radical, but sealing microwave leakage at a rotating joint is hard and the added learning is unclear.

title: Oven-style drop-down shelf door
new_elements: Bottom-hinged drop door (Door swings down and doubles as a plate shelf)
rationale: Mirrors a familiar oven and gives a place to rest the hot plate.
judge_comment: A drop-down door is familiar and workable, but it is hardly radical and barely changes the operation or the learning curve.

title: Foot pedal door
new_elements: Foot-pedal latch release (Bin-style pedal opens the door when hands are full)
rationale: Hands-full opening removes a fumbling step.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is easy to build, but it adds a new control to learn and does not address the main operating steps.

title: Auto-open at end
new_elements: Spring auto-pop door at timer end (Timer trip releases latch so door pops ajar; replaces bell)
rationale: Done state is physically obvious, no button needed.
judge_comment: A spring pop-open door at timer end removes the bell and makes the done state obvious, and a latch trip is simple to build.

title: Transparent conductive window
new_elements: Fine metal-mesh laminated glass (20 µm mesh in glass gives clear view with Faraday shielding); Clear shielded door glass (Replaces perforated steel mesh)
rationale: Seeing food clearly lets users stop by eye instead of learning settings.
judge_comment: Metal-mesh laminated glass is plausible and improves visibility, but the link to zero learning curve is indirect and the idea is incremental.

title: Doorless choke tunnel
new_elements: Quarter-wave choke tunnel (Conveyor-oven style open mouth attenuates leakage without a door); Open-mouth cavity with choke tunnel (Slide plate in; no door, hinges or latch)
rationale: Nothing to open or close means nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A doorless choke tunnel is radical and removes a step, but leakage safety, heat retention and food containment make it very hard, and it doesn't simplify operation much.

title: Thermochromic progress strip
new_elements: Heated thermochromic bar on door (A resistive strip warms along its length as time elapses, colour shows progress)
rationale: Progress is read at a glance without numbers.
judge_comment: A thermochromic progress strip gives an intuitive glanceable cue, though a heated strip adds some complexity and makes it a substitute for a display only loosely.

title: Wind-up spring timer
new_elements: Clockwork wind-up timer (Spring escapement like an egg timer; no synchronous motor, mains-frequency independent)
rationale: Same twist gesture, cheaper, and ticks audibly so users know it's running.
judge_comment: A wind-up mechanical timer is familiar, cheap and reliable, with an audible tick as feedback, and it clearly fits no learning curve.

title: Heat/Defrost toggle
new_elements: Two-position Heat/Defrost toggle (Defrost = 30% duty via one cam lobe; all other cases full power)
rationale: Removes four meaningless intermediate power levels.
judge_comment: A two-position Heat/Defrost toggle directly cuts choices, is simple to build with a cam, and is easy to understand, though not very radical.

title: Single more/less lever
new_elements: Spring-centred More/Less lever (Push up to add heat, down to reduce; oven maps lever to time and power internally)
rationale: One control expressing only 'more' or 'less'.
judge_comment: A single more/less lever is simple and intuitive, but the mapping of lever input to time and power is vague and only moderately radical.

title: Wave-to-add gesture
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (Each hand wave in front of the door adds 30 s)
rationale: Touch-free, no knob to decode.
judge_comment: Wave-to-add is touch-free and feasible with IR sensors, but it is imprecise and may be less discoverable, and users can trigger it accidentally.

title: Pod-style coded containers
new_elements: Keyed container base reader (Container foot shape presses microswitches that select a fixed programme)
rationale: The dish picks the programme; the user just inserts it.
judge_comment: Keyed containers make the dish select the programme, which is nearly zero-learning, though it requires proprietary containers and limits flexibility.

title: Coloured dish mats
new_elements: Colour-sensing turntable spot (Red/yellow/green silicone mats under the plate encode short/medium/long cook)
rationale: Picking a mat colour is simpler than reading a dial.
judge_comment: Colour mats are simple to use, but colour-to-time mapping must be learned and the mats can get lost or dirty.

title: Mechanical power attenuator shelf
new_elements: Height-adjustable shelf toward antenna (Lifting the shelf nearer the feed increases coupling; lever marked Low/High)
rationale: Power becomes a physical position users can see.
judge_comment: A shelf that adjusts power by coupling is highly novel and visible, but it is technically dubious: power control would be uneven and unreliable, and it does not remove the need for timing.

title: Thermochromic plate + run-until-open
new_elements: Bundled thermochromic plate (Plate glaze turns red when food is hot; oven runs until door opened)
rationale: Doneness is shown on the plate, so no timing is needed.
judge_comment: Plate color feedback removes timing, but thermochromic glaze must survive microwaves and its color shows surface rather than true heat; it also depends on a bundled plate, and running until the door opens is a safety and overcooking concern.

title: Zone-labelled single dial
new_elements: Combined time/power dial with result zones (Dial sectors read Warm cup / Hot plate / Defrost / Cook; each sector sets both cams)
rationale: One knob describing outcomes instead of parameters.
judge_comment: An outcome-labelled single dial with cams is simple, cheap and immediately understandable, though it is a fairly incremental idea.

title: Visible hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip hourglass with sand-weight switch (Flipping the glass starts the oven; empty top bulb trips a lever to stop)
rationale: Everyone understands an hourglass at a glance.
judge_comment: A flip hourglass that starts and stops the oven is intuitive and mechanically plausible, but fixed durations limit flexibility and it only loosely substitutes for a timer.

title: Squeeze-handle door
new_elements: Squeeze-to-release grab handle (Gripping the handle lifts the hooks; the natural grab motion opens the door)
rationale: Opening is the same motion as reaching for the handle.
judge_comment: A squeeze-handle door matches natural motion and is easy to build, but opening a door is rarely the main learning barrier, so the gain is small.

title: Evaporation-loss auto-stop
new_elements: Load cell detecting mass loss (Stops when evaporated-water mass loss indicates boiling point reached)
rationale: Closed-loop stop removes the timing decision entirely.
judge_comment: Auto-stop from mass loss removes timing decisions, but load cells in microwaves and the variable relation between mass loss and boiling make it unreliable for many foods.

title: Listen-for-done microphone
new_elements: Cavity microphone (Stops on sizzle/pop pattern decline (popcorn, soups))
rationale: Mimics how people already judge doneness by ear.
judge_comment: Acoustic doneness detection removes the need to set a time and matches how people already judge food, though a microphone in a microwave cavity is a hard environment and the sound patterns need reliable classification.

title: Pass-through tunnel door
new_elements: Front and rear doors (Load from kitchen side, serve from table side)
rationale: Removes carrying and turning steps around the appliance.
judge_comment: A front-and-rear door is novel, but it does little for operational simplicity and makes microwave shielding and the cabinet fit harder.

title: Push-push door latch
new_elements: Cabinet push-push latch (Press the door itself to pop it open; no button)
rationale: Any push anywhere on the door opens it.
judge_comment: A push-push latch is simple, proven and intuitive, which removes the button, but it is a modest idea and not radical.

title: Roll-up shutter door
new_elements: Flexible metal-mesh roller shutter (Shutter rolls up into the top; no swing clearance)
rationale: Lifting a shutter is obvious and needs no swing space.
judge_comment: A roll-up shutter door is intuitive and saves space, but RF sealing, cleaning and the mesh make it hard to build.

title: Result-preview dial
new_elements: Dial with illustrated outcome window (Rotating shows pictures of steaming cup, hot plate etc. in a window)
rationale: Users choose what they want to see, not a number.
judge_comment: An outcome-picture dial replaces numeric input with intent and has almost no learning curve, and it can be built with a mechanical dial and preset programs.

title: Exhaust-air thermostat stop
new_elements: Bimetal thermostat in vent (Cuts magnetron when exhaust air reaches a set temperature; 10-cent part)
rationale: Cheapest possible auto-stop with a single Start press.
judge_comment: Cheap single-press auto-stop, but exhaust air temperature is a poor proxy for food doneness and could over- or under-heat, with limited novelty.

title: Reflected-power defrost sensing
new_elements: Directional-coupler load sensing (Ice-to-water dielectric change shifts reflected power; detect end of defrost); Auto-defrost sensing loop (One Defrost button, stops itself)
rationale: Defrost, the hardest setting, becomes a single button.
judge_comment: Reflected-power sensing is a real physical effect and turns defrost into one button, though reliable end-point detection is difficult.

title: Timer that pops the door
new_elements: Timer cam linked to latch lever (At zero the cam both stops heating and lifts the latch)
rationale: Done equals open; no bell to interpret.
judge_comment: A simple mechanical cam that stops heating and pops the door is easy to build and removes interpretation, but it doesn't help with setting the time.

title: Speaking knob
new_elements: Knob with voice readout (Rotating announces 'one minute, two minutes' from a sound chip)
rationale: No reading of small scales for low-vision users.
judge_comment: A sound-chip voice readout is easy and helps low-vision users, but it adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Toy pull-string timer
new_elements: Pull-string spring governor timer (Pull ring sets time; string retracts under governor; stops at home)
rationale: One pull, hear the whirr, done when quiet.
judge_comment: A wind-up pull-string governor timer is intuitive, playful and mechanically plausible, and truly radical in its simplicity.

title: Chain-mail curtain door
new_elements: Conductive bead-chain curtain with choke (Push plate through a grounded metal curtain; combined with choke tunnel for leakage)
rationale: Walking food through a curtain needs no instructions.
judge_comment: Wild and intuitive, but a bead curtain is unlikely to contain microwave leakage safely, and it's unclear how it works as a door.

title: Lift-off door
new_elements: Drop-in pin hinges, removable door (Door lifts off for cleaning; no tools)
rationale: Cleaning the window is as simple as lifting it off.
judge_comment: A removable door helps cleaning but does little for operating simplicity, and it raises interlock and safety concerns.

title: Capacitive touch door pad
new_elements: Large capacitive 'touch to open' pad (Whole door front acts as release; solenoid lifts hooks)
rationale: No target to aim for; touching anywhere works.
judge_comment: Touch-anywhere opening is easy to use, though it risks accidental opening and is only a small part of operation.

title: Timer-driven turntable
new_elements: Timer motor that also turns the turntable (One synchronous motor drives both cam and turntable via gear train)
rationale: Visible plate rotation doubles as the 'it's running' indicator.
judge_comment: A single timer motor driving the turntable is simple and cheap, and the rotation signals running, but it is a familiar approach with modest gains in ease of use.

title: Weight-plus-IR single Start
new_elements: Scale and IR fused controller (Mass sets power, IR sets stop; panel has only Start)
rationale: Entire interface collapses to one Start button.
judge_comment: Reducing the interface to one Start button with automatic power and stop control directly removes the learning curve, though reliable IR and weight sensing is challenging.

title: Door-weight interlock lid
new_elements: Gravity-sealed lid, no latch (Heavy top lid seals by its own weight; lift to stop, lower to start)
rationale: No latch mechanism to understand or wear out.
judge_comment: A gravity-sealed top lid that starts when lowered and stops when lifted makes operation intuitive and replaces the latch, though it needs a reliable microwave-leakage seal and safe interlock switching, and a top-loading format sacrifices some ergonomics.

title: One-button 'Hot' microwave
new_elements: Single illuminated HOT button (Press once: full power until humidity sensor says food is hot; press again to stop.); Humidity-sensor cooking termination (Steam burst in cavity exhaust indicates food reached serving temperature.)
rationale: Replaces two knobs with a single button so there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-button operation maximally serves zero learning curve, though humidity-based termination is unreliable across foods and sealed or dry items.

title: Weight-sensing turntable sets time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable spindle (Strain gauge under the turntable motor measures dish mass and derives heating time.)
rationale: The user just puts food in; the oven computes duration from weight, eliminating timer guesswork.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing removes guesswork, but mass alone doesn't determine heating needs (frozen vs. not, density), so results would be inconsistent.

title: Food-icon dial replaces power knob
new_elements: Pictogram rotary dial (cup, plate, pizza, frozen block) (Each icon maps to a preset power-and-time combo; no numbers anywhere.)
rationale: Replaces abstract watts and minutes with pictures anyone understands instantly.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is simple, cheap and easily understood, but it resembles existing preset or auto-cook menus and isn't radical.

title: Magnetic pull-door, no button
new_elements: Rare-earth magnetic door closure (Magnets hold the door shut against the choke; a simple pull opens it, like a fridge.)
rationale: A fridge-style pull is a universally known gesture, removing the hidden release button.
judge_comment: A fridge-style pull door is intuitive, but a magnet-only closure raises serious microwave safety and interlock concerns and the benefit is small.

title: Hall-sensor door detection
new_elements: Redundant Hall-effect magnetic position sensing (Two solid-state sensors plus a relay replace three mechanical microswitches with no wear.)
rationale: Door closes with a gentle push and always 'just works', with no clunky latch feel to learn.
judge_comment: Hall-effect sensors are a plausible, concrete component swap, but the user-facing benefit to ease of operation is marginal and mostly internal.

title: Mode-stirrer fan instead of turntable
new_elements: Ceiling mode-stirrer paddle (Metal fan in waveguide outlet scrambles field pattern, giving even heating on a flat floor.)
rationale: Flat floor means any plate shape fits anywhere, so no positioning rules to learn.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are well-established in real microwaves, and the benefit to operation is only indirect, since users still set time and power.

title: Rotating under-floor antenna
new_elements: Rotating feed antenna beneath ceramic floor (Motor spins the RF feed rather than the food; floor is a fixed wipe-clean slab.)
rationale: No removable glass plate to wash, re-seat or misalign.
judge_comment: Rotating-antenna designs exist, and they make cleaning easier but do little to simplify operation.

title: Steam-sniff auto-stop timer
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam rise that marks food reaching temperature and cuts power.)
rationale: The oven decides when it is done, so users never set a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop is already used in sensor-cook models, but it removes time setting and fits the no-learning-curve need well.

title: IR thermopile 'done at 70 °C' stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Reads food surface temperature through a mica window and stops at a safe serving temperature.)
rationale: Temperature-based stopping replaces time arithmetic and avoids overheated liquids.
judge_comment: An IR temperature stop removes time guesswork and adds safety, though surface-only readings and uneven heating limit accuracy.

title: Bowl-size dial
new_elements: Three-position 'mug / bowl / plate' dial (Portion size is the only input; power and time are derived internally.)
rationale: Users already know what container they are holding; nothing else needs to be understood.
judge_comment: A single portion-size dial is very simple and intuitive, but it is a modest and fairly obvious preset approach.

title: Spoken 'your food is ready'
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (Replaces the mechanical bell with a short spoken phrase in the user's language.)
rationale: An explicit sentence needs no interpretation, unlike a generic ding.
judge_comment: A spoken completion message is clear and cheap, but talking appliances are already common and it only addresses the end-of-cycle signal.

title: Colour-glow door replaces bell
new_elements: Edge-lit RGB door frame (Red while heating, green when done; silent and visible across the room.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are universally understood, zero learning.
judge_comment: Red/green status light is intuitive and silent, though it does not simplify operation beyond the completion cue.

title: Edge-lit glass door instead of cavity lamp
new_elements: LED edge-lighting of tempered door glass (LEDs in the door frame inject light through the glass, lighting the cavity from outside the RF field.)
rationale: No bulb to replace and food is always visible, so users check progress at a glance.
judge_comment: A plausible lamp substitute with a clear mechanism, but it has little effect on ease of operation, and the light-leak and RF-shielding challenges in the door are real.

title: Fibre-optic daylight pipe
new_elements: Ambient-light fibre bundle to cavity (Optical fibres collect room light at the top of the casing and emit it inside; no lamp, no wiring.)
rationale: Removes a failure-prone lamp so the oven never needs user maintenance.
judge_comment: Ambient fibre lighting is inventive, but it would be dim and unreliable, and fibres entering the cavity compromise RF shielding; it barely touches the simple-operation need.

title: Inductive power pad instead of cord
new_elements: High-power wireless induction coupling (Ki standard) (Microwave sits on a countertop coil; no cord, plug or outlet hunting.)
rationale: Place it and it works; nothing to plug in.
judge_comment: Wireless power is bold, but delivering about 1 kW or more through Ki-standard induction is wildly impractical, and removing the cord does not help operation much.

title: Battery-pack picnic microwave
new_elements: Swappable LiFePO4 battery module (Tool-battery style pack powers a low-power inverter magnetron for a few heating cycles.)
rationale: Works anywhere with one click-in pack, no outlet or cable management.
judge_comment: Battery portability is interesting, but it mostly addresses power source rather than operation simplicity, and the energy needed for a magnetron makes it impractical.

title: Thermal fuse cast into magnetron
new_elements: Integral one-shot thermal fuse in magnetron heatsink (Cheaper than a snap-disc; cuts anode supply at a fixed temperature.)
rationale: Invisible safety that never asks the user to intervene or reset.
judge_comment: A plausible cost-saving safety part, but it is invisible to the user and barely touches learning curve.

title: Switch-mode inverter replaces doubler
new_elements: High-frequency inverter HV supply (Replaces transformer, diode and large capacitor; no lethal stored charge, continuous power control.)
rationale: True continuous power means 'low' really is gentle, so results match expectations without trial and error.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies are real in existing microwaves and give true power control, which modestly reduces trial and error.

title: Solid-state GaN RF source
new_elements: GaN solid-state 2.45 GHz amplifier with reflected-power sensing (Replaces magnetron and HV chain; auto-tunes to the load and self-detects empty cavity.)
rationale: Oven senses the food and adjusts itself, removing most user decisions.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing enables truly self-adjusting cooking, directly serving no-learning-curve use, though cost and power remain hurdles.

title: Auto-shorting discharge relay
new_elements: Normally-closed discharge relay across HV capacitor (Shorts the capacitor the instant power is removed, replacing a bleeder resistor.)
rationale: Makes the appliance safe to handle immediately after unplugging without any user knowledge.
judge_comment: A feasible safety tweak, but it has little relevance to ease of operation.

title: Conductive elastomer door gasket
new_elements: Silver-loaded silicone RF gasket (Soft conductive seal replaces the precision quarter-wave choke; tolerates sloppy door closure.)
rationale: Door seals even if closed casually, so there is no 'correct way' to shut it.
judge_comment: Forgiving door seal is a plausible substitution, but it only marginally affects operation simplicity and users already just shut the door.

title: Silicone mat instead of glass turntable
new_elements: Dishwasher-safe silicone turntable mat (Unbreakable, rolls up, keyed to the motor hub.)
rationale: Nothing to break or re-align; the mat drops in any orientation.
judge_comment: Practical and feasible, but silicone must withstand heat and the benefit to operation learning is minor.

title: Glazed ceramic waveguide window
new_elements: Sintered alumina waveguide cover (Wipe-clean glazed ceramic replaces the fragile mica sheet that users damage when cleaning.)
rationale: Removes the one interior part that requires special care, so cleaning is foolproof.
judge_comment: Ceramic cover is feasible and reduces care needs, but concerns cleaning rather than operation and is hardly radical.

title: Drawer-style cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity on ball slides (The whole floor slides out like a kitchen drawer; the fixed front wall seals when closed.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to open a drawer; no hinges, no button, food loads from above.
judge_comment: Drawer metaphor is intuitive and novel, though RF sealing of a sliding cavity and spill containment are challenging.

title: Top-loading lid microwave
new_elements: Hinged top lid with gravity seal (Cavity opens like a rice cooker; lid weight closes the RF seal and interlock.)
rationale: Lift lid, drop bowl in, close lid — the pot metaphor requires no instructions.
judge_comment: Rice-cooker-style top lid is a familiar metaphor with gravity-closing seal, though reaching into deep cavity and RF leakage need engineering.

title: Iris-aperture door
new_elements: Metal iris diaphragm front (Overlapping leaves twist open like a camera shutter; closed position forms the RF seal.)
rationale: A single twist gesture opens and closes, with no latch, hinge or button to understand.
judge_comment: Very novel, but an iris door is nearly impossible to RF-seal reliably and doesn't simplify the actual operation of heating.

title: NFC food packaging sets the program
new_elements: NFC reader in turntable hub (Reads a tag printed on the meal package and applies the manufacturer's heating program.)
rationale: Ready meals heat themselves correctly without reading the box.
judge_comment: Zero-input heating for packaged meals is plausible with NFC, though it only works for tagged packaging.

title: Camera food recognition replaces knobs
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-device food classifier (Identifies coffee, soup, leftovers or frozen block and picks the program.); Computer vision (Image classification on embedded hardware.)
rationale: The appliance looks at the food so the user never has to describe it.
judge_comment: Camera recognition removes user input, but classification accuracy and steam or splatter on the lens are practical problems.

title: Time-only dial, power auto-managed
new_elements: Single large time dial with adaptive power firmware (Power ramps automatically from high to low as the humidity sensor detects doneness.)
rationale: Removes the confusing power knob entirely; users only ever turn one thing.
judge_comment: Simplifies to one dial with sensor-driven power, which is practical and builds on existing sensor cooking.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Large momentary 'heat while pressed' pad (RF is on only while the pad is held; release stops instantly.)
rationale: Perfect for 10-second tasks; the user is the timer and nothing can be set wrong.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive and easy to build, but it is impractical for longer heating tasks.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Length of cord pulled equals heating time; cord retracts as it cooks, like a pull-string toy.)
rationale: A visible, physical length of cord is an intuitive representation of remaining time.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer is an intuitive, no-numbers interface, but a retracting cord is mechanically fiddly and imprecise, and it only partly substitutes for the dial.

title: Pressure-sensitive power pad
new_elements: Force-sensing start pad (Light tap = gentle reheat, firm press = full power; cooks until humidity sensor stops it.)
rationale: Maps intensity of intent to intensity of heating without numbers or modes.
judge_comment: Pressure-mapped power plus humidity auto-stop removes settings, though light versus firm presses are ambiguous and humidity sensing is unreliable for some foods.

title: Vibrating floor prevents superheating
new_elements: Piezo-vibrated cavity floor (Replaces the turntable motor; gentle vibration nucleates boiling and evens heating.)
rationale: Users no longer need to know the 'put a spoon in the mug' rule.
judge_comment: A piezo-vibrated floor is a creative replacement for the turntable, but it is aimed at a safety rule rather than operation, and vibrating heavy loads is questionable.

title: Built-in boiling chips in turntable
new_elements: Micro-textured ceramic turntable (Rough surface provides nucleation sites so liquids boil visibly instead of superheating.)
rationale: Safety is built into the plate, so no special cup-handling knowledge is needed.
judge_comment: A textured ceramic plate is cheap and plausible and gives passive nucleation, but it mostly addresses safety rather than simple operation.

title: Ferrite crisper floor
new_elements: Ferrite-loaded ceramic turntable (Absorbs microwaves and heats to ~200 °C, browning the underside of pizza and bread.)
rationale: Crisping happens automatically without a separate grill mode to learn.
judge_comment: A ferrite-loaded plate is feasible and mirrors existing crisper plates, and it removes a mode, but it is not very radical.

title: Transparent conductive film door
new_elements: ITO / silver-nanowire RF-shielding film on glass (Replaces perforated metal mesh with a clear conductive coating.)
rationale: Crystal-clear view lets users judge doneness by eye, the most natural feedback.
judge_comment: Clear view helps judge doneness, but microwave-grade RF shielding with transparent films is hard and the learning-curve benefit is modest.

title: Retractable cord reel
new_elements: Spring-loaded cord reel in base (Vacuum-cleaner style reel; pull to length, tap to retract.)
rationale: Setup is pull-and-plug, with no cable tangle for first-time users.
judge_comment: Feasible and easy to use, but it addresses setup rather than operation and is a minor tweak.

title: Scent-release doneness cue
new_elements: Fan-driven aroma vent at cycle end (At the end of cooking the fan vents cavity aroma into the room instead of ringing a bell.)
rationale: Smelling your food is a primal, zero-learning notification.
judge_comment: A zero-learning cue is intuitive, but venting food aroma is unreliable, may be unwanted, and replaces a useful audible alert.

title: Pneumatic air-switch interlock
new_elements: Door-compressed air bellows to pressure switch (Closing the door squeezes a bellows; air pressure holds the HV enable switch, as used in spa tubs.)
rationale: Fail-safe with no electrical contacts in the door, so the door never 'needs a harder slam'.
judge_comment: A clever substitution for the interlock, but it is invisible to users and barely affects operational simplicity; safety certification would also be a hurdle.

title: Transformer tap selector for power
new_elements: Two-tap HV transformer with toggle (Replaces the duty-cycle cam with a real high/low voltage tap, giving genuine continuous low power.)
rationale: A simple high/low toggle behaves exactly as users expect, with no pulsing surprises.
judge_comment: A true high/low toggle matches user expectations and removes pulsing confusion, though a tapped HV transformer costs more and low-power magnetron operation is tricky.

title: Removable silicone cavity liner
new_elements: Pull-out moulded silicone cavity liner (Catches splatter; lift out and rinse instead of scrubbing stamped steel.)
rationale: Cleaning becomes a single obvious action, lowering the ownership learning curve.
judge_comment: Practical and simple, but it addresses cleaning rather than operation, and silicone liners are a known concept with some microwave-compatibility concerns.

title: Fan-driven magnetic turntable
new_elements: Magnetic coupling from cooling fan shaft (Geared take-off from the existing fan spins the plate through the floor; no separate motor.)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail and a smooth floor with no coupler to align.
judge_comment: Clever parts substitution, but it has no effect on how simple the microwave is to operate for the user.

title: Add-30-seconds only button
new_elements: Single '+30 s' start button (Each press adds 30 s at full power and starts immediately; the entire control surface.)
rationale: The most-used microwave action becomes the only action.
judge_comment: Very easy to use with essentially zero learning curve, though it limits flexibility, and similar buttons already exist.

title: Two-position reheat/defrost switch
new_elements: Rocker switch: REHEAT / DEFROST (Replaces the 5-step knob with the only two settings people actually use.)
rationale: Two words, two positions, nothing to misinterpret.
judge_comment: Two clear settings are easy to understand, but time control is unclear and the idea is not very radical.

title: Slot-machine lever control
new_elements: Spring-return pull lever (Lever travel sets time, it ratchets back as cooking proceeds; one gesture replaces both knobs.)
rationale: A big lever invites use and shows remaining time by its position.
judge_comment: Playful, intuitive single gesture that shows remaining time physically; a mechanical ratchet timer is plausible but lacks power control.

title: Foot-pedal door opener
new_elements: Floor pedal cable release (Pedal under the counter pops the door, like a pedal bin, for hands-full users.)
rationale: Pedal-bin gesture is already learned by everyone.
judge_comment: Familiar gesture and easy to build with a cable release, but it only helps with opening the door and does not simplify operation overall.

title: Door auto-opens when done
new_elements: Solenoid latch tied to timer end (The bell moment also fires a solenoid that swings the door ajar, venting steam and signalling done.)
rationale: Opening the door is the notification and the next step, with no button to find.
judge_comment: A solenoid latch tied to the timer end is simple and cheap, and it removes a step and makes the finish obvious, though the door swinging open unexpectedly could be a nuisance.

title: Magnetron current sensing replaces thermostat
new_elements: Anode current monitor with cut-off (Microcontroller watches magnetron current to infer empty cavity or overheating and stops.)
rationale: Protects against running empty or with metal, so beginner mistakes are harmless.
judge_comment: Current sensing makes mistakes harmless and is plausible, but users never see it, so it does little for learnability and only replaces a thermostat.

title: Thermal camera door display
new_elements: Low-res thermal imager with door e-ink overlay (Shows hot and cold zones on the door instead of lighting the cavity.)
rationale: Users see whether food is hot through, without probing or guessing.
judge_comment: A thermal imager and e-ink overlay on the door is novel but costly and hard to build, and it adds information that makes operation more complex rather than simpler.

title: Shape-memory alloy door release
new_elements: Nitinol wire actuator latch (A touch on a capacitive pad heats SMA wire which retracts the hook; no lever mechanism.)
rationale: Any touch anywhere on the door opens it, so there is no specific button to locate.
judge_comment: A touch-anywhere door release using a Nitinol wire is a radical substitute for the lever and needs no learning, but SMA wires are slow and risk accidental opening.
