title: Hourglass-style countdown window
new_elements: Visible mechanical sand-glass timer (Flipping the hourglass module starts the oven; sand runout trips the stop switch and shows time left.)
rationale: An hourglass is self-explanatory across all ages and languages.
judge_comment: An intuitive flip-to-start hourglass replaces keypad and digital timer with a simple mechanism, though fixed-duration glasses limit flexibility (requires multiple sizes or swaps) and a sand-triggered stop switch is somewhat imprecise, but it is plausible and clearly serves zero-learning operation.

title: One-touch 30-second button
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (existing 0-30 min dial); Single +30s start button (each press adds 30 s and starts immediately); Set heating time (user specifies duration)
rationale: One button, one gesture; nothing to read or dial.
judge_comment: Simple and already common (+30s button), so low novelty, though it clearly removes learning; the new elements list is somewhat muddled.

title: Food pictogram dial replaces power knob
new_elements: 5-step power knob (existing duty-cycle cam); Pictogram dial (cup, plate, frozen box, popcorn) (detents map to preset power+time combos); Select heating intensity (choose energy delivery)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating, not abstract watts or minutes.
judge_comment: Pictogram detents mapping to preset power and time are intuitive and easily built mechanically, but presets may be imprecise.

title: Weighing turntable auto-sets time
new_elements: Glass turntable (existing rotating plate); Load-cell turntable (weighs food and computes duration); Strain-gauge load cell (cheap kitchen-scale sensor)
rationale: Removes the time decision entirely; place food, press go.
judge_comment: A load-cell turntable removes the time decision, but weight poorly predicts heating time and a rotating weighing platform adds engineering challenges.

title: IR thermostat replaces timer
new_elements: Infrared food thermometer (stops heating when surface reaches target); Stop when food is hot (outcome-based termination); Thermopile IR sensor (non-contact temperature)
rationale: Users want hot food, not minutes; the oven decides.
judge_comment: Outcome-based stopping is exactly what users want, but IR reads only surface temperature and is unreliable through covers and containers.

title: Steam sensor GO button
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust (detects steam burst and ends cycle); Single GO button (the only control)
rationale: Zero settings; the appliance senses doneness itself.
judge_comment: A single GO button with steam detection is radically simple, though it works only for foods that steam and risks over- or under-heating.

title: Door-close starts, door-open stops
new_elements: Door push-release button (existing latch release); Door-as-switch interlock (closing the door begins a default cycle); Start heating (initiate cycle)
rationale: The one action everyone already knows (closing a door) is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start a default cycle removes the interface entirely and is highly relevant, though it risks accidental starts and the default cycle is vague.

title: Magnetic soft-close door
new_elements: Magnetic latch with pull handle (no button; pull to open, push to shut)
rationale: Eliminates the hunt for the release button.
judge_comment: A pull-handle magnetic door is easy to build and removes the release-button hunt, but it is a modest change that doesn't touch operation of the controls.

title: Mode stirrer instead of turntable
new_elements: Flat ceramic floor + rotating antenna (even heating without moving plate); Distribute microwave energy evenly (avoid cold spots)
rationale: No plate to seat, break, or re-align; any dish shape fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common in flat-bed microwaves, so the idea is feasible and concrete, but it has little to do with operation simplicity.

title: Spoken 'done' instead of bell
new_elements: Mechanical bell (existing end signal); Voice chip speaker (says 'your food is ready' in local language)
rationale: Unambiguous signal needs no interpretation.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap and feasible and makes the done signal clearer, but it adds a part rather than substituting a simpler one and covers only the end of the cycle.

title: Room-visible colour halo
new_elements: RGB halo ring around door (red while heating, green when done); Signal completion (notify user)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are universally understood.
judge_comment: An RGB status ring is simple and easy to read, but it only signals status and is a fairly obvious feature.

title: Dead-man's hold-to-heat pad
new_elements: Hold-to-heat pad (runs only while pressed; release stops)
rationale: Like a garden hose: hold for as long as you want heat.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive and has zero learning curve, and it is easy to build, but it is tiring for longer heating and substitutes only the controls, not radically.

title: Foot pedal start
new_elements: Floor foot pedal (tap to start default cycle, hands stay free)
rationale: Sewing-machine simplicity with no hands on controls.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is simple and cheap to build, but it adds a floor accessory, offers little time control, and does not remove any decisions.

title: Container-recognising camera
new_elements: Cavity camera (recognises mug vs plate vs bowl, picks preset); Embedded image classification (tiny on-device model)
rationale: The oven reads the situation so the user doesn't have to.
judge_comment: Camera-based container recognition removes user decisions, but a cavity camera is hard to keep clean and heat-safe, and container type is a weak proxy for food and heating needs.

title: Barcode scanner reads package instructions
new_elements: Front barcode scanner (swipe ready-meal, oven sets time and power); Barcode lookup (local or cloud database)
rationale: No reading tiny instructions, no translating to settings.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning is feasible and removes the need to read packaging, but it works only for packaged meals, needs a database, and is not very novel.

title: NFC tag reader in floor
new_elements: NFC reader under cavity floor (reads tagged packaging or tagged dishes)
rationale: Place and go; the dish carries its own program.
judge_comment: The place-and-go concept is elegant, but NFC under a metal cavity floor is technically difficult and needs tagged packaging that does not exist.

title: Dimming lamp as countdown
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp (existing 20-25 W bulb); Progress-dimming LED lamp (brightness fades to zero as cycle ends); Show remaining time (progress feedback)
rationale: Progress is read at a glance without numerals.
judge_comment: Dimming lamp is an intuitive, near-free progress cue, but it addresses feedback rather than operation, and the idea muddles incandescent and LED.

title: LED progress bar on door edge
new_elements: Door-edge LED bar (shrinks like a battery gauge)
rationale: Replaces dial reading with a universally understood bar.
judge_comment: Easy and clear progress indicator, but common and doesn't simplify input.

title: Dial in 'cups of coffee' units
new_elements: Portion-unit dial (marked 1 cup, 2 cups, 1 plate, 2 plates)
rationale: Users think in portions, not minutes.
judge_comment: Portion-based dial directly removes the need to know times, though calibrating for food variety is imprecise.

title: Fixed full power, no power knob
new_elements: Blank panel (power knob deleted) (always 700 W)
rationale: One fewer decision; most users never change power anyway.
judge_comment: Removing power control simplifies operation and is trivially feasible, though full power overheats some foods.

title: Colour-zoned timer dial
new_elements: Colour-band timer knob (green=drink, yellow=plate, red=frozen zones instead of numbers)
rationale: Turn to the colour that matches your food.
judge_comment: Color zones cut numeric reading and are simple to build, but food categories are coarse.

title: Drop-in time tokens
new_elements: Token slot (wooden '1 min' / '3 min' tokens trigger fixed cycles); Mechanical coin-switch (vending-style actuator)
rationale: Physical tokens are tangible and self-explanatory.
judge_comment: Tangible tokens make operation self-explanatory and are easy to build, but fixed durations limit flexibility and tokens can get lost.

title: Smart dishes tell the oven
new_elements: Dish with resonant RF tag (cavity detects which dish, applies its program); Passive RF resonator sensing (detuning detection via magnetron load)
rationale: The bowl you own encodes the settings.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is compelling, but RF tags inside a microwave cavity risk arcing and detuning detection is unreliable.

title: Lawnmower pull-cord timer
new_elements: Pull-cord spring timer (cord length pulled = minutes; retracts as it runs)
rationale: Visible cord length is an intuitive analog of time.
judge_comment: A pull-cord gives an intuitive physical analog of time and is mechanically simple, though its precision is modest and it is a bit gimmicky.

title: Kettle whistle doneness
new_elements: Steam whistle vent with bimetal cutoff (food steam whistles and trips power)
rationale: Everyone knows what a whistling kettle means.
judge_comment: Whistling is a familiar cue, but steam varies widely by food and many foods won't whistle, so doneness detection is unreliable.

title: Door pops open when done
new_elements: Spring-eject door (door swings ajar at end, releasing steam)
rationale: Completion is unmistakable and the next step is pre-done.
judge_comment: An unmistakable completion cue that needs no learning, though it does nothing to simplify setting the cook and raises safety concerns about hot steam.

title: Bimetal exhaust-air timer
new_elements: Bimetal strip in exhaust (cuts power when exhaust air reaches humid-hot threshold)
rationale: Self-stopping with zero electronics and zero settings.
judge_comment: Wildly novel zero-electronics auto-stop that removes settings, but exhaust humidity is unreliable and could over- or under-heat many foods, and it lacks a way to start or adjust.

title: Voice command module
new_elements: Offline voice chip (responds to 'heat', 'stop', 'more'); Keyword spotting ASR (no cloud needed)
rationale: Speaking is the interface nobody has to learn.
judge_comment: Offline keyword-spotting chips are readily available and speaking needs no learning, but voice-controlled microwaves already exist and ambiguity of 'more' remains.

title: Button-on-the-mug remote
new_elements: Microwave-safe mug with start button (press mug button after placing; oven runs mug preset)
rationale: The control lives on the object being heated.
judge_comment: Control on the object is intuitive, but a wireless button in a microwave-safe mug is technically awkward and only serves mug heating.

title: Linear pictogram slider
new_elements: Horizontal slider with icons (left=warm drink, right=cook frozen)
rationale: Less-to-more on a line is more intuitive than rotation.
judge_comment: Simple and easy to build, but it's an incremental interface swap with limited range of foods, not radical.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (pushing drawer shut starts default cycle)
rationale: Load like a drawer, no door, no plate to align.
judge_comment: Drawer with close-to-start default is easy to use, but the choke/sealing design is challenging and a single default cycle limits versatility.

title: Toaster-style lever
new_elements: Top-load lid with push-down lever (press lever to start, pops up when done)
rationale: Borrows the most universally known kitchen gesture.
judge_comment: A toaster-like lever is instantly understood and removes the learning curve, though it still needs some way to set the time and top-loading is less convenient.

title: Wind-up crank timer
new_elements: Visible crank handle (wind it; heating runs while it unwinds)
rationale: Effort-in equals time-out; tangible and obvious.
judge_comment: Wind-up timers are already used in old microwaves, and the crank makes operation obvious and mechanically simple, so it is feasible but not very novel.

title: Thermal-image door glass
new_elements: Door display showing thermal map (food glows red when hot throughout); Low-res thermal array (8x8 to 32x32 sensor)
rationale: See hotness directly instead of guessing from time.
judge_comment: It gives clear feedback on how hot the food is, but it adds a display and may actually add complexity for the user, and thermal sensing through a metal-mesh door is hard.

title: Conveyor tray ejects food
new_elements: Belt tray (carries food in, out when done)
rationale: Food arriving at the front is the clearest 'done' signal.
judge_comment: The idea is radical and the done signal is clear, but a belt inside a microwave cavity is hard to build and clean, and it doesn't address how to start or set cooking.

title: Thermochromic door glass
new_elements: Thermochromic window film (window tints as cavity warms)
rationale: Passive, zero-power status cue needing no explanation.
judge_comment: A passive cue is cheap and simple, but it only shows cavity temperature rather than food state, so it does little to simplify operation.

title: Gentle/Fast rocker switch
new_elements: Two-position rocker (gentle (defrost/soften) or fast)
rationale: Two words replace five numbers.
judge_comment: Simple two-word choice reduces complexity, but it hides the time setting and the substitution is modest.

title: Two big buttons: 1 min, 3 min
new_elements: Red 1-min and blue 3-min buttons (colour coded, tactile)
rationale: Covers 90% of uses with no dial to interpret.
judge_comment: Very easy to use and clearly specified, but similar to existing quick-start buttons and limited in flexibility.

title: Plunger timer
new_elements: Push-down plunger (depth = time; rises as it runs, clicks at top)
rationale: Depth is a direct, visible analog of remaining time.
judge_comment: Intuitive physical analog of time that needs no instruction, though the mechanical plunger mechanism is complex and wear-prone.

title: Target-temperature dial only
new_elements: Thermostat knob (warm/hot/boiling) (IR sensor stops at target)
rationale: Choose how hot you want it, like a radiator.
judge_comment: Outcome-based control matches the user's mental model, but IR sensing of food temperature through containers is imperfect.

title: Glowing turntable rim
new_elements: Electroluminescent rim on floor (lights the dish from below, no bulb)
rationale: No bulb to replace; visibility is maintenance-free.
judge_comment: Addresses bulb maintenance, not operation simplicity, and electroluminescence inside a microwave is questionable.

title: Handle-pull actuates latch
new_elements: Lever handle latch (pulling the handle itself releases the door)
rationale: One affordance (a handle) instead of a handle plus a hidden button.
judge_comment: Sensible and easy to build, but many microwaves already work this way, and it is not radical or a big improvement for a no-learning-curve interface.

title: Fully transparent cavity
new_elements: Transparent conductive-film door (clear ITO/mesh film blocks RF without perforations); Transparent RF shielding film (indium-tin-oxide or fine metal mesh)
rationale: Kitchen light does the job; nothing to switch or replace.
judge_comment: Transparent RF shielding is a concrete substitution, but it has little to do with simple operation, since microwaves already have see-through mesh doors.

title: Tactile embossed pictograms
new_elements: Embossed icon fascia (replaces printed text labels with raised shapes)
rationale: Language-free, readable by touch, legible in dim light.
judge_comment: Embossed pictograms are cheap, language-free and tactile, which helps ease of use a little, but the idea is incremental.

title: Mug-only micro-microwave
new_elements: Mug-shaped cavity with insertion switch (inserting a mug starts a fixed 60 s); Single-purpose appliance (one job, zero choices)
rationale: Form dictates use; there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug microwave that starts when a mug is inserted removes all choices, which is radical and fits the need, though it limits what the appliance can do.

title: Light-curtain fill sensor
new_elements: IR light-curtain in cavity (estimates food volume, sets time)
rationale: Bigger load, longer cycle, decided automatically.
judge_comment: Setting time automatically from a volume estimate removes a decision, but IR volume sensing is unreliable and ignores food type.

title: Flashing lamp as end signal
new_elements: Blinking interior LED (flashes until door opened)
rationale: Reuses the lamp; silent, persistent, obvious.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive end signal, but it is a minor, incremental tweak that does not address operation and is hardly radical.

title: Capacitive dial drawn on glass
new_elements: Touch ring on door glass (trace a circle to add time, like a volume ring)
rationale: No protruding parts; gesture mirrors the familiar knob.
judge_comment: A familiar ring gesture with no protruding parts, but a touch ring on door glass is a bit hard to discover and needs heat-tolerant sensing.

title: Wave-to-start proximity sensor
new_elements: Hand-wave IR sensor (wave once to start, wave again to stop)
rationale: Touch-free, single gesture, works with messy hands.
judge_comment: Wave to start is simple, but it gives no way to set time and can trigger accidentally, so it only covers part of the job.

title: Tilt-to-time handle
new_elements: Rocking door handle with tilt sensor (tilt up to add time, down to subtract)
rationale: The handle you already grip becomes the only control.
judge_comment: An unusual handle-based control, but tilting to add or subtract time is not obvious and so needs learning, which defeats the goal.

title: Egg-timer sand glass front
new_elements: Flip hourglass start switch (flipping a visible sand glass closes a reed switch for its duration)
rationale: The oldest timer in the world needs no instructions.
judge_comment: A visible hourglass that flips to start and shows the time left is radical and self-explanatory, though fixed durations and the mechanics limit it.

title: Weight-sets-time turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable base (Strain gauge under roller ring weighs the dish and sets duration automatically); Mass-proportional heating rule (Seconds = k × grams; one lookup, no user input)
rationale: User just puts food in and closes the door—time is derived from weight, nothing to set.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is ideal for the need, though weight is a poor proxy for heating time across foods and the load cell must cope with the heat and RF environment.

title: Single +30 s tap button
new_elements: One big add-30s button (Each press adds 30 s and starts immediately; no other control exists)
rationale: One button, one rule: tap more for longer—zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Very simple and already common on commercial units, so it is easy to build but not radical.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retractable pull-cord timer (Pull the cord out; it retracts over minutes like a tape measure, length = time); Escapement-governed spring retraction (Clockwork escapement meters cord return speed)
rationale: Remaining time is a visible physical length—intuitive even for children and elderly.
judge_comment: A visible, tactile time metaphor that anyone can read, and a clockwork escapement is plausible, though a long cord is bulky and imprecise.

title: Absorber mats replace power knob
new_elements: Colour-coded RF absorber mats (Silicone mats loaded with carbon/ferrite soak up a fixed share of RF; blue mat = defrost); Passive dielectric dummy-load power sharing (Lossy mat absorbs part of the field so food sees lower effective power)
rationale: Power level becomes a physical object you place under the food—no knob to decode.
judge_comment: A wild substitution of a physical object for a power knob, but absorber mats waste energy, heat unevenly and risk arcing and safety problems.

title: Picture dial
new_elements: Food-icon single dial (One knob with detents showing a mug, plate, frozen block, butter stick; each detent encodes time+power cams)
rationale: Point the knob at the picture of what you are heating—no numbers, no two-knob coordination.
judge_comment: A single icon dial with cam-encoded time and power is intuitive and easy to build, though it is limited to preset foods and has been done in similar forms.

title: Steam-stop sensor
new_elements: Vent humidity sensor (Cheap capacitive RH sensor in exhaust path stops cooking when steam burst detected)
rationale: Food tells the oven when it is hot—user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Steam-triggered stop is a known sensor-cook concept and already exists in some microwaves; it removes settings, though it's unreliable for dry foods and needs a start-up learning period.

title: IR done-temperature cutoff
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Non-contact sensor stops heating at a fixed 70 °C surface target)
rationale: Every dish stops at eating temperature automatically—one outcome, no settings.
judge_comment: A fixed-temperature IR cutoff gives a true one-button outcome, but IR only reads the surface and a single target doesn't suit all foods.

title: Pull-handle magnetic door
new_elements: Magnetic-catch pull handle door (No button or latch lever; magnets hold door, hall sensors feed interlocks)
rationale: Open it like a fridge—the most universally understood door gesture.
judge_comment: A magnetic pull-handle door is highly feasible and intuitive, but it only changes the door and leaves the control interface alone.

title: Drawer microwave
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (Food sits in a sliding drawer; rails carry choke seal and interlocks)
rationale: Pull, place, push—no swinging door or hidden release button to find.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist already, so the gesture is clear, but the choke seal and rail engineering are difficult and it doesn't simplify controls.

title: Roll-top shutter door
new_elements: Conductive tambour shutter (Interlinked metal slats roll up into the top like a bread bin)
rationale: Bread-bin gesture everyone knows; nothing swings into the kitchen.
judge_comment: A roll-top metal shutter door is quirky and memorable, but microwave sealing on the slat gaps and the cleaning problems make it hard to build.

title: Voice 'ready' chip
new_elements: Speech-chip announcer (Greeting-card class voice chip says 'Your food is ready')
rationale: A spoken sentence needs no interpretation, unlike codes of beeps.
judge_comment: A cheap voice chip replacing the beep removes ambiguity about when food is done, but it is an obvious and not very radical substitution.

title: Toaster-style auto-eject door
new_elements: Spring auto-pop door (Timer cam releases the latch at zero so the door springs ajar)
rationale: Done = door open; the signal and the next action are the same thing.
judge_comment: A toaster-style spring door that pops open at zero merges the done signal with the next action, which is intuitive and mechanically simple, though it can cause spills.

title: Filament-winding LED lamp
new_elements: LED strip on 3 V filament winding (Sealed LED bar powered from the transformer's filament tap, lifetime of the oven)
rationale: Light that never burns out means the user never faces a dark, confusing cavity.
judge_comment: A long-life LED on the filament tap is a clever substitution, but it only weakly serves simple operation, and the transformer tap may not suit LEDs.

title: Transparent-conductor glass door
new_elements: ITO-coated clear glass door (Transparent conductive oxide film shields RF without mesh; kitchen light enters); Transparent conductive thin-film shielding (Indium-tin-oxide layer below skin depth for 2.45 GHz)
rationale: You simply see the food like through a window—no mesh squinting, no lamp to fail.
judge_comment: ITO glass would give a clear view of the food, but it is hard to make RF-tight at 2.45 GHz with seams and chokes, and it would be costly and fragile.

title: EL-panel cavity wall
new_elements: Electroluminescent back-wall panel (Thin EL sheet behind microwave-transparent ceramic glows uniformly)
rationale: Shadow-free glow makes food state obvious at a glance.
judge_comment: An EL panel behind a ceramic wall would give shadow-free light, but EL panels are exposed to microwaves, heat, and steam, and the benefit to simple operation is modest.

title: Mode stirrer, flat floor
new_elements: Fan-driven waveguide mode stirrer (Metal paddle in the waveguide exit scrambles the field; cavity floor is a flat ceramic plate)
rationale: No tray to seat correctly or knock off—just put the plate anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers with flat floors already exist in commercial microwaves, so it is feasible but not radical, and it helps operation only modestly.

title: Rotating under-floor antenna
new_elements: Sub-floor rotating feed antenna (Slow-turning antenna under a ceramic floor sweeps the field pattern)
rationale: Oversize dishes don't jam—the user never thinks about fit.
judge_comment: Under-floor rotating antennas already exist in some models, and they remove the fit concern, but they add only a small benefit to operating simplicity.

title: Two-way cook/gentle rocker
new_elements: Cook / Gentle rocker switch (Binary switch: full duty or 30 % duty for defrost and melting)
rationale: Two words replace five abstract power levels.
judge_comment: A two-position switch is simple and easy to understand, and it cuts the complexity of power levels, though the idea is not very radical.

title: Press-the-dial gentle mode
new_elements: Push-to-toggle timer dial (Single clockwork dial; pushing it in engages a cam for low-power cycling)
rationale: One control object on the whole front panel.
judge_comment: A single dial with a push action reduces the number of controls, but the push-to-toggle behavior is hidden and may not be obvious to users.

title: Hold-to-heat touch pad
new_elements: Dead-man heating pad (Magnetron runs only while a palm rests on a large pad; lift hand to stop)
rationale: Direct cause-and-effect like a tap—no concept of a timer at all.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is radical and has intuitive cause and effect, but it is tiring to use, and the safety and interlock design is nontrivial.

title: NFC-tagged dishware
new_elements: Dish tag reader (NFC coil in the floor reads a tag in the bowl or mug that encodes time and power)
rationale: The soup bowl knows how to heat soup—the user only closes the door.
judge_comment: Tagged dishware removes all input, though it requires special dishes and an NFC reader that works inside a microwave cavity.

title: Package barcode reader
new_elements: Door-frame barcode scanner (Reads the ready-meal barcode on insertion and applies the printed instructions)
rationale: Packaged food self-programs the oven; no reading tiny instructions.
judge_comment: Barcode-driven programming is plausible and removes manual entry, but it only works for packaged food with a database behind it.

title: Mug-only mini microwave
new_elements: Single-mug cavity with one button (Cylindrical cavity for one cup; one button heats to drinking temperature)
rationale: A device that does one thing has nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-button mug unit is simple but narrow in scope, and it is more of a subtraction than a substitution.

title: Spoken-minutes control
new_elements: Offline keyword voice module (Recognises 'one minute' to 'ten minutes' and 'defrost' locally)
rationale: Say what you want in plain words—hands free, no panel to study.
judge_comment: Offline voice recognition is feasible and intuitive, but voice-controlled appliances are already common, and it is noisy and awkward for some users.

title: Reed-switch interlocks
new_elements: Magnet-and-reed door sensing (Reed switches replace mechanical microswitches; door closes with light touch)
rationale: No slamming or re-seating the door to satisfy stiff latches—it 'just works'.
judge_comment: Reed switches are a modest component swap with only indirect benefit to learning, and safety interlocks need redundancy.

title: Elbow push panel
new_elements: Full-height elbow push plate (Whole side of fascia is the release paddle, operable with elbow or hip)
rationale: Nothing small to locate—push anywhere with anything.
judge_comment: Easy door-release for hands-full use, but it addresses only opening, not the operation of settings, so it only partly serves the need.

title: Embossed tactile fascia
new_elements: Raised-icon tactile fascia (Moulded raised symbols and detent clicks convey settings by touch)
rationale: Settings are readable by fingertips alone—no glasses, no manual.
judge_comment: Tactile icons and detents make settings intuitive and accessible and are easy to mold, though not very radical.

title: Gravity weight timer
new_elements: Descending-weight timer (Lift a visible weight on a track; it sinks over minutes and trips the switch at the bottom)
rationale: Time left is literally how high the weight is—visible from across the room.
judge_comment: A mechanical weight timer needs no learning, is visible and wildly different, but is hard to make accurate and safe in a microwave.

title: Thermochromic window
new_elements: Thermochromic door glass (Inner pane tints red as cavity air passes 60 °C)
rationale: Red means hot—colour feedback replaces guessing a time.
judge_comment: Air temperature is a poor proxy for food readiness, thermochromic glass in a microwave door is problematic, and it does not replace a timer.

title: Flashing-lamp ready signal
new_elements: Blink-at-end lamp driver (Timer cam puts the cavity lamp into blink mode until the door opens)
rationale: One component does light and signal; a blinking box is universally 'done'.
judge_comment: A cheap blinking-lamp done signal is intuitive, but it only covers end-of-cycle feedback, not operation overall.

title: Bell-jar lift-top
new_elements: Lift-up metal dome cavity (Food sits on a fixed plinth; a counterbalanced dome lowers to seal)
rationale: Cover the plate like a cloche—no door, no reach-in, no button.
judge_comment: A radical cloche-style dome removes the door, but RF sealing, a counterbalanced mechanism and the still-unaddressed controls make it hard to build and only partly serve simplicity.

title: Silicone floor mat
new_elements: Dishwasher-safe silicone cavity mat (Lies on a flat floor; lifts out with spills)
rationale: Nothing to align, break, or re-seat after cleaning.
judge_comment: A silicone mat is easy to make and clean, but it barely affects operating simplicity, which is the target need.

title: Auto-soak timer cam
new_elements: Taper-end timer cam (Cam profile drops to 40 % duty in the final fifth of any set time for standing/evening)
rationale: Even heating happens inside the one timer knob—the power knob disappears.
judge_comment: A taper cam folds power control into the timer knob, removing a control and giving more even heating, which is a clever mechanical substitution.

title: Colour-change turntable
new_elements: Thermochromic glass tray (Tray rim glows orange when plate underside exceeds 55 °C)
rationale: Feedback is in the tray itself; check doneness without touching food.
judge_comment: Thermochromic feedback is intuitive, but it helps with checking doneness rather than operating the oven, and a glowing tray rim is hard to realize.

title: Toaster lever microwave
new_elements: Push-down lever with depth stops (Press the lever to a notch (1–5 min); springs back up at end with a clack)
rationale: Borrows the toaster's zero-learning gesture everyone already owns.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever with depth stops uses a familiar gesture and removes the learning curve, and it is mechanically plausible.

title: Wave-to-open door
new_elements: IR proximity door opener (Spring door releases when a hand hovers in front of the handle zone)
rationale: Hands full of plates? The door opens before you touch anything.
judge_comment: Hands-free door opening is convenient but doesn't reduce the learning curve of operating the microwave, and it adds parts rather than substituting simpler ones.

title: Detachable timer puck
new_elements: Magnetic clip-off countdown puck (The timer dial lifts off and keeps counting, chiming in your pocket; oven stops via its own cam)
rationale: Set it like an egg timer, carry it like an egg timer—a mental model already learned.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer mental model with a portable puck is intuitive, though wireless or magnetic stop coordination and safety interlocks add complexity.

title: Glow-in-dark big-numeral dial
new_elements: Photoluminescent oversize dial scale (Three marks only (1, 3, 5 min) in 25 mm luminous numerals)
rationale: Fewer, bigger choices are read instantly in any light.
judge_comment: A simple, cheap, readable dial that reduces choices, but it is an incremental change, not a radical one.

title: Steam whistle done-signal
new_elements: Kettle-style vent whistle (Exhaust port carries a reed whistle that sounds when steam flow rises)
rationale: Passive, battery-free 'kettle logic': it whistles when the food is steaming hot.
judge_comment: A passive whistle signal is intuitive and battery-free, but steam from microwaved food is inconsistent and covered dishes would muffle it.

title: Solid-state RF self-stopping
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing (Transistor amplifier monitors return loss; impedance shift when food warms triggers stop); Solid-state RF module (Replaces magnetron, transformer, capacitor and diode)
rationale: The oven senses the food through the RF itself and stops—no timer to set.
judge_comment: Auto-stop sensing through reflected RF would remove the need to set anything, which is radical and highly relevant, but reliably detecting doneness across foods is hard and GaN modules are costly.

title: Airflow-spun turntable
new_elements: Pinwheel turntable driven by cooling air (Fan exhaust spins a vaned hub under the tray; no second motor)
rationale: Fewer parts to fail means fewer confusing failure states for the user.
judge_comment: A clever part substitution, but it does almost nothing for ease of operation, and a cooling fan's airflow is questionable for driving a turntable reliably.

title: Portion-count dial
new_elements: '1 plate / 2 plates / frozen' dial (Three detents encode combined time and duty cams)
rationale: Users think in portions, not minutes and watts.
judge_comment: A portion-based dial with cam-encoded presets is simple, cheap and intuitive, though not very radical.

title: Foot-pedal door
new_elements: Bin-style foot pedal release (Pedal under the counter edge pops the door)
rationale: Kitchen-bin gesture needs no instruction and frees both hands.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is intuitive and hands-free, but it is a minor part of operation and awkward for a countertop unit.

title: Door-opens-at-end plus shelf light
new_elements: Under-door amber floor light (At cycle end an amber LED lights the countertop in front of the oven)
rationale: A silent, room-visible cue that works for deaf users and noisy kitchens.
judge_comment: A simple, feasible visual cue that helps accessibility, but it only marginally reduces the learning curve.

title: Weight+IR closed loop
new_elements: Weight-and-temperature controller (Load cell sets initial power, IR thermopile ends the cycle)
rationale: Both knobs vanish; the front panel is just a door.
judge_comment: Removing all controls via weight and IR sensing directly eliminates the learning curve, though IR sensing accuracy through steam and containers is challenging.

title: Cavity-is-the-cup dock
new_elements: Insulated docking cup with RF seal (Dedicated lidded cup slides into a tight cylinder; cup rim forms the choke)
rationale: Dock the cup like a phone—there is nothing else to understand.
judge_comment: Docking a dedicated cup is intuitive, but a cylinder-sized cavity with a reliable RF choke limits what can be cooked and is hard to build.

title: Hourglass-visible clockwork
new_elements: Exposed clockwork timer with sweep flag (Transparent fascia shows a big red flag sweeping back to zero)
rationale: Progress is visible motion, not a number to decode.
judge_comment: A visible mechanical sweep flag makes progress easy to read and is easy to build, though it only addresses the timer display and not the rest of operation.

title: Smart lid replaces power knob
new_elements: Vented defrost dome (Perforated metal-mesh dome placed over frozen food shades it to ~30 % power); Partial-aperture field attenuation (Mesh dome with sub-wavelength holes passes a controlled fraction of RF)
rationale: Defrosting means 'put the dome on'—a physical, obvious act.
judge_comment: A mesh dome that physically sets defrost power is a clever substitute for a power knob, but attenuation would be uneven and the mesh could arc.

title: Open-door-to-stop only
new_elements: Door-closed-equals-on control (Closing the door starts full power; opening stops it; a 5-min safety cam is the only timer)
rationale: The door is the only control—closed means cooking.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start cooking removes nearly all controls, but running at full power with only a fixed cutoff risks overcooking and unsafe operation.

title: Seatless flat ceramic floor
new_elements: Fixed glass-ceramic floor with rotating field (Flat sealed floor; a slow mode stirrer above the cavity evens heating)
rationale: Wipe-flat interior with no loose parts removes a whole class of user mistakes.
judge_comment: A flat fixed floor with a stirrer above is feasible and common in practice, but it does little to remove the learning curve.

title: Aroma-vent done cue
new_elements: End-of-cycle aroma purge flap (Fan reverses for 5 s at the end, pushing food scent into the room)
rationale: You smell dinner being ready—the most primal, learning-free signal there is.
judge_comment: A scent-based done cue is an inventive replacement for the beep, but it only signals completion and does nothing to simplify setting up the cook, and it is unreliable for low-odor foods and may not count as a true substitution of a part.

title: Food-picture dial replaces timer + power knobs
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (mug / plate / frozen / butter) (One cam-driven rotary selector where each pictogram position sets a fixed time and duty cycle simultaneously.)
rationale: Two abstract knobs become one knob whose positions are pictures of what you are heating, so there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single pictogram dial with fixed time and duty cycle is simple and intuitive, though presets are coarse and the idea is not very radical.

title: Weighing turntable sets the time
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable support (Roller ring sits on a calibrated spring; food mass displaces a cam that pre-winds the timer proportionally.); Mass-to-time mechanical cam coupling (Vertical deflection of a spring platform translated into cam-shaft rotation of the clockwork timer.)
rationale: The user never sets a time; putting the plate in is the setting.
judge_comment: Weighing the food to set the time removes the setting step entirely, but mass is a poor proxy for heating time and a mechanical cam coupling would be hard to calibrate.

title: One big button, one minute per press
new_elements: Single ratchet push button (+1 min per press) (Each press advances the clockwork cam one minute; countdown and bell unchanged.)
rationale: Press once for a mug, three times for a plate; counting presses is a zero-training interface.
judge_comment: A one-button +1 minute ratchet is easy to build and use, but it is close to existing microwave quick-start buttons.

title: Toaster lever instead of timer, start and bell
new_elements: Spring-loaded toaster-style cook lever (Push lever down to start; a dashpot releases it at the end and the pop-up is the 'done' signal.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster works; the same gesture now runs the microwave.
judge_comment: A toaster lever draws on a familiar mental model and replaces the start control and bell, but it gives no way to set the time unless the dashpot duration is adjustable.

title: Door pops open when done (door replaces bell)
new_elements: Timer-released spring door latch (At zero the timer cam trips the latch lever; the door springs ajar, cutting power and signalling completion.)
rationale: An open door is an unmistakable, silent and intuitive 'ready' cue requiring no interpretation.
judge_comment: The door springing open at the end is an intuitive done signal that replaces the bell, though it could startle users and spill or cool the food.

title: Closing the door is the start button
new_elements: Door-wound spring timer (Swinging the door shut winds a fixed 60-second escapement; the microwave runs when the door closes and stops when it unwinds.)
rationale: There are zero controls; close the door to heat, open it to stop.
judge_comment: Zero-control, door-wound timer is radical and needs no learning, but a fixed 60 seconds is inflexible and the door must be reopened to repeat.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Pull-cord clockwork timer with length markings (Pulling a cord out winds the spring; cord length (short = mug, long = dinner) is the time; it retracts as it counts down.)
rationale: Remaining time is read by cord length at a glance and set by a single intuitive pull.
judge_comment: A pull-cord clockwork timer is intuitive, with a visible countdown, and is mechanically simple and plausible, though cord length to time mapping needs some learning.

title: Set a temperature, not a time
new_elements: Cold-to-hot thermopile dial (An IR thermopile aimed at the food trips a relay when the dialled surface temperature is reached.); Non-contact infrared thermopile sensing (Thermopile measures food surface radiance through a cavity aperture.)
rationale: People know how hot they want food, not how many minutes it takes, so the dial speaks their language.
judge_comment: A temperature dial matches the user's mental model, but IR surface sensing is inaccurate through the cavity and with covered or uneven food.

title: Steam-triggered auto stop (no timer at all)
new_elements: Bimetal steam sensor in cavity vent (Existing snap-disc technology placed in the exhaust path opens the circuit when hot steam appears.)
rationale: Press start and walk away; food steaming is the universal sign of 'hot' and the oven reads it for you.
judge_comment: Press start and walk away is ideal simplicity, though steam detection is unreliable for many foods and risks overheating or underheating.

title: Three preset buttons replace both knobs
new_elements: Mug / Plate / Defrost mechanical preset buttons (Three push-buttons each engage a fixed cam profile (time + duty cycle) on a common clockwork.)
rationale: Three labelled buttons cover 95 % of uses and remove all numeric decisions.
judge_comment: Three labelled preset buttons are very easy and feasible, but are an incremental and common approach rather than radical.

title: Two-position Cook/Thaw rocker replaces 5-step power knob
new_elements: Cook / Thaw rocker switch (Simple rocker selects 100 % or 30 % duty cycle cam; no intermediate levels.)
rationale: Five power levels nobody understands become a binary choice in plain words.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible binary Cook/Thaw choice that cuts complexity, but it's an incremental simplification rather than radical.

title: Passive attenuator lid replaces power knob
new_elements: Perforated metal 'defrost dome' accessory (A sub-wavelength-perforated dome placed over food reflects part of the field, giving gentle heating with the magnetron at full power.)
rationale: Low power becomes a physical object you place over the food instead of a setting you must remember.
judge_comment: Creative passive attenuator concept, but a metal dome in a microwave risks arcing and unpredictable heating, and it adds an accessory to remember.

title: Solid-state RF source with a light-dimmer power knob
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF power amplifier (Transistor amplifier at 2.45 GHz with continuously variable output, fed from low-voltage SMPS.); Continuous power dimmer knob (A single potentiometer sets RF output 0-100 % like a lamp dimmer.)
rationale: 'More or less heat' on one smooth knob is as intuitive as a dimmer and removes the HV safety mystery.
judge_comment: A solid-state RF source with a dimmer knob gives intuitive continuous control and is real technology, though costly for consumer ovens today.

title: Inverter supply replaces transformer, capacitor and diode
new_elements: High-frequency inverter power supply (Switch-mode converter driving a small ferrite transformer; lighter, no lethal charge storage, true variable power.)
rationale: Enables a single intuitive continuous power control and a lighter oven anyone can lift and place.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies are already in the market and enable simpler control, but the user-facing simplicity benefit is indirect.

title: Fridge-style magnetic door replaces push-button latch
new_elements: Magnetic gasket door with simple handle (Flexible magnetic strip holds the door; pull to open, push to close; reed switches sense closure.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to open a fridge; no hidden button to find.
judge_comment: A familiar fridge-style door is intuitive, but microwave RF sealing needs choke design and it addresses only a minor part of operation.

title: Drawer replaces hinged door
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Food sits on a tray that slides out like a kitchen drawer; the drawer front carries the choke seal.)
rationale: No reaching into a hot box; place food on the open tray and push it in, like closing a drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar metaphor that needs no learning, and microwave drawers already exist, though the choke seal on a moving drawer front is a real engineering challenge.

title: Lift-off dome replaces door entirely
new_elements: Cake-dome lid on a pedestal base (A metal-meshed transparent dome with choke rim lifts straight off a base containing magnetron and tray.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is the most primitive kitchen gesture; nothing to latch, press or align.
judge_comment: Lifting a dome is very intuitive and radical, but sealing microwave leakage with no latch or interlock is a safety problem.

title: Roller-shutter door
new_elements: Tambour metal roller shutter with choke slats (Conductive overlapping slats roll up into the top of the cabinet; a pull tab opens it.)
rationale: No swinging door to clear, so placement and use are obvious even in tight kitchens.
judge_comment: A roller shutter is novel and saves space, but keeping the slats RF-tight and clean is hard, and it does little to make operation simpler.

title: Foot pedal opens the door
new_elements: Pedal-operated latch (bin-style) (A cable from a floor pedal lifts the door hooks, as on a pedal bin.)
rationale: Hands full of plate? Step on the pedal; the bin metaphor needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A pedal-bin mechanism is simple and familiar and clearly feasible, but it only helps with opening the door and is a niche convenience.

title: Transparent conductive door panel replaces mesh
new_elements: Indium-tin-oxide / silver-nanowire conductive glass (Optically clear coating with sheet resistance low enough to reflect 2.45 GHz.)
rationale: A clear window shows food status instantly, removing the need to interpret anything else.
judge_comment: Conductive glass is plausible in principle, but it only improves visibility and barely affects operational simplicity.

title: Daylight light-pipe replaces the lamp
new_elements: Acrylic light guide from top panel into cavity (Room light is piped through a microwave-opaque waveguide-below-cutoff tube into the cavity; no bulb, no wiring.)
rationale: Nothing to burn out or replace; the cavity is simply always lit like the room.
judge_comment: Clever bulb-free lighting, but a room-light pipe gives dim, unreliable interior light and barely touches operation simplicity.

title: Photoluminescent cavity coating replaces lamp
new_elements: Strontium-aluminate glow enamel (Cavity enamel loaded with long-persistence phosphor charged by ambient light whenever the door is open.)
rationale: A softly glowing interior shows the food with zero parts to fail or settings to toggle.
judge_comment: Phosphor glow is novel but would be too dim to see food well, and the enamel would face heat and microwave exposure; it has little effect on the learning curve.

title: LED strip behind the fascia replaces incandescent
new_elements: Mains-driven LED module with 20-year life (Capacitive-dropper LED array behind a mica window; also blinks at end of cycle.)
rationale: Light that never needs replacing means the user never meets a maintenance task.
judge_comment: A long-life LED is feasible and concrete but incremental, and it has little to do with ease of operation.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable, ring and motor
new_elements: Fan-driven metal mode stirrer behind ceiling mica (Cooling-fan airflow spins a reflective paddle that scrambles standing waves; flat fixed floor.)
rationale: No tray to centre, re-seat or trip over; any dish on the flat floor just works.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are proven technology, and removing the turntable eliminates a setup step so any dish just works.

title: Rotating antenna replaces turntable
new_elements: Motor-swept feed antenna under the floor (The waveguide terminates in a rotating slot antenna beneath a ceramic floor, sweeping the field across static food.)
rationale: Square dishes fit, nothing rotates in view, and wiping the floor is the only cleaning step.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas exist in commercial ovens, and the design removes the tray and eases cleaning, which helps simplicity.

title: Non-rotating ceramic floor with multi-mode cavity shape
new_elements: Asymmetric faceted cavity with fixed glazed floor (Non-parallel walls break up standing waves so a turntable is unnecessary.)
rationale: Removing the turntable removes a whole category of user errors and misplaced parts.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable removes a part, but users rarely struggle with it, and uneven heating from a fixed floor is a real risk.

title: Reed-switch interlock replaces three microswitches
new_elements: Dual reed switches with door magnet (Hermetic reed contacts actuated by a magnet in the door; no mechanical plungers to misalign.)
rationale: The door needs no precise slam to register as closed, so the oven never mysteriously refuses to start.
judge_comment: Reed switches are plausible and tolerant of door misalignment, but users don't see the change and it's an incremental swap.

title: Door itself is the mains switch
new_elements: Hinge-cam master switch (A cam on the hinge pin directly opens/closes the mains contactor; closing the door enables, opening kills power.)
rationale: Door open equals off, door shut equals ready, a rule anyone grasps in a second.
judge_comment: Door-as-mains-switch is an intuitive rule, but mains switching through a hinge cam is a safety problem and microwave interlocks already work this way.

title: Mechanical flag replaces the bell
new_elements: Mailbox-style pop-up 'DONE' flag (Timer cam releases a spring flag on top of the cabinet, visible across the room.)
rationale: A persistent visual flag can't be missed or forgotten, unlike a one-shot ding.
judge_comment: The pop-up flag is a simple, visible cue that needs no learning, but it must be reset by hand and doesn't help with operating the oven.

title: Steam whistle replaces bell
new_elements: Kettle-style whistle in the vent louvre (Hot exhaust air passing a reed whistle sounds continuously while food is hot, not only at zero.)
rationale: Borrowing the kettle's whistle gives a 'hot and ready' cue everyone already understands.
judge_comment: A kettle whistle is a familiar cue, but microwave exhaust is not reliably tied to food temperature and the cue would be noisy and unreliable.

title: Aroma pellet signals 'done' by smell
new_elements: Timer-released scent capsule in exhaust (At zero a tiny heated wax pellet releases a vanilla scent into the vent stream.)
rationale: Smell is noticed without attention or hearing, giving effortless feedback.
judge_comment: Wild and original, but scent feedback does not simplify operation and is a poor substitute for existing signals, and the smell may be unwanted or mix with food odors.

title: Detachable egg-timer knob you carry away
new_elements: Magnetic pull-off clockwork timer puck (The timer knob is a self-contained wind-up kitchen timer; a second, slave cam in the oven mirrors its setting.)
rationale: The familiar wind-up egg timer is the control, so the user already knows how it works and can take it to the sofa.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer interface needs no learning and is portable, though syncing the slave cam adds mechanical complexity.

title: Pneumatic dashpot timer replaces clockwork
new_elements: Air-bleed dashpot delay (door-closer principle) (A piston with adjustable air bleed returns to zero at a set rate; far fewer parts than a geared motor timer.)
rationale: Same turn-and-release gesture but silent, cheaper and independent of mains frequency.
judge_comment: A plausible simpler, cheaper timer mechanism, but the user-facing operation is unchanged, so it gives little gain for the need.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand timer with optical cut-off (User flips a sand glass on the fascia; when sand clears a photo-interrupter the circuit opens.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible as falling sand, the oldest and most intuitive timer humans know.
judge_comment: An intuitive visible timer, but flipping and fixed durations are imprecise and the optical cut-off is a bit gimmicky.

title: Quartz countdown knob replaces cam timer
new_elements: Rotary encoder with large 2-digit countdown (One knob, one big display; precise to the second with no menus.)
rationale: Keeps the one-knob simplicity while fixing the vagueness of short mechanical settings.
judge_comment: A one-knob digital countdown is simple and highly feasible, but it is the most conventional idea and not radical.

title: Linear slider with cup/plate icons replaces timer knob
new_elements: Large horizontal slide-fader timer (A rack-and-pinion fader drives the clockwork; icons along the track instead of minutes.)
rationale: A slider shows 'how much' spatially, easier for children and elderly than reading a dial.
judge_comment: A spatial slider is intuitive and cheap, but it is an incremental swap of a dial rather than a radical idea.

title: Dish with a mechanical key sets the oven
new_elements: Keyed container set + floor follower (Each supplied bowl/mug has a notched base ring; a follower pin in the floor reads the notch and sets time and power.)
rationale: Choosing the right bowl is choosing the right programme; no panel interaction at all.
judge_comment: Keyed bowls that set the programme remove the panel entirely and are highly novel, though they lock users into proprietary dishes and the floor follower pin complicates the cavity.

title: Single-mug microwave with one button
new_elements: Mug-sized cylindrical cavity with one fixed-cycle button (~1 L cavity tuned for a mug; one button runs a fixed 90 s at full power.); Single-serve hot drink on the desk (Office and student contexts where only mugs are heated.)
rationale: When the product does exactly one thing, its only control is 'go'.
judge_comment: One button and one function means zero learning, which is very feasible but limited in usefulness and not especially novel.

title: Removable dishwasher-safe cavity liner
new_elements: Slide-out glass-ceramic liner tub (A microwave-transparent tub lines the steel cavity and lifts out for washing.)
rationale: Cleaning becomes 'take it out and wash it', no scrubbing technique to learn.
judge_comment: A removable liner makes cleaning simpler but barely addresses operation without a learning curve.

title: Tactile raised-symbol fascia replaces printed text
new_elements: Moulded-in raised pictogram and braille fascia (Icons and detents moulded directly into the thermoplastic panel; no printing, no language.)
rationale: Felt pictograms work for every language, lighting condition and eyesight, with nothing to read.
judge_comment: Moulded tactile pictograms are cheap and inclusive, but they help recognition more than they simplify operation itself.

title: Colour-zone knob scale replaces numbers
new_elements: Green/amber/red arc timer scale (Timer scale shows short/medium/long colour bands instead of minute figures.)
rationale: Users think 'a bit' or 'a lot', and the scale now matches that mental model.
judge_comment: Simple, feasible and matches users' mental model, but colour-coded dials are an incremental, familiar idea rather than a radical one.

title: Thermochromic tray tells you when it's hot
new_elements: Thermochromic-rimmed ceramic tray (Tray rim turns red above 60 °C, giving a visual 'hot/ready' and 'safe to touch' cue through the window.)
rationale: Glance, see red, eat; no timer reading or guessing required.
judge_comment: A thermochromic rim is a clever substitution of a visual cue for reading a timer, but the ceramic tray is heated indirectly and the color change may lag or not reflect food temperature.

title: Door handle doubles as timer twist
new_elements: Rotating door handle with time detents (Pull to open; after closing, twist the same handle to wind time, so one grip does everything.)
rationale: The hand is already on the handle; one continuous gesture replaces hunting for controls.
judge_comment: Combining the handle and timer into one gesture is intuitive and original, though the mechanical complexity and a twist-to-start affordance still need to be worked out.

title: Self-closing gravity door
new_elements: Canted hinges with gravity close and soft damper (Hinge axis tilted so the door falls shut on its own; no latch spring or button.)
rationale: Nobody can leave it open or fail to latch it, eliminating the commonest 'why won't it start' confusion.
judge_comment: A self-closing door removes one failure mode, but the safety interlock must still work, and it doesn't address how to operate the controls.

title: Passive chimney cooling replaces fan
new_elements: Oversized finned heatsink with convective stack (Magnetron bolted to a tall extruded heatsink venting through a top chimney; no motor.)
rationale: A silent oven with fewer moving parts behaves predictably, with no confusing fan run-on.
judge_comment: Passive cooling is a concrete substitution, but a magnetron needs substantial airflow, so it is poorly feasible, and it only weakly serves learning-curve simplicity.

title: Hand-wound spring motor replaces timer motor
new_elements: Escapement-regulated mainspring timer (User's twist of the knob stores the energy; an escapement regulates run-down, no synchronous motor.)
rationale: Identical turn-knob gesture worldwide, independent of 50/60 Hz, so one simple product fits all users.
judge_comment: Wind-up mechanical timer is a real, historically used approach (old microwaves used mechanical timers) and gives a zero-learning knob, though it's more retro than radical.

title: Bimetal thermal-delay timer
new_elements: Self-heating bimetal delay switch with 3 fixed taps (A heater coil warms a bimetal strip; three button-selected heater resistances give 1, 3 or 6 minutes.)
rationale: Three buttons, no dial to read, and the timing element is a part the oven already uses.
judge_comment: Three-button bimetal delay is simple and plausible, but accuracy and ambient temperature drift are issues, and fixed times limit usefulness.

title: Cavity light goes out = done
new_elements: Lamp state signals cooking status (Lamp on while cooking, off at end; the bell is deleted.)
rationale: Lit means busy, dark means ready, a binary visual rule with no sound to miss or interpret.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive cue, but removing the bell lowers feedback and many ovens already light the cavity during cooking.

title: Fixed-dose 'cup' measuring timer
new_elements: Water-cup dosing timer (User fills a small side reservoir with the same water they will heat; a float valve drains it at a fixed rate and trips a switch when empty.)
rationale: More liquid in the cup means more time, a physical proportion the user feels rather than calculates.
judge_comment: Wild and intuitive proportional idea, but a water-driven timer in a microwave is messy, inaccurate for non-liquid foods, and hygiene/safety risky.

title: Magnetic-coupled turntable replaces coupler and roller ring
new_elements: Sealed-floor magnetic drive puck (A magnet rotor under a flat sealed floor spins a magnetically coupled tray; no holes, no ring, no coupler.)
rationale: Drop the tray anywhere and it just spins; no fiddly alignment of ring and spindle.
judge_comment: Removes alignment fuss, but the turntable is a minor part of operation and magnetic coupling in a microwave cavity is challenging.

title: One food-pictogram dial replaces both knobs
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (cup, plate, defrost, popcorn) (One rotary cam that sets both duration and duty-cycle from a fixed lookup of food icons.); Selects a complete cook recipe in one motion (Time and power chosen together.)
rationale: Two abstract scales collapse into one picture-based choice, removing any need to understand minutes or watts.
judge_comment: A picture-based single dial is simple and cheap, though icon-to-recipe mapping is imprecise and the idea is somewhat incremental.

title: Dead-man cook bar
new_elements: Hold-to-cook front bar (Magnetron runs only while the user holds a large bar; release stops it.); Momentary-contact power switching (Simple normally-open high-current switch.)
rationale: No timer to set at all: you watch, you hold, you let go—nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Hold-to-cook needs no timer and is intuitive, but it is tiring for long cooks and has safety and regulatory questions.

title: Single +30 s button
new_elements: One big '30 seconds' button (Each press adds 30 s; cooking starts on first press; cheap MCU or stepper cam.)
rationale: A single affordance with one obvious behaviour replaces reading a dial.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is very easy to learn and already common on real microwaves, so it is low on novelty.

title: Weighing turntable sets time automatically
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Food mass sets cook duration via a fixed J/g curve.); Strain-gauge load cell (Low-cost kitchen-scale sensor.)
rationale: Put food in, close door, done—the machine infers duration so the user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Weighing food to set the time means zero user input, but mass is a poor proxy for the cook needed and the load cell is hard to integrate with a rotating turntable.

title: IR temperature-target knob replaces timer
new_elements: Target-temperature knob with IR thermopile (User picks 'warm/hot/boiling'; magnetron stops when food surface reaches it.); Non-contact IR thermometry (Thermopile behind waveguide-shielded window.)
rationale: Users think in 'how hot', not minutes, so closed-loop heat targets remove guesswork.
judge_comment: Closed-loop temperature targets are intuitive, but IR only reads the surface, and sensing through the cavity is difficult.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor in vent (Stops cooking when steam release spikes; no timer needed for reheating.)
rationale: One 'Go' press and the food tells the oven when it is done.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop genuinely removes timing decisions and exists in some sensor-cook ovens, so it is less radical but highly effective.

title: Three-zone traffic-light timer
new_elements: Colour-zone timer knob (green/amber/red) (Only three coarse stops: warm, heat, cook; no numbers.)
rationale: Removing numeric precision removes the decision burden for elderly users.
judge_comment: Simple and easy to build, but coarse stops limit usefulness and it is an incremental simplification.

title: Toaster-style lever timer
new_elements: Push-down slider lever (Push down to start; lever creeps back up and pops at end like a toaster.); Bimetal/solenoid toaster latch (Decades-proven cheap timing mechanism.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster lever works—zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Toaster lever metaphor is familiar and cheap, though it still needs some way to set duration.

title: Pull-tape timer
new_elements: Retracting tape-measure timer (Pull tape out to the picture you want; it winds back as it cooks and clicks off at zero.)
rationale: Remaining time is a visible length, instantly readable without any dial.
judge_comment: Visible tape length is intuitive and novel, but it is mechanically awkward and the 'picture' wording is unclear.

title: Hourglass-style sand timer with optical trip
new_elements: Flip sand-glass timer module (User flips the glass; optical sensor cuts power when sand finishes.)
rationale: A universally understood timing object replaces a mechanism people fail to read.
judge_comment: Sand-glass is a recognizable metaphor and quirky, but fixed durations and accuracy limit its practicality.

title: Spring escapement timer (no motor)
new_elements: Wind-up escapement timer (Egg-timer clockwork; independent of mains frequency.)
rationale: Twisting an egg timer is already intuitive and it behaves identically in any country.
judge_comment: Wind-up mechanical timers are proven and intuitive, though similar to old mechanical microwave dials, so not very radical.

title: Pneumatic dashpot timer
new_elements: Air-dashpot delay switch (Push plunger; air bleeds out at fixed rate and releases switch.)
rationale: One push-in plunger whose depth is the time is cheaper and plainer than a geared dial.
judge_comment: A push-plunger dashpot is quirky and simple to use, but its timing accuracy varies with temperature and humidity, and push depth is hard to map to time.

title: Potentiometer + 10-cent MCU timer
new_elements: Analog pot knob read by microcontroller (Same knob feel, accurate seconds, buzzer, any mains frequency.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar single knob but makes short times reliable, so the first try works.
judge_comment: A pot read by an MCU is very feasible and keeps a familiar knob, but it is a modest and fairly obvious substitution.

title: Minute-token slot
new_elements: Coin-slot timer with 1-min tokens (Drop tokens; each is one minute, counted by a mechanical pawl.)
rationale: Counting tangible tokens is more concrete than reading a scale.
judge_comment: Tokens make time concrete, but losing tokens and the extra handling add friction, and the pawl mechanism is more complicated than a knob.

title: Twist-count timer
new_elements: Ratchet knob: one full twist = one minute (Each click-twist adds a fixed minute; no scale printed.)
rationale: 'Twist it three times for three minutes' is a rule anyone remembers.
judge_comment: A one-twist-per-minute rule is nearly zero-learning, and a ratchet is cheap, but it handles sub-minute times poorly.

title: Colour-coded containers set the cook
new_elements: Bundled containers with magnetic/ferrite code (Red bowl = 3 min high, blue = 6 min defrost; reed switch in floor reads code.)
rationale: Choosing a bowl replaces choosing settings.
judge_comment: Choosing a coded bowl replaces setting selection and is a novel substitution, but it locks users into bundled containers and covers few food types.

title: Packaging barcode / NFC sets timer
new_elements: Door-mounted NFC/barcode reader (Reads cook instructions from ready-meal packaging.); Low-cost NFC tag reading (13.56 MHz reader IC.)
rationale: The package knows the time; the user only taps and closes the door.
judge_comment: Tapping the package to set the cook is intuitive and NFC readers are cheap, but it needs packaging standards and doesn't cover non-packaged food.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Offline keyword-spotting mic ('Heat two minutes' recognised by a tiny on-device model.)
rationale: Speaking a request requires no interface literacy.
judge_comment: Voice control is intuitive and offline keyword spotting is feasible, but it is already common and not very radical.

title: Foot-pedal cook switch
new_elements: Floor pedal for start/stop (Hands stay free for plates; pedal toggles magnetron.)
rationale: One pedal, one meaning—like a bin lid.
judge_comment: A single pedal is simple, but it doesn't set time or power, so it adds an awkward accessory instead of removing learning.

title: Delete the power knob: fixed soft profile
new_elements: Fixed ramp cam (no user power control) (Always starts low then rises; good enough for 95% of reheats.)
rationale: Fewer controls is the simplest control.
judge_comment: Removing power control is simple, cheap and feasible, but the fixed profile limits versatility and still leaves timing to the user.

title: Two-position rocker: Reheat / Defrost
new_elements: Rocker switch with two icons (Full power or 30% duty, nothing between.)
rationale: Binary choice with pictures is understood at a glance.
judge_comment: Simple pictorial two-way switch is easy to understand, but it is a modest, fairly obvious simplification with limited flexibility.

title: Inverter gentle-to-fast slider
new_elements: Inverter continuous-power magnetron drive (True continuous output rather than on/off cycling.); Linear 'gentle ↔ fast' slider (Unlabelled slider mapped to continuous power.)
rationale: Behaviour becomes a smooth, predictable slider like a tap, not cryptic 'P-levels'.
judge_comment: Inverter drive with a continuous slider is intuitive and plausible, since inverter microwaves exist, though the slider swaps one control for another.

title: Triac phase-control power dimmer
new_elements: Phase-angle dimmer on transformer primary (Light-dimmer circuit sets magnetron anode power.)
rationale: A dimmer-style knob feels exactly like a household light dimmer users already know.
judge_comment: The dimmer analogy is familiar, but phase control on a magnetron transformer primary is technically problematic because of the high-voltage and rectifier circuit.

title: Power set by shelf height
new_elements: Two-level rack with position switch (Upper rack = gentle (defrost), floor = full power.)
rationale: Where you put the plate is the setting—no knob to interpret.
judge_comment: Shelf position setting power is a quirky, wild idea that removes the knob, but it is awkward in practice, as it ties power to height and reduces cooking-geometry flexibility.

title: Auto-power from weight
new_elements: Weight-derived duty-cycle selector (Light items get low power automatically to avoid splatter.)
rationale: Removes the power decision entirely.
judge_comment: Auto power selection removes the decision entirely and best fits zero learning curve, but weight alone is a crude proxy and the mechanism is vague.

title: Tactile giant knob with raised icons
new_elements: Oversized knob with embossed symbols and hard detents (Readable by touch, high-contrast; replaces printed scale.)
rationale: Substituting print with tactile shapes makes operation accessible without instruction.
judge_comment: Tactile knobs are plausible and clearly reduce learning, but they are common on existing microwaves and not radical.

title: Pull handle replaces push button
new_elements: Full-width pull handle with cam latch (Pulling the handle lifts the hooks; no separate button.)
rationale: Opening like a cupboard needs no discovery of a hidden button.
judge_comment: Pull handles already exist on many microwaves, so it is practical and intuitive but not novel.

title: Magnetic catch, no latch lever
new_elements: Magnetic door catch with reed interlock (Door just pulls open; magnet holds it shut; reed switches form the interlock.)
rationale: Fridge-door simplicity: pull to open, push to shut.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch is intuitive, but it has to hold up as a safety interlock and keep a reliable microwave seal, so feasibility is moderate.

title: Drawer-style cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity on slides (Food sits on a drawer floor; no swinging door, hinges, or button.)
rationale: Loading a drawer is a motion everyone performs daily.
judge_comment: A drawer is a very intuitive motion and fairly novel (microwave drawers exist), though sealing and spill handling are challenges.

title: Top-loading lid like a rice cooker
new_elements: Hinged top lid with gravity close (Lid falls shut under its own weight; no latch button.)
rationale: Lift lid, drop food, close—a pot metaphor with no latch to learn.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid is a distinctive idea, but gravity-close raises safety and seal concerns and the lid is awkward under countertop cabinets.

title: Roller-shutter door
new_elements: Tambour shutter of linked metal slats (Rolls up into the top; slats overlap to keep Faraday seal.)
rationale: No swing arc in front of the counter and a single obvious 'roll up' gesture.
judge_comment: A roller shutter is a novel gesture, but keeping the RF seal on flexible slats is hard and it does little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: Sliding pocket door
new_elements: Side-sliding door on rails (Slides into a pocket beside the cavity.)
rationale: A slide is a one-axis motion with nothing to press.
judge_comment: A sliding door is plausible and simple to use, but it is only a modest change that adds a sealing challenge and takes up side space.

title: Door pops open at end (door is the alarm)
new_elements: Timer-released spring door ejector (Cam end-of-cycle trips the latch; door swings 5 cm open; bell deleted.)
rationale: Done-ness is self-evident and the next action (take food) is physically cued.
judge_comment: A door that pops open at cycle end replaces the bell with a physical cue, is cheap and mechanical, and makes the next step obvious.

title: Flag indicator replaces bell
new_elements: Pop-up red flag at cycle end (Mechanical flag rises; visible from across room, works for hearing-impaired.)
rationale: A visual state the user cannot misread.
judge_comment: A mechanical flag is simple and accessible, but it adds a part rather than simplifying operation, and a flag is not a radical idea.

title: Hand-wave proximity opener
new_elements: IR proximity sensor + solenoid latch (Wave at door with full hands; it unlatches.)
rationale: Touch-free opening removes the button hunt when carrying plates.
judge_comment: A hand-wave opener is intuitive and works when hands are full, but it is costlier than a handle and risks false triggers.

title: Knee-bump opener
new_elements: Lower-front bump plate linked to latch (Push with knee or hip to release door.)
rationale: Large target, no fine motor skill, nothing to find.
judge_comment: Easy hands-free opening, but it only addresses door opening, not the cooking operation, and it risks accidental bumps.

title: Polymer living-hinge door
new_elements: Metallised polymer living hinge (One moulded part replaces steel hinges; conductive coating keeps the seal.)
rationale: Fewer parts, no misaligned hinge play, door always closes cleanly first time.
judge_comment: A metallised polymer living hinge is a clever substitution, but it barely affects ease of use and it is hard to make durable and keep RF-tight.

title: Crank handle winds timer and closes door
new_elements: Door crank that winds the clockwork (Closing door and turning the crank once per minute wound starts cooking.)
rationale: Closing and setting become one physical gesture.
judge_comment: Merging closing the door and setting the time into one gesture is intuitive and radical, but a crank adds mechanical complexity and the time-per-turn mapping needs explaining.

title: Door-close starts fixed 1-minute cook
new_elements: Door-close trigger with 60 s monostable (Shutting the door starts 60 s; open and re-close to repeat.)
rationale: Zero controls: the door is the only interface.
judge_comment: The door is the only interface, so there is no learning curve and it is trivially cheap to build, though a fixed 60 s limits flexibility.

title: Transparent ITO-coated door, no mesh
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide shielding glass (ITO/silver nanowire film gives Faraday attenuation with full clarity.)
rationale: Seeing food clearly lets users stop by eye instead of trusting settings.
judge_comment: A clear door helps users judge doneness by eye, but transparent conductive shielding at microwave attenuation levels is technically doubtful and only indirectly supports simple operation.

title: Stair-step dish dial
new_elements: Stepped cam dial with 6 named dishes (Each hard stop is 'soup', 'leftovers', 'milk', etc., encoding time+power.)
rationale: Users choose what they are cooking, not how.
judge_comment: Dish-named dial is intuitive and easy to build, but similar preset dials already exist and it is not very radical.

title: Paddle depth = time
new_elements: Single spring paddle: press depth sets minutes (Deeper press winds more; paddle returns to flat as time runs.)
rationale: One control, one motion, with progress visible as the paddle rises.
judge_comment: A single paddle where press depth sets time is intuitive and visual, though precision and a safe mechanical timer are questionable.

title: Pull-cord start
new_elements: Retracting pull cord winding the clockwork (Longer pull = longer cook; cord recoils as it counts down.)
rationale: A satisfying single-gesture start with no mains-dependent motor.
judge_comment: A clockwork pull cord is a fun substitution for the timer, but it adds effort, and some users, such as the elderly, may struggle with it.

title: Big wireless 'Heat' button for elderly
new_elements: Single-button RF remote (fixed 2 min) (Placed anywhere; one press runs a safe default cycle.)
rationale: One huge button with one outcome is the minimum possible learning.
judge_comment: A one-button fixed cycle has minimal learning but is inflexible, and a remote start raises safety concerns.

title: Plate-memory RFID
new_elements: Turntable RFID reader + user's tagged plates (Each plate remembers its last good cook; oven repeats it.)
rationale: Routine meals require no settings the second time.
judge_comment: RFID plate memory is highly novel and removes settings on repeat use, but it needs tagged plates and a learning phase and is costly, so it isn't a cheaper substitute.

title: Weight-driven gravity timer
new_elements: Falling-weight clock escapement (Lift a brass weight to a notch; its descent runs the timer like a cuckoo clock.)
rationale: Visibly falling weight shows remaining time with no reading of dials.
judge_comment: A mechanical weight-driven timer is a charming and plausible substitute for the electronic timer, but lifting a weight to a notch is still a learned action and gives only coarse timing control.

title: Light-sensing 'bubble' stop
new_elements: Optical boil/bubble detector (Photodiode sees surface motion of liquids and stops before boil-over.)
rationale: Prevents the commonest novice mistake without any setting.
judge_comment: Optical boil detection removes one setting and prevents a common mistake, but it covers only liquids and its reliability through steam and containers is questionable.

title: Acoustic popcorn-style listener
new_elements: Cavity microphone end-detector (Stops when sizzling/popping cadence drops.)
rationale: The oven listens so the user needn't.
