judge_comment: Acoustic end-detection is already used for popcorn and could be extended, but it works poorly for non-sizzling foods and is noisy to implement.

title: Always-on while door shut, shut-off by opening
new_elements: Door-position-only control with 5-min hard cap (Closed = cooking, open = off; thermal fuse cap for safety.)
rationale: There is literally nothing to operate but the door.
judge_comment: A door-only control gives zero learning curve, but a fixed 5-minute cap makes it unsafe and impractical for varied foods, since the heat can't be matched to the food.

title: Removable lift-off door on pins
new_elements: Lift-off door on gravity pins (Door sits on two pins; lift and set aside to load; magnetic interlock.)
rationale: Removes hinge stiffness and buttons; also cleans like a plate.
judge_comment: A lift-off door is a wild substitution, but it risks microwave leakage and safety problems, and removing and setting aside a door is awkward, so it adds little to simplicity of operation.

title: Thermochromic 'done' window
new_elements: Thermochromic ink stripe on door glass (Stripe turns from blue to red when cavity air hits serving temp—user stops by colour.)
rationale: Replaces mental timing with a colour cue that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A colour cue is intuitive, but cavity air temperature does not reflect food temperature in a microwave, so the stripe could mislead. It also doesn't remove the need to set a time, and thermochromic ink on a door with a mesh screen has durability and safety issues, so it is only a partial fit for the need and not very radical.

title: One-Touch 'Until Hot' Button
new_elements: Single start button with IR food-temperature sensor (Thermopile reads food surface temperature; one press heats until target is reached, then stops.); Thermopile infrared thermometry (Non-contact IR sensing of food surface temperature through a mesh aperture.)
rationale: Two knobs become one button; the user never estimates time or power.
judge_comment: A single button with IR sensing removes all time and power decisions, though surface-only readings and uneven heating limit accuracy.

title: Weigh-to-Time Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Roller ring on strain gauges weighs the food; cooking time is derived automatically from mass.)
rationale: Put food in, press start; the oven calculates duration so no timer knowledge is needed.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time is plausible and removes the timer, but food type still affects the right duration.

title: Steam-Stop Humidity Sensor
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor auto-stop (Cheap capacitive humidity sensor in the vent path stops heating when food begins to steam.)
rationale: Replaces the countdown with closed-loop 'stop when steaming', eliminating time guessing.
judge_comment: Steam detection is a known sensor-cook approach and works for many foods, but not for dry items or for items that don't steam.

title: Hold-to-Heat Lever
new_elements: Spring-return dead-man heating lever (Magnetron runs only while the big lever is held down; release stops it instantly.)
rationale: Zero settings: hold to heat, let go to stop, as intuitive as a tap.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is very intuitive and radical, but tiring for long cooks and it raises safety and wear concerns.

title: Toaster Pop-Up Microwave
new_elements: Toaster-style push-down lever and pop-up food cradle (Push lever lowers the cradle into the field and latches; a bimetal release pops the food back up when done.)
rationale: Borrows the universally understood toaster gesture so nobody has to learn a new interface.
judge_comment: The toaster metaphor is wildly intuitive, but a bimetal release can't sense when food is done and a moving cradle in the RF field is hard to build.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord spring timer (Pull a cord out by a visible length (marked in minutes); it retracts as the time runs.)
rationale: Length pulled equals time left — a physical metaphor readable at a glance from across the room.
judge_comment: The pull-cord is a vivid physical metaphor for time left, but the cord length limits the maximum time and the retraction mechanism must be accurate and safe.

title: Hand-Crank 30-Second Timer
new_elements: Ratchet hand-crank timer (Each click of a crank adds 30 s with tactile and audible feedback; no fine dial reading.)
rationale: Counting clicks is simpler than reading a minute scale and is precise for short drinks.
judge_comment: The ratchet crank is mechanically simple and gives clear tactile feedback, but counting clicks is a small learning step and long times take many turns.

title: Food-Icon Dial
new_elements: Pictogram-only timer dial (Dial positions show a mug, bowl, plate, frozen block instead of numbers; cams map each icon to a preset.)
rationale: Users choose what they are heating, not how many minutes, removing the mental conversion.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial with cams mapping to presets directly removes time conversion and is cheap and plausible, though portion size variation limits accuracy.

title: Colour-Gradient Power Slider
new_elements: Blue-to-red gradient power slider (Linear slider with a cold-to-hot colour band replaces numbered power steps.)
rationale: Colour needs no explanation; 'more red, more heat' is grasped instantly.
judge_comment: A colour-gradient slider is intuitive and easy to build, but it only addresses power level, which most users never touch.

title: Heat / Defrost Rocker
new_elements: Two-position rocker switch (Heat/Defrost) (Binary rocker selecting 100% or 30% duty cycle replaces the 5-step cam.)
rationale: Five ambiguous power levels collapse to the only two choices most people ever make.
judge_comment: A two-position rocker is trivially simple and cheap and cuts out ambiguity, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Inverter Continuous Slider
new_elements: Switch-mode inverter HV supply (High-frequency inverter replaces the shunt transformer and allows continuous power control.); Continuous power slider (Single analogue slider from gentle to full, no steps or cycling.)
rationale: A smooth slider behaves like a stove knob the user already understands.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist and a slider is familiar, but it still asks the user to pick a power level and a time, so it does little for zero learning.

title: Target-Temperature Probe Dial
new_elements: Bimetal food probe thermostat dial (Insert probe, set 'warm / hot / piping'; a bimetal snap contact cuts power at the chosen food temperature.)
rationale: Users say how hot they want it rather than guessing time and power.
judge_comment: Setting a desired doneness instead of time and power is intuitive, and a bimetal probe is cheap and plausible, though a metal probe inside a microwave is a design challenge.

title: Attenuating Defrost Shelf
new_elements: Removable RF-attenuating mesh shelf (A second shelf under a partially absorbing/reflective mesh receives reduced field; place food there to defrost.)
rationale: Power level becomes a spatial choice (top or bottom shelf) instead of a setting.
judge_comment: Turning power level into shelf position is clever and needs no controls, but predictable field attenuation and safety are doubtful, and it only covers defrosting.

title: NFC Mug Tap-to-Cook
new_elements: NFC tag reader in fascia with tagged crockery (Tap a tagged mug or bowl against the panel; the tag carries its own time and power.); Passive NFC tagging (13.56 MHz passive tags embedded in heat-safe crockery bases.)
rationale: The container knows its own programme, so the user does nothing but tap.
judge_comment: Tapping a tagged mug removes all settings and NFC is cheap and proven, though it depends on special crockery and is not really a cheaper substitute.

title: Repeat-Last Single Button
new_elements: Single 'same as last time' button with memory (One button repeats the last cycle; a long press cycles through three household presets.)
rationale: Most households repeat the same few tasks; one button replaces repeated dial setting.
judge_comment: A one-button repeat is very simple and easy to build, but it is incremental, and the first cycle still needs manual setup.

title: Close-to-Start Mailbox Drawer
new_elements: Sliding food drawer that starts a default cycle on close (Push the drawer shut and a fixed 90 s reheat begins; pulling it open stops heating via the interlock.)
rationale: Loading the food is the only action; closing is starting.
judge_comment: Closing the drawer to start a default cycle removes every control, though a fixed 90 s limits flexibility and raises safety questions about unintended starts.

title: Door-Wound Clockwork
new_elements: Door-hinge-wound spring timer (Swinging the door closed winds a spring escapement for a fixed 2-minute run; no knob, no motor.)
rationale: The timer disappears into the door motion the user already performs.
judge_comment: A door-wound spring timer is wildly simple and motor-free, but a spring escapement controlling magnetron power is hard to make reliable and safe, and the fixed 2 minutes is rigid.

title: Voice Command Chip
new_elements: Offline keyword-recognition voice module (Low-cost on-device speech chip accepts 'two minutes', 'defrost', 'stop'.); Embedded keyword spotting (Small neural model on a microcontroller recognising a fixed vocabulary without cloud.)
rationale: Speaking a request is the oldest interface humans know; no symbols to decode.
judge_comment: Offline voice control is intuitive and feasible, but it is a common idea and adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Fridge-Style Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic gasket door with pull handle (Door held shut by a magnetic strip; pulling the handle opens it and releases the interlocks, no button.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to open a fridge; the hidden release button is gone.
judge_comment: A magnetic fridge-style door is easy and familiar, but it only fixes door opening and leaves the start and time controls untouched.

title: Foot-Pedal Door Release
new_elements: Foot pedal door opener (bin-style) (Pedal linkage lifts the latch so the door swings open while both hands hold a hot dish.)
rationale: Opening becomes the same unthinking motion as a pedal bin, hands-free.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is feasible and handy with full hands, but it adds a mechanism and does little for operating the controls with no learning curve.

title: Tambour Roll-Top Door
new_elements: Conductive slatted roll-top shutter (Metal tambour slides up into the cabinet; overlapping slats form the RF seal; no hinge, latch or button.)
rationale: One slide-up gesture replaces button-latch-hinge, and nothing swings into the user.
judge_comment: A slide-up shutter is an intuitive single gesture, but sealing RF across moving slat joints is very difficult.

title: Top-Loading Saucepan Lid
new_elements: Lift-off metal lid on a pot-shaped cavity (Cylindrical cavity with a choke-rimmed lid; lifting the lid breaks the interlock like lifting a pan lid.)
rationale: Mugs and bowls drop in from above exactly as into a pot — a gesture every cook knows.
judge_comment: The pot-and-lid metaphor is familiar and a choke-rimmed lid is plausible, though a cylindrical cavity and top loading raise some practical issues.

title: Bell-Jar Mesh Dome
new_elements: Glass dome with embedded fine conductive mesh (Transparent lift-off dome shields RF through sub-wavelength mesh; ambient light shows the food from all sides.)
rationale: Nothing is hidden: lift the dome, place food, replace dome — visually self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A mesh-embedded glass dome is self-explanatory and visible, but RF leakage and the durability of a lift-off dome are concerns.

title: Auto-Pop Door at End
new_elements: Timer-released spring door ejector (The timer cam trips the latch instead of a bell; the door springs ajar to show food is ready and vent steam.)
rationale: An open door is an unmissable, language-free 'done' signal and saves a button press.
judge_comment: A spring-ejected door gives a clear done signal and is mechanically simple, but it mainly addresses the end of the cycle and is less radical.

title: Pop-Up Flag Indicator
new_elements: Spring-loaded mechanical 'READY' flag (Timer cam releases a bright flag that pops out of the top; reset by pushing it down.)
rationale: A persistent visual state means the user never has to remember whether the ding happened.
judge_comment: A mechanical flag is easy to build and clear, but it is peripheral to operation and adds only a minor change.

title: Spoken 'Done' Announcer
new_elements: Voice playback chip (Cent-level sound chip says 'Your food is ready' and repeats every minute until the door opens.)
rationale: Plain speech needs no interpretation of what a ding means.
judge_comment: Spoken completion alert is easy to understand and cheap, but it only addresses end-of-cycle and is a fairly obvious feature.

title: Status-Colour LED Lamp
new_elements: RGB LED cavity lamp (red cooking, green done) (LED replaces the incandescent bulb and doubles as the end-of-cycle signal by changing colour.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours communicate state instantly to anyone.
judge_comment: A colour-changing LED lamp is a simple, plausible substitute for the bulb, though it is incremental and covers only status.

title: Dimming-Lamp Progress Bar
new_elements: Lamp brightness tied to timer cam (A cam-driven rheostat dims the cavity lamp as time runs out; dark means done.)
rationale: Remaining time is readable from across the room without reading any scale.
judge_comment: Dimming the lamp as a progress indicator is a clever, intuitive mechanism that replaces a scale, though 'dark means done' may be ambiguous.

title: Ceiling-Projected DONE
new_elements: LED gobo projector on top panel (Projects a glowing 'READY' icon onto the kitchen ceiling until the door opens.)
rationale: A room-scale visual cue needs no listening or reading of the appliance itself.
judge_comment: A ceiling-projected icon is novel and needs no learning, but it is a gimmick that adds cost and does little for operating the microwave.

title: Detachable Carry-Along Timer Knob
new_elements: Magnetically docked portable timer puck (The knob is a battery egg-timer; set it, dock it to start, or pocket it to be alerted anywhere.)
rationale: Same single twist gesture, but the familiar kitchen egg-timer now travels with you.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer knob that docks to start and travels with you substitutes the knob and alert in one, keeping operation to a single twist.

title: Piezo Repeating Chime
new_elements: Piezo buzzer with repeat-until-opened logic (Replaces hammer-and-bell; chimes again every 60 s until the door is opened.)
rationale: No need to stand by or remember; the oven keeps reminding until the user acts.
judge_comment: Practical and cheap, but a repeating buzzer is an incremental swap that only mildly helps ease of use and isn't radical.

title: Fog-Window Ready Indicator
new_elements: Thermochromic 'HOT' decal on door glass (Passive ink on the window turns from clear to a red HOT word when cavity air exceeds 45 °C.)
rationale: A passive, zero-cost indicator tells the user what the food state is without any control or sound.
judge_comment: A passive thermochromic indicator is a clever, cheap substitute, though it conveys hot cavity air rather than whether food is done, so its usefulness is limited.

title: Mode Stirrer, No Turntable
new_elements: Fan-driven metal mode stirrer behind ceiling cover (Rotating reflector blades scramble standing waves; the cavity floor is flat and fixed.)
rationale: No tray to seat, re-align or knock off its ring — food goes anywhere on a flat floor.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common in microwaves, but removing the turntable does cut a user-facing part and requires nothing new to learn.

title: Rotating Antenna Under Ceramic Floor
new_elements: Bottom-fed rotating antenna under flat ceramic floor (The waveguide feeds a slowly spinning antenna beneath a sealed flat floor instead of rotating the food.)
rationale: Removes the only loose, mis-positionable part the user ever had to deal with.
judge_comment: A rotating antenna under a flat ceramic floor is a real approach that removes the loose tray, is easy to clean, and needs no user learning.

title: Your Plate Is the Turntable
new_elements: Three-point silicone drive pins for any dinner plate (Spring-loaded rubber pins on the motor coupler grip and spin an ordinary plate directly.)
rationale: One fewer object to understand, wash or lose; you just put your plate in.
judge_comment: Spinning an arbitrary plate with grip pins is novel, but it is mechanically unreliable and doesn't remove a part so much as add complexity.

title: Quartz Timer Movement
new_elements: Quartz stepper timer with same twist knob (Battery-free quartz oscillator and stepper drive the cam; accurate to the second and mains-frequency independent.)
rationale: Keeps the familiar twist knob but makes 30-second settings trustworthy, so users stop re-checking.
judge_comment: A quartz timer is a plausible substitution for the mechanical timer, but it does little to cut the learning curve and is not radical.

title: Press-to-Start Encoder Knob
new_elements: Single rotary encoder with push-to-start and 30 s detents (Turn for time (clicks), press to start, press again to stop; power fixed at full.)
rationale: One knob, two gestures (turn, press) — the entire interface fits in one hand motion.
judge_comment: A single knob that turns to set time and presses to start is very simple and highly feasible, though similar designs already exist.

title: Handle-Twist Timer
new_elements: Door handle that twists to set time (The grip you already hold to close the door rotates like a throttle to set minutes; fascia removed.)
rationale: Close and twist in one continuous motion; there is no separate panel to find or understand.
judge_comment: A twisting handle that sets time is an intuitive and fresh interface, though it needs a start mechanism and some sealing and safety engineering.

title: Gravity Lift Door
new_elements: Counterweighted vertically sliding door (Door slides up like a garage door and drops closed by gravity; no latch, button or spring.)
rationale: Lift and let go — closing is automatic so the user cannot leave it half-latched.
judge_comment: A counterweighted gravity door removes latching errors, but it has little effect on operating the controls and raises interlock and safety concerns.

title: Boil-Sound Auto-Stop
new_elements: Microphone boil/sizzle detector (Cavity microphone detects the acoustic signature of simmering liquid or sizzling and stops heating before eruption.)
rationale: Milk for breakfast needs no timing judgement — it stops itself when it sounds right.
judge_comment: Acoustic boil detection removes timing decisions, but it is unreliable with noise, varied foods and the microwave's own sounds, and it covers only some uses.

title: Mug-Shaped Dock Presets
new_elements: Floor with mug and bowl recesses that trigger presets (Placing a mug in the mug-sized recess presses a microswitch selecting 'drink' time/power; the bowl recess selects 'meal'.)
rationale: Where you put the food is the setting; the shape of the recess guides the user.
judge_comment: Recess shape selects the preset with simple microswitches, so no learning is needed, though it only covers a few container types.

title: Visible Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Flip-to-start sand hourglass with optical end switch (User flips a 2-minute hourglass mounted on the fascia; an optical sensor on the empty bulb cuts the magnetron.)
rationale: Flipping an hourglass is a millennia-old gesture; progress is visible and delightful.
judge_comment: An hourglass is intuitive and charming, but a fixed duration is inflexible and the optical sensing adds complexity.

title: One Knob Only
new_elements: Single time knob with built-in pulsed defrost zone (Power knob deleted; a marked 'defrost' sector at the long end of the dial engages a cam-driven 30% duty pattern.)
rationale: Halves the controls while keeping the one capability (defrost) users actually seek.
judge_comment: Simplifies the controls and is very feasible, but it is an incremental step similar to existing dial microwaves.

title: Tactile Braille Dial
new_elements: Raised-relief fascia with braille and shape-coded knobs (Moulded ridges, braille numerals and distinct knob shapes replace printed labels.)
rationale: Settings can be felt, not read, so operation is learnable by touch in seconds.
judge_comment: Helps accessibility but does not really reduce the learning needed for general operation.

title: Scan the Packet
new_elements: Barcode reader in door frame (Cheap CCD scanner reads ready-meal barcodes; a built-in table (or printed cook code) sets time and power.)
rationale: The packaging already knows the instructions; the user just shows it to the oven.
judge_comment: Scanning packaging removes the need to read instructions or enter settings, but it depends on a code database and only works for packaged food.

title: Presence-Mat Heating
new_elements: Floor pressure mat enabling the magnetron (Oven heats only while someone stands on the mat in front of it; step away and it pauses.)
rationale: No timer logic at all — stand there until it looks hot, walk away and it stops.
judge_comment: Zero-learning operation, but forcing users to stand on a mat the whole time is annoying and the safety interlock concept is questionable.

title: Steam Whistle Ready Signal
new_elements: Kettle whistle in the exhaust vent (Food steam carried by the fan passes a reed whistle that sounds when humidity and airflow peak.)
rationale: The kettle whistle is a sound everyone already associates with 'hot and ready'.
judge_comment: The whistle is an intuitive cue, but it depends on steam, which many foods don't produce, so it's unreliable and doesn't help with operation.

title: Music-Box Finish
new_elements: Timer-wound music-box comb (Setting the knob winds a tiny music box that plays a short tune when the cam releases it.)
rationale: A pleasant, unmistakable finish cue with no electronics and the same single knob gesture.
judge_comment: A mechanical music-box timer is feasible and charming, and it keeps the single knob, though it only improves the finish cue.

title: Single +30 s Button
new_elements: One momentary '+30 s' button (Each press adds 30 s and starts immediately; holding adds a defrost-pattern minute.)
rationale: The only control is 'more', which cannot be misunderstood.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is very simple, easy to build and easy to understand, though not very radical.

title: Exhaust-Heated Progress Strip
new_elements: Thermochromic strip warmed by vent airflow (Warm exhaust air progressively colours a strip along the top edge, giving a passive elapsed-cooking bar.)
rationale: Progress feedback appears with zero controls or displays to interpret.
judge_comment: A passive progress bar is a clever idea, but thermochromic response to exhaust air would be slow and inaccurate and gives no control.

title: Food-pictogram single dial
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (legacy 0-30 min mechanical timer); 5-step power knob (legacy duty-cycle cam selector); Pictogram dial (one knob with icons (mug, plate, popcorn, frozen meal) that sets time+power together); Select program by food picture (user matches food to icon, no numbers)
rationale: Two numeric knobs collapse into one picture choice, removing all mental arithmetic.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is simple and highly intuitive, but it resembles existing auto-program dials and mechanical-timer microwaves, so it is not very radical.

title: Weighing turntable sets the time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (glass tray on strain gauges; mass computes heating time); Strain-gauge weighing (cheap kitchen-scale sensor); Auto-derive time from mass (heavier food heats longer automatically)
rationale: User places food and presses nothing numeric; the scale decides.
judge_comment: Weighing the food to set the time removes numeric input, but mass alone is a poor proxy for food type and power needs, so results would be unreliable.

title: One big GO button
new_elements: Single GO button (each press adds 30 s at full power; nothing else on the panel); Incremental one-touch heating (press count equals cooking amount)
rationale: A single control with one behaviour cannot be misused.
judge_comment: A single GO button is extremely simple, but it exists in some form already and gives limited control over the cooking result.

title: Package barcode reader
new_elements: Barcode/QR scanner (reads packaged-food instructions and runs them); Optical code recognition (low-cost camera module); Execute printed instructions automatically (no reading or dialling by user)
rationale: The package already knows the settings; the user only shows it to the oven.
judge_comment: Scanning package codes automates settings, but it depends on packages carrying standardized machine-readable instructions and does not cover non-packaged food.

title: Foot-pedal door
new_elements: Door push-release button (legacy latch release); Foot pedal release (bin-style pedal pops door open); Hands-free door opening (open while carrying a plate)
rationale: Opening becomes as intuitive as a pedal bin, with full hands.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is a feasible and concrete change, but it only affects door opening and barely serves the no-learning-curve operation need.

title: Drawer instead of door
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (whole cavity slides out like a kitchen drawer; closing starts heating); Load from above (no reaching into a hot box)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a drawer works.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive familiar gesture, but a sliding cavity with microwave sealing and a heavy load is hard; closing-to-start is an elegant, simple operation.

title: Roll-top shutter
new_elements: Tambour shutter door (roll-top slides up, no swing clearance, no latch button); Slide-to-open access (one motion, no hinge)
rationale: A single sliding gesture replaces button-then-pull.
judge_comment: A roll-top door simplifies opening to one motion, but a tambour shutter needs RF sealing and adds little beyond a simple door.

title: Flat floor with mode stirrer
new_elements: Glass turntable (legacy rotating tray); Mode-stirrer fan + flat ceramic floor (rotating metal paddle above cavity spreads field); Even heating without moving parts under food (no tray to misalign or break)
rationale: Nothing to seat, clean around or re-fit; any dish just goes in.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers with flat floors are already common in commercial products, so it is feasible but not radical, and only modestly helps ease of use.

title: Rotating antenna under floor
new_elements: Rotating waveguide antenna (spinning feed antenna beneath a fixed floor); Field rotation instead of food rotation (oversized dishes allowed)
rationale: Removes the 'will it fit and turn?' decision for the user.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas under a ceramic floor exist in products and remove the turntable, a modest usability gain.

title: Thermochromic viewing window
new_elements: Interior incandescent lamp (legacy 20-25 W bulb); Thermochromic window film (window shows colour map of food temperature); See doneness as colour (no light bulb, instant readout)
rationale: User reads 'hot/not hot' at a glance without interpreting visuals.
judge_comment: A thermochromic window would give an instant readout, but it is hard to realize because food temperature cannot be sensed through the window and the film would be exposed to the microwave environment; it addresses feedback rather than operation.

title: Spoken end-cue
new_elements: End-of-cycle bell (legacy mechanical bell); Voice chip (says 'Your food is ready, let it stand a minute'); Plain-language completion notice (instruction included in signal)
rationale: A sentence needs no decoding, unlike a bell.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap, but it only improves the end signal, so the operating interface is unchanged and it is not radical.

title: IR thermometer stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR temperature sensor (stops magnetron when food surface hits target); Thermopile IR sensing (ear-thermometer grade sensor); Heat to temperature not time (user picks 'warm' or 'hot' only)
rationale: Time guessing disappears; outcome is specified directly.
judge_comment: A warm/hot choice removes time guessing, but IR only reads the surface temperature and a metal-free sensor is needed in the cavity, so accuracy is limited.

title: Humidity sensor auto-stop
new_elements: Vent humidity sensor (detects steam burst and ends cycle); Steam-based doneness detection (common in high-end ovens, here as the only control)
rationale: Press start, walk away; the oven senses when to stop.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto-stop already exists in many microwaves, so it is proven and simple but not radical, and it works poorly for non-steaming foods.

title: Voice command only
new_elements: Offline voice module (understands 'heat my soup' / 'two minutes'); Edge speech recognition (no cloud, few dozen phrases); Speak the instruction (no panel to learn)
rationale: Talking is the zero-learning interface.
judge_comment: Offline voice control is plausible and needs no learning, though it adds cost and risks noise errors, and it is not a cheaper substitute.

title: NFC smart dishes
new_elements: NFC reader in floor (reads tag in dish base carrying program); Tagged dishware set (soup bowl, pasta plate, baby bottle holder with embedded tags); Dish selects program (placing dish is the command)
rationale: The container knows its contents; the user learns nothing.
judge_comment: Placing a tagged dish as the command is a bold zero-learning idea and NFC is feasible, but it requires proprietary dishware and has limited flexibility.

title: Three physical preset buttons
new_elements: Mug / Plate / Frozen buttons (three big moulded buttons shaped like the objects); Shape-coded preset selection (tactile, language-free)
rationale: Choices are reduced to three recognisable objects.
judge_comment: Simple and tactile with minimal choices, but preset buttons are a fairly common and incremental substitution.

title: Pull-cord timer
new_elements: Retractable pull-cord (pull length winds spring timer; cord retracts as time elapses); Set time by how far you pull (visible remaining cord shows time left)
rationale: Physical length is more intuitive than knob angle and shows progress.
judge_comment: A spring-wound pull-cord timer is intuitive and shows progress, though it is a bit gimmicky and imprecise for short times.

title: Linear food-icon slider
new_elements: Slide fader with icons (horizontal slider: cup, bowl, plate, frozen block); Left-to-right 'more heating' metaphor (monotonic single axis)
rationale: A slider's position is self-explanatory at a glance.
judge_comment: A single-axis icon slider is easy to grasp and cheap to build, but mapping food type to heat level may be ambiguous.

title: Warm/Hot rocker switch
new_elements: Two-position rocker ('Warm' or 'Hot'; sensors handle duration); Binary outcome choice (lowest possible decision load)
rationale: Two options need no manual.
judge_comment: The two-option rocker is the lowest decision load, but it depends on reliable sensors and gives limited control.

title: Pass-through conveyor
new_elements: Conveyor belt tunnel (food enters one side, exits other; belt speed fixed); Put in, wait, take out (no door, no timer)
rationale: The toaster-conveyor model is universally understood.
judge_comment: A conveyor with no door or timer is radical and familiar from toasters, but microwave shielding and leakage at open ends are major hurdles, and fixed belt speed fits few foods.

title: Door pops open as the signal
new_elements: Spring-eject door (door opens a few cm at cycle end instead of ringing); Visible completion state (open door means done, like a toaster)
rationale: Status is embodied, not signalled.
judge_comment: Cheap, simple spring-eject door substitutes for the beep and is intuitive, but it only signals completion and does nothing to simplify starting or setting the cook.

title: Camera doneness AI
new_elements: Cavity camera + classifier (recognises food and stops when bubbling/steaming); Embedded vision model (tiny CNN on microcontroller); Watch the food so the user doesn't (replaces timer and lamp)
rationale: Delegates judgement entirely to the appliance.
judge_comment: Removes the need to set time or power at all, which is the ultimate zero-learning-curve approach, though a reliable classifier in a microwave cavity with steam and a metal-shielded environment is hard, and it is not a cheaper substitute.

title: Wave-to-start gesture
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (wave once per minute of heating); Touch-free counting gesture (works with dirty hands)
rationale: Counting waves is simpler than reading a dial.
judge_comment: Counting waves is arguably no simpler than pressing buttons and is less discoverable, so it adds a new thing to learn.

title: Counter-projected guidance
new_elements: Pico projector (projects 'put food here, press this' arrows onto counter and panel); Just-in-time instructions (replaces paper manual)
rationale: Guidance appears where the hand is, so nothing must be learned beforehand.
judge_comment: Contextual projected guidance directly attacks the learning curve, but a pico projector is costly, can be washed out by bright light, and does not simplify the underlying controls.

title: Electroluminescent cavity walls
new_elements: EL-coated cavity liner (walls glow uniformly; colour shifts as time runs out); Illumination that also shows progress (no bulb to replace)
rationale: Light itself communicates state without reading a display.
judge_comment: Glowing walls with colour progress are intuitive, but EL coatings are unlikely to survive microwave fields and heat, and the idea covers status only, not operation.

title: Recipe card slot
new_elements: Punched-card slot (insert a laminated card for the dish; notches set time and power mechanically); Physical program token (cards stored on fridge, no menus)
rationale: Choosing a card is a tangible, memorable act.
judge_comment: Mechanical punched cards remove menus and are very intuitive, though card management and variability in food portions add some friction.

title: Solid-state RF self-tuning
new_elements: Solid-state RF amplifier (replaces magnetron; reads reflected power to self-adjust); GaN RF power transistors (closed-loop frequency and power control); Automatic power matching (power knob becomes unnecessary)
rationale: The oven senses the load and picks power, removing a knob.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with closed-loop sensing is real and removes the power knob, but it is expensive and not a cheaper substitution, and it only partly addresses operation simplicity.

title: Window clears when done
new_elements: Electrochromic door glass (frosted while cooking, transparent when finished); Glanceable done/not-done (no bell, no numbers)
rationale: One visual state communicates everything.
judge_comment: Electrochromic door glass gives a clear done-state signal but doesn't simplify the input side, and it adds cost.

title: Defrost/Cook pictogram toggle
new_elements: Snowflake/Flame toggle (two icons replace five power levels); Iconic power choice (language-independent)
rationale: Only the two power levels people actually use remain.
judge_comment: Two-icon power toggle is simple and cheap and cuts choices, but it is an incremental and fairly obvious simplification.

title: 1-2-3 minute buttons
new_elements: Three numbered buttons (1, 2 and 3 minutes; pressing again adds); Direct minute entry (no rotary estimation)
rationale: Pressing '2' is unambiguous where a 0-30 dial is not.
judge_comment: Fixed minute buttons with press-to-add are nearly zero-learning and trivially feasible, though already common on some microwaves.

title: Hand-crank energy input
new_elements: Crank-wound heating budget (turning a crank winds a spring that meters heating; stop cranking, stop heating); Effort equals heat (bodily metaphor for energy)
rationale: An embodied control needs no abstraction.
judge_comment: Embodied and intuitive, but cranking for the whole heating duration is tiring, and a spring can only store limited energy, so it only partly serves a simple, no-learning-curve operation.

title: Weight-triggered swing shelf
new_elements: Counterbalanced loading shelf (placing plate on outer shelf swings it into cavity and seals); Loading is closing (door button eliminated)
rationale: One physical act replaces open-place-close.
judge_comment: Merges open, place and close into a single act, but it still needs a way to start and set heating, and a sealed, weight-triggered shelf adds mechanical and safety complexity.

title: Thermochromic serving plate
new_elements: Colour-change ceramic plate (bundled plate turns red when food is hot enough); Doneness on the dish (no timer judgement, no bell)
rationale: The plate tells you; nothing to interpret on the oven.
judge_comment: A feasible and clever doneness cue, but it addresses only the finish and leaves the start and setting of the cook untouched.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Momentary heat button (heats only while held; release stops); Continuous manual control (like a tap or a drill trigger)
rationale: Cause and effect are immediate and obvious.
judge_comment: Very simple and immediately understandable, and easy to build, but it is an obvious approach and holding the button through a long cook is a burden.

title: Cake-dome lid cavity
new_elements: Lift-off shielded dome (food sits on open plinth; drop metal-mesh dome over it to start); Cover-to-cook (no door, latch or button)
rationale: Covering food is a gesture every cook knows.
judge_comment: Covering food is a highly intuitive gesture, but a mesh dome that must contain microwave leakage safely is very doubtful, and it gives no setting for the heat.

title: Heat-map cavity walls
new_elements: Thermochromic liner paint (walls show hot zones so users see where to place food); Self-explaining placement (no 'edge of turntable' tips needed)
rationale: The oven visually teaches placement without a manual.
judge_comment: Thermochromic walls are a clever visual cue, but microwave hot spots are standing-wave patterns that shift with load and the paint would need to react quickly, so it is neither reliable nor an operating simplification.

title: Phone buzz instead of bell
new_elements: BLE notifier (sends 'done' to phone or wrist); Reach the user wherever they are (no listening for a bell)
rationale: Users need not learn to stay within earshot.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but it adds a pairing step and a notification feature, which makes operation more complex rather than simpler, and it does not substitute a part with something simpler.

title: Door-closing winds the timer
new_elements: Door-driven spring timer (the door swing itself winds a fixed 90 s spring; slam harder, nothing changes); Closing starts a standard cycle (zero controls)
rationale: There is literally nothing to set.
judge_comment: A door-wound mechanical timer with zero controls substitutes a simpler part and gives a radically simple operation, though a fixed 90 s cycle is limiting.

title: Reflected-power load sensing
new_elements: Directional coupler sensor (measures reflected RF to infer food mass and water content); Infer load without weighing (sets power and time automatically)
rationale: The oven figures out the food; the user presses start.
judge_comment: Sensing the load from reflected RF removes the need for settings and is plausible, though accurate inference of food type is hard.

title: Scale-plate floor
new_elements: Fixed weighing floor (flat floor doubles as scale; display shows grams and suggested button); Weigh and recommend (turntable and timer dial removed)
rationale: Doubles as a kitchen scale and removes guesswork.
judge_comment: A weighing floor is plausible and removes some dials, but a weight-based recommendation still asks the user to interpret the display and press a button, and removing the turntable hurts heating evenness.

title: Tactile-shape knobs
new_elements: Shape-coded knob set (time knob is a clock-hand shape, power knob is a flame shape, with raised detents); Identify control by touch (no labels to read)
rationale: Shape tells function instantly, including in the dark or to visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Shape-coded tactile knobs are practical and aid intuitive use, but mildly incremental and not very radical.

title: Colour-coded giant preset buttons
new_elements: Four colour pads (red=meal, blue=drink, white=defrost, yellow=popcorn; whole front face); Colour as program (toy-like clarity)
rationale: Children and elderly can operate it from the first use.
judge_comment: Colour-coded presets are very easy to learn but fixed programs limit flexibility and the concept is fairly common.

title: No clock, no standby
new_elements: Clockless always-ready controller (removes time-of-day display and set-up flow entirely); Plug in and use (nothing to configure after power cut)
rationale: Eliminates the most common confusing microwave interaction: setting the clock.
judge_comment: Removing the clock eliminates a known pain point simply, though it addresses only one interaction.

title: Shrinking colour arc timer
new_elements: Mechanical arc indicator (coloured wedge behind the knob shrinks as time elapses); Pre-attentive time remaining (no digits)
rationale: Remaining time is seen like a fuel gauge, not read.
judge_comment: A shrinking colour wedge gives glanceable remaining time without digits and is mechanically plausible.

title: Kettle-whistle vent
new_elements: Steam whistle vent (food steam passes through a whistle; it sings when food is steaming); Food itself signals readiness (no timer or bell electronics)
rationale: Everyone knows a whistling kettle means hot.
judge_comment: A whistle-based readiness cue is radical and intuitive, but microwave steam is inconsistent and it does not replace controls or safely stop heating.

title: Icons replace numbers on the dial
new_elements: Icon-graduated timer bezel (same clockwork timer, bezel printed with cup, bowl, plate, frozen meal at calibrated positions); Turn to picture (near-zero cost change)
rationale: Replaces the numeric mental model with a pictorial one for a few cents.
judge_comment: Pictorial dial markings are cheap and intuitive, though quite incremental and not radical; it fits the substitute operator well.

title: Removable tray is the plate
new_elements: Serving-tray floor (the cavity floor lifts out as a tray you eat from and wash); Cook and serve on one surface (no turntable to realign)
rationale: Fewer parts and steps between oven and table.
judge_comment: A removable tray reduces steps but does little for operating simplicity, and a lift-out cavity floor raises heat and microwave design concerns.

title: Cradle-shaped program selector
new_elements: Mug and bowl cradles (cavity has a mug ring and a bowl ring; a switch under each selects program); Placement selects program (no panel interaction)
rationale: Where you put the food is the entire instruction.
judge_comment: Placement-based program selection removes the panel entirely and is intuitive, but the sensing switches and the limited set of container types constrain it.

title: Auto standing time
new_elements: Latched rest timer (door stays locked 60 s after heating for standing time, then releases); Enforce correct standing without knowledge (removes a step from instructions)
rationale: Users need not know microwave lore about standing time.
judge_comment: Locking the door for standing time is easy to build but is arguably annoying, and it removes knowledge rather than simplifying operation.

title: Peel-and-stick wall tags
new_elements: Reflective tag reader + sticker tags (stick a reflective tag on any favourite container; optical sensor recognises pattern and runs saved program); Teach once, never set again (household containers become presets)
rationale: Daily operation collapses to 'put it in'.
judge_comment: Teach-once stickers make daily use 'put it in', but setup adds a learning step and optical reading inside the cavity is a challenge.

title: Magnetic pull handle, no latch button
new_elements: Magnetic seal handle door (fridge-style magnetic strip and handle; interlock by reed switch); Pull to open, push to close (mirrors a fridge door)
rationale: Borrows a door behaviour everyone already uses daily.
judge_comment: Fridge-style magnetic door is intuitive and substitutes the latch simply, but door opening is already easy on most microwaves, and a magnetic seal may not meet microwave leakage or safety interlock requirements. It is also not very radical.

title: Food-pictogram single dial
new_elements: Pictogram program dial (One knob with icons (cup, plate, pizza, ice) replacing both timer and power knobs)
rationale: User chooses what, not how long or how hot.
judge_comment: Simple and practical, replaces two knobs with one icon dial, but pictogram presets are fairly common and not radical.

title: Weight-sensing auto-timer
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Weighs dish and sets heating time automatically); Strain-gauge weighing (Cheap kitchen-scale load cell)
rationale: No time to set; heavier food simply cooks longer.
judge_comment: A load cell under the turntable is cheap and concrete, though weight alone is a crude proxy for heating time and the rotating platform complicates the mounting.

title: Temperature-target knob
new_elements: IR thermometer with 'how hot' dial (Dial labelled warm/hot/boiling; IR sensor stops when reached)
rationale: People think in temperature outcome, not minutes.
judge_comment: Outcome-based dial matches how people think, but IR only reads surface temperature and covered or uneven food makes it unreliable.

title: Humidity auto-stop button
new_elements: Steam sensor one-button (Single start button; heating ends when exhaust humidity spikes)
rationale: One press, no settings at all.
judge_comment: A single start button with steam-sensing stop is truly zero-setting, but it works poorly for dry foods and sensor-based cooking already exists on high-end models.

title: Door is the only control
new_elements: Close-to-start, open-to-stop (Closing the door starts heating; no start or timer input)
rationale: The gesture everyone already does becomes the whole interface.
judge_comment: Radical and intuitive, but starting on close with no duration input is unsafe and undefined, and it would trigger accidental runs.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button
new_elements: Momentary heat paddle (Heats only while pressed; release stops, nothing to set)
rationale: Zero configuration, instant feedback, impossible to forget food.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat removes all settings and is very intuitive, though it is tiring for longer heating and similar to existing dead-man controls.

title: Foot pedal heating
new_elements: Floor pedal (hold to heat) (Sewing-machine pedal controls heating; hands stay free)
rationale: Intuitive like a car pedal; more press, more heat.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is novel and hands-free but awkward for a countertop appliance, and holding a pedal for minutes is impractical.

title: One big +1 minute button
new_elements: Single oversized button (Each press adds one minute at full power and starts)
rationale: Only one possible action; nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Simple and easily built, but similar to existing quick-start buttons and offers limited control.

title: Push-depth tray timer
new_elements: Sliding dish tray (How far you push the tray in sets the time; it slides back out as it cooks)
rationale: Loading the food and setting time are one motion.
judge_comment: Merging loading and time-setting into one tray motion is clever and radical, but the mechanics and safety of a retracting tray with hot food are difficult.

title: Drawer instead of door
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (Dish sits in a drawer; closing it starts heating)
rationale: Drawer is universal; no latch button to find.
judge_comment: A drawer with auto-start on close is familiar, but sealing against microwave leakage is hard and time-setting is not addressed.

title: Auto-opening door as 'ding'
new_elements: Spring door release at end (Timer trips the latch; door pops open to signal completion)
rationale: The result announces itself and removes the button step.
judge_comment: Door pop-open replaces the bell and the button press, but it only handles the end of the cycle, not the setup, and a door that springs open could spill hot food or surprise users.

title: Spoken completion
new_elements: Voice chip 'food is ready' (Replaces bell with a plain sentence)
rationale: No ambiguity about what the sound means.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap and easy, but it only clarifies the finish alert and does nothing to simplify operation, so it is a minor tweak.

title: Voice-command heating
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognition (Recognises 'warm', 'hot', 'defrost', 'stop'); Microphone control (Replaces all knobs)
rationale: Say what you want in your own words.
judge_comment: Offline keyword recognition removes the controls and the learning curve, but it is a known concept and may struggle with kitchen noise and with setting times.

title: Package barcode reader
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Reads ready-meal barcode and applies printed instructions)
rationale: Wave the box past, no reading of instructions.
judge_comment: Scanning a barcode removes the need to read instructions, but it only works for packaged meals and needs a database of cooking instructions.

title: RFID dish tags
new_elements: Tagged household dishes (Mug, bowl, plate carry tags that select the program)
rationale: The container chooses the setting.
judge_comment: Tagged dishes that select the program are clever, but tagging household dishes is impractical, RFID cannot be used in a microwave cavity, and the setting depends on the food as well as the dish.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Edge vision classifier (Recognises soup, pizza, frozen block, liquid); Cavity camera (Also replaces lamp and window)
rationale: Put food in, close door, it decides.
judge_comment: Zero-interaction operation fits the no-learning-curve need perfectly and the camera usefully replaces the lamp, though reliable recognition and heating control for varied foods is hard.

title: Plain-language power dial
new_elements: Dial labelled 'melt / warm / cook' (Three words replace percentage power steps)
rationale: Removes abstract power percentages.
judge_comment: Easy to build and understand, but it is a modest relabeling of existing dials rather than a radical substitution.

title: Two-button rocker
new_elements: Defrost/Heat rocker switch (Only two choices; auto time via sensor)
rationale: Binary choice is learned instantly.
judge_comment: A two-choice rocker with sensor-driven auto time is simple and plausible, but it limits flexibility and resembles existing sensor-cook presets.

title: Hourglass timer
new_elements: Flip sand hourglass trigger (Flipping a visible hourglass starts heating; empty = stop)
rationale: Universally understood, visibly shows remaining time.
judge_comment: A flip hourglass is intuitive and shows remaining time visibly, but it is imprecise and awkward to integrate with a sealed, safe heating cycle.

title: Pull-string timer
new_elements: Toy-style pull cord (Pull length sets time; cord retracts as it cooks)
rationale: Single playful gesture, no scale to read.
judge_comment: A playful pull cord is a memorable, simple gesture, but the cord-length-to-time mapping is unclear and the cord may wear out or pose safety concerns.

title: Token-per-minute slot
new_elements: Coin-op token mechanism (Each token dropped = one minute; tokens return after)
rationale: Counting tokens is simpler than reading a dial.
judge_comment: Tokens make time tangible and are mechanically simple, but they add a small item to keep track of and are less flexible than a dial.

title: Clock-face end-time dial
new_elements: Analog clock hands (Move hand to when you want it done, like an alarm clock)
rationale: Leverages the alarm-clock mental model.
judge_comment: The alarm-clock mental model is familiar, but end-time setting is less intuitive for short microwave durations and it substitutes more than it radically changes.

title: Wind the turntable
new_elements: Hand-wound turntable spring (Rotating the plate by hand winds the timer; it unwinds while cooking)
rationale: Placing and spinning the dish is the whole setup.
judge_comment: A wound spring timer folds setup into placing the dish and removes electronics, but the plate can only set limited durations and precision is poor.

title: Door handle angle sets time
new_elements: Rotary door handle (Turn to close: quarter turn = 1 min, full turn = 5 min)
rationale: Closing the door is also setting it.
judge_comment: Closing the door doubles as setting the time, which is clever, but it risks accidental settings and it complicates the door-seal and safety interlock.

title: Wave-to-open sensor
new_elements: Capacitive/IR gesture latch (Hand wave releases door, no button to locate)
rationale: Works with full or dirty hands, zero search.
judge_comment: A gesture latch removes the search for a button, but it covers only opening, not operation, and is prone to false triggers.

title: Countertop projected countdown
new_elements: Mini projector (Projects large remaining-time ring onto counter)
rationale: Huge, unmissable display requires no squinting.
judge_comment: A projected countdown is eye-catching but it only improves time display, not operation, and it adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Light beacon instead of bell
new_elements: Slow-pulsing top light (Silent, visible 'ready' signal that stays on until door opens)
rationale: Persistent cue, no missed ding.
judge_comment: A pulsing light that stays on is easy and useful, but it only affects the done signal and is not very radical.

title: Smell cue for done
new_elements: Aroma puff release (Releases a pleasant scent when finished)
rationale: Ambient, non-startling signal understood by anyone.
judge_comment: A scent cue is unusual, but cartridges, odor mixing and refills make it impractical, and it does little for operation.

title: Dish-shaped slots
new_elements: Mug slot and plate slot (Two openings sized for mug or plate, each with fixed program)
rationale: Physical fit replaces every setting.
judge_comment: Slots shaped for a mug or plate with fixed programs remove nearly all settings through physical affordance, which directly gives zero learning curve, though the mechanics are complex.

title: Top-loading pot microwave
new_elements: Lidded cooking pot cavity (Lift lid, drop food, close lid to start)
rationale: Behaves like a saucepan everyone knows.
judge_comment: A saucepan-like top-loading pot uses a familiar mental model, but it faces serious microwave-physics, safety and usability problems with plates and containers.

title: Self-centring knob flick
new_elements: Spring-return flick knob (Flick right for more, left for stop; no scale)
rationale: Removes precise positioning on a dial.
judge_comment: A spring-return flick knob is simple and easy to use, but there is no feedback on duration and the control is ambiguous, and it substitutes the dial only mildly.

title: Pressure mat time
new_elements: Cavity floor pressure mat (Mechanical spring mat: heavier dish compresses longer timer)
rationale: Purely mechanical automatic timing.
judge_comment: Zero-input timing is appealing, but dish weight is a poor proxy for heating time, so it would be unreliable and even unsafe.

title: Water-drip timer
new_elements: Visible water clepsydra (Fill cup to a line; heating stops when it drains)
rationale: Filling a cup is intuitive and the level is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A water clepsydra is whimsical and radical, but it adds water near the electronics, makes timing awkward and imprecise, and is less simple than a button.

title: Program cartridges
new_elements: Insertable program cards (Cards labelled 'popcorn', 'soup' slot in and set cams)
rationale: Pick a card, no dials.
judge_comment: Labelled cards that set cams make a believable, no-learning-curve interface, though they add loose parts that can get lost.

title: Companion dish lid with timer
new_elements: Smart lid (Lid thermometer tells oven when contents are hot)
rationale: Cover food and forget; stops itself.
judge_comment: Cover and forget is highly intuitive, but a thermometer lid that works in a microwave and communicates with the oven is hard to build, and the idea is vague on how.

title: Fixed full power only
new_elements: No power knob; automatic duty via load sensing (Magnetron current sensing adapts power to food)
rationale: One fewer decision for the user.
judge_comment: Removing power choice simplifies use, but magnetron current sensing as a load-adaptive method is vague and not very radical.

title: Tilt-to-set
new_elements: Tilting front panel (Tip panel back a little for short, a lot for long)
rationale: Gross motor gesture, no fine reading.
judge_comment: Tilt gesture is novel and low-precision, but a moving panel adds mechanical complexity and is not obviously intuitive.

title: Big touch strip
new_elements: Full-width slider strip (Slide finger from cold to hot pictures)
rationale: Continuous gesture mirrors desired outcome.
judge_comment: A slider with pictorial cues is easy and cheap, though similar to existing touch interfaces.

title: Haptic stop knob
new_elements: Knob with hard stops at 3 presets (Clicks only at 'cup', 'plate', 'frozen')
rationale: Impossible to set a wrong value.
judge_comment: A three-preset detent knob is very easy to use and trivially buildable, but fairly conventional.

title: Door window as e-ink display
new_elements: E-ink door panel (Shows camera image plus one word: 'heating' / 'ready')
rationale: Status and view in one glance.
judge_comment: An e-ink door with camera status is eye-catching but is about feedback rather than operation, and e-ink over a shielded window is technically hard.

title: Phone-free NFC tap
new_elements: NFC tap zone (Tap a tagged recipe card or packaging to set and start)
rationale: One tap, no menus.
judge_comment: NFC tap on tagged packaging is plausible and simple, but it requires tagged items and is only moderately novel.

title: Mechanical bell replaced by door glow
new_elements: Electroluminescent door frame (Frame glows green when done)
rationale: Visual, silent, located exactly where you reach.
judge_comment: A glowing door frame is easy to build, but it only signals completion and does little for operating the microwave.

title: Boil-detect microphone
new_elements: Acoustic boil sensor (Hears bubbling or popping and stops)
rationale: Popcorn and liquids stop themselves.
judge_comment: Acoustic boil detection lets popcorn and liquids stop themselves, though noisy kitchens and varied foods limit reliability.

title: Fingerprint user presets
new_elements: Fingerprint start button (Repeats each person's last setting on touch)
rationale: Habits replace settings.
judge_comment: A fingerprint button that repeats each person's last setting is feasible and speeds repeat use, but the first use still needs setup and it adds cost.

title: Door auto-start on close with auto-stop
new_elements: Fully autonomous cycle (Weight + steam + IR fuse; user only loads and unloads)
rationale: Zero controls is the ultimate no-learning-curve interface.
judge_comment: A fully autonomous cycle with no controls is the ideal no-learning-curve interface, but reliably sensing different foods is very hard and potentially unsafe.

title: One-knob 'how hot' dial replaces timer + power knobs
new_elements: Single doneness dial (cold to piping hot) (One rotary control whose cam simultaneously sets duty cycle and run time along a single 'more/less heat' axis.); Coupled dual-cam single-shaft timer (One shaft drives both the time cam and the power cam with a fixed mapping.)
rationale: Two abstract controls collapse into one intuitive 'how hot do you want it' knob, removing the time-vs-power mental model.
judge_comment: A single 'how hot' dial is intuitive and mechanically plausible with coupled cams, though the fixed time/power mapping will suit some foods poorly.

title: Weighing turntable sets cooking time automatically
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable platform (Turntable sits on a calibrated spring; displacement mechanically selects run time via a lever on the timer cam.); Mass-to-time mechanical linkage (Heavier load compresses spring further and advances timer cam proportionally.)
rationale: User sets nothing: putting the plate in is the input, so there is literally no control to learn.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is appealing, but mass does not determine heating time reliably (food type, starting temperature, and container weight all matter), and a spring scale under a rotating turntable is awkward.

title: Hold-to-heat dead-man button replaces timer
new_elements: Large hold-to-heat paddle button (Magnetron runs only while the paddle is pressed; release = stop, no timer at all.); Momentary high-current paddle switch (Spring-return paddle in series with interlocks.)
rationale: Pressing a button while something happens is the most primitive interaction there is; short heats become trivially precise.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is very simple to understand, but it is tiring for longer heats and the safety and regulatory case for a high-current paddle switch is questionable.

title: Steam-sensor auto-stop, single 'Heat' button
new_elements: Cavity humidity sensor + single Heat button (Oven runs at full power until a humidity rise slope indicates the food is steaming, then stops.); Capacitive humidity sensing (exhaust vent) (Low-cost RH sensor in exhaust airflow detects food steam onset.)
rationale: One button and the oven decides when food is hot, so no numbers, times or power levels are needed.
judge_comment: A single Heat button with humidity-based auto-stop is highly intuitive and feasible, but sensor cooking already exists in many microwaves.

title: IR food thermometer replaces the timer dial
new_elements: Ceiling-mounted IR thermopile with 'Hot/Warm' switch (Non-contact sensor reads food surface temperature; oven stops at 60 °C (warm) or 85 °C (hot).); Thermopile IR temperature sensing through mica window (8-14 µm IR sensing behind a microwave-opaque, IR-transparent port.)
rationale: Users think in 'warm' or 'hot', not minutes; the oven translates for them.
judge_comment: A warm/hot switch driven by an IR thermometer matches how people think, but it reads surface temperature only and needs an IR-transparent, microwave-blocking window that adds some cost and complexity.

title: Door-close-to-start, no control panel at all
new_elements: Door-actuated fixed 60 s cycle (Closing the door winds a fixed 60 s clockwork; opening stops it; repeat for more time.); Door-hinge wound spring escapement (Hinge motion charges a spring escapement timer like a music box.)
rationale: Zero controls: the only action is the one every user already knows, shutting the door.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is very intuitive and removes the controls, though a fixed 60 s cycle and a hinge-wound spring are limiting and the door-open safety interlocks need care.

title: Pull-string timer like a toy
new_elements: Pull-cord timer with length-graduated handle (Pull the cord out to the marked length (cup, bowl, plate); it retracts via spring governor and stops heating when fully home.); Governor-regulated cord retraction (Centrifugal governor sets constant retraction rate.)
rationale: A visibly retracting cord shows remaining time without numbers and is as intuitive as a pull-string toy.
judge_comment: A visible retracting cord is an intuitive timer and a governor is plausible, but the graduated lengths still need some learning and the mechanism adds wear and cost.

title: Picture dial: cup, bowl, plate, butter instead of numbers
new_elements: Icon-only preset cam dial (Dial positions are food pictograms; each position encodes both time and duty cycle in the cam profile.); Multi-track cam encoding presets (Each dial detent maps to a pre-cut time/power cam pair.)
rationale: Users point the knob at the thing they are heating, no arithmetic about minutes or watts.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are easy to use and cheap with a cam timer, but similar presets already exist, so novelty is low.

title: Where you put the dish sets the power level
new_elements: Two-zone cavity floor (Full / Gentle) (Fixed floor with a partially shielded 'gentle' zone under a perforated plate that attenuates field for defrost/melt.); Graded perforated-plate RF attenuation (Sub-wavelength hole pattern density sets local field attenuation.)
rationale: Power level becomes a spatial choice ('put butter on the soft side') rather than a numeric setting.
judge_comment: Setting power by where the dish sits is a wild and intuitive idea, but a perforated plate that attenuates the field locally is physically doubtful and gives uneven, unpredictable heating.

title: Cooking tokens: drop a coin for a cup, two for a plate
new_elements: Token slot timer (Plastic tokens of different thickness/colour insert into a slot; thickness mechanically sets time and a notch sets power.); Token-gauged cam preset (Token depth pushes timer cam to fixed position; token returns when cycle ends.)
rationale: Physical tokens labelled with pictures make the choice tangible and child/elder friendly, with nothing to dial.
judge_comment: Tangible picture tokens are easy for children and elders and mechanically simple, but they can get lost and add a handling step.

title: Voice chip replaces the control fascia
new_elements: Offline keyword-spotting voice module (Recognises ~10 words ('one minute', 'defrost', 'stop') with no network; drives relays in place of cams.); Embedded keyword spotting (tiny neural net on MCU) (Sub-dollar MCU with on-device speech keyword model.); Speech processing (Automatic speech recognition at the edge.)
rationale: Saying 'one minute' requires no instruction and works for users who cannot read dials.
judge_comment: Offline keyword voice control is plausible and removes dials, but it is not cheaper than a mechanical timer and noisy kitchens hurt reliability.

title: Magnetic pull-handle door replaces push-button latch
new_elements: Magnetic soft-catch door with bar handle (Door held by magnets, opened by pulling a full-width handle; interlocks still actuated by the door.); Ferrite magnetic catch (Low-cost magnetic latch as used on cabinet doors.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is universal; the hunt for a release button is eliminated along with the lever mechanism.
judge_comment: Simple and cheap, but it only addresses opening the door rather than the full operation, and magnetic latches raise interlock and safety concerns.

title: Drawer microwave: pull out, load, push in to start
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity with push-to-start (Cavity is a drawer; fully pushing it home closes the RF seal and triggers a fixed cycle.); Drawer-rail choke seal (Quarter-wave choke around drawer face frame.)
rationale: The load and start actions merge into one familiar drawer gesture with no door button or dial.
judge_comment: Pushing the drawer closed to start merges load and start into one gesture, though the RF choke on a drawer is challenging and a fixed cycle limits use.

title: Toaster-lever microwave
new_elements: Push-down start lever with pop-up end (Push lever down to start (like a toaster); it pops up with a clunk when done and unlatches the door.); Latched lever with timer-released solenoid/clockwork (Mechanical latch holds lever; timer trips release.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster works, so the interaction model transfers with zero learning.
judge_comment: The toaster lever uses a familiar mental model and a mechanical timer, giving near-zero learning, though a fixed time setting is still needed.

title: Foot pedal door opener
new_elements: Foot pedal / knee bar door release (Bowden cable from a floor pedal or front knee bar pops the door, hands-free.); Bowden cable actuation (Sheathed cable transfers pedal motion to latch.)
rationale: Like a pedal bin, the action needs no explanation and works when both hands hold a hot dish.
judge_comment: A hands-free door opener is a convenience, but it does not simplify the actual operation of setting and starting a cook.

title: Door pops ajar when done (no bell)
new_elements: Timer-released door pop-open (Timer cam trips the latch so the door springs 3 cm open: RF stops, steam vents, and the open door is the visual signal.); Cam-tripped latch release (Timer cam end-stop pushes latch lever.)
rationale: Done-state is self-evident across the room and food is never left forgotten behind a closed door.
judge_comment: A door that pops ajar is an intuitive done signal that also stops RF, and cam-tripped latch release is mechanically plausible, though a door left ajar may cool food and shouldn't spring open unexpectedly.

title: Talking end-of-cycle chip replaces bell
new_elements: Speech playback module ('Your food is ready') (Greeting-card class sound chip plays a spoken message and repeats every 30 s until the door opens.); One-time-programmable voice playback IC (Sub-dollar OTP audio chip and piezo speaker.)
rationale: A spoken message is unambiguous for first-time, elderly or visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Cheap, proven voice chip clearly communicates completion, but it is a fairly obvious substitution and language-specific.

title: Pop-up flag indicator replaces bell
new_elements: Mechanical pop-up 'READY' flag (Timer end-stop releases a spring flag on top of the cabinet, visible across the room, reset by opening the door.); Spring-loaded mailbox flag mechanism (Cam-released flag, door-linkage reset.)
rationale: A persistent physical state ('flag up = ready') cannot be missed or misread, unlike a transient ding.
judge_comment: A mechanical flag gives a persistent, unmistakable ready state with simple cam and linkage, though it adds a part and the top-of-cabinet location may be unusual.

title: RF-harvesting LED glow replaces lamp
new_elements: In-cavity rectenna-powered LED strip (Small antenna + Schottky rectifier harvests stray 2.45 GHz field to light LEDs only while microwaves are present.); Rectenna RF energy harvesting (Antenna-rectifier converts incident RF to DC.)
rationale: Light on = energy on is an honest, wiring-free status indicator that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Clever wireless status light, but the user sees it only while running, rectennas in a high-field cavity risk arcing, and the sealed-cavity safety is questionable.

title: Phosphorescent cavity paint instead of a lamp
new_elements: Glow-in-the-dark enamel cavity (Strontium-aluminate phosphor in the enamel is charged by kitchen light and glows softly to silhouette the food.); Long-persistence phosphor coatings (SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy phosphor in a food-safe enamel.)
rationale: Removes a failing part and wiring, keeping the one thing novices need: seeing their food.
judge_comment: A phosphor glow is novel, but it would be too dim to see food clearly, and the enamel's durability and food safety are uncertain, so it only weakly serves ease of use.

title: Electrochromic door tint as the 'cooking' indicator
new_elements: Amber-tinting electrochromic door glass (Door glass turns amber while the oven runs and clear when done; a low-power LED behind mesh provides view light.); Electrochromic film (Low-voltage reversible colour change layer.)
rationale: The whole front face communicates busy/ready, so status is readable at a glance by anyone.
judge_comment: Clear status cue helps a little, but it adds cost and does not substitute a part or simplify operation much.

title: Mode stirrer replaces turntable, motor and roller ring
new_elements: Fan-driven waveguide mode stirrer and flat ceramic floor (Rotating metal paddle in the waveguide randomises field pattern; cavity floor is a fixed wipe-clean ceramic slab.); Airflow-driven mode stirring (Cooling-fan exhaust spins the stirrer, no extra motor.)
rationale: No tray to seat, misplace or break: any dish anywhere just works, which is what simplicity means for a novice.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are proven and remove the tray, a real simplification, though the control interface remains unchanged.

title: Rotating antenna under a flat floor
new_elements: Bottom-feed rotating antenna (Waveguide feeds a slowly rotating radiating antenna under a flat glass-ceramic floor, replacing the turntable system.); Rotating radiating antenna feed (Rotary joint distributes field; used in commercial flatbed ovens.)
rationale: Removes the 'is the tray on properly?' failure mode and lets users place rectangular dishes freely.
judge_comment: Rotating antenna under a flat floor is real commercial tech and removes the tray, but it is not very radical and is only indirectly about operation.

title: Solid-state RF source replaces magnetron and HV chain
new_elements: GaN solid-state 2.45 GHz power amplifier module (Low-voltage (48 V) RF source with reflected-power sensing; no transformer, capacitor, diode or filament.); GaN HEMT power amplification (Wide-bandgap transistors deliver hundreds of watts at 2.45 GHz.); Semiconductor device physics (Wide-bandgap transistor engineering.)
rationale: Reflected-power sensing lets the oven self-stop when food is done, enabling a true one-button product.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is plausible and enables sensing, but it is costly today and the relevance depends on the sensing feature.

title: Reflected-power 'cook until done' single button
new_elements: Waveguide directional coupler + comparator cut-off (Monitors reflected power; as food heats and its dielectric loss changes, a threshold crossing ends the cycle.); Directional-coupler VSWR sensing (Diode-detected forward/reflected ratio in the waveguide.)
rationale: The appliance senses doneness through the food's own RF signature, so the user never estimates time.
judge_comment: Doneness sensing for one-button cooking directly removes the learning curve, though reflected power may not track doneness reliably across foods.

title: Packaging-tag reader replaces knobs
new_elements: NFC/barcode instruction reader at door (Tap the ready-meal package on the door; the oven reads time and power from the tag and starts when the door shuts.); Passive NFC instruction tags (13.56 MHz tag storing a tiny cook program.); Packaging & identification technology (Machine-readable packaging.)
rationale: The food package programs the oven, removing the step of reading and transcribing instructions.
judge_comment: Tapping the package to program the oven removes setup steps, and NFC is plausible, but it depends on food makers adopting the tags and the idea is not entirely new.

title: Tactile embossed dial rings replace printed scales
new_elements: Embossed tactile/contrast knob bezels (Raised bumps and high-contrast moulded icons replace silk-screen numbers; detents click per 30 s.); In-mould tactile relief (Relief features moulded directly into fascia polymer.)
rationale: Settings can be felt and heard, so operation needs neither eyesight nor reading.
judge_comment: Easy to build and helpful for accessibility, but it is an incremental tweak to existing knobs and not a radical substitution.

title: Thermochromic plate tells you it's done, oven just heats
new_elements: Thermochromic dinnerware set + hold-to-heat oven (Included plates and mug change colour at 65 °C; the oven itself only has a hold-to-heat paddle.); Leuco-dye thermochromic glaze (Reversible colour change pigment in food-safe glaze.)
rationale: Feedback moves to the dish you are already looking at, so there is nothing to set and nothing to decode.
judge_comment: Colour-changing dishes are a creative way to give feedback, but hold-to-heat with no timer is awkward, uneven heating makes the cue unreliable, and it only works with the bundled dishware.

title: Detachable chirping timer puck you carry away
new_elements: Magnetic detachable timer puck (The timer knob is a battery-free wind-up puck; set it on the oven to start, pull it off and pocket it, it rings where you are.); Reed-switch docked clockwork timer (Docked puck's magnet closes the oven circuit; a twin clockwork in the oven mirrors its countdown.)
rationale: It behaves like the kitchen egg timer everyone already understands, with no extra steps to learn.
judge_comment: A detachable wind-up puck timer is intuitive and familiar like an egg timer, and the reed-switch docking is workable, though the mirrored clockwork is somewhat fiddly.

title: Mechanical waveguide shutter replaces interlock switch logic
new_elements: Door-linked waveguide guillotine shutter (Opening the door mechanically drops a metal shutter across the waveguide and breaks a single mains switch; RF physically cannot enter the cavity.); Below-cutoff waveguide blocking (Metal plate across the guide reflects RF back to a dummy load.)
rationale: Safety becomes a visible mechanical fact rather than hidden logic, reassuring novices and simplifying service.
judge_comment: This is a safety mechanism that barely affects ease of use, and a mechanical waveguide shutter with a dummy load is complex and costly compared with standard interlocks.

title: One big button: press to start, press to open
new_elements: Single illuminated mega-button (One 8 cm button: press = start fixed 45 s burst (repeat presses add bursts); press-and-hold = door pops open.); Dual-action (tap/hold) mechanical push switch (Short stroke closes timer, long stroke engages latch lever.)
rationale: A single affordance means there is nothing to choose between, which is the definition of no learning curve.
judge_comment: A single tap/hold button removes all choices and is plausible, though fixed 45 s is a limitation and the idea is not very radical.

title: Top-loading 'microwave pot' with lid
new_elements: Top-loading cylindrical cavity with hinged lid (Drop a mug or bowl in from above like a pot; closing the lid starts a fixed cycle; gravity seals the choke.); Cylindrical cavity with lid choke ring (Circular quarter-wave choke on lid rim.)
rationale: Mimics putting a pot on the stove, a gesture even non-users of microwaves already know.
judge_comment: A top-loading pot-style microwave is radical and intuitive, but sealing the lid against leakage and the fixed cycle are difficult, and a stove-like gesture is not guaranteed to be learned-free.

title: Single-purpose mug-warmer microwave
new_elements: Mug-sized cavity with one 'Hot drink' button (A 1.5 L cavity tuned for a mug; fixed power and auto-stop by cup-wall IR temperature.); Load-matched small cavity design (Cavity dimensions optimised for a single mug load.)
rationale: A product that does one thing with one button cannot be misused.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug warmer is very simple and feasible, but it is narrow in function and not very radical.

title: Slider ruler: pull to the size of your plate
